- An Empirical Study of LLM-Generated Specifications for VeriFast (2026)
    - what: # An Empirical Study of LLM-Generated Specifications for VeriFast (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Wen Fan, Minh Tran, Sanya Dod, Xin Hu, Marilyn Rego, Danning Xie, Jenna DiVincenzo and Lin Tan, arXiv:2606.26490v1, 25 June 2026. This is an empirical study of LLM-written specifications and auxiliary proofs for C programs checked with VeriFast. It reports 855/2,727 outputs passing verification (31.4%), 91% source-behavior preservation and 92% contract preservation. The last figure combines equivalent and strengthened contracts; it is not an equivalence rate. The released verification CSVs contain 856 “yes” rows, one more than the paper. No general correctness theorem or end-to-end proof of an LLM verifier is given (Q1,Q8,Q9,T3–T6,C8).  ## Reading and source scope  Read all 13 PDF pages, sections I–VIII, both figures, all eight tables, displayed code/specifications and all 83 bibliography entries. All 13 individual page renders were inspected. There is no appendix, checklist, numbered theorem/proof or separately numbered algorithm. Figure 1 is a complete append-tail verification example; Figure 2 diagrams the study. References were read as bibliography entries, not recursively followed.  The inventory PDF matches its recorded SHA256. Acquired the paper's §VIII replication package, Zenodo record 19570523, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19570523; its 17,362,580-byte ZIP matches the published MD5 8c8335ee601057daf18c27d3cf9097e3. Inventoried 14,646 ZIP members. The archive's ISSRE26 filename does not establish a publication venue. Its metadata identifies an anonymous replication package published 14 April and updated 20 April 2026, preceding the arXiv version; correspondence to every reported run is not established.  Read the root and two infrastructure readmes, all selected analyzer and generation scripts, four original append-tail inputs/ground truth, three generated append-tail FBP outputs and four generated files containing literal assume(false). The 15 released CSVs were parsed as plaintext to count labels, unique benchmark names and selected rows; modified.txt was counted, not semantically reviewed. In total 43 plaintext assets are retained, with per-asset reading boundaries. A bounded lexical scan covered the 2,727 primary full-study C outputs, without treating it as whole-output semantic reading. XLSX workbooks, remaining inputs/outputs, retrieved examples/tutorial bodies, libraries, raw checker/API logs and recursively cited papers were not read. No author code was executed/imported, verifier rerun, model/checkpoint loaded or experiment reproduced. Quotes retain exact source bytes and LF/character pointers; arithmetic and static control-flow findings are reader checks, not new experimental results.  ## Task, logic and benchmark assumptions  Separation logic describes ownership of disjoint heap regions. VeriFast uses symbolic execution, contracts, predicates, loop invariants, folding/unfolding statements and lemma calls to check safety and specified behavior. The paper describes Z3 as the default solver. Although background mentions VeriFast 25.11, actual experiments use 24.08.30 with default integer-overflow and heap-leakage checks. The record therefore does not transfer outcomes to another release or to Verus/Rust (Q2,Q7,Q8).  The dataset has 303 functions from 60 small single-file C programs: 258 functions from 50 public examples and 45 from ten author-written programs. Selection starts with 770 repository programs, narrows to 160 single-file example/tutorial programs, then removes 46 lacking code or SL specifications, 49 duplicates or prompt-tutorial examples, ten with unresolved verification errors and five without prepared inputs. This deliberately retains known-verifiable programs, not arbitrary industrial code. Overall ground truth averages 43 source and 81 specification lines, with ranges 3–143 and 5–600. The public and new subsets average 44/91 and 34/32 lines respectively (Q3).  Each function receives one mutually exclusive feature tag, prioritizing concurrency, then loops, then recursive predicates: 45 concurrent, 39 loop, 134 recursive-predicate and 85 other functions. A function tagged concurrency may also contain a loop; these are not independent feature effects. The authors' ten new programs resemble the public set and are used for both selection and the full study. Their non-leakage is asserted, not independently established; a low overall verification rate cannot itself measure contamination (Q3,Q12).  Three inputs retain executable code but differ in guidance: NL gives informal behavior, FB formal pre/postconditions, and FBP adds allocation ownership or integer constraints needed for verification. FBP is closer to a complete solution and asks a different completion task from NL. Paper Table I's append-tail example specifies an acyclic input/output list; Figure 1's contract tracks ownership and acyclic shape, not a value sequence, preserved prefix or insertion of exactly one value. A program satisfying only that contract has not thereby proved the full usual append operation. The retained artifact's list nodes omit the value field and its append_tail takes only head; this is a simpler example variant, not a byte-identical implementation of Figure 1 (Q2,Q3,T1,F1,C10).  ## Prompt/model selection and measured workflow  Four prompt contents, Basic, chain-of-thought, sparse retrieval and dense retrieval, cross whole-program versus function input for eight choices. The first pilot uses GPT-4o and the 45 new functions' FBP variants. Sparse retrieval with function splitting verifies 64%, versus at most 56% for alternatives, with 63 errors versus more than 67; its three logical errors and two behavior changes also influence selection. These are selection-set results, not independent held-out estimates (Q4).  A second pilot chooses Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro and GPT-4o from ten models: selected models verify at least 60%, have at most 73 errors and at most two behavior changes. A follow-up crosses ten models with eight prompts over the same 45 FBP functions; however, deprecated Claude 3.7 is replaced by Haiku 4.5. It therefore supplies broader prompting evidence without evaluating exactly the same model set. Sparse split and unsplit tie at median 16 verified functions; selected model families' reported medians are 23, 22.5 and 20.5, versus at most 15 for the rest. It does not remove reuse of the selection set or isolate all input/model interactions (Q5).  The full study fixes sparse retrieval with splitting and evaluates three models × three input types × 303 functions, producing 2,727 outputs. Temperature is zero, with one output per condition, not repeated sampling. Sparse retrieval uses BM25, dense retrieval TextEmbedding, and vectors reside in Qdrant. The retained prompt code retrieves ten program/library entries and five tutorial entries, caps concatenated example text at 300,000 characters and extracts C-fenced blocks. Main generation calls each model once per input, without a verifier-feedback loop. The code's active model list is the later ten-model configuration including Haiku, not a preserved exact full-study configuration; historical correspondence needs logs (Q4–Q8,Q12,C6,C7).  Reported local hardware is a Yoga 14sACH 2021, 16 AMD Ryzen 7 5800HS CPUs, 16 GiB RAM, 1 TB SSD, Ubuntu 24.04 and Python 3.12; Qdrant has 0.5 vCPU, 1 GiB RAM and 4 GiB disk. Full-study API costs per model are Gemini $233, Claude $232 and GPT-4o $171. The paper supplies no repeated-run uncertainty, formal significance test for its “significantly” wording or complete token/latency account (Q7,Q10).  ## What the outcomes establish  RQ1 manually compares source behavior and contracts, with at least two authors coding independently and resolving conflicts. Source changes include compiler errors as well as semantic changes. Table III has 246 changes: NL 64, FB 82, FBP 100; Claude 86, Gemini 98 and GPT-4o 62. Source inter-rater Cohen's kappa is 0.73. The prose divides 246 changes into 102 semantic edits and 143 compile-related cases, which sum to 245. Their overlap or an omitted case is not resolved by the paper (Q6,Q8,T3).  Table IV reports 2,375 equivalent, 146 strengthened, 116 weakened and 90 other contracts. The advertised 92% combines 2,375+146=2,521, while exact-equivalence coding is 87.1%. The authors define strengthening jointly for pre- and postconditions, without a formal behavioral-refinement criterion. A stronger postcondition can add guarantees; a stronger precondition can exclude previously allowed inputs. Thus eq+str does not automatically mean preservation of the original contract on its whole domain. This is a logical qualification, not a finding that all strengthened examples are wrong. NL accounts for 114 of 116 weakened cases; 66/90 other cases have missing or duplicate specifications. Contract-coding kappa is 0.38, explicitly “fair” in §IV-A2, despite §V calling the pair “moderate to substantial”; more than 275 NL coding conflicts were resolved (Q6,Q9,Q12,T4).  RQ2's 31.4% is a checker-success rate, not a reported joint rate of unchanged source, adequate original contract and complete verification. Table V gives NL/FB/FBP averages 24.6/29.5/39.9%, and Claude/Gemini/GPT-4o averages 29.8/39.7/24.5%. Gemini is highest for every input type; Claude FB is lower than its NL result, so formal guidance does not improve every individual cell. FBP success also changes the supplied information, rather than proving a particular prompting mechanism causes better reasoning (Q8,Q10,T5).  Table VI's feature averages are 51.2% other/basic SL, 30.9% recursive predicates, 12.3% concurrency and 11.4% loops. Gemini's hard-case figures are 21.5% concurrency and 21.4% loops, versus Claude 10.4/9.4% and GPT-4o 5.2/3.4%. These describe this curated, tagged dataset and one output per condition; they do not establish distribution-free model rankings (T6,Q10,Q12).  ## Error analysis and concrete cases  RQ3 selects 50 low-success functions, then examines their 354 failing variants. It is not a random sample of every failure: category success thresholds are 33/33/44/56%, quotas 7/7/22/14, all eligible author cases are chosen first and public cases fill remaining quotas randomly. Authors repair each failing output until verification, record errors/severity/location/fix and reconcile independent analyses, preferring fewer modifications when repairs differ. The coding and repair order affect which errors become visible; no RQ3 agreement metric is reported (Q6,Q11,Q12).  Table II gives four useful distinctions. Misplaced queue pre/postconditions cause a compile error. Opening heap predicates reveals that both null heaps have INT_MAX minimum values, a practical automation step. A list-segment concatenation lemma restores an invariant after advancing a pointer. An array loop invariant recording only ten arbitrary elements is logically too weak to prove ten zeros and needs an initialized-prefix invariant. The last example is a genuine missing property, not merely absent predicate unfolding (T2).  Tables VII–VIII contain 1,652 coded errors: 383 compile, 1,167 practical and 102 theoretical, or 93.8% in the first two categories. Component totals are predicates/contracts 381, open/close/assert/leak 767, lemmas 331, invariants 61, source 55 and other 57. The 94% headline is this operational taxonomy; it does not experimentally identify models' internal knowledge or prove that errors are unrelated to general reasoning. There are 858 required-heap-chunk failures, 51.9% of all errors, and 58 missing/incorrect malloc-block cases. These are errors in selected failing outputs, not percentages of all generated functions (Q11,T7,T8).  Of the 767 open/close/assert/leak errors, reported causes are missing 58%, redundant 31%, misplaced 7% and wrong 4%. Lemma errors are 62% missing and 23% redundant. Invariant errors include 20% missing, 25% too weak and 20% too strong. For the 381 predicate/contract errors the prose's 44% compiler share matches 167/381, but its syntax 22% plus type 13% totals only 35%; the missing percentage is not explained. The table, finer prose fractions and denominators should remain distinct (Q11,T7).  The authors report VeriFast's automatic folding/unfolding can fix 39.4% of open/close errors. This is not 39.4% of all errors, all functions, or an evaluated end-to-end increase in passing functions. Heap-state feedback, better error messages and retry loops are proposals; the measured main study does not deploy a feedback agent (Q11,Q13).  ## Static artifact checks and trust boundary  The analyzer keeps a named target function and replaces other parsed executable bodies with `//@ assume(false)`. Therefore passes concern a selected function under remaining declarations/contracts; they are not whole-program proofs that all generated callees were independently verified. The extractor accepts C function declarations and function typedefs as well as definitions, while target eligibility checks names rather than requiring a body. This further limits treating every row as verification of an implemented function. These are inspected source behaviors, not measured false-positive rates (C1–C3).  The subprocess wrapper labels success by the substring “0 errors found”; it does not check the process exit status, set a timeout or reject assumption markers. The contract prefilter compares nonempty dumped AST strings of declarations and initial definitions, then marks the rest “unknown” for manual review. That is syntactic triage, not a proof of semantic equivalence or strengthening. The shell source prefilter strips comments, preprocessor directives and whitespace before diffing; it is also triage. Neither prefilter replaces the paper's manual resolved coding (C1,C4,C5).  Each of the nine verification CSVs has 303 distinct benchmark names. Their yes counts in Claude/Gemini/GPT order are NL 79/109/36, FB 73/118/77 and FBP 119/135/110, totaling 856. In particular Gemini FBP is 135/303=44.55%, whereas Table V prints 44.2% (compatible with 134/303). The current wrapper emits “parse error” or “other error”, but the released CSVs use “no”; source and published reports therefore cannot be assumed to be an unchanged exact run snapshot. The six formal-contract CSVs contain 1,307 syntactically equivalent and 511 unknown cases; these are prefilter results, not the 2,375 final manually equivalent count that also includes NL. The source-change prefilter lists 780 candidate paths, not 780 final semantic changes. No raw logs or resolved XLSX coding were inspected to settle provenance or join all outcome dimensions (C8,C9,reader-static-scan.json).  A lexical scan finds “assume” in 32/2,727 primary output files and exact “assume(false)” in four. The four were then read whole. Gemini's generated thread_start explicitly uses contradiction to trust its stub; its CSV label is “no”. Claude's charreader contains an assumed helper lemma and is also “no”. Gemini's barrier_thread2 is “no”; barrier_main is “yes”, but its assumptions occur in a non-target barrier helper. The analyzer removes that helper's executable body when checking main, so this does not establish that the passing target relied on those exact assumption statements. It does establish that a “yes” row and unchanged executable behavior do not by themselves document the complete proof trust boundary. These literal counts are neither counts of unsound verified targets nor exhaustive checks for all spellings of assumptions (C11–C14,C8).  All three retained generated append-tail FBP outputs are “no” in their CSVs. They attempt segment lemmas/invariants but differ from ground truth; this is a concrete artifact example of proof-structure difficulty, not a reader-reproduced verifier failure. Shape contracts and the artifact's simpler value-free node representation remain explicit (C10,C15,C8).  ## Contribution to the requested topics  The authors position this study as an extension of Rego et al.'s preliminary separation-logic work: “We extend and refine their preliminary work to explore more LLMs, prompting approaches, and benchmarks.” They additionally claim function-level analysis, error severity coding and actionable insights as extensions. Their AutoVerus comparison explicitly distinguishes its multiple-agent refinement from this study's lack of LLM feedback loops. These are the authors' related-work comparisons (§VI,p11,Q14); the cited studies were not independently read as part of this record.  This directly informs evaluation of LLM-written specifications and proofs: report checker success alongside contract meaning, allowed source changes, proof assumptions, function-versus-program scope, dataset selection, repeated sampling and evidence provenance. Its error examples explain why heap ownership, unfolding and segment lemmas challenge automation even when the intended property is understood. The manually coded dataset and released outputs can support further work, subject to the recorded discrepancies and unread coding workbooks.  There is no distributed protocol theorem, Verus/Rust development or TLA+ model in this study. Concurrency is a C benchmark category, not a proof of a message-passing distributed service. Applying its lessons to Verus agents or distributed-system proof pipelines is a reader proposal: preserve the original code/contracts, audit trusted assumptions, distinguish auxiliary-proof completion from specification synthesis, and count the joint validated outcome rather than checker acceptance alone. The paper does not measure those proposed pipelines.

- Ang-Pirlea-Mathur scenario proofs (2026)
    - title: Scenario Proofs for Verification of Distributed Protocols
    - what: Introduces scenario proofs: regular-expression-like representative executions with ghost variables, guards, phases, and loops; coverage modulo sound semi-commutation plus Hoare-style correctness replaces monolithic inductive-invariant discovery. The semantics has structure, variable, feasibility, and commutativity layers. Coverage is reduced to syntax-directed inclusions J1K⊆JsK and Js·aK⊆JsK; correctness checks only feasible representatives using weakest preconditions and supplied loop invariants; local pairwise soundness of semi-commutation justifies reordering. The Paxos scenario defers negative Promise/Accept actions, orders positive rounds ascending, and proves agreement because each later round sees a quorum intersection with completed earlier rounds. Additional appendixed proofs cover two-phase commit, a decentralized lock (empty commutativity), and two Ivy multisignature-payment variants.
    - number: 6 protocol case studies
    - number: 3 proof obligations: coverage, correctness, semi-commutation soundness
    - number: Paxos positive and negative scenario parts
    - limits: Protocols are modeled as finite-action transition systems with feasible runs; semi-commutation must preserve feasibility and final states and is checked locally. Scenario authors must invent representative expressions, coverage derivations, and loop invariants; iteration still requires user invariants. Results are proof case studies, not an automated prover or runtime evaluation; paper notes page-limited appendix and leaves automation/decision procedures open.

- CertiFlash reusable FTL proofs (2026)
    - title: CertiFlash: A Formal Verification Framework for Flash Translation Layers in Computational Solid State Drives
    - what: CertiFlash models FTLs as deterministic state machines with a global invariant covering mapping, isolation, integrity, ownership, and allocation, then packages reusable Rocq proofs so modified FTLs discharge five design-specific hypotheses instead of re-proving the full invariant. The framework proves invariant preservation, stepwise simulation, command precondition soundness, read-after-write correctness, and cross-address non-interference. It identifies five SSD failure surfaces and demonstrates ten reachable attacks when command bundles are unchecked. Four case studies cover new state, reimplemented operations, new operations, and changed invariants; inherited proofs and local obligations are measured in lines.
    - number: Rocq development has 21,884 lines, 432 definitions, and 778 closed theorem statements
    - number: base framework contributes 16,489 inherited lines; four case studies add 27–3,231 lines
    - number: clean build takes 93 seconds on Apple M5 Pro
    - number: ten failures across five attack surfaces are proved reachable when command preconditions are unchecked
    - limits: The reusable certificate assumes the custom FTL projects onto CertiFlash’s FTLState and proves five pure hypotheses over its operations; fields outside the projection are not automatically covered. The threat model treats faulty or malicious commands as possible, and each failure theorem is conditional on its stated hypothesis. Security follows Rocq kernel checking and no admitted axioms in the reported development, but implementation integration remains model/refinement dependent.

- DissProve (2026)
    - title: DissProve: Automated Verification of Asynchronous Distributed Protocols with Affine Communication
    - what: DissProve performs backward abstract interpretation of P actor protocols from a negated safety property. Separation logic tracks local actor state/control, linear logic tracks pending messages, and ordered histories constrain causal execution. Goal-directed materialization, causal reduction, message segments and entailment refute unsafe states for unbounded actor populations. [Q1,Q3–Q18,Q23–Q25] Complete election quorum-bug/refutation, aliasing-aware actor materialization, affine sender-count bounds, handler-independence requirement for message segments, five causal graph edges, counter-summary versus entailment cycles, conditional acyclic-graph termination, full appendices and exact mechanization assumptions. All seven evaluation rows, query counts and capped ablations are preserved. Corrects unsupported Raft-timeout and Theorem 4.1-only mechanization claims. [Q3–Q49]

    - number: 16 states Bakery;9275 Atomic Broadcast
    - number: Two-Phase Commit 5888 states,1:08:46;Atomic Broadcast 9275 states,1:12:46
    - number: 25000 state cap without entailment;Barrier 87 versus 35 states
    - limits: Affine means at most one message type per sender/receiver in the modeled round; initialization precedes other messages, Main-only creation/deployment is outside analysis, no shared memory or message duplication. Properties are prenex universal; no liveness proof. Segment soundness requires independent/reorderable handler invocations and sound recurrence abstraction. Termination requires acyclic causal dependencies and terminating handler analysis. Authors report Lean proof of Theorem 4.1 with assumed concretization lemmas and also Worklist-LemmaB.8; Section 5 segment semantics and full termination are not fully mechanized. Paxos several-hour noncompletion is reported; no separate Raft run is stated. Formula notation and graph/branching definitions have reader-identified ambiguities, without any artifact conclusion. [Q1,Q3,Q9–Q10,Q16–Q22,Q32–Q47] The introduction defines affine communication per sender/type/receiver [Q1], but §3.1.3 says no two messages of the same event type may carry different payloads from one sender, without the same-receiver qualifier [Q10]. The latter wording additionally excludes receiver-specific different payloads. This apparent prose discrepancy remains unresolved; no implementation condition is inferred.

- Guidelines for Producing Concise LNT Models, Illustrated with Formal Models of the Algorand Consensus Protocol (2026)
    - what: # Whole-paper read: Guidelines for Producing Concise LNT Models, Illustrated with Formal Models of the Algorand Consensus Protocol (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Hubert Garavel. MARS2026, EPTCS443,pp43–83,doi10.4204/EPTCS.443.5;arXiv2604.05006,41pages. The paper refactors a finite LNT model of Algorand's BBA* phase and reports equivalence/model checks. Its strongest directly measured result is model compaction with strong bisimilarity checked for two four-node configurations. It supplies a detailed transformation sequence, printed model code and property scripts. It does not establish correctness of the deployed Algorand implementation or arbitrary-size Byzantine consensus. [Q0,Q1,Q2,Q10,Q11]  ## What changes, and what is preserved  The original Urbino model has967LNT lines. Application-specific changes produce U0 with769lines. These changes include new observations, merged/split events, a different attacker and a fair-coin correction; the paper explicitly says many “do not preserve bisimilarity properties.” Thus equivalence of U0–U4 does not imply equivalence with the original967-line model. [Q2,Q11,Q14]  Four generic transformations then produce U1–U4: extract shared modules, replace duplicated control branches with data parameters, merge common sequences, and replace mutually recursive tail calls with assignments and explicit loops. Strong bisimilarity means corresponding states can match every labelled transition in both directions. Authors report BCG_CMP checks for A4,0(four honest nodes) and A2,2(two honest/two malicious), with incremental checks after individual changes. They give structural/algebraic explanations, not a mechanized theorem covering every use of every transformation. The common-suffix choice law is explicitly qualified as failing for common prefixes. [Q3,Q4,Q5,Q6,Q7]  The §2.2 table gives total/nonblank-noncomment lines: U0=769/705,U1=607/552,U2=320/282,U3=288/250,U4=250/212. U0→U4 therefore removes67.49%of total lines and69.93%of substantive lines, ratios3.076and3.325 respectively; these are reader arithmetic. The original967→250comparison also includes semantic changes. Readability and reduced maintenance effort are the author's qualitative judgments; there is no reader study or maintenance-cost experiment. [Q3,Q11]  State counts illustrate that fewer source lines need not produce fewer unminimized states. For the honest-node/malicious-node/A4,0/A2,2 LTSs, U0 has1740/3190/24230/42509states; U1 is identical; U2 has1761/3190/24599/42509;U3 has1681/3046/20665/34679;U4 has1723/3130/20905/35059. After strong-bisimulation minimization every version has558/840/12059/19486states. Identical minimized counts alone would not prove bisimilarity; the reported equivalence checks supply that evidence. No runtime or memory benchmark is given. [Q3]  ## Concrete transformation cases  U1 extracts duplicated node/counter code and splits data definitions into types/constants/channels. U2 merges honest, malicious and disguised behaviors using a MORALITY parameter; node IDs≤H identify honest nodes. U3 factors common suffixes/prefixes and reduces NODE's process calls22→9. Its final branch-factorization example is acknowledged as harder to understand despite being shorter. U4 exposes an inner three-step coin loop inside an outer block-processing loop, replacing12recursive calls across node/counter code with3loops. [Q4,Q5,Q6,Q7]  The loop discovery uses pairs of control location and step residue, rather than control locations alone. The initial random-bit process had combined graded-consensus abstraction with a later fair coin; separating these roles restores the nested-loop structure. The earlier probability P_H used for the later coin is corrected to0.5 among the specific changes before the equivalence-preserving sequence. The counter independently accepts propagated/self-propagated bits, increments K0/K1 and resets them after TALLY. AnnexB prints U2/U3/U4 node code and recursive/imperative counter variants, enabling direct comparison. [Q7,Q14,Q15,Q16]  ## What is verified  Visual checking first hides irrelevant events and minimizes by branching bisimulation, which allows matching behavior across internal steps. Four-node models have roughly12000–20000strongly minimized states,43000–69000transitions and131labels. SYNC-only slicing exposes alternating BEGIN/END barriers. The block interface exposes proposal bits0/1 and commit-proposed/commit-empty events: for H≥T the observed model allows acceptance or rejection; for H<T the illustrated attacker systematically rejects bit1 proposals. Earlier pre-v5models have visible deadlock traces. These are observations of the stated abstract models and attacker, not an arbitrary-fault resilience theorem. [Q8]  Equivalence checks compare sliced systems with small hand-written expected processes: TALLY events form a cyclic four-dimensional hypercube; SELF_PROPAGATE has a more involved loop with optional per-node propagation. Hidden bit/counter values are renamed toX, so those checks establish event-pattern behavior after abstraction, not correctness of discarded values. SET_BIT slices remain difficult to inspect, motivating value-passing MCL formulas. [Q9,Q10]  AnnexC reports16named property scripts checked on both U4configurations: P1deadlock absence;P2SYNC alternation;P3aTALLY counter sum≤4 andP3bhypercube;P4a/bPROPAGATE patterns;P5a/bSELF_PROPAGATE patterns;P6a/bselection P_IN/P_OUTpatterns;P7a/bP_ZERO/P_ONEpatterns;P8ablock-interface classification;P9a/b/cper-node SET_BITinitialization and step progression. The latter formulas require an eventual next bit-setting event or, in P9b, a new proposal, without intervening conflicting events. They are local sequencing checks. The conclusion leaves formulas connecting all nodes' votes to the expected consensus decision as future work. The printed P9cdescription is grammatically incomplete, while its formula explicitly targets SET_BIT(ID,0,any). [Q17,Q18,Q19,Q20]  The models have infinite loops. Absence of deadlocks does not itself prove eventual block commitment. The paper does not report probabilistic model checking or almost-sure termination; probability values occur in observable choice labels, and probabilistic verification is proposed as future work. The evaluated equivalences and MCL results should not be turned into a quantitative probability-of-failure guarantee. Larger configurations of6,8,10nodes are mentioned as explored compositionally, without this paper providing comparable property outcomes or resource measurements for them. [Q10,Q11,Q15,Q16]  ## Model assumptions and limits  AnnexA fixes node population, honesty and equal stake; omits money/rewards, cryptography and leader election; abstracts graded consensus by a probability; reduces step numbers modulo3; and synchronizes every voting phase with global BEGIN/ENDbarriers. Committees are independently selected possibilities ranging from0toNmembers rather than fixed sizeC. The attacker does not fork: it manipulates votes to reject selected proposed blocks. U0 replaces shared BOYCOTT synchronization with independent malicious behavior triggered by proposal bit1. Therefore the model covers one censorship-style strategy, not all Byzantine behavior or dynamic corruption. [Q12,Q13,Q14]  Two documented interpretation choices are fresh committees per step rather than per round, and a persistent per-node bit across steps. Printed constants use N=4,C=3,T=2,H=2(or4),P_V=C/N,and P_H=p²(1+p−p²),p=H/N. The main process synchronizes nodes on proposals, propagation, barriers and both commit events. Reader observation: agreement at those shared commit events is constrained by the model composition; the paper's checks do not independently establish all implementation behaviors fit that composition. Relaxing synchrony and moving from historical BBA* to deployed ABFT remain future work. [Q12,Q13,Q15,Q16,Q11]  For this collection, the paper contributes a concrete workflow for simplifying distributed-system specifications while checking equivalence and targeted temporal properties. Its relevance to LLM-generated specifications is my inference: proposed cleanup should retain an explicit preservation target, and success on self-chosen event slices should not substitute for the intended protocol guarantee. The paper has no Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment.  ## Read and evidence scope  Read all41pages, §§1–8,29reference entries and AnnexesA–C, including all32specific changes,9model-code subsections,16property scripts and auxiliary processes. Inspected all5figures, the full §2.2table and dense formula/code renderings; complete extracted text supplied the remaining material. No external author artifact was linked or acquired beyond the full code printed in the paper. Official arXiv and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. Publisher PDF differs in66bytes but yields identical raw extracted text; hashes and comparison saved. No author code, compiler, model checker, solver or generated LTS was executed or loaded. All reported tool results remain attributed to the author.
    - limits: boundedfixedsynchronousmodel;restrictedattacker;abstractGC/crypto;equivalenceamongrefactoringsnotoriginal/deployedprotocol

- ICEPICK API model checking (2026)
    - title: Systematic API Testing Through Model Checking and Executable Contracts
    - what: Introduces ICEPICK, a black-box REST API testing framework that models API state in TLA+, exhaustively explores the TLC state-space graph, extracts call sequences, and checks execution with GLACIER first-order contracts. The paper specifies a two-phase pipeline: CRUD/OAS contract generation, manual semantic predicates, a conservative TLA+ abstraction, TLC state-space preprocessing, coverage-guided BFS path selection, and execution with an emulator that evaluates preconditions, postconditions and invariants. PUT updates are inserted into post/delete paths; results are classified OK, WARN, ERR or NOT_TESTED. State coverage is complete for generated paths, while transition coverage can miss parallel transitions represented by the same abstract state pair. In the evaluation, Tournaments, Petstore and Features-Service expose distinct scalability and compliance behavior; injected delete and referential-integrity faults are detected, but non-REST APIs block useful inference.
    - number: 17 SSG configurations
    - number: 30–99.4% SSG size reduction after preprocessing
    - number: 5–21 GB models complete within about an hour
    - number: 467 GB and 16 h 16 min for Tournaments size 12
    - limits: The approach requires resource-oriented REST APIs, accurate schemas and HTTP status semantics; generated contracts are intentionally partial and domain invariants may require manual predicates. TLA+ models are abstractions that can diverge from implementations. TLC and path extraction face state explosion: on the reported hardware about 5–21 GB SSGs finish within an hour, while a 467 GB model takes 16 h 16 min; a 100 GB heap handled about 46K states/349K transitions. Only three systems were evaluated, and three-value configurations produced infeasible request counts.

- PerF fault-aware performance prediction (2026)
    - title: A Formal Framework for Predicting Distributed System Performance under Faults (Extended Version)
    - what: Introduces PerF, a Maude framework that composes a distributed-system model with a reusable actor-based fault injector and uses statistical model checking to predict throughput, latency and other metrics under configurable single or combined faults. The paper defines seven fault types (message loss, duplication, delay, tampering, equivocation, node crash, partition) as message-manipulating actors. A scheduler samples normal latency and orders in-flight messages; a priority-aware controller selects eligible behaviors; handlers can modify, duplicate, delay, drop or trigger environment changes. Composition preserves system rules and proves absence of nondeterminism (AND), enabling PVeStA/QuaTEx analysis. Preprocessing labels message-producing rules; transformation adds event monitors for throughput/abort metrics. The six-system study spans 2PC+CTP, Raft, PowerDNS, Cassandra, RAMP/OPW and Fast-HotStuff, and explicitly evaluates mixed equivocation+partition faults.
    - number: Six case studies; model/implementation LoC: 2PC 314/354, Raft 536/1400, PowerDNS 2200/4887, Cassandra 465/1402, RAMP 2523/7977, Fast-HotStuff 304/4247. PVeStA uses 95% confidence and 0.01 error margin on 2.4-GHz quad-core Xeon Emulab machines. Model curves for throughput/latency align closely with deployment evaluations; RAMP shows markedly higher latency than OPW as loss increases; Fast-HotStuff throughput declines with more equivocators and only moderately with combined partition.
    - number: six systems evaluated with model-versus-deployment curves
    - number: PerF uses 95% statistical confidence and 0.01 error margin
    - number: formal models range from 220 to 2,523 LoC and implementations from 354 to 7,977 LoC
    - limits: Maude probabilistic rewrite semantics and absence-of-nondeterminism are required for SMC. Delays come from user-chosen distributions (lognormal, Weibull, exponential), and fault rates/times/targets are configured abstractions. Accuracy is judged by curve trends up to an unknown deployment/model time-scale factor, not absolute values. The framework models faults as message interception, so faults outside message effects or inaccurate distributions are not covered. Experiments use six systems, one deployment per system and 95% confidence/0.01 error; deployment implementations and models differ in size and platform. Dynamic actor/message populations challenge automata-based alternatives but are not claimed solved generally.

- Rocq out-of-order multiprocessor refinement (2026)
    - title: Formal Verification of an Out-of-Order Multiprocessor against an In-Order Weak-Memory ISA
    - what: Mechanizes an unbounded refinement proof that a multicore out-of-order RISC-V implementation with weak-memory behavior refines an in-order ISA, using a clean core specification to eliminate excess executions and then serializing memory/inter-core behavior. The proof decomposes n·Coreᵢ+ShMem⊆ISA into core refinement Coreᵢ⊑Coreₛ and system inclusion n·Coreₛ+ShMem⊆ISA. Coreₛ stores instructions in a single program-order list, allowing invalid excess instructions to be dropped; lightweight option-lifting encodes pure method preconditions without changing the refinement metatheory. Rocq mechanizes module refinements, arbitrary traces, and arbitrary design parameters.
    - number: end-to-end refinement is fully mechanized in 64k Rocq LOC
    - number: Theorem 1 holds for all instantiations and arbitrary execution lengths

    - limits: The design is a single-issue out-of-order RV32I core with LR/SC, an axiomatized coherent shared memory, and promising/RISC-V memory semantics. The precondition encoding is deliberately limited to pure predicates, and the proof abstracts implementation details through specified modules. LLM-written proofs remain trusted only after Rocq kernel checking; performance or silicon behavior is outside the formal theorem.

    - what: Introduces inductive proof decomposition and the Scimitar tool for interactively constructing compositional safety proofs. - Show Me The Money: An Exercise in Proof-Driven Software Understanding (2026)
    - what: Retrospective human-led analysis of Stellar SDEX exchangeV10 uses LLM-generated PVS abstractions, interactive theorem proving and SeaBMC symbolic C++ harnesses to recover rounding invariants and test a supposedly unreachable exception. Authors report 37 of 38 lemmas/typechecker obligations proved, establishing P1–P3 in their model. The remaining P4 obligation leads to an executable local exception witness; reachability through upstream production callers is left unresolved. Records the actual human/LLM/prover division of work, the distinction between generating and discharging type obligations, the asymmetry of the one-percent bound, exact harness assumptions and concrete exception inputs. Separates PVS model proofs and parallel code-property checks from a general abstraction-to-C++ refinement theorem. Preserves unresolved caller assumptions, schematic figure issues and the absence of a measured maintenance or controlled LLM experiment.
    - limits: §§1–3: the target is a mostly functional arithmetic function in deployed blockchain infrastructure, not consensus, network behavior, smart contracts or the entire order book. Source has 1344 C/C++ lines plus 758 comment lines; abstraction has 260 PVS lines plus 84 comment lines. Code structure and substantial informal invariants are important favorable inputs. §3.1: humans copied full source to ChatGPT 5 Pro, fed PVS errors back and repeated with Claude Opus 4 with qualitatively similar results. Invalid DIV, misplaced IMPORTING and invented libraries needed repairs. Models originally represented exceptions as unused booleans. Humans split theories into three files and supplied interface preconditions. This is not autonomous proof generation. §3.1 footnote4: passing the initial typechecker phase means name resolution and sound generation of type-correctness conditions (TCCs), not their discharge. TCC generation itself is distinct from a complete checked proof. §3.2: the introduction says 16 generated lemmas and 22 generated proof obligations were proved, but the detailed account reports 37/38 and one failed P4 obligation. Retain the detailed denominator; do not claim all 38 obligations or absence of exceptions were established. §§2–3/Figs3–4: P1 favors the offer remaining in the book. P2 bounds relative rounding error by 1% for a single matched offer. P3 permits path-payment asymmetry: error favoring the wheat seller can be unbounded, whereas the sheep-favoring case remains bounded; non-path exchanges exceeding the bound are rejected. These claims depend on input bounds and formalized preconditions. §3.2/Fig5: PVS assert/grind use Shostak reasoning; Yices2 handles nonlinear arithmetic. Type subranges and explicit bounds matter. The displayed Price uses uint32 fields although the source comment says int32_t; uint32 includes zero while the shown posint64 obligations require 100*n>0 and 100*d>0. The schematic includes ellipses and does not show all premises, so it alone neither proves positivity nor establishes unsoundness of the full artifact. §3.3: C++ unit proofs encode PVS type constraints as assumptions, call the implementation and assert corresponding properties; SeaHorn lowers harness and source to LLVM for SeaBMC. These are parallel property checks and a sanity check on relevance. The paper supplies no general relational refinement/equivalence theorem covering the PVS abstraction and all C++ operational semantics. §3.3/Fig6: price n,d are nondeterministic signed 32-bit integers with n>0,d>0. Four maxima are signed 64-bit; assumptions constrain maxWheatSend>=0, maxSheepSend>0 and maxWheatReceive>0. No positivity assumption is shown for maxSheepReceive. The postcondition is !res.wheatStays || (res.numSheepSend>0 && res.numWheatReceived>=0). §3.3/Fig7: a counterexample confirms local exception behavior for the stated harness domain. Developers believe upstream code excludes it; that caller claim is not proved. A failed PVS proof alone would not establish a code bug, and the witness does not establish an exploitable end-to-end production vulnerability. Algorithm2: graphical line14 asserts round=PPS_SEND implies Ss≠0; extracted text loses the negation. Prose p.237 calls it line15, but printed line15 zeroes amounts. The function declaration omits several variables used by its body, so the pseudocode is schematic rather than a complete executable specification. §4/Fig8: revised prompt asks for total mathematical functions, explicit bounds and exceptions converted to preconditions/subtypes. It explicitly excludes full C++ semantics and asks only to state lemmas. Reader inference: strengthening a precondition can remove the failing behavior from the model; callers must separately establish it. No memory, exception or arithmetic semantic correspondence follows from well-typed PVS alone. §4: claims of low manual effort, transfer to larger codebases and useful continuous integration are qualitative. No attempt counts, token costs, elapsed human/prover/model-checker times, resource limits, unroll bounds, solver configurations, controlled comparison or repeated-run variance are reported. §4: exchangeV10 did not change during the exercise. Maintenance/evolution benefits and automatic harness/proof updates are proposed opportunities, not measured longitudinal outcomes. Conclusion still says specification finalization and broader coverage are ongoing. Trusted components include human interpretation, abstraction/precondition selection, PVS and its proof/solver integration, source-to-LLVM compilation, SeaBMC and harness construction. No independent artifact execution, proof replay or upstream-call analysis was performed for this record. No Verus, Rust or TLA+ result is reported.

    - what: Introduces Taco, a modular toolsuite for developing and verifying threshold-based distributed algorithms modeled as monotonic or extended threshold automata, with SMT, ZCS/BDD, and ACS/WSTS model checkers plus semi-decision support for reset/decrement extensions. - Towards System-Oriented Formal Verification of Local-First Access Control (2026)
    - what: # Whole-paper read: Towards System-Oriented Formal Verification of Local-First Access Control (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Florian Jacob, Johanna Stuber and Hannes Hartenstein; arXiv2604.23560v1,26April2026,PaPoC2026-related manuscript,8PDFpages. The contribution is a capability-based authorization design and three deliberately restricted Verus implementations. The paper explicitly says its full §3target has not yet been met. Its results concern simplified authorization/query functions assuming a valid eventually consistent chronicle; they do not verify Matrix, Keyhive, a cryptographic hash implementation, or a deployed replication stack. [Q0,Q1,Q3,Q10,Q13]  ## Threat model and intended semantics  A local-first entity acts on its own replica and exchanges events asynchronously. The threat model permits any strict subset of entities to be Byzantine, f/n<1, including selective omission, equivocation and backdating. Events are assumed authenticated and integrity-protected. The underlying hash chronicle is assumed Byzantine fault-tolerant, append-only and eventually consistent; collision-resistant identifiers fix an event's causal past. This is the input contract for the authorization layer, rather than a new proof of the replication or cryptographic layer. Eventual dissemination requires the stated chronicle/anti-entropy assumptions; it does not follow merely from having one honest participant. [Q2,Q4,Q9]  The mathematical design uses four event kinds:create,grant,revoke,assign. A grant specifies subject, recipient and operation capability; a use presents the grant's identifier; revocation references that identifier. Events combine an invocation and a downward-closed set of precursor identifiers. The printed identifier contract idealizes collision resistance as equality of identifiers iff equality of events. A valid group has one creation event, no event concurrent with creation, and valid timestamps. Logging appends an event after the current history; joining takes set union. The name query returns the latest authorized assign events, allowing multiple concurrent names. These are the intended §3semantics, not all jointly verified features. [Q5,Q6]  Authorization requires a matching authorized grant in the event's causal past, no matching authorized revocation in its past or concurrent history, and, for a revoke, a referenced grant in its past. Creation and setup precursors are authorized by definition. Extending revocations to concurrent uses prevents an attacker from bypassing a revocation by backdating a new use. It also makes authorization non-monotonic: new information can invalidate an earlier result. [Q6,Q7]  The paper distinguishes authorization based only on immutable precursors (“precursive”) from authorization based on the available group including concurrent events (“discursive”). A subtle example is revocationa concurrent with useb, followed by revocationc concurrent witha but afterb: revokinga can reauthorizeb even thoughc followsb. Concurrency is not transitive. Thus a property's dependence cannot safely be inferred just by looking at direct time order. This motivates distinguishing what may be stored/broadcast from what currently affects queries. [Q7]  The three stated security invariants are:precursor-based authorization is unchanged by adding events, while current authorization can change through authorized revocations; a changed query result requires an authorized newly added event; and an invocation unauthorized now remains unauthorized when backdated. These are specifications of the intended behavior. The paper's explanation that the full Spec.2supports them is not itself a mechanized proof of all Spec.2features. [Q8]  ## What the Verus case study reports  The three verified restrictions separate the difficult features. First, assign capabilities are fixed before creation and cannot later change. Second, the creator may grant assign rights after creation, but nobody may revoke. Third, assign rights are initially granted and the creator may revoke them, but new grants are not introduced afterward. The third case permits concurrent assign/revoke conflicts; it avoids mutually revoking equally privileged entities. Supporting both grants and revocations in one algorithm, post-creation delegation, query/membership capabilities, self-revocation, public joining, sparse replication and group changeover are future work. [Q10,Q11,Q12]  Specification functions describe pure mathematical behavior; executable functions have contracts linking their results to it. Figure4illustrates a log contract accepting exactly the events authorized by the specification, with an explicit fresh-identifier availability precondition. It is a shortened code example with ellipses, not the complete executable implementation. Authors report total and pure queries, precursor authorization as a group type invariant, and the restricted constructions supporting current authorization/revocation safety. If correct replicas eventually hold the same chronicle, deterministic total queries give the same answer. That conditional convergence argument does not prove dissemination, bounded latency, or settlement in a perpetually changing history. [Q9,Q10,Q11]  Totality has a material trust boundary. Authors report modifying vstd to add no_unwind contracts, assuming standard-library functions terminate and allocation/randomness system calls do not panic. They also add the assumption that cloning a HashSet preserves its elements, conditional on Rust std correctness. Ghost specifications and proofs impose no runtime checks according to the paper; the paper provides no throughput, memory or latency experiment demonstrating a numerical runtime saving. Its “zero runtime cost” refers to erasing verification annotations, not to a proof that the algorithms execute for free. [Q9,Q11]  The evaluation is a proof-of-concept experience report. It supplies no complete table of proof obligations, solver times, source/proof line counts, hardware measurements, test-population results or comparative performance study. The artifact README says verification “should complete in a hand full of seconds”; this is an informal expected duration, not a saved timing measurement. A practical difficulty was replacing unsupported iterator combinators with for loops and proving their invariants; authors call this among the most time-consuming parts. Their claim that Verus is accessible/future-proof is an author judgment, not a measured user-study result. [Q11,Q13,S0]  ## Static artifact comparison  The paper-linked repository was retrieved at commit3d6bdaf63c192ada9039f4f61127744465827ed0. Its README identifies Verus release0.2026.01.23.1650a05. The Makefile invokes Verus on main.rs, which imports separate modules for the chronicle, three authorization variants, types, helpers and assumed specifications. I inspected the whole Rust source tree. The HashSetclone assumption is explicit; the only external_body in these sources wraps printing. No assume/admit proof escape appeared beyond that declared assume_specification and imported library axioms. This describes these project files, not the full trusted Verus/vstd closure. [S0,S1,S2,S3,S4,S5,S6,S7,S8,S9]  The source makes further simplifications concrete. EntityID/EventID areu64, and Chronicle::find_free_id scans from0 for a locally unused identifier under an explicit availability precondition. Events contain the full predecessor set. There is no cryptographic hashing/signature verification, replica transport or join operation in these project modules. Grant/Revoke operations target an entity's SetName authorization, without the full Spec.2grant-identifier/delegation structure. The immutable case consults setup_grants; the monotonic case permits creator grants; the non-monotonic case treats all entities as initially able to SetName and disables that right when a matching revocation appears in the relevant history. A type invariant requires all stored events to be causally authorized. name's executable result must equal its specification's latest concurrently authorized SetName values. These contracts support the stated restricted authorization layer; they do not implement the complete hash-chronicle data type. [S1,S3,S4,S5,S6,S7]  main.rs supplies four hand-written scenarios with proof assertions: reject Dave's unauthorized assignment and retain two concurrent names; reject an unauthorized grant and a use concurrent with its grant; accept a causally valid backdated assignment but exclude it from current name results; and observe{name1}→{name1,name2}→{name1}when a concurrent revocation arrives. I read these scenarios without executing or re-verifying them. Some chronicle clones are executable statements labelled “for verification purposes only”; the general proof-erasure statement should not be read as a measured guarantee that this entire example has no verification-related executable work. [S8]  The paper's reported no_unwind experiment cannot be reconstructed from this snapshot alone: no no_unwind annotation or modified-vstd patch occurs in the acquired project files. The Nix/Cargo metadata point to external Verus/vstd sources, which I did not inspect. Thus the paper's conditional totality claim remains attributed to the authors; absence in the project snapshot does not establish that their separate experiment failed. The README's expected fast verification was not reproduced. [Q9,S0,S1,S8,S9]  ## Contribution and read scope  This paper directly adds a verified-Rust authorization case study to the distributed-systems collection. It isolates the trust placed in replication, cryptographic identity, library specifications and resource-related behavior. Its potential use in evaluating proof-writing agents is my inference: assess the exact restricted capability policy and trusted library additions before calling a whole system verified. The paper has no TLA+ or LLM experiment. [Q9,Q10,Q11,Q13]  Read all8PDFpages,37references,all4figures,both complete mathematical specification boxes and all3security-invariant formulas; inspected every page render. The final PDFpage contains all37references. Read all9Rust source files,README,Makefile,Cargo.toml,flake.nix and relevant lock metadata;15static text files acquired withSHA256/Gitblobidentities. External Verus/vstd dependencies and repository scenario images were not inspected. Official arXiv and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. No author execution, compiler, solver or prover run.

- ACL2 dynamic-stake DAG BFT nonforking (2025)
    - title: Formal Verification of Blockchain Nonforking in DAG-Based BFT Consensus with Dynamic Stake
    - what: Formalizes a DAG-based BFT consensus protocol whose validator set and stake can change at every block, and machine-checks blockchain nonforking in ACL2 under a less-than-one-third faulty-stake condition for every active committee. The labeled transition system models validators, certificates, DAGs, network messages, rounds, dynamic bonding/unbonding, lookback active committees, anchor elections/commitments and block generation. Bonding changes become active only after a fixed lookback, resolving the DAG/blockchain circular dependency. The proof establishes interdependent invariants for committee agreement, certificate and DAG nonequivocation, previous quorums, anchor presence/voters/paths/nonforking, and blockchain nonforking. Anchor nonforking uses voter/quorum stake intersection; certificate nonequivocation uses signer quorum intersection, and both are proved together because each depends on the other through committee agreement. The ACL2 development has about 20,000 lines and verifies in under one minute on an Apple M3 Max (under two minutes single-core), applying to arbitrarily long executions and arbitrarily large states. The model intentionally includes deadlocking and other executions beyond an implementation, so safety transfers to implementations as subsets but liveness is not established.
    - number: faulty stake < one third of each active committee
    - number: lookback lkbk≥1; committee can change completely every block
    - number: about 20,000 ACL2 lines
    - number: under 1 minute on Apple M3 Max 16 cores; under 2 minutes single core
    - limits: Correct validators follow the abstract protocol and faulty validators are Byzantine; each active committee must have faulty stake at most fstk(w)<nstk(w)/3, with quorum stake qstk=nstk−fstk. Signatures/addresses are idealized and cryptographic details are omitted. The model is nondeterministic and a superset of implementation executions; validators can advance without certificates and deadlock, and the authors explicitly note that proving liveness would require augmenting the model. Only blockchain nonforking and related invariants are proved; performance, synchronization, transaction validity, fairness and implementation behavior are not evaluated. The ACL2 state-transition system and nonforking predicate are trusted modeling boundaries.

Messages carry sender identities; arbitrary Byzantine forgery or compromised hosts are not modeled. History is proof state, not a measured runtime logging cost. §3: Network provenance links a sent message to an adjacent pair of historical sender states and a matching send step. Host provenance for witness q requires q now, no initial state satisfying q, and a historical crossing from not-q to q through a candidate modifying step. These statements concern well-formed initialized protocol executions, not arbitrary malformed history sequences. §§3.3,5.3: Provenance alone identifies a past producing event. Monotonicity/non-equivocation invariants are needed to move from past sender conditions to present facts. Ownership invariants/labels are inherited from Kondo; generated invariants are individually/local mechanically checked, not assertions trusted merely because the generator produced them. §4.1: An atomic shard is a subset of local variables always modified together. If the current tuple is not an admissible initial tuple, it was established in one candidate update step. Maximal shards retain shared-message correlations lost by independent singleton witnesses. This does not mean every member of a collection remains correlated with the latest scalar value. §4.2: Static footprints overapproximate variables a step may update; excess candidates weaken the resulting provenance disjunction. Underestimating footprints would produce incorrect invariants. Prototype rejects a step updating different variables under different conditions, e.g. if c then x:=5 else y:=6. User must split this into separately guarded steps. §§4.2,5.3: Collection fields also receive refined singleton shards, allowing each noninitial set/map entry to be traced to its insertion step. Prototype supports explicit Dafny record-update syntax only, rather than general relational updates. A step can receive and send together; multiple sends/broadcasts in one step are described as an easy extension but not implemented or evaluated. §5.4 reader qualification: Formal obligations are Init⇒I∧φ and I∧φ∧Next⇒I′∧φ′. Thus the actual method proves safety with induction on I∧φ and may use current φ in the step proof. Figure 5/prose describing a proof that I implies safety must not be read as requiring or establishing the stronger standalone I⇒φ in every example. The final safety proof remains user-written. §§5.4,6.4: Failure may reflect a too-weak generated invariant or an unsafe model; the verifier points to the failing host-step obligation, but does not automatically decide which explanation is true. Reader qualification: SMT proof failure can also arise from solver incompleteness. Additional provenance witnesses or manually written invariant clauses may be needed; Basilisk is explicitly incomplete for undecidable logics. §6: First six protocols were used to develop/refine provenance and atomic sharding; the remaining ten were applied later. All sixteen models/invariants are reported outside EPR. This is an author-built benchmark suite, not a blinded independent user study or proof of completeness for all protocols outside EPR. §§6.1–6.2: Zero manually supplied invariant clauses across 16 does not mean zero user reasoning. Six of 64 host-provenance invariants need explicit witness hints, across Paxos-Dynamic, Raft election and Multi-Paxos; monotonicity annotations, ownership labels and safety lemmas remain. Distributed Lock and both ShardedKV variants already had fully automatic Kondo ownership proofs. §6.2: Kondo comparisons cover only ten protocols and modify models to split receive/send; Kondo also needs synchronous protocol definitions. Final proof LOC excludes failed/revised proof attempts and does not measure person-time, cognitive difficulty or novice success. Basilisk uses more proof LOC for some simple cases and is not faster for every ownership example. §6.3: Timings check final history-preserving asynchronous proofs including generated/user invariants and lemmas; Kondo synchronous-proof verification is excluded. Invariant generation is under two seconds in every case. Table 1 reports Multi-Paxos 61.5 seconds; the prose phrase in a minute is approximate, not a strict sub-60-second bound. No repetitions/variance or controlled proof-authoring experiment is reported. §6.4: Epoch resets create implicit multi-step relations that sharding cannot infer. Adding an event at current year and clearing events on year increment requires a witness relating every current entry to current year; merely finding its historic insertion year is too weak. All three hinted benchmark protocols have collection resets at epoch changes. Footprint imprecision is another possible weakness, not observed by authors in these protocols. §6.4: Safety specification is trusted. The user must trust the model describes actual code or separately prove correspondence; this work does not verify production implementations. Dafny, dependencies and hardware are trusted. Crash-fault safety is the scope; no liveness or Byzantine correctness proof is provided. §§6–8,Appendix A: No runtime throughput, production bug-finding or LLM-agent experiment is evaluated. Artifact developed/tested on M3 MacBook Pro with MacOS Sequoia; this appendix statement is not an explicit platform declaration for every published timing. Artifact and external proof bodies were not executed in this reading.

- CADP model of Algorand BBA* (2025)
    - title: Formal Modeling and Verification of the Algorand Consensus Protocol in CADP
    - what: Builds a probabilistic process-algebra model of Algorand’s BBA* phase, translates it to CADP/LNT and checks equivalence-based noninterference. Honest nodes are modeled first; malicious nodes can coordinate a boycott that forces an empty-block commit, exposing when adversarial behavior changes observable outcomes. Models committee self-sortition, bit propagation, three step types (coin fixed 0/1 and genuinely flipped), vote counters and commit thresholds. The malicious extension uses a high-level boycott action; CADP compares hide(BOYCOTT) and cut(BOYCOTT) under weak and branching bisimilarity. Parameters instantiate four nodes, committee size three, threshold two and honest stake 0.8; the model explicitly documents stronger synchrony and honest-majority abstractions.

- CCF smart casual verification (2025)
    - title: Smart Casual Verification of the Confidential Consortium Framework (CCF)
    - what: Industrial experience applying TLA+ specification/model checking, weighted simulation and implementation trace validation to the existing C++ Confidential Consortium Framework. Separate node-consensus and client-history specifications are aligned with production protocol details and incorporated in CI. The paper reports six consensus bugs found/fixed and a clarified read-only consistency limitation, plus tooling/effort and state-exploration measurements. Reconstructs all six safety/liveness cases and the unsuccessful first fix, distinguishes trace compatibility from universal implementation refinement, records granularity alignment via composition/stuttering and incomplete-state reconstruction. Saves all scale/coverage rows, effort figures, counterexample sizes and issue pointers. Preserves TEE/model trust, bounded exploration and non-linearizable read-only semantics; no all-executions C++ correctness theorem is claimed.
    - number: Six subtle bugs found, five concerning safety and one liveness
    - number: 400 LoC Trace spec; 88 commits to it and 107 changes to the consensus spec; implementation 63 kLoC C++
    - number: six subtle bugs found
    - number: 63 kLoC in C++ (§2)
    - limits: §§1–2: CCF runs application logic inside trusted execution environments while treating operators, host OS/hypervisor, network and storage as corruptible. This paper checks distributed protocol behavior under modeled failures, not hardware/firmware isolation, enclave security, cryptography, all 63k C++ LOC, or arbitrary Byzantine behavior of the protected consensus code. Production use in Azure Confidential Ledger is context, not evidence that every production behavior is covered. §§1.1,4,8: Smart casual verification combines formal specification, finite model checking/simulation and tests/trace checks. Consensus spec is unbounded but exhaustive checking restricts terms, requests and reconfiguration sequences. No TLAPS safety/liveness proof for all sizes or universal code-refinement proof is reported. Most CI exploration relies on bounded simulations because sufficiently realistic exhaustive exploration is too expensive. §2: CCF returns transaction results before replication; clients separately query Pending/Committed/Invalid status. A returned result may later be invalidated. Committed read-write transactions are strictly serializable; committed read-only transactions are serializable and may be stale. Pending branches offer fork-like consistency rather than arbitrary results. Broad prose about all committed transactions being linearizable needs the explicit read-only exception. §2: Transaction IDs are lexicographic term/index pairs. If two transactions commit, ID ordering agrees with execution ordering. Ancestor Commit says committed <t,i> implies same-term <t,j>, j≤i, committed. This concerns transaction identity/status, not a proof that any stale read immediately observes the newest committed write. §2.1: CCF customizes Raft with signed Merkle-root transactions, messaging without RPC correspondence, optimistic sentIndex advances, express catch-up, CheckQuorum, bootstrapping/reconfiguration and retirement/ProposeVote. A transaction is committed only after a subsequent signature is committed. The actual combined protocol needs verification; citing the base Raft proof does not establish these extensions. §2.1 reader qualification: Early description says an AE-ACK carries the last transaction in the follower log, while the Inaccurate AE-ACK bug/fix later constrains that index to the end of the received AE. The historical/protocol-description distinction must be retained rather than treating the early sentence as the final safe response rule. §§2.1,4: Reconfiguration needs majorities in each active configuration, rather than a majority of their union. A removed node remains retiring until retirement information is safely committed for future leaders. CheckQuorum steps down an isolated leader, but absent delivery/scheduling assumptions this is not a theorem that all executions make progress. §4: Consensus has 17 actions/13 variables, 12 local-state mappings plus network. Parameterization includes every nonempty initial node subset with any member as initial leader. Locally initiated timeout/signature/candidacy/step-down choices impose no clock synchrony. LogInv compares pairwise committed-log prefixes; AppendOnlyProp prevents committed-prefix rollback over time. Another 27 properties include MonoLogInv, requiring term increases only after signatures. §4: Simulation explores behaviors to bounded depth under a time quota; authors manually downweight failures to promote forward progress. Q-learning was implemented in TLC but no state-hash feature set beat manual weighting. More progress-rich traces may help find bugs but do not constitute exhaustive failure coverage or proof of liveness. §5: Client model uses append-only history and logBranches, independent of node count. History includes read-only/read-write requests/responses and status responses, but omits status requests/Pending replies. A simple shared value appends transaction identifiers so conflicts and observations are visible. It is a deliberately selected application workload, not a proved reduction of all arbitrary CCF application semantics. §5: A new branch can be any prefix of an existing branch containing the last committed transaction. Requests may execute at any still-active leader/term. PrevCommittedInv checks same-term committed ancestor statuses; ObservedRoInv demands that a subsequently committed read-only response observe a read-write transaction whose response preceded its request. The latter expectation is falsified and documented, not a proved CCF invariant. §6.1: Scenario driver serializes consensus execution deterministically and mocks governance/networking/other components, injecting loss/reordering/partition/delay. Original 13 scenarios and about 1.6k unit-test/2k Python end-to-end LOC precede the effort; Table 1 gives later exact scope counts. Initial fuzzing was abandoned for insufficient interesting coverage. Driver/mock accuracy is a boundary, as demonstrated by retirement bugs. §6.1: Driver uses a global logical ordering clock; distributed Lamport/vector alternatives are suggested but not implemented here. Fifteen added logging statements capture stable states at message and role-change points, immediately after a global lock for state changes. Constant-space values such as log lengths are recorded, not full log entries. Production logging compiles out, so the checks use instrumented test executions rather than continuous production monitoring. §6.1/§6.5: Traces initially remove/deduplicate bootstrapping events because early consensus spec omits that phase; later specification is expanded to model bootstrapping more faithfully. These describe successive coverage stages. A successful preprocessed trace validates only its retained observations and modeling assumptions, not excluded initialization behavior. §6.2: Trace spec checks existence of a spec behavior consistent with observed events/values: T∩S is nonempty. Nondeterministically reconstructed hidden state is existential. A successful finite trace check is evidence for those observations, not proof that all completions, all execution traces or unlogged state transitions meet the spec. If logging or mappings omit a decisive distinction, an incorrect implementation could remain compatible. §6.2: Send actions constrain current state, invoke high-level action and assert matching successor messages. Network changes from set to multiset to represent duplicate/resend occurrences. Trace network abstractions also explore ordering/duplication/loss guarantees. Such abstraction choices affect what is observable and accepted; they are not runtime network guarantees inferred from traces. §6.2.1 Listing 5: UpdateTerm·HandleAppendEntriesReq composes two model actions into one implementation receive. IsFault·Next admits unlogged network faults before a step; send-response events may stutter high-level variables when already modeled by another action. Composition hides intermediate states and stuttering changes observation granularity, so correctness depends on the mapping retaining semantically important events. Merely making a mismatch disappear is not an independent proof. §6.2.2–6.3: Start with a happy-path trace, add many assertions and cross-references, debug source and formulas. Invalid traces may indicate bogus logging, incorrect mapping, specification error or implementation bug; failure lacks an ordinary model-checking counterexample. Longest matching prefixes, unreachable-state graphs, failing subformulas and an unsatisfied breakpoint support diagnosis. §6.4: DFS stops after finding one compatible behavior, avoiding BFS enumeration of alternatives; a consistency trace goes from about one hour to under a second. This is an author example without trace-size distribution or controlled speedup suite, and does not mean all traces validate in under a second. Existential acceptance is essential to that optimization. §6.5: Logging/driver enhancements took about one day. Consensus alignment/tooling took two engineer-months over four months, including TLC composition/DFS/debug support, discrepancy diagnosis and abstraction design. Writing about 400 lines of Trace was minor; Table 1 counts 369. Trace saw 88 commits and consensus spec 107 changes. This is observed project effort, not a controlled productivity study. §6.5: Client consistency validation uses REST observations without source instrumentation, reconstructs other clients’ hidden transactions from observed IDs, and took about one engineer-week over two weeks, mainly by CCF experts. Smaller spec, previous experience and reused TLC changes confound a simple comparison with initial consensus effort. §7 Table 1: Approximate state counts/rates are measured on Azure DC8s v3. A log line is largely equivalent to a model action, according to authors, not a formal equality of semantic coverage. Different abstraction sizes, bounds, durations and distinct/generated-state counting prevent treating orders-of-magnitude state counts as a calibrated defect-detection probability. §7: Six serious consensus bugs comprise five safety issues and one liveness issue, found by combined modeling, source scrutiny, trace mismatch, simulation and functional/end-to-end reproduction. They are not six independent discoveries by model checking alone. Read-only non-linearizability is an additional documented consistency ambiguity and accepted behavior, not a seventh fixed consensus bug. §§7–8: Authors report all six fixed before user impact/customer reports; software had already been deployed. One-node-at-a-time operational reconfiguration masked the election bug, and absence of an incident from the first bad commit fix was attributed to chance. No external incident audit, current repository verification or independent bug reproduction was done in this reading. §§8–9: Paper chooses model checking for developer accessibility rather than deductive proof, despite compute cost. AI-assisted proof search is future possibility with a reference to neural theorem proving, not an experiment using LLM agents. Related-work sentence says IronFleet and Verdi both proved Raft; reader qualification: IronFleet uses a Paxos-based replicated state machine, so do not propagate that comparison as fact.

    - title: ChonkyBFT: Consensus Protocol of ZKsync
    - what: Presents ChonkyBFT, a partially synchronous committee BFT protocol for ZKsync with one voting round, single-slot finality, quadratic communication, and n≥5f+1. Safety, validity, and partial-synchrony progress are proved by quorum and timeout lemmas. The Quint specification and Apalache symbolic checking found pseudocode type/definition errors and attack paths; an 18-lemma inductive invariant was checked for bounded parameters. A deployment evaluation measures failure-free throughput, latency, resource use, and replication lag.

Liveness additionally assumes block synchrony, periodic retransmission, bounded clock drift, and eventual correct leaders. Formal Apalache checks restrict to six replicas, at most one fault, three views, bounded message/QC sets, so they are model-level evidence. Performance tests are failure-free and exclude block synchronization.
