- Crossword (2025)
    - title: Crossword: Adaptive Consensus for Dynamic Data-Heavy Workloads
    - what: # Crossword: Adaptive Consensus for Dynamic Data-Heavy Workloads (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Guanzhou Hu, Yiwei Chen, Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau and Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau, arXiv:2509.07157v1, 8 September 2025. This reading covers all 30 PDF pages: design, implementation, every evaluation, discussion, 144 references, complete PlusCal/TLA+ specification and model-checking configuration. All eight contact sheets and close views of pages 5, 8, 10–12 and 19–30 were read. PDF and printed page numbers agree. The findings below distinguish author reports from static reader reasoning; no author code or checker was run. [Evidence: Q0, title, abstract and §1, PDF pp.1–2; Q24, Appendix A model-check report and explicit finite scope, PDF pp.19–19; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Crossword changes how much erasure-coded data each replica must durably store before a log entry commits. More data per replica permits a smaller reply quorum; less data requires more replies. Its motivating Figure 1 profiles Raft payloads under 200-warehouse TPC-C in TiDB and CockroachDB: “~45% are 4KB” and the distributions reach 290 KB and 63 MB, respectively. The paper derives a shard-survival condition, combines it with majority voting, and implements per-entry adaptation in Rust and in a CockroachDB Go prototype. Followers exchange missing shards after commitment. Its evidence is algebraic design reasoning, a reported finite model check, tests and system measurements. The paper says, “It has been model-checked for both linearizability and fault-tolerance properties” and immediately names the finite inputs. The artifact supplies neither an unbounded proof nor a refinement from the model to Rust or Go. [Evidence: Q4, §3.3 complete derivation and Figure 4, PDF pp.5–5; Q7, §3.6 complete protocol changes, PDF pp.7–7; Q8, §4 implementation and Gazette/CockroachDB, PDF pp.7–7; Q24, Appendix A model-check report and explicit finite scope, PDF pp.19–19; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]  ## Assumptions and the actual contract  The system model uses an odd number n of replicas, asynchronous communication and fail-stop failures. Set m=ceil(n/2) and f=n−m. Balanced policies use Reed–Solomon (n,m) coding, so any m distinct shards reconstruct a payload. A vote means both acceptance of a ballot and durable storage of its assigned shards: “s votes yes to the ballot number of this Accept message and has durably remembered the shards it carried.” The leader retains the entire payload in memory but persists only its assignment. Background gossip remains in memory. Restart recovery, Byzantine behavior and cryptographic shard authenticity are outside this model. Time-based read leases separately assume bounded clock drift; the asynchronous network model alone does not establish lease correctness. [Evidence: Q1, §2 complete background, system model and motivation, PDF pp.2–3; Q3, §3.1–3.2 assignments and Figure 3, PDF pp.4–5; Q4, §3.3 complete derivation and Figure 4, PDF pp.5–5; Q6, §3.5 gossip and Figure 5, PDF pp.6–7; Q11, §4.3 heartbeats, snapshots and leases, PDF pp.8–8; literal spans in quotes.json.]  For an acceptance pattern ap, C1 requires at least m distinct replying nodes, including the leader. C2 requires at least d distinct recoverable shards after removing any f replying nodes, with d=m for the balanced family. Majority intersection preserves the voting argument; the second condition preserves payload availability after the allowed crashes. These are different obligations. C2 alone does not prove preservation of the chosen value across changing ballots and assignments, and neither condition promises termination in an arbitrary asynchronous execution. [Evidence: Q4, §3.3 complete derivation and Figure 4, PDF pp.5–5; Q7, §3.6 complete protocol changes, PDF pp.7–7; Q28, Appendix A PreparedConditionAndCommand, PDF pp.22–23; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Balanced round-robin policies assign c consecutive shard indices to each node, wrapping around the n indices, with 1≤c≤m. The derived valid region is n≥q≥m and q+c≥n+1; the candidate performance boundary is q+c=n+1. For n=5,m=3,f=2, its three choices are (c,q)=(1,5),(2,4),(3,3). Full replication and single-shard coding become endpoints of one family. Section 3.2’s written range s through s+c would contain c+1 shards if both endpoints were included; the figures and Appendix A’s upper endpoint ShardToIdx[r]+na−1 establish the intended c-shard interpretation. Figure 2 gives the motivating failure: with single shards and q=4, crashing the leader and another accepting node leaves only two shards, below the three needed. The paper's RSPaxos/CRaft comparisons commonly use f=1, whereas Crossword retains f=2. Their throughput comparisons therefore include different availability guarantees, which the graphs label. [Evidence: Q2, §2.4 failure example, Figure 2, PDF pp.3–3; Q3, §3.1–3.2 assignments and Figure 3, PDF pp.4–5; Q4, §3.3 complete derivation and Figure 4, PDF pp.5–5; Q5, §3.4 tradeoff, PDF pp.6–6; literal spans in quotes.json.]  One printed intermediate bound needs a saturation qualification. The paper writes SubCover(ap,f)≥q−f+c−1, but shard coverage cannot exceed n. Reader example: n=5,q=5,c=3,f=0 gives a right side of seven although only five distinct shards exist. The round-robin lower bound should be capped by n. The later threshold test against m≤n, including q+c≥n+1 at f=n−m, is unaffected. This is arithmetic about the displayed derivation, not an implementation finding. [Evidence: Q4, §3.3 complete derivation and Figure 4, PDF pp.5–5; literal spans in quotes.json.]  ## Protocol, adaptation and concrete cases  Each Accept message carries the chosen per-instance assignment; recipients persist their assigned bytes before acknowledging. On failover, a majority Prepare exchange preserves a reconstructible highest-ballot value; the paper permits replacing it with a new command if fewer than d shards of that value can be recovered. The appendix selects a maximum-ballot command and combines reported shards for that command, including matches at other ballots. A complete correctness argument must connect that rule to chosen-value preservation over all earlier ballots, not just count surviving shards in one acceptance pattern. This reading identifies that proof obligation without claiming a counterexample. [Evidence: Q3, §3.1–3.2 assignments and Figure 3, PDF pp.4–5; Q7, §3.6 complete protocol changes, PDF pp.7–7; Q28, Appendix A PreparedConditionAndCommand, PDF pp.22–23; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Figure 5 distinguishes committed-but-partial data from committed-and-known data and execution. Followers periodically request missing shards from peers; reconstructed shards are memory-only. Requests are batched about every 20 ms and normally exclude the last 400 KB of accumulated payloads. A peer without a reconstruction reply for ten cycles is skipped. A new leader reconstructs its partial tail synchronously. Low-traffic tails, retrying skipped peers, eventual delivery and leader recovery consequently matter to progress; the text provides mechanisms and experiments rather than a temporal proof covering them. [Evidence: Q6, §3.5 gossip and Figure 5, PDF pp.6–7; Q10, §4.2 gossip details and Figure 6, PDF pp.8–8; Q11, §4.3 heartbeats, snapshots and leases, PDF pp.8–8; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The default chooser fits per-follower response time t_s(v)=d_s+v/b_s from a two-second sliding window, updates every 200 ms, and discards the slowest five percent of observations. It considers balanced assignments and uses the (q−1)th smallest follower response-time estimate, because the leader already counts toward q. The stated limitations are no automated unbalanced search and no reaction to fluctuations shorter than roughly one second. Heartbeats and random 300–600 ms election timeouts track failures; the healthy-node count limits q. The CockroachDB integration instead uses payload thresholds, not this regression chooser. [Evidence: Q8, §4 implementation and Gazette/CockroachDB, PDF pp.7–7; Q9, §4.1 complete regression chooser and limitations, PDF pp.7–8; Q11, §4.3 heartbeats, snapshots and leases, PDF pp.8–8; literal spans in quotes.json.]  A concrete source inconsistency occurs in §4.1, PDF p.8: the chooser evaluates t_s(v_p/c). Each of c assigned shards actually has v_p/m bytes, so the bytes per recipient are c·v_p/m. With n=5,m=3, c=1 sends v_p/3 but the printed expression predicts v_p; c=3 sends v_p but predicts v_p/3. Thus the printed expression reverses the size trend. It should not be used as the specification of an implementation without resolving the mismatch. No repository revision was inspected, so this is not a claim about executed code or the validity of measured results. [Evidence: Q3, §3.1–3.2 assignments and Figure 3, PDF pp.4–5; Q9, §4.1 complete regression chooser and limitations, PDF pp.7–8; literal spans in quotes.json.]  ## Implementations and measured evidence  Gazette is async Rust/Tokio with channels. The paper lists 12.7k infrastructure lines and six implementations: Chain Replication 1.1k, MultiPaxos 2.3k, Raft 2.3k, RSPaxos 2.5k, CRaft 2.6k and Crossword 3.4k. It reports “extensive unit tests and fuzz tests” but gives no counts, fault schedules or coverage. The Go prototype modifies CockroachDB v24.3.0a by approximately 1.6k lines. Those listed amounts total 26.9k lines, slightly below §1’s “a sum of 27.3k lines of async Rust”; the paper does not reconcile the counting scope. The paper promises to open-source the code; this reading establishes no repository version or reproduction. [Evidence: Q8, §4 implementation and Gazette/CockroachDB, PDF pp.7–7; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Gazette experiments use CloudLab c220g2 hosts, 40 cores, 160 GB RAM and Linux 6.1.64. The regional setting has 1 Gbps links and 4 ms average delay; the wide-area setting spans CloudLab datacenters with about 200 Mbps and 30 ms average delay. Clients share hosts with servers but use disjoint pinned cores; batching is one millisecond. Default static tests have five servers and fifteen closed-loop clients. Requests are half lease-local Gets and half Puts, with eight-byte keys and small, 128 KB or mixed payloads whose normal distributions have ten percent standard deviation. Reported throughput includes reads; latency curves show means and arrows mark P95, not confidence intervals. [Evidence: Q12, §5 evaluation questions and §5.1 setup, PDF pp.8–9; Q13, §5.1 Figure 7 complete static comparisons, PDF pp.9–9; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Figures 7–9 report that Crossword follows the favorable endpoint across small, large and mixed data: up to 1.9× coded-protocol throughput for small data, 2× MultiPaxos for large data, and 2.1× alternatives in the mixed workload. Figure 8 varies payload means from 8 B to 256 KB, replica counts 3/5/7/9 and write shares 10/50/100%; at ≥64 KB, the chosen c=1,q=5 case exceeds MultiPaxos throughput by four times in the plotted setting. Figure 8’s cluster-size/Put-share sensitivity reports “up to 2.3x over MultiPaxos” and 1.4× over RSPaxos in its tested settings. These are workload-specific ratios, not universal bounds. At 64 KB Figure 9 reports 71% less critical-path data-transfer/WAL time and logs of 913 MB versus 1,467 MB, a reader-calculated 37.76% storage reduction. [Evidence: Q13, §5.1 Figure 7 complete static comparisons, PDF pp.9–9; Q14, §5.1–5.2 Figures 8–9 and storage/critical-path measurements, PDF pp.9–10; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Figure 10 changes conditions about fifteen seconds apart: payload size 64→4 KB, bandwidth 1 Gbps→100 Mbps→1 Gbps, and then two replicas with tenfold worse delay and bandwidth. Throughput is sampled once per second. Adaptation is shown by time traces, not a regret or convergence guarantee. Figure 11 crashes leaders at 15 and 55 seconds, uses a special 1.5-second timeout and disables snapshots. Crossword's first recovery gap is about twice classic protocols' gap because of tail reconstruction; afterward it selects c=2,q=4. RSPaxos becomes unavailable after the second crash, whereas CRaft completes its fallback before it. These particular separated failures do not test every crash spacing. [Evidence: Q15, §5.2 Figure 10 adaptation measurements, PDF pp.10–10; Q16, §5.3 Figure 11 crash measurements, PDF pp.10–11; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Figure 12 manually chooses an unbalanced assignment for follower links of 1/1/0.4/0.1 Gbps, using the (8,5) codeword example with 5/5/3/1 assigned shards. It obtains roughly 1.4× MultiPaxos or balanced Crossword throughput. Automated unbalanced adaptation remains future work. Figure 13 forces c=1 and compares 0/400/800 KB deferral gaps at 3/10/100 ms write intervals, measuring follower version distance from the leader. Section 5.5 says, “The replies are not linearizable but sequentially consistent,” followed by “possibly stale versions in the history”. This is evidence about staleness, not a history-based proof of the text's sequential-consistency claim. Figure 14, at fixed throughput, reports 13% less follower-to-follower bandwidth from batching; it moves two-thirds of payload replication to that background path. The 13% is not a reduction of all network traffic. [Evidence: Q17, §5.4 Figure 12 unbalanced assignment, PDF pp.10–11; Q18, §5.5 Figures 13–14 staleness and gossip traffic, PDF pp.10–11; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Figure 15 uses YCSB-A key popularity on 1,000 keys, but all requests are Puts with a TiDB-derived size distribution. Five partitions rotate leaders over the same five regional servers. Crossword's peak throughput exceeds MultiPaxos but falls below RSPaxos and CRaft, which omit its background gossip. Chain Replication has the highest unsaturated latency from chain propagation and does not reach its throughput limit over the plotted load range. This experiment tests shared follower bandwidth, not the usual half-read YCSB-A operation mix. [Evidence: Q19, §5.6 Figure 15 partitioned-store experiment, PDF pp.11–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The CockroachDB TPC-C experiment uses twelve nodes, 200 warehouses, five replicas per range and 400 workers. It disables leader/leaseholder rebalancing and write pipelining. The chooser uses two shards above 4 KB and one above 8 KB. Aggregate throughput is 2,520 tps for vanilla, 3,330 for Crossword and 2,450 for an always-one-shard variant; reader arithmetic gives 32.14% gain over vanilla. The reported “up to 44%” refers to transaction-specific speedup. Table 1 separately measures RS(5,3) coding on 32 cores with SIMD: 4/16/64/256 KB and 1/4 MB take 1/4/16/77 μs and 1/6 ms; reported per-request leader CPU overhead is about 1.24–1.26%, with reported memory 1.6 KB through 1.6 MB. These costs have a different measurement denominator from throughput ratios. Repetition counts, warm-up and confidence intervals are not reported; the dynamic plots show their trace duration. [Evidence: Q20, §5.7 Figure 16 CockroachDB experiment, PDF pp.11–12; Q21, §5.8 Table 1 coding overhead, PDF pp.11–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]  ## What the formal appendix actually checks  Appendix A reports three replicas, at most one failure, two ballots, three requests and both balanced choices over three shards with two data shards. The supplied configuration specifically has three writes, no reads, CommitNoticeOn=FALSE and NodeFailuresOn, replica/write symmetry, TypeOK and Linearizability invariants, and deadlock checking. It gives no TLC version, explored-state counts, timing or run log. “These inputs should be large enough to explore all the distinct, interesting execution paths of the protocol” is the authors' belief; no parameterized theorem justifies it. In particular, three nodes cannot instantiate the interior five-node policy c=2,q=4 or the unbalanced example. [Evidence: Q24, Appendix A model-check report and explicit finite scope, PDF pp.19–19; Q27, Appendix A coverage and valid round-robin assignments, PDF pp.21–22; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The PlusCal model represents shard identifiers, abstract command values and votes. It does not encode Reed–Solomon byte algebra, disk operations, the Rust or Go program, gossip/reconstruction messages, the chooser, leases, snapshots or reconfiguration. The single rloop label makes the macros atomic transitions; messages accumulate in a set. Nodes fail permanently. ReplicaCrashes additionally requires balMaxKnown<MaxBallot, suppressing crashes after learning the maximum modeled ballot: “∧node[r].balMaxKnown < MaxBallot” (Appendix A, PDF p.28). This is an explicit state-space restriction, not the protocol's ordinary fail-stop rule. [Evidence: Q25, Appendix A constants, assumptions and state types, PDF pp.20–21; Q27, Appendix A coverage and valid round-robin assignments, PDF pp.21–22; Q29, Appendix A message types and commitment condition, PDF pp.22–24; Q35, Appendix A remaining process and MC definitions, PDF pp.29–29; Q34, Appendix A crash guard and process loop, PDF pp.28–29; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The model's Linearizability predicate is conditional: “terminated ⇒” a complete order exists that respects observed real-time precedence and old values. Terminated means no pending requests and all requests acknowledged. Therefore the checked expression constrains fully completed runs; arbitrary incomplete finite histories are not checked by that expression. Writes return their old value, so the all-write model still has meaningful observable ordering constraints, but it does not exercise read operations or leased local reads. Request identities are unique, admission picks the first unseen pending command, and InitPending fixes writes before reads under a stated W.L.O.G. reduction. Its comment says, “all other cases are either symmetric or less useful” (Appendix A, PDF p.21). No theorem establishes that reduction for a larger mixed workload. [Evidence: Q26, Appendix A initial request order and server states, PDF pp.21–21; Q30, Appendix A main state, termination and observation helpers, PDF pp.24–24; Q32, Appendix A complete new-request and Accept handling, PDF pp.26–27; Q36, Appendix A complete observable-order predicate, PDF pp.30–30; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]  No fairness condition or eventual-completion temporal property is supplied. CHECK_DEADLOCK tests the absence of an enabled next step under TLC's deadlock semantics; it is not a proof that every admissible execution eventually completes. With CommitNoticeOn=FALSE, the loop can select a branch whose conditional body does nothing while a node remains live, illustrating why a no-progress execution need not be a deadlock. The displayed theorem statements have no TLAPS proof. Thus the author's “fault-tolerance” report must be read together with the configured invariant, finite crash restriction and deadlock check, rather than promoted to unbounded liveness. [Evidence: Q34, Appendix A crash guard and process loop, PDF pp.28–29; Q35, Appendix A remaining process and MC definitions, PDF pp.29–29; Q36, Appendix A complete observable-order predicate, PDF pp.30–30; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Two further model-to-design obligations are concrete. TakeNewRequest puts all Shards in the leader's voted.shards while its own AcceptReply records only assign[r]; the prose persists only assigned shards but expressly keeps the complete codeword in leader memory. Since failures are fail-stop with no restart, the abstract full-shard knowledge is consistent with a live leader’s memory. A refinement must explain that knowledge and its lifetime; this difference does not establish a crash-recovery durability counterexample. CommitNotice has only an index, no ballot or origin, and its handler applies a local command without shard reconstruction; the supplied configuration disables that handler. These are source differences and missing coverage, not checked exploit traces. The prepared-value fallback also spells a field “shard” rather than “shards”; HandlePrepareReplies awaits exam[s].prepared for every slot before reading shards, so that false-prepared branch alone does not establish a missing-field failure. No translator was run. The handler also overwrites cmd/shards while preserving a Committed status and sends its own reply before its voted record is updated by any later self-Accept. Chosen-value preservation and consistent self-voting must justify those intermediate states; no reachable counterexample is established. [Evidence: Q3, §3.1–3.2 assignments and Figure 3, PDF pp.4–5; Q28, Appendix A PreparedConditionAndCommand, PDF pp.22–23; Q29, Appendix A message types and commitment condition, PDF pp.22–24; Q32, Appendix A complete new-request and Accept handling, PDF pp.26–27; Q33, Appendix A commit and CommitNotice handlers, PDF pp.27–28; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]  ## Contribution to the human's topic  For distributed verification, this is a useful case separating voting intersection from durable data reconstructibility while policies change per instance. A proof would need cross-ballot chosen-value preservation, shard-survival and data-known/executed invariants, plus explicit assumptions for eventual gossip and failover. TLA+ can express the distributed contracts; Verus could connect assignment bitmaps, persistence-before-ack and reconstruction to Rust execution. Those are reader-proposed next steps, not supplied proofs. The static chooser mismatch gives a precise specification-to-code question. [Evidence: Q4, §3.3 complete derivation and Figure 4, PDF pp.5–5; Q7, §3.6 complete protocol changes, PDF pp.7–7; Q9, §4.1 complete regression chooser and limitations, PDF pp.7–8; Q8, §4 implementation and Gazette/CockroachDB, PDF pp.7–7; literal spans in quotes.json.]  For evaluating LLM-generated specifications or proofs, the artifact offers concrete scope checks: whether an agent notices the all-write/CommitNoticeOn=FALSE configuration, completed-run predicate, ballot-dependent crash restriction, atomic actions, idealized shards and leader-knowledge abstraction. A convincing generated proof would have to state which model and which property it proves and show the link to implementation. The paper makes no claim of LLM-generated specifications, proofs or evaluation, and references Verus only as related verification work. Its strongest contribution here is a nontrivial Rust systems case with a published finite specification and measurable adaptation, together with explicit gaps a later proof effort must close. [Evidence: Q22, §6 discussion and §7 conclusion, PDF pp.12–13; Q24, Appendix A model-check report and explicit finite scope, PDF pp.19–19; Q32, Appendix A complete new-request and Accept handling, PDF pp.26–27; Q34, Appendix A crash guard and process loop, PDF pp.28–29; Q36, Appendix A complete observable-order predicate, PDF pp.30–30; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]
    - limits: Odd n, fail-stop, asynchronous network; majority m=ceil(n/2), f=n−m; balanced RS(n,m), c consecutive wrapped shards, q+c≥n+1. Durable assigned shards before ack. Bounded clock drift separately assumed for read leases. Printed chooser uses inverse shard count instead of assigned bytes; intermediate coverage bound needs saturation; cross-ballot preservation proof obligation; finite formal scope/reductions/crash restriction/completed-run predicate; leader-knowledge abstraction requires refinement; disabled commit notices; no Rust refinement; heterogeneous policies manual; <1s fluctuations outside chooser scope; f1 baselines differ; staleness not a consistency proof. Prose RR interval endpoint differs from intended c-shard range; listed line counts total26.9k versus headline27.3k; prepared-state overwrite/self-vote obligations remain conditional static observations.

- Extended threshold automata (2025)
    - title: Parameterized Verification of Round-Based Distributed Algorithms via Extended Threshold Automata.
    - what: Extends threshold automata with decrements and resets of shared variables, develops sound and complete semi-decision procedures for general coverability and reachability, and evaluates an implementation on fault-tolerant distributed algorithm models. The counter-system model retains arbitrary process counts satisfying a linear-arithmetic resilience condition. Parametric intervals abstract shared counters; an abstract counter system leaves location counts unbounded. Lemmas 1–2 relate concrete paths to non-spurious abstract paths using quantifier-free linear-integer constraints, including acceleration multiplicities. Lemmas 3–4 establish a well-structured system with effective predecessor bases. Algorithm 1 must preserve transitions from subsumed states to enumerate all abstract error paths, because one spurious path cannot settle verification. Corollary 2 and Lemma 5 give soundness/completeness; Theorem 1 proves termination for nonnegative updates without resets. A second abstraction keeps only occupied/empty location bits, allowing zero tests in reachability specifications; PRA implements this symbolically. General coverability can express two leaders at the same location, whereas ordinary positive-location coverability cannot. Experiments reveal the narrower scope of the phase-king and full Red Belly results than the abstract suggests.
    - number: PRA vs ByMC: bosco validity 0.73s vs 42.22s; cf1s validity 0.42s vs 380.81s
    - number: c1cs 0.23s, RB 1.03s, RB-Simpl 61.77s with ByMC timing out at 1.5h
    - number: PRA slower on nbacg 0.36s vs 0.18s and RB-bc 0.49s vs 0.32s
    - number: multiR-floodMin 0.3s; multiR-RelBrd 0.1s; multiR-RB-Simpl 6859s; multiR-RB timeout at 2h
    - limits: Results concern threshold-automaton models, not executable protocol code. Finite local locations/shared-variable sets, nonnegative counter values, parameter-linear threshold guards, and linear-integer resilience conditions are assumed; the standard example is n > 3t and t >= f with n-f modeled correct processes. All possible finite orders of parametric thresholds must be considered. Abstract transitions can be spurious and require SMT concretization. The extended model is undecidable; error-path unfolding can diverge on cycles containing decrements/resets. Termination holds for monotone increments/no resets, acyclic error graphs, or cycles without decrements/resets. Detailed formal proofs are referred to the extended version, rather than machine-checked proof artifacts here. Evaluated properties are selected safety/reachability properties, not full liveness or implementation refinement. Full multi-round Red Belly times out; phase-king validation is partial correctness and a bug in an incorrect model.

- Model Checking and Synthesis for Optimal Use of Knowledge in Consensus Protocols (2025)
    - what: # Model Checking and Synthesis for Optimal Use of Knowledge in Consensus Protocols (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Alpturer, Huang and van der Meyden use MCK to check whether small synchronous consensus protocols decide as soon as their available information permits, and synthesize concrete decision predicates from knowledge-based programs. The contribution is empirical and methodological. They “do not attempt to give a full characterization or a proof” of general optimality (§1, p.3, Q3). The 22-page arXiv 2505.02353v1 is the full version of the PODC 2025 paper, ACM pp.131–140, DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733552 (Q37; saved arXiv metadata). No new parameterized proof or new synthesis engine is presented.  ## Assumptions and specification (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The system has synchronous message rounds and two layers: an information exchange defines observed state, messages and updates; a decision protocol chooses noop or a decision. Failures are crashes or sending omissions. A crashing agent can send an arbitrary subset of its messages in the crash round and then sends nothing; an omission-faulty agent can omit sends but receives messages sent to it (§3, pp.5–6, Q6–Q7). “Byzantine Agreement” names the coordination problem here; the experiments do not evaluate arbitrary malicious message values, asynchronous scheduling or a cryptographic implementation.  The base simultaneous agreement specification requires at most one decision per agent, agreement at the same time among nonfaulty agents, and a decision value initially held by some agent, possibly faulty. The paper explicitly says “termination is not a requirement of this specification,” while reporting additional termination checks in its scripts (§4, p.6, Q8). Eventual agreement permits different decision times (§8, Q20). These distinctions matter when calling a synthesized result correct.  Optimality is relative to the same information exchange and failure model, comparing runs with identical initial preferences and failure patterns (§4, p.7, Q9). The paper distinguishes an optimum protocol, which decides no later than every competitor, from an optimal protocol, which no competitor systematically improves. This is not optimality across arbitrary messaging designs or execution costs. The semantic order as printed compares every agent; this record does not silently narrow its quantifier to nonfaulty agents.  MCK uses finite variables and ordered binary decision diagrams. The chosen clock semantics gives an agent its current observable variables plus the time, rather than perfect recall. Synthesis replaces boolean template variables with local predicates equivalent to knowledge tests (§6, pp.8–9, Q11–Q12). Uniqueness under clock semantics and the optimality characterizations are attributed to prior theory, not proved anew. EBA’s simpler knowledge-based program P0 also requires technical side conditions on information exchange: learning 0 through decision-message chains and suitable possibilities involving nonfaulty agents (§8, pp.11–12, Q20).  ## Concrete cases and results (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Four SBA information exchanges are modeled: FloodSet, FloodSet plus current received-message count, the Count variant plus previous count (“Diff”), and the concrete Dwork–Moses protocol. Two EBA exchanges, Emin and Ebasic, respectively send decision values and additionally send initial 1 messages with a count. The models have parameters n agents, t maximum failures and the decision-value set. The main FloodSet/Count timing table fixes two values (§§7–11, Q13–Q28).  FloodSet retains values seen and broadcasts their union. The naive earliest-knowledge hypothesis t+1 fails at n=3,t=2. Revised Eq 2 uses time=n−1 when t≥n−1, otherwise t+1; model checking and synthesis agree in the instances checked (§7.1, pp.9–10, Q14–Q15). The authors report an all-n proof in companion work [7]; this read does not include that proof (Q17). Adding the current message count exposes the early condition count≤1, meaning only the agent’s own message was received (§7.2, Q16). Diff gave no stronger SBA stopping condition than Count in checked cases, although previous-count memory can help a different EBA specification (§7.3, Q18).  The printed Count formula needs reconciliation at a boundary. Eq 3 uses “time = t” in its t≥n−1 branch (§7.2, p.10, Q16), whereas FloodSet Eq 2 uses time=n−1 (Q14). At n=3,t=3,time=2,count=3, Eq 2 is true and Eq 3 false. Count adds an observation while retaining FloodSet’s values and clock; its stated earliest condition should not require later knowledge on that account. No-crash histories allow count 3 even when t=3 is the failure upper bound. This is a reader-derived discrepancy in the printed conditions, not a replayed MCK counterexample or a refutation of the companion theorem. The benchmark inputs needed to resolve it were not obtained. The source’s formulas are retained unchanged in Q14/Q16 and static-witnesses.json.  There is a second printed EBA ambiguity. Ebasic’s jd update stores 0 on receiving 0 and otherwise ⊥, but its decision 1 rule includes “jd𝑖 = 1” (§9.2, pp.12–13, Q22). Under that update description the jd=1 branch cannot be reached. I have not silently repaired the update or inferred which rule the actual model used.  Appendix A gives a complete FloodSet synthesis example for n=3,t=1,two values. It uses finite time 0..3, communicates while time<2 and has four decision templates for knowledge times 1 and 2 (pp.18–21, Q32–Q35). The reported output makes both time 1 predicates false; at time 2 the predicate for v is values_received[v], with 0 taking priority in the decision code. The authors report that the accompanying formulas all hold (p.22, Q36). State at time m means information after round m; the decision follows in the next modeled round (§7, Q13). This accounts for the appendix’s AX3 completion check.  The appendix checks ordinary and uniform agreement, validity and termination at AX3, and knowledge predicates. Its printed agreement formulas compare values when both agents have decided; they do not explicitly require simultaneous decided flags (Q34). Thus the displayed formulas alone are not a direct check of every SBA clause. The knowledge-based theory may establish simultaneity; no counterexample to the synthesized protocol is claimed. Likewise the finite AX3 termination check is not a general unbounded liveness proof. The appendix uses currently ALIVE agents in knowledge tests, which should not be casually substituted for permanently nonfaulty agents without the cited crash-theory correspondence.  ## Evaluation and limits (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The experiments used one core of a 3.7 GHz six-core Intel Core i5 with 256 KB L2, 9 MB L3 and 32 GB memory. The final run’s timeout was 10 minutes (§10, p.13, Q23). Early exploratory trials sometimes ran 5 hours or 2 days; those are not the table timeout. No MCK build/version, BDD variable ordering, repetition count, variance, raw trial set or memory measurements are supplied. The measured costs are model-checking and synthesis runtime, not consensus latency or deployment throughput.  All three timing tables are transcribed with printed values and converted seconds in numeric-evidence.json: 16 parameter rows in Table 1, 15 in Table 2 and 6 in Table 3, totaling 118 timing cells. TO remains a timeout rather than a measured 600-second completion. Representative results show the steep scaling:  - FloodSet at n=5,t=2: checking 34.635 seconds, synthesis 162.015 seconds; synthesis times out at n=5,t≥3. Checking still finishes at n=6,t=1 in 72.863 seconds, while n=6,t=2 times out (Table 1, Q24) - Count at n=4,t=2: checking 23.328 seconds, synthesis 120.892 seconds; synthesis times out for t=3/4 and both tasks time out at n=5 in the listed rows (Table 1) - Diff at n=3 takes roughly 258–304 seconds depending on failure bound/rounds; Dwork–Moses times out for every listed n=3 case. Both time out at n=4,t=1,one round (Table 2, Q26) - Emin EBA synthesis succeeds through the listed n=3 cases, with crash costs 31.219–178.142 seconds and omission costs 11.371–66.735 seconds. Every n=4,t=1 cell times out. Ebasic succeeds only at n=2 in Table 3 (Q28)  Table 3’s prose says Emin scales to 4 agents before blowup, then names Emin again for the worse count-containing model. The table has no successful 4-agent row, and §9.2 attributes the extra count to Ebasic. This record preserves the cells and flags the prose ambiguity instead of recording 4-agent success or swapping labels without evidence. Receiving/general omissions are reported to have similar successful cases, but no separate timing rows are provided (§11, Q28).  For comparison, the authors report 125 seconds for purely temporal SAT-based SBA checking of Dwork–Moses at n=5,t=4 (§13, p.16, Q30). This checks a different obligation with a different algorithm from the BDD epistemic runs, so it is not a like-for-like solver speedup. They suggest quadratic messages and BDD size explain the difficulty; the paper does not measure a causal ablation. Their conclusion is appropriately limited: “a manual proof of correctness and optimality will” still be needed for all numbers of agents and failures (Q30).  ## Contribution to the requested topic and evidence scope (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  This adds concrete epistemic verification and protocol-synthesis benchmarks for distributed consensus, including examples where stronger local observations permit earlier decisions but make automated analysis harder. It supports a workflow of synthesizing small instances, checking hypotheses on larger finite instances, then proving the general claim manually. That workflow is the authors’ proposal; this paper does not demonstrate LLM agents. There is no Verus or verified Rust experiment. Appendix A calls its nondeterministic transition construct “refinement calculus/TLA action style” (Q33); it does not report TLA+/TLC verification.  For LLM-generated specifications and proofs, I infer evaluation lessons from the record: state the failure and information-exchange scope, declare observation/recall semantics, distinguish agreement from simultaneous agreement, inspect every printed guard and boundary case, separate finite checking from general proofs, and retain timeouts and source/script mismatches. These are reader-derived lessons, not measured LLM results.  Read every one of 1099 layout-text lines, all 22 pages, all 39 references and the complete appendix input/output. Inspected 11 contact sheets and fullsize pages 10,13–15,19–22; the paper has three tables and no figures. The bundle retains 44 literal excerpts with line/character/page anchors, 19 diagnostics, all 37 timing rows and raw hashes. Local/official PDFs are byte-identical. The paper identifies no benchmark archive/repository link. The primary MCK site links a related consensus demonstration. I read its page/loader and all 551 logical lines (550 newline characters) of four static source scripts: FloodSet, optimized FloodSet, Count and Dwork–Moses. They are pinned by content hashes and fetch times; no direct association with the paper’s benchmark version was established. The demo FloodSet/Count scripts read and update w in place, allowing later senders to forward values received earlier in the same round; Appendix A instead snapshots old_w before delivery. Demo FloodSet crash delivery is also selected per value. These differences prevent treating the demos as interchangeable benchmark inputs or evidence against the paper’s reported results (Q38–Q44, D19). No demo Verify action or stored .result output was invoked or loaded. Two MCK subpage links returned 404 and were not retried within five minutes. No author code, compiler, model checker, prover or solver was executed; no serialized scientific/model/results data were loaded. Reported checks and synthesis outputs are statically inspected author results, not independent reproductions.
    - limits: Synchronous rounds, crash or sending omissions, and finite MCK clock semantics using current observations and time. Optimality is relative to a fixed information exchange and failure model. Base SBA omits termination. EBA P0 requires technical information-exchange side conditions. The paper checks finite instances and supplies no all-n proof. Count Eq. 3, the Ebasic jd update and Table 3 prose have unresolved printed discrepancies; the appendix lacks an explicit simultaneity formula. Related static demo models differ from the appendix; the exact benchmark revision and independent reproduction are unavailable.

- PoWER (2025)
    - title: PoWER Never Corrupts: Tool-Agnostic Verification of Crash Consistency and Corruption Detection
    - what: PoWER encodes crash consistency as a precondition on each storage write: every durable state introduced by a partial write must be permitted by a ghost permission. Prophecy-based storage views and recovery-equivalent writes simplify proofs. A bounded-bit corruption model and an eight-byte corruption-detecting Boolean support atomic data/checksum updates. CapybaraKV in Verus and CapybaraNS in Dafny demonstrate the method, with coarse concurrent KV variants and performance comparisons. Records exact permission quantification, prophecy flush semantics, state versus transition and blanket versus single-use permissions, all four write strategies and concurrency restrictions. Includes correspondence-proof trust boundaries, CRC corruption bounds, Tick-Tock counterexample and CDB protocol, full type/LOC/startup/resource tables, all workload setups and adverse performance cases. Separates conditional detection from arbitrary-media-error recovery and reported proofs from independent proof replay.
    - number: CapybaraKV 5,531 executable / 14,255 spec+proof / 5,244 trusted lines; CapybaraNS 278 / 673 / 414
    - number: verification 54 s single-thread, 23 s eight-thread for KV, 12 s for NS
    - number: Table 2 KV total: 5244 trusted, 14255 spec/proof, 5531 implementation lines; notary 414/673/278
    - limits: Core technique requires Hoare pre/postconditions, ghost variables and quantification over crash states. Each asynchronous write requires all chunk-wise old/new durable outcomes to satisfy its permission; executable annotations erase. Soundness depends on every actual storage mutation using the controlled API, correctness of the storage model and a meaningful allowed-recovery predicate. A permission that allows all states proves no useful crash property. Natural storage semantics distinguish readable last-written bytes from outstanding writes. Atomic persistence chunks can survive independently until flush. The prophecy model instead stores read_state and one prophesized durable_state; write updates all readable bytes and chooses a subset of chunk subwrites for durable state. Flush constrains these two states to agree without changing either in the ghost model. This is a logical modeling device, not a runtime ability to predict crash outcomes. The authors report a Verus proof implementing the prophecy model over a natural model using prophecy variables. The PoWER-to-Crash-Hoare-logic proof in Rocq/Perennial is metalogical and trusts a translation of PoWER semantics, since PoWER was not implemented in Rocq. The Verus correspondence to crash invariants is entirely machine-checked within Verus. Formal theorem bodies are in artifacts; this reading examined paper explanations only. Crash states can be specified through rec(bytes), commonly allowing pre-operation or post-operation abstract state. Transition permissions instead authorize pairs of durable states. Blanket permissions cover arbitrary recovery-equivalent transitions; single-use permissions authorize a mutating transition once and are consumed or invalidated. A blanket permission can manufacture single-use permissions only for its allowed transitions. Initial recoverability and all permission constructions remain proof obligations. Tentative writes change only addresses irrelevant to rec and need no value-specific proof. Committing writes are a single aligned atomic chunk, typically after flushing tentative data, so only old/new durable states matter. Recovery writes rely on idempotent recovery that overwrites all possibly torn bytes on retry. In-place writes can use weaker specifications with many allowed outcomes, but the authors have no verified examples or helper-library support for that category. Atomic PoWER adds durable ghost resources owned by atomic invariants, proof callbacks and completion objects for consumed transition permissions. Completions witness an issued/applied operation even if another thread later changes its key. This extension needs concurrency facilities beyond the minimal core features; a tool-agnostic core does not imply arbitrary concurrent proofs in plain sequential Dafny. Concurrency allows multiple readers, or disjoint statically allocated storage regions with exclusive access during writes. It excludes read/write or write/write overlap within one region because callers must know its current logical state. Sharded wrappers establish linearizable individual create/read/update/delete/list operations, not cross-shard transactions. The reusable inner implementation still supplies a transactional API to wrappers. Corruption is modeled by a fixed device bitmask with at most c potentially faulty physical bits. A zero mask bit reads correctly; a marked bit can return either value independently on each read. The trusted CRC axiom distinguishes byte strings at Hamming distance 1 through c. Current ECMA CRC-64 implementation uses c=1 for arbitrary lengths; the cited c=3 for data shorter than about1 GiB is not exploited. Detection is conditional on that device-wide bound, not a guarantee against arbitrary bursts, malicious rewrites, rollback or unbounded media failure. Reader qualification: integrity proofs must cover corrupted data and checksum bytes, repeated/noncontiguous address mappings, and the chosen CDB codeword distance under the same physical-bit bound. The paper reports verified checking and a trusted CRC library; it does not derive an unrestricted cryptographic collision-resistance guarantee. Detecting a mismatch permits reporting corruption, not necessarily repairing damage or preserving availability. Tick-Tock’s old-checksum/new-data mismatch after a crash is not a small-bit corruption event relative to the old data. CRC(D0) can collide with CRC(D1-prime) even if D1-prime differs by only bounded media corruption from D1, because D0 versus D1-prime may differ arbitrarily. The paper gives a logical counterexample to the algorithm in its model, not an independently reproduced NOVA-Fortis artifact exploit. CDB stores one of two known eight-byte values CRC(0) and CRC(1), with aligned crash atomicity and sufficient corruption separation assumed/proved for the primitive. Two data/CRC slots accompany it. Write the inactive slot and checksum, flush, atomically switch CDB, flush. The selector identifies the committed slot independently of potentially matching stale checksums. This costs extra storage and flushes; it does not remove hardware atomicity assumptions. CapybaraKV values contain a fixed-size item and a list of fixed-size elements, with fixed-size keys. The abstract state has on-abort and on-commit maps. Ordinary operations affect the latter; abort restores it from the former; commit publishes it to the former. A crash during commit may commit or abort, while other uncommitted operations abort. Reads within a transaction see tentative operations, so visible results need not already be durable. Implementation uses main/item/list tables, per-field CRCs, validity CDBs, copy-on-write updates and a physical redo journal. Journal commit writes a CRC of pending entries then flips a CDB; replay installs operations and clears the journal. Volatile key index and free lists rebuild on startup. Correctness depends on recovery traversal, bounds, allocation and CRC checks, not merely the commit selector. Capacity is statically allocated at initialization with maximum key/item/list counts and sizes. No dynamic resizing, partial-value updates or range queries. All keys reside in a volatile Rust HashMap and must be indexed again at startup. Designed target is small records on tens of GiB of dedicated PM in a cloud-storage service. Prototype integration into an Azure Rust system is reported, not evidence of production deployment of all verified variants. Trusted pmcopy bridges Verus and compiler-generated representations. It requires repr(C) and derive(PmCopy), implements PmSafe/PmSized/Clone/PartialEq, generates specifications and static layout assertions checked by Rust. PmSafe includes numeric types, bool and char; composites require safe fields. Casts still require correct layout, valid discriminants/values and prior corruption checks. Compiler assertions caught a u128/i128 layout change; this is a concrete consistency check, not a proof of the macro or compiler. CapybaraNS stores a 64-bit logical timestamp and last hash. Advance increments and atomically persists them using CDB; Sign signs their binding. A trusted C# wrapper supplies CRCs, cryptography and serialization. This paper does not supply a complete distributed-notary protocol, a cryptographic implementation proof, remote attestation argument or availability theorem. Counter overflow handling and full security assumptions require the external specification. PM model permits independent eight-byte chunk reorderings until flush; backend write uses PMDK non-temporal stores or mov followed by clflushopt/clwb, and flush uses sfence. It deliberately overapproximates strongly ordered clflush and same-cache-line hardware ordering, including potential compiler reorderings. Eight-byte alignment/atomicity, backend calls and hardware behavior remain trusted. PoWER can use other models; current model is not a universal storage-device specification. Table 2 counts unverified pmcopy source but not its generated code. KV trusted count includes mock byte-vector PM plus Windows/Linux backends, concurrency and sharding wrappers. Trusted versus proved LOC therefore should not be interpreted as executable core size alone. Reported proof/code ratios are2.6 KV and2.4 NS; LOC is not a measure of specification adequacy. KV design, implementation and verification took about1.5 years by a team of experts and newcomers; headcount and person-time are unspecified. After that experience, porting the PM spec to Dafny took under an hour, porting helper lemmas about an hour, and implementing/verifying NS about nine hours after its spec and C# wrapper were already written. This is author experience, not a controlled productivity comparison. On Linux6.9.3 with i7-11850H eight physical cores and32 GB RAM, KV verifies in54s with one thread or23s with eight; NS takes12s with one. Appendix expects KV1–2min serial or15–40s parallel on other hardware. Paper gives no independent proof replay in this reading and no controlled comparison against alternative verification approaches. Performance setup is a two-socket32-core machine with128 GB RAM and one128 GB Optane DC PMM, Debian Trixie/Linux6.12.10. All KV runs use the sharded variant with one shard per thread. Redis client/server run together but retain communication overhead; RocksDB uses memory-mapped files and non-temporal log appends; Viper preallocates enough capacity except in utilization measurement. Different supported features and durability architectures affect comparison. Microbenchmarks use25M records,64-byte keys,1 KiB values and8-byte list elements. Append adds16 elements per record in random order; read-list returns the entire list; trim removes it. Other operations run once per record. Figure2 uses logarithmic latency axes and95% confidence intervals. KV matches or beats RocksDB but Viper is faster on several operations, including most writes; Redis is slowest. Windows/Azure20 GiB battery-backed DRAM tests run only KV, with up to2× improvement; other systems lack Windows support. YCSB uses15M keys,24-byte keys,1140-byte values and five executions per system. RunE range queries are omitted and RunA/RunB partial updates become full-value updates. X is uniform75% updates,5% read-modify-write and20% reads; Y/Z use50/50 or5/95 read/update with90% accesses to10% records. LoadE is omitted only from Figure4 as similar to LoadA. These modified workloads must not be called an unmodified full YCSB suite. At one thread KV is broadly comparable to Viper and often slightly slower. At16 threads it substantially leads Viper on update/read-heavy run phases but not every load phase; the broad prose claim of outperforming other systems needs this figure-level qualification. Viper is tested on one non-interleaved NVDIMM despite optimizations for interleaved PM. Authors attribute scaling issues partly to CCEH semaphore costs nearly doubling1→16 threads. This is reported profiling attribution, not isolated causal proof. Figure 4 read-heavy B/C/D scale better than write-heavy phases. Approximate 16-thread throughput is RunC 3.5 Mops/s, RunB/RunD 3.0, RunA 1.25, LoadA 0.4, RunF 1.1, RunX 0.9, RunY 1.2, RunZ 0.8 and LoadX 0.4. Values are visual estimates. Hash sharding distributes hot keys across shards, so this does not demonstrate performance under all accesses contending on one shard. Full-instance startup fills each store to its own out-of-space point with64-byte keys/1 KiB values; capacities and record counts can therefore differ. KV/Viper startup is seconds because volatile indexes rebuild, whereas RocksDB is milliseconds. Full Redis startup fails with memory allocation error. Table3 utilization instead uses YCSB LoadA and optimally provisions KV at18 GiB with no further growth. Comparing those startup/resource numbers requires keeping these distinct experiments separate. Artifact branch osdi25-artifact and Zenodo15306499 include implementations, scripts and proof guidance; CHL formalization lives in the Perennial repository rather than being bundled. Exact performance reproduction requires at least128 GB Optane, with128 GB DRAM/32 cores recommended; emulation can check workflow but changes performance. Default artifact experiments are smaller than paper runs. No artifact or external proof was executed here; no LLM, TLA+ model-checking or distributed network liveness experiment appears.

    - what: # Reusable Formal Verification of DAG-based Consensus Protocols (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Nathalie Bertrand, Pranav Ghorpade, Sasha Rubin, Bernhard Scholz and Pavle Subotić, arXiv2407.02167v2,18March2025. The inventory year2024 identifies the original submission; this read uses the retained2025revision. The authors report TLA+/TLAPS safety proofs for five protocol models by combining three DAG-construction components with two ordering components. The five are DAG-Rider, Cordial Miners, Hashgraph, Eventually Synchronous Bullshark and a minor variant of Aleph. The result concerns Integrity and Total Order; eventual delivery, probabilistic progress and implementation correctness remain outside it (Q0,Q1,Q2,Q12).  ## Reading scope and source identity  Read all21PDFpages, sections1–6 and51reference entries, all three figures including both panels of Figure2, seven listings and numerical Table1. Individually viewed pages6–16, covering the figures, listings, refinement mapping and numerical table. The paper refers to “Appendix ??” but includes no appendix. References were read as bibliography entries, not recursively read papers.  Acquired the paper-linked repository's complete nontruncated tree and22static blobs at9e4c9629eb283c7c34b6ffcf7956bc72a3e26e5d,22December2024, the latest retained commit before this paper revision. This selects a historical version without establishing that it produced the reported timings. Whole reads cover README and the five component Specification.tla files. Proof files and complete-protocol sources are inspected only in explicitly recorded ranges. Acquisition of a file does not imply its whole read. No author code, specification, checker or solver was executed/imported; no serialized experimental data or model was loaded.  ## What is proved and how composition works  A vertex embeds its entire rooted causal history, rather than only an opaque identifier. Thus two processes possessing the same vertex have identical histories for it. A separate anchor-agreement property requires processes that have selected anchors for a frame to select the same anchors. Delivering each frame's previously undelivered causal-history vertices in a fixed deterministic order then prevents duplicate delivery and gives consistent delivery order. A lagging process may deliver a shorter prefix; the proof is not simultaneous equality of local delivery states (Q2,Q3).  The decomposition is three construction models, reliable structured, unreliable structured and unreliable unstructured, plus Global Perfect Coin (GPC) and Virtual Voting (VV) ordering. Reliable construction ensures one agreed vertex per position. Unreliable structured construction allows equivocation and uses ratification to agree on a vertex at a position. GPC ordering separately agrees on leader positions; combining these properties establishes anchor agreement. Hashgraph first converts its unstructured events to a structured witness DAG. Reference consistency constrains witnesses' predecessor references; VV establishes agreement on famous witnesses (Q4,Q6,Q7,Q8).  The full protocol maps constants and new state variables into an INSTANCE of the ordering specification. Each construction action performs an appropriate ordering action or leaves its mapped variables unchanged. Protocol-specific refinement obligations remain necessary: five reusable components do not eliminate the proofs connecting five concrete models to them. DAG-Rider and ES Bullshark share reusable components but differ in wave lengths and commit/leader rules. Aleph is explicitly a variant; neither the paper nor its one-line repository README gives a precise delta against every published Aleph rule (Q4,Q9,C6).  ## Assumptions and abstractions  The system explanation assumes signed identities and fewer than one-third Byzantine processes. Reliable broadcast is weakened to integrity because validity and eventual agreement support liveness. Its model retains the first broadcast for each creator/round; the authors argue a faulty process's chosen delivered message could equivalently have been sent first. This is an abstraction argument to retain in correspondence work, not a separately measured implementation equivalence (Q1,Q5).  Unreliable communication copies a vertex from another local DAG; Byzantine participants can insert arbitrary modeled vertices. Procedures retain input/output behavior while omitting internal loop states. GPC becomes an arbitrary fixed function shared by all processes: randomness, unpredictability and fairness are absent. Agreement of the function's answers suffices for the stated safety argument; it supplies no probability-one termination theorem or implementation of a cryptographic coin (Q5,Q7,Q8).  The retained component models use finite symbolic bounds on waves/rounds or event IDs, with no fixed numerical test instance. Proof claims quantify over their parameters; a single TLC run at one bound would not establish that claim. The record does not independently establish an infinite-execution refinement beyond these bounded model families. The VV component incorporates its reference-consistency premise directly into both the prestate and poststate of Next. Its source proof of that premise therefore depends on the action restriction; a concrete protocol still must justify the mapping (C1–C5).  ## Consequential findings in the retained artifact  The printed self-referential VertexSet listing is explanatory shorthand. ReliableStructuredDAGconstructionSpecification.tla instead constructs vertices recursively by decreasing round with UntilRoundVertex. That resolves the apparent circular-definition concern for this component. However, its received/added-vertex guards access v.edges, while the actual constructed records contain strongedges and weakedges. This is a static field mismatch in the saved model; no checker error or reachable protocol failure was observed (C1).  In the unreliable structured component, Approves(v,u) requires Observes(v,u) and forbids observing every vertex with u's source and round. Taking that quantified vertex to be u yields both Observes(v,u) and its negation. Thus the literal definition admits no approval. With n-f positive under3f<n, ratification requires a nonempty set of approving sources and cannot occur under this reading. Since ratified vertices initialize to Nil, the displayed agreement property can hold without any ratification progress. This is a reader derivation from the retained definitions, not a claim that the real Cordial Miners protocol fails (C2).  The unstructured component's DonotSeeFork(v,u) has the same self-including universal condition. Taking x=u contradicts its Path(v,u) conjunct. Its Sees predicate consequently cannot witness a seen ancestor under the intended reflexive Path interpretation. This is another source-definition concern to resolve before trusting correspondence to actual Hashgraph behavior; the paper excludes liveness and no safety counterexample is established (C3).  VVOrderingProofs.tla contains several named lemma statements without proof text. Most concretely, intInv14 asserts, for integers a,m, that a>=m and m+a>2f imply m>f. The permitted assignment f=1,a=2,m=1 makes both premises true and its conclusion false. The file cites this lemma in its Inv1 preservation proof. The nearby intadd statement has the plausible intended conclusion a>f with strict a>b. This suggests a proof-support defect or mistaken statement in the retained artifact; it does not show a checker accepted a false theorem. The actual preservation goal is a majority-count fact that can be mathematically true even though this cited general lemma is false (C7,C8).  The same proof preamble asserts, without accompanying proof text, that every witness has more than2f predecessor sources in the preceding frame. Combined literally with its positive finite frame range and predecessor-frame condition, that leaves no nonempty witness set: a witness of minimum frame would require an earlier witness. This preamble should not silently become an established domain theorem. A simpler nonvacuity concern appears in the VV specification itself: all witness-DAG cells initially are empty, while adding a witness requires more than2f predecessor sources already present. With f nonnegative and no genesis exception, no first witness can be added under the intended typed interpretation. Whole proof closure and tool handling of unproved declarations have not been replayed. These artifact findings limit independent confirmation of the paper's mechanized-proof claim; they do not refute the high-level decomposition or establish a reachable fork (C5,C7).  ## Evaluation and significance  Table1 reports, in order reliable structured/unreliable structured/unreliable unstructured/GPC/VV: specification lines403/160/230/272/136; invariants6/6/7/10/18; proof lines460/594/554/822/2120; maximum proof depths10/9/8/9/13; maximum degrees7/8/7/7/11; leaf obligations633/895/665/1302/3316; and checking seconds49/68/74/125/651. Environment:2.10GHzCPU,8GBRAM,Windows11,TLAPS1.4.5. These are author-reported component checks, not reader replications or total timings for every full-protocol refinement. No repeated-run variability or controlled comparison appears (Q10).  The authors report approximately14person-months across five people. Their “almost half” proof-effort claim corresponds to reducing an illustrative ten separate construction/ordering components to five reusable ones. There is no controlled person-time baseline or ablation demonstrating a50% labor saving; refinement work and component complexity also differ. A reusable component count is concrete, while a measured causal labor reduction remains unestablished (Q0,Q4,Q10,Q12).  This is directly relevant to reusable TLA+ specifications and distributed-protocol proofs. It has no Verus/Rust artifact or LLM-agent experiment. A reader proposal for evaluating proof agents is to score specification correspondence, nonvacuous progress examples, closure of helper lemmas and refinement obligations separately from reported leaf-obligation throughput. The retained field/predicate/lemma issues make those distinctions concrete without treating static concerns as observed solver results.

- Sync/Async functional distributed verification (2025)
    - title: Functional Reasoning for Distributed Systems with Failures
    - what: Defines twin Rocq-embedded languages Sync and Async to make high-level functional reasoning about asynchronous distributed protocols precise, then proves that compiled Async executions are included in Sync denotations. The authors mechanize the framework and safety proofs for Bosco and Sequential Paxos. Sync is a choreography language whose typed programs are ordered communication steps over role-indexed vectors; its power-set denotation explicitly enumerates message loss, reordering, truncation and arbitrary Byzantine injections. The configuration model separates good, crash-prone and Byzantine nodes and uses a Netwk relation as an executable over-approximation. Finite loop unwinding supports safety proofs for nonterminating protocols. Bosco proofs derive a strong one-step theorem for n>7f and an inductive univalence/agreement invariant for n>3f. SeqPaxos proofs use a weakest precondition UC_D to show once a value is decided, later iterations decide it or abstain when n>2f; the condition is weaker than the protocol’s strongest postcondition and exposes optimization opportunities. Async is a monadic node LTS plus single-use channel LTS; alignment permutes arbitrary interleavings into channel order, and adequacy (Theorem 5.1) follows through aligned traces, big-step semantics and channel-erasure lemmas. The Rocq development is about 2.5k lines and includes endpoint projection/executable extraction.
    - number: Rocq mechanization about 2.5k LoC
    - number: Bosco one-step threshold n>7f; agreement threshold n>3f
    - number: SeqPaxos agreement threshold n>2f
    - number: SimpleVote example n_R=4, f_R=b_R=1
    - limits: Sync excludes branches and loops inside a body, cryptographic primitives, and arbitrary communication order; it therefore targets streamlined communication-closed protocols. Network messages are authenticated, nonduplicated, eventually delivered between correct nodes, and well typed; signatures and parsing are assumed rather than modeled. Byzantine behavior is over-approximated and can inject values it could not know. Safety is proved for finite loop unwindings, not termination/liveness. The Async adequacy theorem is inclusion (compiled outputs are in the denotation), and correctness depends on the stated channel-ordering and synchrony-reduction restrictions.

- VEP: A Two-stage Verification Toolchain for Full eBPF Programmability (2025)
    - what: VEP separates eBPF verification into C-level symbolic execution and SMT proof generation in user space, compilation that translates code, assertions and proofs, and independent bytecode symbolic execution/proof checking intended for kernel space. Separation logic describes owned memory and helper-acquired resources. Annotations expose loop invariants and contracts unavailable to fully automatic verifiers. The paper reports acceptance/rejection, time, memory and annotation/proof sizes on 41 small programs, and claims Coq proofs of the separation-logic transformation properties. It does not present a mechanized soundness/refinement theorem for the entire executable toolchain. Records proof-generation/checking boundary, trusted helper specifications and bytecode semantics, assertion restrictions and conversion rules, compilation passes and source-property loss, safety versus intended functionality and termination proof limits, concrete string/list/socket examples, all Table 2–5 results and deployment/version uncertainty. Separates sample success from universal no-error/full-programmability claims; checks discrepancies in memory/speed/acceptance prose and proof-line terminology; preserves printed illustrative inconsistencies without claiming implementation defects.
    - limits: §§2/5: Claimed small trusted computing base excludes the C verifier, compiler and SMT solver because bytecode is checked again. Guarantee still depends on correct executable bytecode checker, faithful eBPF instruction/memory/arithmetic semantics, actual helper contracts, and correspondence with kernel execution/JIT. The paper supplies no whole executable-checker soundness or code-to-kernel refinement theorem. §5 specifically reports Coq proofs for separation-logic transformation properties, not all these components. §§2.1/3/5: VEP-C computes strongest postconditions, eliminates spatial entailments, and uses its own SMT solver producing cvc5-style proof terms. VEP-eBPF independently symbolically executes bytecode and checks spatial/pure proof steps without solving. Checked proof terms remove the need to trust SMT answers only to the extent proof rules and their checker/semantics are correct. Kernel-space deployment is the intended architecture; evaluation does not clearly distinguish an in-kernel deployment benchmark from standalone checker measurements. §§2.2–2.3/7: Introduction and capability section claim functional correctness, but §2.3 explicitly makes user intent the user’s responsibility and §7 lists functional correctness as future work. The reported Key_connection annotations are expressly memory-safety-only. Accepting bytecode safety does not establish intended lookup/copy semantics or preservation of arbitrary source assertions. §2.2: Termination within finitely many steps is claimed. The shown loop reasoning uses invariants and exit conditions; no explicit general ranking-function, decreasing variant or fuel/step-bound rule is explained. Invariant preservation alone establishes partial correctness, not termination. This is a limit of the presented justification, not a reproduced checker counterexample. §§2.1/6.2/Appendix B: Full programmability and no false positives/negatives are author claims. Finite examples and annotations do not establish completeness for all safe programs; general entailment is acknowledged undecidable. Spatial-expression scope restrictions reject some natural quantified array assertions, requiring custom predicates. Appendix B DNF normalization can multiply branches, so approximate linear symbolic-execution cost in statement/assertion length excludes assertion-size growth and SMT solving. §3: Memory ownership uses disjoint spatial conjunction; duplicated ownership is inconsistent. Built-in helper contracts are derived from documentation, not proved against kernel helper implementations. Resource acquire/release soundness depends on their completeness and accuracy, including permitted null returns, flags and sizes. Contract variants are selected for supported contexts. §§2.3/4: Source C undefined behavior can compile into memory-safe bytecode. Early source rejection protects source semantics beyond kernel bytecode safety. Maliciously altered bytecode with a valid safety proof may pass without matching original program intent. Neither final safety checking nor an unverified compiler automatically proves C-to-bytecode functional refinement. §4: Compiler uses nanopasses, member-to-offset conversion, calling convention transformation, iterated register coalescing, and explicit stack frame preconditions. Few optimizations supported. Dead source variables become existential logical variables. Figure 14 deliberately turns a false source assertion x==1 after x=0 into satisfiable exists _x,_x==1; source assertion truth is lost even though bytecode safety can survive. §4 Figures 13/15, Appendix A: Printed illustrations contain apparent inconsistencies. Figure 13 sets R1=0 then asserts R1==*(R10-4)+1 while stack value is0. Figure 15 declares fields x,next but accesses l.head. Appendix A transforms forall n,v!=n*n into forall n,n!=n*n, which fails for n=0/1 and is not generally equivalent. These are source illustration issues; artifact behavior was not tested. Appendix A prose also describes x as a nonsquare although displayed condition constrains v with x=2*v. §3 Figures 4/6/9/12: An arbitrary owned output list proves initialized memory/ownership, not that memset filled every byte or strncpy copied/padded correctly. Figure 9 uses stronger repeat(v,n) content predicate; Figure 6’s displayed successful strncpy postcondition is weaker than complete C-library functionality. Keep actual predicate content when evaluating generated proofs. Appendix B: Internal assertions separate program-variable addresses, pure facts and owned memory; logic variables in spatial facts require permitted existential binding. Printed array-address conversion shows V(e1+e2) without explicit element-size scaling; semantics/type conventions would need inspection before inferring a compiler defect. §6: Evidence is 41 selected small C programs, not large production services or adversarial bytecode fuzzing. Linux Kernel5.15 and PREVAIL August2024 used. Hardware, trial repetitions, confidence intervals, human annotation time/user study and whole-tool LOC are not specified. No independent reproduction performed. §6 Tables 2–5: Passing rate means acceptance for safe cases and rejection for unsafe cases. All ten unsafe cases stop at VEP-C; compiler/eBPF columns are dashes. Thus data demonstrate C-front-end rejection, not independent final-checker rejection of ten crafted attacks. Safe VEP outcomes are 30 category samples plus one Key_connection, all accepted. §6.2: Linux 6/10 acceptance is for the PREVAIL sample category, not all safe programs; Linux category is9/10 and Stringlib3/10, with Key0/1. PREVAIL10/10,8/10,1/10 and Key0/1. Source attributes PREVAIL variability to SMT dependency/nondeterminism although introduction describes abstract interpretation; no experiment establishes that causal claim. Claimed version regressions30%/20% lack paired version tables, and no cross-version VEP study is shown. §6.1: Claimed predictable2–3MB VEP-eBPF memory is contradicted by Linux sample maximum8034KB (lathist); VEP-C maximum32569KB. Linux average.94ms applies to its accepted Linux sample subset, not all benchmarks, and Stringlib maximum2.69ms. Claimed3–5x faster than PREVAIL is not uniform: Linux category12.48/8.42≈1.48x, while39.46/8.42≈4.69x relative to VEP-C. Different acceptance sets complicate average comparisons. §6.3: Table3 labels proof counts as proof lines, while prose calls64840 proof obligations. Do not infer64840 independent obligations. Annotation lines are a size proxy, not measured effort or expertise. Key proof5819lines in table versus about5800 in text; preserve rounding. §7: LLM generation of annotations, broader functional correctness and advanced optimization support are proposed future work. No LLM agent experiment, Verus/verified Rust/TLA+ proof, distributed-protocol theorem or code execution reported in this reading.

- Bythos (2024)
    - title: Compositional Verification of Composite Byzantine Protocols
    - what: Embeds TLA in Coq and assumes that message delivery is weakly fair (a message that stays deliverable is eventually delivered). Proves that pending packets are eventually delivered and that protocol phases finish. The method: for each phase, find a finite set of packets that is enough. Show that delivering them starts the next phase. Chain the phases with the transitivity of the leads-to relation (for example init ∧ □next ∧ WFDelivery ⊢ sent ~~> output). Covers Provable Broadcast, Reliable Broadcast, Accountable Confirmer and Accountable Reliable Broadcast.
