- Formally Verifying the Safety of Pipelined Moonshot Consensus Protocol (2024)
    - what: # Formally Verifying the Safety of Pipelined Moonshot Consensus Protocol (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  M. Praveen, Raghavendra Ramesh and Isaac Doidge, arXiv:2403.16637v1, March2024; the PDF identifies FMBC2024 in its metadata. The authors report an IVy proof that honest validators' committed chains are prefix-comparable for arbitrary network sizes under an abstract honest-quorum-intersection assumption. This is a safety verification of a high-level model, using190 reported invariants and23 monitors. Liveness is future work; cryptographic checking, executable implementation refinement and transaction validity are outside the demonstrated result (Q1,Q4,Q6,Q8,Q11).  ## Reading and evidence scope  Read all17PDFpages: sections1–7,30bibliography entries, AppendixA, the complete Figure1 protocol pseudocode, the unnumbered proof-dependency diagram, both tables and the appendix IVy listing spanning pages15–17. No numbered theorem/proof, evaluation plot or checklist appears. Individually inspected renders5,9,10,15,16,17 to verify the protocol, numerical table, proof diagram and appendix code. Complete extracted text was read for every page; visual scope is limited to those six renders. References were read as entries, not recursively followed.  Fetched the paper-linked GitHub repository metadata and a complete nontruncated tree. Chose commit1eae7974044d6981b214aa231d4e1c7d6f1bc1b3, the most recent commit affecting suprabft before26March2024. Its date is8February2024. This is a documented historical-source selection, not proof that this exact commit produced every reported check. The current repository has later changes; the record does not substitute current HEAD for the paper-era source. Nine retained files have SHA256 and matching Git-blob identities. Read README, types.ivy, ubd_seq.ivy, network.ivy, moonshot.ivy, quorum_verification.ivy, check_all.sh and Isolates.txt whole. Read selected safety.ivy ranges1–140,703–875,1007–1115,1170–1195 and1230–1309, plus search hits for axioms/assumptions/isolates. This is not a whole1,309-line proof-file audit. Large IVySummary/IVyTrace logs, slides, backup/trial proof files and external tool-library modules were inventoried but not read. No author code, IVy model, checker or SMT solver was executed/imported; no model/checkpoint/serialized experiment data was loaded.  ## Exact property and fault model  Each validator maintains committed blocks and its latest committed block. Safety requires that for any two honest validators one committed blockchain is a prefix of the other. The model may allow one validator to lag arbitrarily far behind another; it need not require equal states at every instant. The retained full_safety definition makes three conditions explicit: the first tip equals or precedes the second; every block of the first set is in the second; and every extra block in the second descends from the first tip. The invariant requires this relation in either direction for honest participants (Q4,C8).  The protocol explanation assumes n=3f+1 and quorums of2f+1, with at most f Byzantine validators. The mechanized abstraction does not prove a cardinality theorem with this arithmetic. It axiomatizes that every pair of quorums shares an honest member, and that an f+1 timeout group has an honest member. For the stated cardinalities, ordinary set counting justifies the honest intersection: two2f+1 subsets of3f+1 participants overlap in at least f+1, exceeding f faulty members. That arithmetic connection is reader reasoning, not a separate IVy run (Q2,Q5,C1).  The paper motivates partially synchronous operation, but the safety network is asynchronous: messages may be lost, duplicated or reordered. Timers are Boolean expiration events that may occur nondeterministically. Neither eventual delivery nor a known time bound is needed for the stated prefix invariant; those abstractions cannot establish eventual commits or latency. The source explicitly says liveness would require fairness for timer execution and additional handling of directly received prepare quorums (Q5,Q6,C5).  Byzantine validators can send arbitrary modeled messages under Byzantine identities, including impersonating other Byzantine validators. They cannot forge an honest identity. Digital signatures and hashes are abstracted: block identity replaces digest computation; global records of honest sent messages validate a certificate's claimed members. These monitors are proof instrumentation, not a deployed trusted coordinator. Their faithful relationship to actual cryptographic validation remains an implementation/refinement obligation (Q5,Q6,C2,C3).  ## Protocol cases  Views have rotating leaders and three voting/proposal paths. A normal proposal extends the block certified in the preceding view. A fallback proposal carries a timeout certificate and extends the block whose included quorum certificate has the highest view. Optimistic proposals let the next leader propose a child immediately after voting, before receiving the current block's certificate. Honest voting guards constrain prior optimistic/normal/fallback votes and timeouts; certificates aggregate votes of one type. An honest validator may vote at most twice in a view under the displayed rules (Q2,Q3).  A validator advances with a quorum or timeout certificate, updates the locked highest-view certificate, and resets its timer. It commits a block when that block and its child are certified in adjacent views, then commits uncommitted ancestors. The one-block-per-network-hop and three-hop finalization claims describe the normal-path design in the cited protocol work; this verification paper supplies no throughput/latency experiment or implementation performance result (Q2,Q3).  The source separates message receipt from processing. A normal proposal must be received from the current leader, contain a constructed block and appropriate certificate, satisfy timer/first-processing conditions and the vote predicate; it may process the certificate first and propose the next optimistic block. Timeout/fallback handlers require embedded certificates to have been processed, explicitly constraining the environment to perform those steps first. This is a modeling convention to retain in any source correspondence argument, rather than evidence that every implementation obeys the ordering (C4,C5).  The eight whole source reads expose additional concrete abstractions. Fresh blocks are chosen from initially present unconstructed objects. Genesis has its own certificate and all participants in its quorum. The optimistic-last-block variable initially uses a separate unused block rather than the paper's genesis digest; a comment calls this a proof-performance shortcut. Honest/block validity invariants are separate from the top safety invariant. These details are not silently normalized to the informal algorithm (C1,C3).  ## How the proof is organized  IVy generates initiation/preservation obligations for inductive invariants and asks Z3 to discharge them. Isolates expose selected supporting properties to control formula size and logical fragments. Passing one isolate while assuming dependencies is only part of a complete verification; those dependencies also need checking. The paper reports completing that process but this read does not replay it (Q5,Q7,Q8).  The principal argument establishes that certified blocks proposed in later rounds descend from the directly committed block. This ordering concerns proposal rounds, not the time a delayed certificate is received. Additional invariants establish ancestry among each honest validator's committed blocks, closure under committed ancestors, and ancestry comparability of different honest tips. These establish prefix comparability. The paper supplies a five-step informal proof outline and a dependency diagram, not the full text of all obligations. The retained source supplies the exact omitted blockchain_prefix formula (Q7,Q8,C8).  The difficult descendant lemma uses induction over rounds. The paper says “The principle of induction is taken to be an axiom” (§4.3,p10). The source includes an explicit parameterized induction schema in quorum_after_ldc_descendant; related predecessor/successor results also use schemas. These are mathematical assumptions/rules requiring an intended natural-number interpretation, not automatically inferred from a bare arbitrary total order. The retained ubd_seq defines immediate successor using the absence of an intermediate element and supplies a nat implementation; no such implementation was executed or proved anew here (Q8,C1,C6,C13).  Transitive closure is not directly definable in first-order logic. A monitor incrementally records ancestors when blocks acquire quorums; supporting invariants establish parent inclusion, transitivity, no divergent ancestors and recovery of the immediate-parent relation from ancestry. The commit update is in safety.ivy rather than simply the core moonshot module: commit_candidate requires local direct commit, descent from the current tip, processed-certificate conditions for ancestors, and maximal eligible round; its after-qc-processing monitor updates the committed set/tip. Thus the exact model being verified includes proof-file actions, not just moonshot.ivy alone (Q8,Q9,C7,C12).  No contradiction or reachable fork was established by this read. Static source inspection is insufficient to certify every isolate dependency, axiom, abstraction or proof result. The paper's categorical statements that verification conclusively rules out design/logic errors should be understood relative to this formal model, stated axioms, tool behavior and intended correspondence, rather than as a theorem about arbitrary implementations or all blockchain security properties (Q4,Q11).  ## Reported evaluation and retained artifact  Table1 reports338lines of Types,110Network,642Moonshot,165Quorum verification and1,309Safety, totaling2,564. These counts exactly match physical line counts of the five retained files at the selected historical pin. The printed ratio of program code to proof is approximately1:3; that partition is descriptive, since files also contain comments, data abstractions and monitors. The authors report190invariants and23monitors, but do not specify a counting convention. A simple line-prefix count finds188invariant declarations in safety.ivy and211across those five files, including other invariants; do not equate that lexical count with semantic proof obligations or silently replace the published number (Q7,C9).  The reported effort is about140person-hours after the protocol specification stabilized,10%modeling and the remainder proofs. Fourteen modeling and126proof hours are reader arithmetic, not a time log. Earlier protocol revisions and proof/specification iterations are discussed but excluded from that clearly stated starting point. No verification wall-clock benchmark, hardware specification, exact IVy/Z3 version, variance, isolate runtime table or controlled cross-tool comparison appears (Q7,Q9,Q10).  The README gives a full-file checking command; check_all.sh instead lists116individual isolate checker invocations separated by date commands. Static shell inspection finds no fail-fast option or aggregate-status check and a final date command. Therefore running the script can return success even if an earlier checker command fails. This is a wrapper-status limitation, not evidence that a particular historical obligation failed or that the README's separate command masks failures. Isolates.txt lists an older basic_safety structure, so it is not used here as a certificate of current full_safety dependency coverage. Unread trace/summary logs are not evidence of successful complete checking in this record (C10,C11).  The authors describe solver stalls, inlining nested subroutine calls, explicit intermediate facts and fine dependency selection. Their concrete ancestry example adds two intermediary ancestor facts so that transitivity becomes easy for Z3. These are useful proof-engineering observations without controlled ablations or measured universal speedups. The claimed lower effort than Coq and preference over TLA+/TLAPS are author experience/opinion, not a matched comparison of equivalent developments (Q1,Q9,Q10).  ## Contribution to the requested topics  This is a directly relevant parameterized Byzantine-consensus safety case study: abstract honest quorum intersection, asynchronous safety despite timer abstraction, certificate-authentication monitors, ancestry instrumentation, round induction and modular solver obligations. It reports human verification work rather than LLM agents. It has no Verus or verified Rust artifact and does not prove a TLA+ model.  For agents writing specifications/proofs, the transfer is a reader proposal: preserve exactly which code and monitor actions define the model; separately check dependencies and axioms; expose small intermediate ancestry facts; retain failures from every checker invocation; and distinguish a proof of an abstract invariant from executable refinement, crypto correctness, liveness and application security. The190-invariant/140-hour development is a potential future study case, not evidence of an agent success rate or measured automation benefit.
    - limits: Honestquorumintersectionandinductionaxioms;unforgeablehonestidentities;Boolean-timer/asynchronoussafetyabstraction;globalcertificate/ancestry/commitmonitors;noimplementation/crypto/liveness/transactionvalidityproof;noauthorcodeexecution

A bounded FIFO producer-consumer example and CLH lock were verified with tool support. Completeness-threshold chapters define thresholds over input sizes, derive verification-condition based approximations, prove modular/transitive/elimination rules, and characterize simple unconditional array accesses.

- Modelling the Raft Distributed Consensus Protocol in mCRL2 (2024)
    - what: # Whole read: Modelling the Raft Distributed Consensus Protocol in mCRL2 (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Bora, Pham Duc Minh and Willemse, MARS 2024, EPTCS 399, pp. 7–20; DOI 10.4204/EPTCS.399.4; arXiv 2403.18916v1, submitted 27 March 2024. Read all 14 PDF pages, §§1–5, Figure 1, Table 1, acknowledgement and 14 references, in text and rendered pages. Also read the official MARS mCRL2 model, all nine property files, README and batch script statically. The downloaded paper matches the indexed PDF byte for byte. No author code, model checker, prover or solver was executed. Raw sources, hashes, scope and exact excerpts are retained separately.  The paper contributes an action-based Raft model and modal µ-calculus formulas, with reported model-checking results for eight finite configurations. It does not establish unrestricted Raft correctness. More specifically, the authors write, “All main properties hold true for all configurations of Table 1; verification of each property takes roughly 2-3 times that of generating the state space” (§3, PDF p. 9 / printed p. 15; Q19). Static inspection also finds differences between the printed formulas, artifact formulas and model indexing. These narrow what a successful check can establish; they are not claimed reachable protocol counterexamples.  ## Model and assumptions  The model follows the TLA+ and LNT specifications and focuses on leader election and log replication: “Features such as cluster membership changes and log compaction have not been modelled” (§2, PDF p. 2 / printed p. 8; Q3). Node, Network and Client processes run in parallel; communicating actions and allow restrictions enforce synchronisation. Analysis requires a “fixed, concrete number of servers” (§2, PDF p. 3 / printed p. 9; Q4), rather than a proof quantified over all cluster sizes.  One client sends a bounded sequence of unique natural command IDs, abstracting away command contents and application behavior (Q5). Client-to-cluster communication is synchronous; communication among servers is asynchronous through the network. The network holds a finite set of payloads, permits reordering and limits capacity (Q7). Thus two identical pending payloads collapse to one set element. Reliable mode supplies no scheduler fairness guarantee. Capacity can block sends; the broadcast admission guard uses the number of servers rather than the exact outgoing set size (Q47). These are model restrictions, not a general unbounded or duplicate-preserving network semantics.  The scope description has a tension worth retaining. Section 2.1 says, “we do not analyse the Raft algorithm in the presence of message loss or duplication” (PDF p. 4 / printed p. 10; Q6). Table 1 nevertheless includes one lossy-and-crashing row, and §3 reports all main formulas true for every row (Q18–Q19). The model supplies an optional loss branch (Q8, Q47). The defensible reading is a primarily reliable model with one reported loss experiment; no duplication experiment is reported.  Each server has role, term, log, commit index, vote state, replication indexes and a pending reply. Figure 1 adds a Crashed role to Follower/Candidate/Leader (Q9–Q10). Entries are Command(term, commandID), stored in zero-based mCRL2 lists; the authors explicitly warn that Raft’s original indexing is one-based (Q11). Only leaders accept client commands. Elections and heartbeats use nondeterministic actions; “we cannot analyse real-time requirements, nor the real-time performance of the algorithm” (§2.2, PDF p. 6 / printed p. 12; Q12). There is no sampling of randomized timeout intervals or elapsed-time state.  A candidate votes for itself and sends vote requests to other nodes not already in its voter set (Q13). Stale RPCs are discarded. A received request computes and stores a reply before the later send, allowing a crash between the state update and reply transmission (Q14). The artifact’s resume transition preserves currentTerm, log and votedFor, but resets commitIndex, voterLog, nextIndex, matchIndex and the pending reply, and returns to Follower (Q46). Reply computation itself is atomic: the authors acknowledge it “does not accurately reflect real-world scenarios where the computation of a reply would involve multiple steps” (§5, PDF p. 13 / printed p. 19; Q35).  Leaders send one log entry at a time; the model uses nextIndex backtracking to find a matching prefix (Q15). Majority replication commits only a current-term entry directly; earlier entries are committed indirectly with it (Q16). This is a protocol model without a refinement proof connecting a Rust implementation, application state machine or storage system to these transitions.  ## What the properties check  The action logic cannot inspect process parameters directly. The model therefore adds self-loop actions exposeLeader, exposeLogLeader and exposeLog (Q19, Q46). Safety formulas compare exposed states across arbitrary later execution, rather than merely reading two process parameters in one state.  **Election Safety.** The printed formula forbids a different node from ever later exposing leadership in the same term (Q20); the artifact agrees (Q52). An additional existential formula asks whether a leader can be exposed at all; another asks whether two different node IDs can eventually expose leadership (Q21). The latter is reported true only with at least two terms. These are witness-existence checks, not eventual election on every execution.  The least-fixed-point formula counts possible leader announcements whose ID differs from the most recently stored ID, starting with id=1 and count=0 (Q22, Q53). It does not compare the associated terms or demand globally distinct IDs; a later reuse of an earlier ID can count. It is therefore more precise to describe its actual counter than to call it a proof of MaxTerm distinct leaders or guaranteed succession.  **Log Matching.** The intended statement is that the same index and term imply identical prefixes through that index. The paper’s guard instead tests complete entry equality, log1.index == log2.index, which is a stronger antecedent and makes the standalone requirement weaker (Q23). The artifact repairs this to term(log1.index) == term(log2.index) and checks both list bounds (Q49).  Both versions compare slice(log,1,index+1). The supplied slice helper begins at zero and excludes its finishing index (Q42). It therefore omits position 0, the first actual entry; initial logs contain no dummy element (Q48). Reader-created one-entry logs [Command(1,1)] and [Command(1,2)] have matching terms at position 0, but both compared slices are empty. This separates the intended first-entry equality requirement from the artifact formula. It does not establish that these two logs coexist in a reachable model state.  **Leader Completeness.** After advanceCommitIndex(old,new,term,log), the formula asks that selected entries occur somewhere in every later-term leader’s exposed log (Q24–Q25, Q51). The membership consequent is weaker than retaining each entry at its original index. There is also an indexing discrepancy: it selects log1.index for old < index <= new, while the model’s getTerm translates Raft index to list position index-1 (Q41). With a singleton log and new=1, the formula selects zero-based position 1 rather than 0. No semantic result for out-of-bounds list selection, checker failure or reachable counterexample is asserted here. For commits in the sole elected term of a one-term configuration, there is no later leader term to test; the auxiliary leader/commit existence checks do not make every main formula nonvacuous.  The event itself has a separate static inconsistency. On the successful AppendEntriesResponse branch, advanceCommitIndex computes its new index from the old matchIndex array, whereas the following Node transition computes commitIndex after incorporating the new acknowledgement (Q45). A local valuation with one entry, old matchIndex=[0,0,0] and an acknowledgement of entry 1 from another server yields event new index 0 but state commit index 1 using the supplied count helper (Q43–Q45). Reachability of that valuation was not established. The source expression mismatch is sufficient reason not to equate the event range automatically with all newly committed entries.  **State Machine Safety.** The intended statement forbids two nodes applying different entries at the same committed index. Paper and artifact compare slice(log1,1,commitIndex1) and the corresponding slice of a later other node with commitIndex2 >= commitIndex1 > 0 (Q26, Q50). Under the artifact helper, position 0 is excluded. For commitIndex1=1 both slices are empty, independent of the first entries. Thus a successful check of this formula alone cannot establish agreement on the first committed entry. Again, this is formula coverage established by symbolic values, not a reachable protocol failure.  An existential companion asks whether two different nodes can expose positive commit indexes in sequence, the later one at least as large (Q27). It does not repair prefix coverage or prove every request eventually commits. Append Entries is omitted as a separate checked property because the authors consider it immediate from the modeled leader operations (Q19).  ## Reported evaluation and concrete cases  The authors used manual interactive simulation and safety formulas throughout development to find model bugs (Q19). Table 1 gives eight configurations, all with three nodes and capacity three. The following preserves the reported rounded sizes and approximate generation times; every row is retained in numeric-evidence.json (Q18, §2.2, PDF p. 8 / printed p. 14):  - 2 commands, 1 term, reliable, no crashes: 2.14×10^5 states, about 1 minute - 1 command, 2 terms, reliable, no crashes: 1.17×10^6 states, about 2 minutes - 1 command, 3 terms, reliable, no crashes: 1.32×10^7 states, about 13 minutes - 2 commands, 1 term, reliable, crashes: 1.79×10^7 states, about 5 minutes - 2 commands, 2 terms, reliable, no crashes: 2.25×10^7 states, about 19 minutes - 2 commands, 1 term, lossy, crashes: 5.97×10^7 states, about 105 minutes - 1 command, 2 terms, reliable, crashes: 1.48×10^8 states, about 24 minutes - 1 command, 3 terms, reliable, crashes: 2.38×10^9 states, about 820 minutes  The first seven times use a 2017 Macbook Pro with 16GB; the last uses an unspecified compute server and is explicitly “not directly comparable to the other runtimes reported” (Table 1; Q18). No repetitions, error bars, exact CPU, per-formula times or implementation latency/throughput are supplied. The paper reports roughly 2–3× generation time for each main property using symbolic verification (Q19, technique reference Q38). The base configuration compresses by almost factor 5 under strong bisimilarity; no exact reduced size is given (Q17).  The artifact README names mCRL2 release 202307.1 and gives explicit and symbolic commands (Q56). Its default model has five servers, two requests, one term, capacity five, no loss/crashes, and PRIORITISE=false (Q40). Seven individually guarded Node instances support the small configured sizes (Q48). The batch script substitutes three servers/capacity three, requests 1 or 2, terms 1–3, and both Boolean loss/crash settings, for 24 combinations (Q57). It includes all .mcf files, including timeout/client-command checks (Q54–Q55); neither the script nor their inclusion is a saved result log. Do not infer that every batch combination or every extra formula was successfully checked. The official archive contains source and instructions, not experiment output or an identified experiment commit.  MAJORITY is ceil(NumberOfServers/2) in the artifact (Q40). That is a strict majority for the odd sizes three and five here, but only half for even sizes. No arbitrary-size correctness claim should be inferred from the configurable constant.  Section 4 illustrates how modeling style changes generated state count. A Boolean process with conditionals after the action yields 3 states/6 transitions; moving the choice before the action yields 1 state/2 transitions, strongly bisimilar to the first (Q29–Q30). The tool can then remove an unused process parameter. The example supports a concrete state-generation lesson; it is not a measured uniform threefold Raft reduction. The claim that an early inexperienced model was “orders of magnitude larger than needed” is an author observation without a controlled Raft benchmark (Q29).  ## Relation to the research topic  The direct contribution is a finite distributed-protocol model and action-logic encodings of selected Raft requirements, with bounded symbolic checking and concrete resource measurements. The authors describe the modal formalizations as apparently new while acknowledging the prior TLA+, LNT and Verdi work (Q2, Q33, Q39). This is useful evidence about specification design, state exposure, state-space growth, crash abstraction and model/property correspondence.  The TLA+ comparison is specific. The authors say TLA+ answers stale requests but drops stale responses; their model follows LNT in discarding both. They follow TLA+ when bounding transmitted commit information, and add reboot behavior they say is absent from the LNT model (Q31). These are attributed source discussions, not an independent audit of all upstream artifacts. Section 4’s view that imperative LNT is more appealing to average engineers is an author opinion, not a user study (Q32).  For evaluating LLM agents writing specifications or proofs, the useful checks are reader inferences: validate a formula against its helper definitions, include first/last-index examples, inspect whether instrumentation exposes the actual state transition, distinguish term equality from entry equality, and separate existential witnesses from inevitable progress. This paper supplies concrete reasons these checks matter, but it contains no LLM-agent, Verus, verified-Rust or implementation-refinement evaluation.  The liveness boundary is explicit: “Stronger liveness requirements, asserting that always inevitably a leader must be elected, are simply not true in our model” (§5, PDF p. 13 / printed p. 19; Q34), owing to crashes/loss and bounded terms. More complex configurations, stronger liveness, finer reply computation and real-time verification remain future work (Q33–Q36). Successful bounded checks therefore support the specified finite model and literal formulas, subject to the correspondence issues above. They do not independently establish the stronger prose requirements.  ## Evidence and review  quotes.json contains 57 literal excerpts with file, section, PDF/printed page where applicable, line ranges and character offsets. combined.quote-source.txt contains every excerpt for database validation. source-files.json retains raw hashes; source-scope.json distinguishes whole-paper and static artifact coverage. numeric-evidence.json preserves all table rows, and static-witnesses.json records reader-created separating values. reader-diagnostics.json separates source claims from reader findings. REVIEW.md and validation-final.json track consultation, independent review and mechanical checks.
    - limits: Fixed finite cluster,client commands,terms and finite-set network capacity; one synchronous client and asynchronous interserver RPC; no membership changes/log compaction; nondeterministic untimed timeouts,atomic reply computation,optional crashes/reboot/loss. Eight reported three-node configurations. No duplication/multiplicity or fairness guarantee. Static indexing/formula/event mismatches qualify property coverage.

- Reward Augmentation in Reinforcement Learning for Testing Distributed Systems (2024)
    - what: # Reward Augmentation in Reinforcement Learning for Testing Distributed Systems (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Andrea Borgarelli, Constantin Enea, Rupak Majumdar and Srinidhi Nagendra propose two reinforcement-learning policies for testing distributed implementations. BonusMaxRL rewards unfamiliar state/action pairs; WaypointRL adds manually chosen predicates that guide exploration toward selected situations. The evidence is an empirical comparison on RedisRaft, Etcd and a Go reimplementation of RSL, plus a cube-world illustration. It provides bug-finding evidence, not a proof of protocol correctness or exhaustive coverage.  This reading covers arXiv:2409.02137v1, 2 September 2024: all 27 pages, 40 bibliography entries, five figures, seven tables and four algorithms. All renders were inspected through seven contact sheets; pages 7,8,18,20,21,22,23 were additionally viewed at full size. Official and inventory PDFs are identical. Selected static files from both linked GitHub repositories were read, with pinned commits and exact source quotations saved separately. Artifact metadata and any further source inspection are distinguished in source-scope.json. No author code or scientific experiment was executed, and no stored scientific results were loaded.  ## Policies and assumptions  The environment is treated as a Markov decision process: the next-state distribution should depend only on the current state and action. The learner uses a table of Q-values, which score state/action choices, and an epsilon-greedy policy: mostly pick a highest-scoring action, occasionally choose randomly (§2.1). Those assumptions describe the learning setup; the paper does not prove that every concrete distributed execution abstraction preserves them.  BonusMaxRL uses an exploration bonus inversely proportional to visits to a state/action pair. Its update combines the larger of that bonus and the discounted next-state Q-value, rather than adding accumulated rewards; Algorithm 2 processes episode transitions backwards (§2.2). The authors explicitly say their algorithm is not optimal for the usual accumulated-reward objective. There is no testing completeness, convergence-to-correctness or fault-coverage theorem.  WaypointRL maintains a separate Q-table for each predicate in a supplied sequence (§2.3, Algorithms 3–4). The first predicate is always true; the last defines the target. The highest-index true predicate selects the active table. Rewards of 2 favor progress to a later predicate and eventual arrival at the final target; the exploration bonus is at most 1. The oneTime flag keeps the final table active after the target has occurred, enabling exploration after an event without encoding its full history in each state. Predicates and instrumentation require human protocol knowledge. This paper does not learn specifications, infer the correct safety property or automate the choice of waypoints.  The cube illustration has dimensions 6×10×10×6,5000 episodes, horizon 80, α=.3 andγ=.99 (§2.4). It illustrates propagation of exploration rewards and guidance toward corners. The distributed evaluation uses different horizons and hyperparameters. Its figures are illustrative empirical curves, not a general sample-complexity bound.  ## Distributed cases and measurements  The test environment groups processes into network partitions, delivers messages within a partition and drops messages crossing partitions (§3). It also provides crashes, recoveries and client requests. Each test step runs a fixed number of clock ticks; a SameState counter distinguishes repeated unchanged configurations until the counter reaches its bound. The learner sees process colors, meaning selected state fields with process identities omitted and counters such as rounds bounded. These choices reduce the explored state space. A finite color-space coverage count is not coverage of all concrete executions, and no sound abstraction theorem or bisimulation is supplied.  Etcd uses its Go Raft implementation; RedisRaft uses an instrumented implementation with a network/control shim. The paper reports about 500 lines of added code for Etcd's roughly 7000 lines and 700 lines for RedisRaft's roughly 10000 lines (§5). RSL is the authors' Go reimplementation of Azure's protocol. The reported new RSL bug belongs to that reimplementation; it must not be attributed to the production Azure implementation.  Target predicates describe synchronized, unsynchronized or mixed process states (§4): all processes in a term, term differences, log-entry counts, a leader coexisting with a candidate, different commit positions, or RSL ballot/decree differences. Intermediate predicates break difficult targets into easier stages. These are testing goals, not complete distributed-system specifications. Choosing a target that correlates with a bug can improve detection without establishing that all relevant bugs share that target.  The common experiment setup has three processes, four ticks per partition action, a SameState counter limit of 5, at most three crash actions per episode and one simultaneously inactive process (§5.1). Each configuration runs 10000 episodes or 8 hours, whichever ends first, with at least 10 trials. Horizon 25 is used for Etcd/RSL and 50 for RedisRaft; early implementation failures can shorten episodes. Coverage curves therefore use time steps. BonusMaxRL/WaypointRL useα=.2, γ=.95, ε=.05; NegRLVisits usesα=.3, γ=.7 and softmax selection. Different policies consequently have different tuning; the comparison is of these chosen configurations.  Table 2 reports final unique-state means±standard deviations for Random, BonusMaxRL and NegRLVisits. RedisRaft:27081.9±2627.31,32818.4±3017.32,33433.2±2972.34; Etcd:19179.3±106.26,22202.7±137.75,24898.6±97.40; RSL:678.9±36.43,2020.9±190.67,751.2±37.24. BonusMaxRL improves over Random on all three, but exceeds NegRLVisits only on RSL (§5.2). The paper explicitly notes the remaining two favor NegRLVisits. It omits an empirical Mallory comparison because the required annotated source was unavailable; no Mallory superiority claim follows.  Across 26 target predicates, the authors report statistically significant target-coverage improvement for 20 (§5.3, Table 4). Exact rows, predicate-sequence lengths and deviations are retained in evaluation.json. Exceptions include RedisRaft OneInTerm(3), Etcd OneLeaderOneCandidate and RSL EntryBallot(2), where an unbiased baseline has a larger mean. Means alone do not establish statistical significance. Section 5.1 prints a Mann–Whitney threshold of “> 0.05”; that direction is opposite the usual small-p-value rejection criterion. No p-values or raw trials were inspected, so this record retains the authors' significance claims with that unresolved reporting ambiguity.  Intermediate rewards can help, but more waypoints do not consistently help (§5.3, Table 5). RedisRaft LogCommitDiff(3) rises from 264±99 without intermediates to 18309±2820 with one, versus 17287±3102 with three; targeting only LogDiff(1) yields 1578±931 in the LogCommitDiff target space. EntryInTerm(2) rises from 22468.1±5295.2 to 28173.7±6935.9 with two intermediates. RSL DecidedDiff(3) rises from 26.4±13.2 to 173.1±70.1 with one intermediate, versus 113.7±46.8 with two. The Table 5 caption's “one example from each benchmark” is inaccurate: it contains two RedisRaft examples and one RSL example.  ## Bugs and limits on the comparison  The paper reports 13 bugs:10 RedisRaft,2 Etcd and 1 in the RSL reimplementation; five are described as new, comprising 3 RedisRaft,1 Etcd and 1 portedRSL (§5.4). RedisRaft's Table 7 distinguishes seven crashes from three safety violations: inconsistent committed logs, loss of committed entries and modification of committed entries. The bugs require implementation and trace analysis; the learner is not itself a correctness oracle.  Table 6 contains nonzero entries for 13 bugs under WaypointRL,10 under BonusMaxRL,7 under NegRLVisits and 11 under Random. Crucially, its WaypointRL column selects the highest average for each bug over target predicates, naming the selected predicate. This is a campaign aggregate with per-bug selection, not one fixed WaypointRL policy finding all 13 under the same total testing budget as a baseline. The paper does not report an equal-total-budget comparison of that campaign; the record does not invent an exact multiplier for its cost.  The selected WaypointRL mean is highest for 11 of 13 bugs. BonusMaxRL has 6499.8 versus WaypointRL 5704.6 for RaftRestoreLog; Random has 4.5 versus WaypointRL 1.3 for ConnIsConnected. The comparison therefore supports frequent reproduction in many selected cases, not universal dominance. No independent reproduction, bug-fix validation or analysis of false-positive/negative rates was performed in this reading.  Etcd's prose conflicts with Table 6. The table gives IncorrectLogRestore only WaypointRL 0.1; NilSnapshotPanic has WaypointRL 0.3 and Random 0.2. The prose says the new incorrect-log-restoration bug was found by biased and random exploration with the same frequency, while the known bug was found only by biased exploration. This appears to swap the two attributions, and its equal-frequency statement also differs from 0.3 versus 0.2. The record preserves both rather than deciding which is correct without traces.  Two smaller paper issues do not establish implementation failures. Its Raft background gives an n/3 crash threshold (§3), whereas majority-based crash consensus conventionally tolerates fewer than half; the actual tested three-process/one-inactive setup is compatible with a majority. Full-size Algorithm 3 confirms its else belongs to the outer reached test, consistent with its explanation; a contrary extraction-based suspicion was rejected. Algorithm 4 omits explicit false/zero initialization for reachedFinal/finalR, and its final-reward distance can be negative after a first target visit if oneTime is false and stages later change. Those are pseudocode completeness/interpretation concerns until tied to a specific implementation version.  ## Static artifacts and contribution  The two linked GitHub repositories are different source snapshots. raft-rl-test is pinned at f9b203642905310a5f61c7f191a0016982e577c8 (15 January 2024); dist-rl-testing at e26c838f16b73fd04616276f47158f371bb040a8 (27 June 2025). The former predates this paper version and the latter postdates it. Neither live default-branch snapshot is assumed to be the evaluated artifact merely because the paper links it. The Zenodo concept pointer 12671211 and version pointer 13166254 both resolve in the fetched API metadata to version 0.3.1, record 13166254. Metadata inspection is separate from any archive files actually read.  Selected live files confirm max-based visit bonuses and manually specified predicate machines, but differ from the paper. raft-rl-test's ordinary bonus updates online; its reward-machine branch updates segments backwards using 2+1/(t+1) for progress and has no global final-target-distance bonus. Its inspected Redis setup disables crashes and uses three partition ticks, unlike the paper's common setup. The later dist-rl-testing hierarchy also lacks the printed final-distance bonus, always latches final-target arrival, initializes the stage to 0 without checking the initial state, and its backward loop usesj>0, skipping the first stored transition of each segment, including every one-step segment. These are static properties of those pins; their effect on the paper's trials is not established.  The 22.3 MB Zenodo 0.3.1 source archive was downloaded and its published MD 5 checked. Its 82 member names were inspected; nine selected source/documentation files were extracted, without extracting or running its binaries. Its bonus/hierarchy policy files are byte-identical to the inspected later live files, so the online-update, missing-final-distance and skipped-segment-transition differences also apply to this released artifact. The archive contains Etcd/RSL and CometBFT source, with no RedisRaft source member. Its README supplies Etcd/RSL reproduction instructions; full virtual machines were not downloaded, so their contents are uninspected.  The released target-coverage analyzer latches the target once seen and counts hashes of multisets of node colors after that point, rather than retaining the partition configuration in that coverage key (Q42). This agrees with the paper’s reported coverage metric, a “multi-set of colors” (§5.1, Q15), which is coarser than the MDP state containing a partition configuration (§3.1, Q8). Its plotting/statistical scripts use one-sided Mann–Whitney calls with alternative="greater", but do not apply a p-value cutoff in the inspected code. Thus that source does not resolve the paper's printed threshold direction. Plots/mean summaries truncate each policy's run arrays to their shortest episode-count length and take time-step coordinates from one run; the significance calls instead use each run's final array element. Those procedures need not compare identical time-step budgets after early failures. No actual discrepancy in the reported numbers was established because outputs were not loaded.  Released Etcd pure-coverage setup assigns MaxCrashedNodes from flags.MaxCrashActions, whereas its hierarchy setup supplies separate MaxCrashedNodes/MaxCrashActions fields. RSL's two inspected setup functions likewise assign MaxCrashedNodes from MaxCrashActions and omit the separate crash-action field. This is a concrete configuration mismatch worth checking before reproduction; its actual runtime effect requires following the environment/default definitions, which are outside the selected source scope. The source archive is linked evidence of what was released, not proof that the paper's measured trials used every inspected branch. No author execution, virtual-machine launch or experiment-output loading occurred.  For the human's topic, the contribution is a concrete way to direct execution testing toward semantically interesting distributed states and an example of how to evaluate that guidance. A possible use with specification/proof-writing agents is to turn stated intermediate conditions into test goals and independently check resulting traces. That is a reader inference, not an LLM-agent experiment in this paper. The paper discusses IronFleet, Verdi and bugs at verified/unverified boundaries, but supplies no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM proof-generation case. Testing success remains distinct from a proof and from validation that a chosen formal specification captures the intended behavior.  Further static review of the released hierarchy shows that action selection passes a default Q-value of 1, while update lookups pass 0; its outOfSpace/end-of-segment branch repeats the same next-state maximum lookup already performed immediately above it (Q38, lines 169 and 187–191). This is a source-level difference from the printed subspace treatment, not an established effect on the measured trials. Released pure-versus-hierarchy configurations also differ in Etcd election/heartbeat ticks (16/4 versus 9/3; Q39) and RSL heartbeat interval (3 versus 2; Q40). Historical trial provenance remains unconfirmed.

- SCION router verification (2024)
    - title: Protocols to Code: Formal Verification of a Next-Generation Internet Router
    - what: Presents end-to-end verification of a production SCION border router: Isabelle/HOL refinement proves path authorization, valley freedom and loop freedom under a strong adversary; Gobra verifies optimized concurrent Go code for memory safety, crash/race freedom, finite processing and protocol conformance. Igloo soundly links protocol and code models. Protocol models progress from weak to Dolev–Yao adversaries and extract an I/O specification for code. Code proofs use four layers, modular function verification, outline statements for large functions and Gobra preprocessing that splits queries/removes irrelevant assumptions soundly. The effort discovered five protocol attacks and thirteen implementation issues; developers confirmed the issues, fixed most, and adopted stronger valley/loop checks. Weekly synchronization and version pinning handled moving code/protocol targets.

One minor protocol attack remained under discussion; implementation verification was laborious and tool performance constrained progress.

- SCYTHE distributed protocol synthesis (2024)
    - title: Efficient Synthesis of Symbolic Distributed Protocols by Sketching
    - what: Introduces SCYTHE, a syntax-guided and counterexample-guided synthesizer for completing TLA+ sketches of parameterized distributed protocols. It enumerates typed expressions with cache/equivalence reduction and short-circuiting, uses TLC to check finite instances, and generalizes counterexamples into pruning constraints for safety, deadlock, liveness, and stuttering. The tool synthesizes protocols including consensus, 2PC, locks, sharded stores, and Raft reconfiguration. The paper formalizes protocol instances, fairness, sketches with pre/post holes and regular-tree grammars, and distinguishes finite-instance synthesis (Problem 1) from all-parameter-instance synthesis (Problem 2). Candidate generation uses cache-based size enumeration and semantic normal forms for Boolean/set/equality expressions; pruning constraints are disjunctions of hole interpretations. Safety constraints are optimal, while deadlock/liveness/stuttering encodings are sub-optimal but non-over-pruning; fairness and explicit implementability/environment constraints prevent vacuous solutions. TLC exhaustive checks each finite instance. In 22 benchmark rows, equivalence reduction cuts generated expressions by orders of magnitude; final TLAPS proofs establish safety for arbitrary instances in all but the two-process-only Peterson cases. Extra-checks expose finite-size overfitting: two Raft variants initially correct up to 3 nodes failed at 4+ and required larger-instance checks.
    - number: 22 benchmark configurations
    - number: up to >3 orders of magnitude expression reduction
    - number: raft-reconfig ID 121: 694,552 to 271 expressions
    - number: 4-node extra-check caught 3-node overfitting
    - limits: Synthesis guarantees only the finite instance checked by TLC unless an independent proof (TLAPS) establishes parameterized correctness; the search problem is generally undecidable. Grammar restrictions, typed symbols, opaque domains, finite-state verifier instances, fairness constraints, and manually specified implementability/environment separation shape results. Liveness pruning is sub-optimal; weak-fairness handling may under-prune. TLC calls dominate many runs, and the final all-instance verification remains a difficult/undecidable step. Benchmarks are adapted from existing specifications and may not represent arbitrary distributed protocols.

- SquirrelFS: using the Rust compiler to check file-system crash consistency (2024)
    - what: A 7500-line Rust persistent-memory file system uses typestate to enforce ordering constraints of synchronous soft updates (SSU). Persistence and operational types restrict legal update sequences; recovery rename pointers provide metadata rename atomicity. A separately authored Alloy model checks bounded concurrent/crash traces, while tests exercise unmodeled code. Evaluation compares runtime latency/throughput and compilation against Ext4-DAX, NOVA and WineFS, and reports SquirrelFS mount/recovery costs and index-memory sizes. Reconstructs six-stage rename/recovery, dirty/in-flight/clean typestate and ownership requirements, mkdir dependencies, backpointer layout and range-type trust. Records all empirical checks/bugs, model bounds, frame-condition failures, compile/mount tables and benchmark baseline numbers. Qualifies complete-checking language as conditional ordering enforcement rather than end-to-end crash consistency, and saves adverse recovery/memory/performance cases.
    - limits: §§1,3.5: Authors explicitly state SquirrelFS is not fully verified. Successful compilation checks ordering encoded in types, assuming those rules, transition bodies, unsafe/FFI/ownership interfaces and Rust compiler are correct. It does not prove data values, inode contents, arbitrary functional behavior or the sufficiency of the rules for crash consistency. Table 1 marks this work Complete, but the later explicit trust/coverage qualifications constrain that label. §§3.1,3.4: x86 PM model assumes aligned writes of at most eight bytes are crash atomic. Cache-line writeback and store fence must make/order writes durable; non-temporal stores still require a fence. No proof of hardware/flush primitive correctness is supplied. Every system call is synchronous and fsync is a no-op; metadata operations are crash atomic, file-data updates are not. §3.1: SSU enforces initialize-before-link, clear-old-pointers-before-reuse and new-link-before-removing-old-link. Synchronous calls and fine-grained updates on byte-addressable storage avoid traditional cross-operation pending-dependency graphs/cycles. This simplification does not prohibit concurrent calls; VFS locking must serialize conflicting resource access. A future asynchronous implementation requires more complex rules. §3.2 Listings 1–2: Persistence types Dirty→InFlight via flush→Clean via fence are independent of operational types such as Free/Init/Alloc/Committed. Transition functions consume old wrapper ownership and return a new type. Compiler can reject inappropriate ordering or redundant persistence calls through this API, but cannot confirm the instruction flushes the right address or a body initializes every required field. §§3.2,3.4: Rust ownership plus VFS resource locking must ensure each durable resource has one owner/type at a time; indexes/allocators have internal locks. Reader qualification: Rust permits shared references, so the paper’s one-owner statement is about the exclusive mutable typestate wrapper discipline, not a claim that Rust forbids every alias. No concurrent implementation-refinement theorem or liveness proof is provided. §3.4: Persistent allocation means any object byte nonzero; validity of dentries/page descriptors is set inode number, validity of inodes is root reachability. Deallocation clears links before zeroing every byte. Volatile allocators/indexes are reconstructed by scanning. Backpointers in page descriptors simplify dependencies at the cost of mount scans/DRAM indexes; per-CPU page allocators and one global inode allocator affect scalability. §§3.4,5.7: Alloy model has roughly one-to-one transition correspondence with Rust typestate transitions, separately authored and not mechanically linked to code. Checks are bounded to two possibly concurrent operations, ten persistent objects and at most thirty steps. Bounded model success is not a proof of every-size/every-length implementation execution. §§4.1–4.3: General initialization typestate combines many field writes, deliberately trading bug coverage for simpler interfaces. Unbounded collections cannot be checked element by element with the chosen Rust types, so one typestate represents a page range and trusted transition loops update every page. This moves the universal obligation into unchecked bodies; it does not prove all range elements were updated correctly. §4.3 reader qualification: The broad claim that universally quantified formulas are undecidable must be read as general unrestricted checking, not a claim that every universally quantified property is undecidable. The concrete limitation is this unmodified Rust/typestate encoding cannot prove all objects in dynamically sized collections meet a property. Richer theorem provers or other encodings may establish particular quantified properties. §4.3: Alloy checking can take days/weeks. Missing frame conditions permit unconstrained state changes and yield false positives; custom syntactic checker demands each transition mention all mutable structures but explicitly cannot detect every issue. Parallel independent checks and split invariants improve turnaround without proving model intent or implementation correspondence. §4.4: No equivalent verified/unverified system exists for controlled development-effort comparison. Authors’ lower-effort/faster-debugging statements are experience and belief. Footnote durable-log three months is one author’s separate experience, not a measured SquirrelFS development duration. Staying synchronized through types applies to encoded API rules, not automatically to omitted requirements or incorrect transition bodies. §5.1: Measurements use two-socket 32-core machine,128GB DRAM,128GB Intel Optane DC PM,Debian Bookworm/Linux6.3. Baselines configured for metadata consistency without data atomicity to match prototype. SoupFS unavailable as closed source; ArckFS excluded for time. Means of multiple trials with plotted min/max; microbenchmarks specify ten trials. No per-system equal-functionality or production-maturity claim follows. §§5.2–5.4: Microbenchmarks do not call fsync, but SquirrelFS already makes each call durable. Filebench defaults; RocksDB/YCSB uses25GB/25M records/25M operations/eight threads and normal syscall interfaces. LMDB100M keys uses mmap, reducing metadata/syscall differences. - TLA+ trace validation (2024)
    - title: Validating Traces of Distributed Programs Against TLA+ Specifications
    - what: Presents an API and TLC-based constrained model-checking workflow that records selected specification-variable updates from Java executions and checks whether the partial trace can be completed to a behavior of a TLA+ specification. The framework traces only chosen variables/events, leaving omitted values existentially open for TLC to reconstruct. It handles stuttering steps and implementation transitions that combine multiple TLA+ actions, and uses shortest BFS counterexamples or constrained DFS for speed. Case studies include Two-Phase Commit, snapshot-isolation key-value store, EWD998 termination detection, two Raft implementations and Microsoft CCF; trace validation found mismatches and exposed a CCF safety bug that became regression tests.
    - number: Counter implementation bug detected in less than one minute with event-only trace for 16 RMs
    - number: Two-Phase Commit 16 RMs event-only trace explores ∞/557k states (BFS/DFS table)
    - number: Key-value 12-agent, 20-key/40-value event-only trace reaches ∞ states at 1-hour timeout
    - number: Five distributed-program case studies all yielded specification/implementation discrepancies
    - limits: Verdicts depend on instrumentation points, trace granularity and the high-level specification. Too-imprecise logs can admit erroneous traces because TLC fills unconstrained values; too much logging causes state explosion. TLC explores finite bounded models and can return no counterexample for an invalid trace when the searched diameter is insufficient. The method detects conformance discrepancies, not a proof that all executions of the implementation satisfy the specification.

- Using Dynamically Layered Definite Releases for Verifying the RefFS File System (2024)
    - what: The RefFS project page links a separate 124-page draft, Progress of Concurrent Objects with Dynamic Dependencies, authored by Mo Zou. Its PDF metadata dates it May24,2024; the project says “A separate paper” illustrates MoLi's metatheory (P1). This is a complete fresh reading of that PODD paper, not an appendix of the OSDI paper and not a new reading of the RefFS implementation. The original RefFS main-paper account remains inherited from formal509. Whether this precise draft proves every rule of the released MoLi framework is not established by the link alone.  PODD makes a thread's progress depend on definite actions, obligations that their owning threads must fulfill once enabled. Actions have state-dependent layers, and dependencies must preserve strict relative order even when numeric layers change. Layers have a total order, not necessarily a well-founded one. Finite dependency sets and decreasing local/stack metrics supply the termination argument. The LIVE-FRM rule extends action/layer context while preserving old ordering, so an acquisition proof can be reused without expanding every nested wait chain. Tokens account for unblocked loop progress and finitely many levels of delaying interference. Theorem4.2 states linearizability and deadlock-freedom; starvation-freedom additionally requires rely and guarantee actions at level0 (S12,S14,S15).  AppendixA supplies the fuller resource/ownership logic, fences, rules and ideal shared-memory semantics. AppendixB first gives judgment simulations with finite-height while stacks: arbitrary-length lexicographic lists would not be well-founded (S31). B.3 expands new while/live-frame cases. B.4 maps these to a common simulation, directly for starvation-freedom and through a lock plus nondeterministically decreasing finite-wait wrapper for deadlock-freedom (S45,S48). B.5 combines thread simulations using finite active-thread dependency sets, scheduler rounds and a lexicographic metric. LemmasB.22–B.30 connect coinductive fair traces to refinement (S54,S57,S58,S66,S69). B.6 defines progress over complete fair traces, permitting abort alternatives, and uses three most-general clients to relate finite refinement to linearizability and fair refinement to linearizability plus starvation/deadlock freedom. The deadlock equivalence wraps the atomic specification; it must not be replaced by the stronger starvation refinement (S72,S74).  AppendixC provides all printed proof outlines for nested TAS/ticket locks, ticket-lock coupling lists, optimistic/lazy TAS lists, and two-list transfers. Ticket queues support starvation-freedom; unfair TAS permits only the weaker deadlock-freedom claim. Lists use local lock obligations, node order and finite traversal metrics. Optimistic/lazy cases retain removed nodes in ghost garbage, not a proved memory-reclamation scheme. Lazy contain is explicitly omitted. Transfers use one mutex to serialize moves, list levels0/1/2 and lexicographic (listlevel,distance-to-tail) layers; their add/remove proofs are referred to earlier lists. The two-list move is a useful dynamic-dependency example, rather than a distributed network/crash model (S87,S90,S94,S102,S109,S116,S122,S124).  Evaluation consists of paper proofs and worked examples; no numerical benchmark, proof-time table or replayed mechanization is supplied here. Section6 explicitly makes mechanization and automation future work (S20). Section5.1 admits that common rely conditions and frame stability can prevent reuse across objects (S17). Assumptions include fair scheduling, an arbitrary fixed finite number of threads, ideal atomic memory actions, safe total abstract methods and the presented non-nested method-call language. No bounded response-time, weak-memory, crash/recovery or implementation-to-binary theorem follows from this reading.  Reader deductions from the literal listings must be kept separate from intended theorems. Figure40's inner ticket loop never increments o; Figure55's elems retains marked values and discards unmarked ones; Figure62's sequential MOVE removes a head before reading the new head. Details and elementary counterexamples are in reader_diagnostics.json, with exact page anchors. These are printed-source defects, not findings about unseen code or a global refutation of PODD. The page also has draft-level omissions: a duplicated strict-comparison branch in the proof on p57, an apparent dependency-set type slip in DefinitionB.12, and an unresolved Fig.?? reference plus omitted scheduler semantics on p58. Underlines/fonts were visually checked before identifying these issues.  Relevance to the requested database is manual liveness proof structure and evaluation of specification/proof agents: track actual fairness and progress strength, stable dependency ordering, finite metrics, abstract-method contracts, omitted cases and intended versus literal specifications. These are reader uses of a concurrency result. This paper does not evaluate Verus, Rust, TLA+, LLM agents or distributed consensus. RefFS/Coq performance and proof counts remain attributed to the inherited OSDI paper, rather than this draft. Records exact WHILE/OBJECT obligations, ticket and abstract-lock metric differences, dynamic-layer/TDep construction, VFS bug cycle and source typo, refcount ownership protocol, non-atomic operation abstraction, conditional theorem and unmechanized metatheory, survey denominators, all LOC cells, workloads, normalized performance limits and graph estimates. Separates checked RefFS proofs from trusted C/runtime/lock/allocator and protocol-only VFS reasoning.

Original21page RefFS main reading inherited from formal509. Separate PODD draft is not a same-title appendix or proof-assistant replay. S12,S15,S72,S74: fair scheduling and arbitrary fixed finite thread count; linearizability plus deadlock-freedom generally, starvation-freedom only under level0 rely/guarantee restriction. Abort alternatives in progress definitions do not establish memory safety by themselves. S10,S22,S23,S27: ideal shared-memory language, primitive atomic operations and specified safe/total abstract methods; presented language excludes nested method calls. No weak-memory, compiled implementation, network/crash/recovery or bounded response-time theorem. S12,S14,S31,S54,S66: total ordering of layers is distinct from well-founded local/stack metrics. Dynamic numeric ranks may change while actual strict dependency relations remain stable. Finite-height stack bound and finite active-thread sets are substantive premises. - Verifying Randomized Consensus Protocols with Common Coins (2024)
    - what: # Whole-paper record: Verifying Randomized Consensus Protocols with Common Coins (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Song Gao, Bohua Zhan, Zhilin Wu and Lijun Zhang. DSN 2024, IEEE, pp.403–415; DOI 10.1109/DSN58291.2024.00047. Read arXiv 2409.17627v1, submitted 26 September 2024, all 13 PDF pages, §§I–VIII, all 27 references, six figures and four tables. Inspected every page image. Publication pagination comes from Crossref; this PDF has no printed page numerals (Q52). Exact extracted passages with PDF pages and source lines are in quotes.json and combined.quote-source.txt. No author code, compiler, checker, prover, solver or serialized experiment/model data was executed or loaded.  ## Contribution and claimed guarantees (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The paper extends parameterized threshold-automaton verification from independent local coins to a shared common coin. It adds a separate coin automaton and communication variables, giving an infinite-state Markov decision process with process-location counters, per-round shared variables and resilience parameters (§III,Q9–17). Byzantine processes are represented through their effect on threshold guards rather than explicit Byzantine automata (§III-A,Q8). This is a verification method for protocol models, not an implementation refinement or verified executable.  Safety and termination follow different reductions. For safety, two one-round invariants imply agreement and binary validity (Proposition 1,Q20–21). Theorem 1 states that any finite schedule can be reordered by rounds while preserving its final configuration and per-round stutter equivalence (Q22). Theorem 2 relates one-round LTL without next-time properties to a single-round system, assuming nonblocking behavior and termination of every fair single-round execution for all initial configurations (Q24). These assumptions matter; it is not an unrestricted equivalence between arbitrary multi-round properties and one bounded run.  For termination the paper distinguishes three categories (§V-B,Q26–28). Category A has no decide event and targets eventual convergence to a common final value. Category B has binary messages and explicit decisions. Category C uses a Binary Crusader Agreement stage that may output ⊥, meaning undecided. C1 requires a uniform positive probability of converging during a round. C2 preserves unanimity; C2′ instead gives a positive probability of deciding when the round starts unanimously. Proposition 3 supplies a two-round geometric argument: the probability of not deciding after 2r rounds is at most `(1−p·p′)^r` (Q29).  Binding fixes a bit at the first relevant execution prefix and excludes its opposite in every continuation. It is a property of sets of executions, beyond ordinary single-execution agreement (Definition 4,Q30). The model refinement introduces N0, N1, N⊥ locations so that five sufficient safety conditions, CB0–CB4, imply binding (Proposition 4,Q31–32). Proposition 5 combines binding and C2′ for termination (Q33). Lemma 2 states that, in the single-round setting, a uniform positive probability under every admissible adversary is equivalent to each adversary having some satisfying path (Q35). That quantifier order is stronger than merely finding one favorable schedule.  The proof record is mixed. Lemma 1 has a one-line justification. Proposition 2 calls its proof trivial after a geometric-tail argument. Propositions 3–5 provide paper proofs; Corollary 1 cites them. Proposition 1, Theorems 1–2 and Lemma 2 explicitly omit proofs for length (Q21,Q24–25,Q35). proof-inventory.json records all ten named results and their assumptions. No proof-assistant artifact was inspected, and this reading does not independently establish their soundness.  ## Assumptions and limits (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The network is asynchronous and reliable: a sent message is “eventually received” without “loss, duplication or modification,” and receivers identify senders (§I(a),Q3). Byzantine faults are bounded by the selected resilience condition. The common coin is a trusted, fault-free abstraction, and only strong coins are considered: both bits are common outputs with probability 1/2. Cryptographic implementation correctness is future work (Q2–3,Q41).  The model separates shared-message guards from coin guards. Correct processes cannot update coin variables; coin rules cannot modify shared variables. Automata are canonical: rules on cycles have zero updates (§III-B,Q10–13). The method is parameterized by the environment's admissible n,t,f values, rather than verifying only the example cluster sizes.  The termination specification is explicitly “under Round-rigid Adversaries” (§IV,Q19). Such an adversary is fair and schedules all actions of round k before those of round k+1 (§III-E,Q17). Removing this restriction is future work (§VIII,Q41). Finite safety-trace reordering does not establish probabilistic termination for arbitrary asynchronous adaptive schedulers.  No benchmark archive, model file or proof-artifact URL is identified in the read paper. The paper says it builds two one-round automaton versions per protocol, but those inputs and their transformations were not available in the inspected sources (Q36–37). This does not assert that no artifact exists elsewhere. No ByMC run was reproduced.  ## Cases and reported evaluation (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The benchmark comprises Rabin83, CC85(a), CC85(b), FMR05, KS16, MMR14, Miller18 and ABY22 (§VI,Q36; Table II,Q45). Their protocol descriptions give different Byzantine bounds: for example Rabin83 uses t<n/10, CC85(b) t<n/6, and CC85(a), KS16 and ABY22 use n>3t. These protocol descriptions should not be substituted for the undisclosed exact checked input environments.  Table II reports model locations/rules, execution-schema counts and verification time for agreement, validity and almost-sure termination. The authors “ran each experiments 10 times” and report averages, without raw trials or dispersion (§VI,Q37). The first six rows use an Intel Core i7-12650H laptop; the final two use a 216-core AMD EPYC7702 server in parallel mode. Times measure verification work, not consensus latency or throughput.  Small examples complete quickly: Rabin83 has 7 locations/17 rules and reported times 0.25s for agreement, 0.20s for validity and 0.43s for its convergence target. CC85(a) uses 342 schemas/4.93s for agreement and an average 171.5 schemas/2.70s for termination. Fractional schema counts are averages. All eight rows and all table values are retained in numeric-evidence.json.  MMR14 has 17 locations/29 rules. Its agreement and validity checks take 298.90s and 8.74s. The termination column says CE, with no time. Separately, §VI reports a CB2 violation “within 10 seconds at best,” with an example witness n=193,t=64 (Q38). A failed sufficient condition alone does not prove nontermination. The authors additionally analyze the returned execution, compare it with a known adaptive attack and describe repeating its final actions to recreate the opposite estimate distribution.  The motivating four-node example has three correct processes and one Byzantine process. Two correct processes obtain the coin result s, while the adversary delays messages to the third until it can force estimate 1−s; the round can repeat (§II,Q7). This is a prior attack, not a new vulnerability discovered by the paper. Miller's 2018 issue credits Ethan MacBrough and explains that the actual coin instantiation lacks the independence assumed by the earlier ABA proof (Q48–49). The issue proposes an extra CONF phase before revealing coin shares (Q50). Its later implementation comments were read as allegations, without auditing the linked code (Q51).  The two repaired category C variants reportedly pass their obligations. Miller18 takes 11h46m47s and ABY22 takes 10h13m14s for all termination conditions, each exceeding 10^8 schemas; agreement takes 605s and 583s, respectively (Table II,Q45). The paper also describes 24-hour timeouts for the earlier technique on category C models, without a controlled cross-hardware speedup comparison (Q37).  Table IV changes milestone counts from 10 to 6 in five same-size ABY22-based automata. Calculated maximum schemas fall from 98,182,294 to 28,918 for CB0 and 7,479,057 to 3,592 for Inv2 (Q39,Q47). These are calculated search bounds, not measured runtime reductions or proof that the variants preserve protocol semantics. Table I supplies MMR14 transition guards and updates; Table III lists selected value 0 formulas and an ellipsis, rather than complete checker inputs. Figures 1–6 provide pseudocode, voting and MMR14 automata, and the binding refinement.  ## Source discrepancies that qualify interpretation (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Three points remain unresolved from the printed sources. They are recorded as static comparisons, not reproduced checker failures or counterexamples to a full theorem.  - Example 2 gives the MMR14 environment `n>5t` (Q9), while §II describes n>3t and §VI reports n=193,t=64. That witness satisfies 193 > 192 but not 193 > 320. The exact checked resilience condition cannot be recovered from the paper alone. - Proposition 5 reasons that no correct process has executed a coin-based rule, “in other words” the coin “is not yet tossed,” and therefore its result is independent of the binding bit (Q33). Figure 4 and Table I instead show rb with guard true, from initial coin location I2 to N0/N1, followed by unconditional rc/rd publishing its outcome (Q13,Q43–44). Under the initial-state and action definitions, a finite round 0 prefix can execute rb then rc before any correct-process transition. The adversary observes configuration histories (Q15,Q17). Thus the stated timing inference needs a further visibility or scheduling condition that is not enforced by these displayed rules. This prefix does not refute the full theorem or a benchmark protocol; it identifies an unsupported step in the supplied model-to-proof account. - Table III labels C1 with a universal implication excluding mixed final values along every path after a 0-valued final event (Q46). Body C1 is a positive-probability convergence condition, reduced through a per-adversary existential-path condition (Q27,Q35). The displayed statements differ. Separate model versions might explain a stronger checked obligation, but their concrete transformation is not supplied here, so the table cannot establish that correspondence.  The coin prefix, resilience arithmetic and quantifier comparison are in static-witnesses.json. All relevant formulas and table entries were checked against rendered PDF pages, rather than relying only on text extraction.  ## Relevance to the requested topic (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  This work directly addresses parameterized verification of randomized Byzantine consensus, especially the relation between common randomness, adaptive scheduling, binding and almost-sure termination. It supplies concrete verification-cost evidence and an example of using failed proof obligations to investigate a known attack. It also shows why a safety-preserving reordering theorem, a probabilistic termination argument and a checker result must retain their separate assumptions.  For evaluating LLM-written specifications or proofs, the reader-derived lesson is to check scheduler quantifiers, coin secrecy and independence, the exact resilience environment, source-to-formula correspondence, proof availability and what a counterexample actually disproves. The paper contains no LLM, Verus or verified Rust experiment. Its TLA proof-system reference concerns related HotStuff work, not this paper's verification method (Q40,Q42). HoneyBadger/Dumbo composition and cryptographic primitive verification remain future work (Q41).
    - limits: Parameterized canonical threshold automata under resilience environments; reliable eventual authenticated-sender delivery, no loss/duplication/modification; assumed strong fault-free common coin. Almost-sure termination only for fair round-rigid adversaries. CategoryA convergence differs from categoriesB/C decisions. Nonblocking and all fair single-round termination are prerequisites for reduction. Several central proofs omitted; printed resilience, coin-visibility argument and C1 formula correspondence unresolved.
