- Design and Verification of the Arm Confidential Compute Architecture (2022)
    - what: Arm CCA isolates Realm VMs from malicious hypervisors using a separate hardware physical-address space and verified RMM/EL3 monitor firmware. VIA verifies an early concurrent C/Arm-assembly prototype through Coq refinement and simulation of an ideal model with explicit declassification. Techniques combine local CPU rely/guarantee with movers, program-specific conditions transferring SC proofs to relaxed Arm memory, and ABI-based accounting for registers hidden by C. Functional tests use an architectural Fast Model; preliminary performance uses modified non-CCA Arm hardware. Records delegation/GPT/GST/PAR semantics and all RMI operations, exact mover/log and RTT uniqueness proof, all six permutation conditions and real reordering bug, detailed ABI/inline-assembly restrictions, six declassification rules and three simulation relations, unverified initialization/crypto/compiler/hardware boundaries, concrete bugs, complete Coq and benchmark tables, workload settings and qualified bar estimates. Preserves 43-versus-45 layer and seven-versus-eight hypercall-register wording differences and distinguishes secure functional model from insecure performance emulation.
    - limits: §§1–2: Protects confidentiality/integrity of VM registers and memory against compromised hypervisor/other VMs, memory remapping/aliasing and DMA under GPT enforcement. VM must not itself disclose private data. No availability guarantee; hypervisor can stop scheduling or reclaim memory, causing protected accesses to halt. Physical attacks, DRAM probing/replay/cold boot, side channels and software-error injection are excluded or require separate mitigations. §3: Hardware must correctly implement Realm/NS/Root/Secure PAS checks, GPT, exception/virtualization and DMA checks. Root EL3M may access all PAS; RMM controls Realm VMs at Realm EL2. Firmware verification does not verify hardware or microarchitecture. Paper focuses NS/Realm interactions; detailed Secure-world behavior is omitted. §3: Hypervisor controls all dynamic resources but must delegate zeroed granules before RMM use. GPT is hardware permission state; separate GST is software bookkeeping for granule use. Protected addresses inside PAR map only private Realm Data; outside PAR may deliberately access shared NS/device data. Untrusted I/O payloads are not covered as confidential private memory. §3: Reclaim zeros and unmaps private memory; future access faults/halts. A previously backed protected IPA cannot be remapped without Realm permission. This is integrity against observing unauthorized changes, not durable data availability or prevention of every malicious deallocation. Remote-attestation initialization hashes IPA/data but relies on unverified crypto. §4.1: Global logical event log abstracts interleaved CPUs. Per-CPU environment oracle yields unseen other-CPU events under rely/guarantee conditions, not a prophetic runtime component or unrestricted assumption. Mover proofs justify rearranging queries, then aggregating local events; right/left/none classifications must be established against permitted environment actions. §4.2/§5.2: Relaxed-memory result is relative to VRM extended Promising Arm model and proved permutation conditions. Decomposition separates DRF code from non-DRF parts. Non-DRF conditions must both hold for allowed hardware reorderings and imply SC-equivalent behavior; arbitrary proposed conditions do not automatically establish arbitrary racy programs correct. §4.3: C/assembly accounting assumes AAPCS64-conforming compilation and the stated C integer/pointer calling shape (≤8 parameters, scalar/pointer return). Tracks unknown caller-saved registers conservatively and requires assembly independence from them. It does not verify an optimizing Arm compiler or establish correctness of every possible C ABI/language feature. §4.3 Figure6: Inline assembly translated to logical input/output registers; supports r,Q,m constraints, prohibits explicit GPR names/goto labels, and requires multi-instruction outputs constrained & or + to avoid unintended overlap. Paper prose says final read by set_pr, whereas code and preceding definition use get_pr; record uses code-consistent get_pr. These are concrete supported cases, not unrestricted inline assembly. §4.4/§5.4: Ideal model gives each Realm private memory and each REC exclusive registers, with six explicit declassification rules. Simulation preserves memory/register observations despite allocation control. This intentionally weaker availability-sensitive integrity property differs from standard noninterference; failure to apply a particular standard formulation does not prove that every generalized noninterference formalism is impossible. §5: Proof covers early prototype RMM/EL3M runtime C/assembly, excluding assembly initialization (.1K RMM/.5K EL3M) and external cryptographic library. Simulation assumes correct initial relation at boot. Later production firmware and current CCA architectures are not automatically verified by this historical result. Roughly .2K Coq ideal specification is trusted security policy, not the total trusted computing base: hardware/model, Coq, compiler/ABI, initialization and crypto remain relevant. §1/§5: Introduction says43refinement layers; §5 says45total layers and gives machine-model, spinlock, three EL3M,39RMM, ideal-model breakdown. Preserve this accounting distinction rather than reporting a single count without context. RTT atomicity takes nine layers; REC.Run takes five. §4.4 Table3 versus §5.4: Table specifies seven hypercall GPRs r0–r6 and four RMM-call GPRs r0–r3, plus system/timer/emulation disclosure. §5.4 concluding prose calls them eight hypercall GPRs. This source inconsistency is retained; no inference that all registers are protected from every intended disclosure. §6: Fast Model has RME functional behavior but is not cycle accurate and too slow for full application performance. N1SDP performance port lacks GPT/Realm hardware and cannot enforce security. Two NS contexts mimic world switching; GPT memory writes occur but register control/check costs are absent. Expectations that GPT cost cancels, future interrupts/passthrough improve costs are predictions, not measured results. §6: N1SDP GIC writes make some userspace exits about800ns more expensive; prototype lacks direct virtual interrupt injection. Thus measurements neither establish actual CCA-hardware performance nor a strict lower/upper bound. Modified KVM/QEMU/guest integration demonstrates functionality without proving the full application/device stack. §6.2: Fifty runs report average/best/worst, not confidence intervals. Mostly<8% overhead and18% MongoDB are author prose claims; plot bars are approximate and some ratios (notably Memcached) do not exactly reproduce that prose. Native baseline normalizes lower-is-better cost; source does not give raw per-workload timings/throughput for every bar. §§7–8: Research relevance is concurrent low-level refinement, specification trust, weak-memory proof and evaluation limits. No direct distributed protocol, Verus/verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent evaluation. Originality/first-proof claims are authors’ historical claims, not an independent literature proof. No artifact appendix/repository pointer in saved PDF; scripts and external claims unexecuted.

- DuoAI (2022)
    - title: DuoAI: Fast, Automated Inference of Inductive Invariants for Verifying Distributed Protocols
    - what: Infers inductive safety invariants for Ivy distributed-protocol models by filtering formulas on reachable simulation states and refining candidates with Ivy/Z3. A finite directed implication graph organizes formula weakening. Runs top-down weakening, bottom-up universal-core strengthening and a universal-only search in parallel. Reports26of27protocols solved, including five Paxos variants; vertical Paxos exhausts memory. Completeness is relative to an adequate finite decidable formula space and graph/optimization correctness, with a reader counterexample to the printed arbitrary-alternation decomposition extension. Supplies exact/approximate implication graphs, sample-preserving coverage theorem, monotonic-refinement proof, counterexample-pruned powerset search proof, quantified-variable/type ordering, mutual-implication optimizations and all benchmark outcomes. Explains which refinement wins per protocol, why hundreds of existential candidates can stall SMT, what human choices baselines require, and how specification/retrofitting differences affect claims of automation. Reader checks distinguish sufficient invariant inference from implemented-system verification and identify a quantifier-dependency flaw in a printed optimization lemma.
    - number: solves 26 of 27 protocols including Paxos variants; Vertical Paxos runs out of memory
    - number: Fast Paxos takes 26,979 seconds (about 7.5 hours)
    - number: solves all but 1 of 27 protocols (Vertical Paxos unsolved)
    - number: evaluation permits a week per tool and protocol
    - limits: Inputs are an Ivy protocol transition model and safety property, not arbitrary executable distributed code. Trusted Ivy/Z3 checks initialization and transition preservation of the conjunction and safety implication for all modeled instances, rather than bounded simulation being the certificate. Scope is safety; no liveness, crash-recovery implementation refinement, verified Rust/Verus proof or LLM-agent evaluation. Sampled states are assumed genuinely reachable; incorrect simulation could discard needed true invariants and compromise completeness, though final sound SMT checks still guard returned results. Finite formula search space uses prenex DNF, relational predicates/equality; extension to uninterpreted functions referred to DistAI. Bounds are quantified variables per sort, max_exists, max_literal, max_and and max_or. Tautologies/contradictions excluded. Nonempty sorts are implicit in universal-to-existential implication. Quantifier alternation must follow a fixed sort order, inferred partly from axioms or supplied by user; absent user choice multiple orders are tried in parallel. The actual full verification condition, including protocol axioms/transitions, must remain in the intended decidable fragment. Exact graph is transitive reduction of strict implication over finite formulas; syntactic implementation instead uses five sound weakening shapes and may connect equivalent formulas. Lemmas1–5 establish claimed acyclicity, implication and coverage of nontrivial formulas from selected roots. No theorem says every semantic implication is an edge/path in the approximate graph; coverage plus sound directed weakening is what enumeration/refinement need. Enumeration checks original variable-length states at multiple finite instance sizes, rather than DistAI incomplete fixed-length subsamples. A candidate is retained if it holds on all sampled states; descendants can be skipped if dominated by an existing candidate. Theorem1 says every true invariant in S is either itself retained or has a stronger retained ancestor. Retained candidates can still be false on unseen reachable states; simulation removes candidates, not proof obligations. Top-down refinement checks conjunction plus safety, replaces a failed candidate by noninvalidated immediate successors not already dominated by a reachable ancestor, and returns NotProvable if safety fails. Reachable ancestor here means a graph path avoiding invalidated nodes, not a reachable protocol state. Theorem2 maintains domination of every member of an adequate inductive solution; finite formulas each invalidated at most once give finite refinement assuming every solver check terminates. Bottom-up first weakens all universal candidates until inductive, explicitly ignoring safety, to obtain universal core. noncore includes existential candidates AND universal candidates not in the core whose inductiveness may require existential support. Enumerates subsets by size, calls top-down on core plus subset, and skips subsets holding on an already returned negative prestate. A failed safety-induction counterexample is a possibly unreachable state that invariants must exclude; strengthening can remove it. Theorem3 eventually tries all noncore, reducing to full top-down, conditional on correct pruning and finite solver decisions. Relative completeness is not a guarantee to prove every correct distributed protocol. Needed inductive solution must be expressible in chosen finite S and decidable fragment, samples/graph/optimizations must preserve it, solver calls must terminate, and resources must suffice. NotProvable means this search space cannot prove the property, not the protocol unsafe. Increasing size in round-robin has no practical resource bound; vertical Paxos memout is concrete failure despite expert invariants existing. Defaults max_literal4,max_or3,max_and3,max_exists1 unless safety already has>=2existentials; quantified variables per sort initially maximum arity occurrence in any relation. On failure increments literal/OR/AND/existential/per-sort-variable bounds round-robin. Runs a third max_exists0top-down worker along with general top-down/bottom-up; benchmark walltimes benefit from parallel simulation/refinement and possible sort-order searches, with no separate CPU-time/worker-count-normalized comparison. Mutual implication optimization suppresses Q if retained P1...Pk jointly imply Q, then reintroduces Q if a supporting candidate invalidated. Equivalence decomposition suppresses a formula permanently only when conjunction of smaller formulas is truly equivalent. Examples separate two independent existential witnesses, same witness, and distinct witnesses: existential dependency matters to logical validity, not just speed. Decomposition can require representation of each component within allowed search space. Reader counterexample to Lemma6 claimed arbitrary-alternation/skolemization extension: sorts A,X each{0,1}, fixed order A before X. Let p(x) iff x=0, q(x) iff x=1, r(a,x) iff a=x. F=exists a forall x.((p(x) AND q(x)) OR r(a,x)) is false. The selected conjunction p(x) AND q(x) has two components sharing no existential variable. Claimed components exists a forall x.(p(x) OR r(a,x)) and exists a forall x.(q(x) OR r(a,x)) are both true, choosing a=1 and a=0 respectively. A globally chosen existential witness in the other disjunct cannot be chosen separately. Proof for forall-X exists-YZ is valid under its independence conditions; extending it to arbitrary alternation is unsupported and false as stated. - Holistic Verification of Blockchain Consensus (2022)
    - what: Parameterized model checking verifies binary Byzantine consensus associated with Red Belly Blockchain under n>3t and0≤f≤t. First verifies binary-value broadcast, then substitutes a smaller specification-based automaton into the outer consensus and checks safety and progress properties with ByMC. Agreement and validity do not require the added good-round fairness; termination does. The verified algorithm is the coordinator/timeout-free pseudocode variant under that fairness, rather than a proof of the deployed implementation or its partial-synchrony mechanism. Makes the decomposition concrete: global sent-message counters replace local receive counts; Byzantine effects lower enabling thresholds by f; four temporal broadcast properties support a replacement gadget; round communication closure reduces selected all-round LTL obligations to one-round checking. Manual meta-arguments connect per-superround invariants to global agreement/validity and good-round existence to eventual decision. Gives a fair-round definition, a nonterminating4-process trace, detailed automaton rules, explicit liveness preconditions and measured schema counts.
    - limits: Fixed n sequential processes communicate through reliable fully connected asynchronous point-to-point links; delays are finite but unbounded, steps interleave, each receive is atomic and sender identities distinguish quorum members. Up to t<n/3 are Byzantine; f≤t is the actual fault count. The threshold abstraction assumes faulty senders cannot impersonate arbitrarily many distinct processes. Communication closure is essential: each process uses only messages for its current round, discards earlier tags and buffers later tags. Monotone send counters and threshold guards admit the prior ByMC reduction. Guarantees do not automatically extend to arbitrary protocols with cross-round data dependencies, timing constraints or changing membership. Reliable communication is encoded by progress assumptions on enabled rules and source-location emptiness. This excludes scheduler executions that indefinitely withhold enabled productive actions. Added consensus fairness is different: some round r has every correct process first deliver r mod2 in that round’s binary-value broadcast. Neither fairness follows from asynchronous reliability alone. Algorithm1 is the DBFT variant without coordinator/timeouts. The second DBFT variant uses partial synchrony, but this paper replaces that mechanism with a good-round assumption. It does not prove a synchronizer, coordinator rotation, timeout correctness or that the deployed environment enforces the assumption. Threshold models describe correct processes and abstract Byzantine influence with f-offset guards; global send counters abstract possible local receipt histories. Parameterized checking ranges over symbolic parameters satisfying n>3t≥3f, rather than testing a list of network sizes. Soundness still depends on faithful manual abstraction and ByMC’s reductions/SMT checks. Inner broadcast verification establishes justification,obligation,uniformity and termination. Replacement must preserve all behaviors relevant to the outer consumer because contestants is shared and the outer algorithm can proceed before the broadcast finishes. The paper argues this and supplies encoded preconditions; it is not a machine-checked source-to-source refinement of production code. ByMC handles a restricted LTL fragment and one-round systems. Cross-superround agreement,initial validity and existential good-round termination require manually chosen intermediate formulas and mathematical composition arguments. The model checker does not directly discharge each final quantified formula as written. The proof covers binary agreement,validity and eventual decision for the displayed algorithm. It does not prove blockchain transaction semantics,multi-value reduction,ledger consistency across all block heights,network/cryptographic code,resource bounds or end-to-end behavior of the deployed Red Belly software. Processes continue participating after deciding so others can finish; only the first decision matters. Text states safe exit after two later rounds but does not supply a verified executable stopping implementation. A process that halts immediately on first decision would change progress assumptions.

- IPA compositional TLA+ checking (2022)
    - title: Compositional Model Checking of Consensus Protocols Specified in TLA+ via Interaction-Preserving Abstraction
    - what: Introduces Interaction-Preserving Abstraction (IPA) for compositional checking of TLA+ consensus specifications. Actions are partitioned into modules, dependency/interaction variables are identified, internal actions are abstracted, and each module is checked in a context formed from abstractions of the others. Strong refinement proves that passing all compositional checks implies refinement of the original specification to the abstract one. IPA defines recursive dependency and interaction-variable sets and four abstraction constraints: abstract dependencies cannot use other modules’ locals; interaction updates depend only on interaction/dependency variables; abstract locals avoid other-module locals; and every externally visible action has a mapped abstract action preserving effects. A strong action mapping is used because ordinary refinement does not record correspondence of omitted actions. Case studies identify polling, centralized control-flow and brute-force replacement of performance optimizations as practical patterns. Raft is split into PreVote, Vote and Replication; ParallelRaft merges Replication into LeaderRecovery when it offers little abstraction. The theorem composes per-module refinements into S⇒A.

    - title: Kalas: A Verified, End-To-End Compiler for a Choreographic Language
    - what: Mechanizes a five-phase compiler from global asynchronous Kalas choreographies to endpoint code and CakeML, composing with CakeML compiler correctness to obtain machine-code guarantees. Proves operational correspondence and network-level deadlock freedom, and deploys a generated producer/filter/consumer system through seL4/CAmkES. Sections 2–3 define asynchronous swapping/deferred-action semantics and endpoint projection, requiring immediate branch notifications when another endpoint’s behavior differs; orphan recursion and divergence introduced at uninvolved endpoints are excluded. Sections 4–6 encode choice as boolean messages, split arbitrary strings into fixed payload chunks with a bookkeeping byte, and convert substitution-based fixpoints into letrec closures, passing variables modified by the body. Section 7 proves weak operational correspondence up to strong bisimilarity with catch-up transitions, then network-level deadlock freedom; local confluence and inert reductions control the interleaving explosion. Section 8 compiles Payload endpoints to CakeML using FFI models, proves FFI irrelevance and forward correctness, and uses proof-producing HOL-function synthesis to discharge each deployment’s environment assumptions. The infinite-execution liveness limitation is discussed explicitly.

Communication assumes a live backend, lossless delivery and unbounded queues; payload size σ is positive, chunks are σ+1 bytes. Machine-code liveness is subject to out-of-memory behavior in CakeML. The deployment uses C send/receive glue and seL4/CAmkES IPC, but its proofs are not formally connected to the kernel/platform proofs. Section 8.1 says the current compiler theorem guarantees global progress but does not exclude endpoint livelock for choreographies with only infinite paths; stronger fairness/receive-matching transfer remains unproved. No Internet/TCP deployment or bounded-queue result is supplied.

    - what: Presents MET, a two-layer workflow that model-checks CRDT designs in TLA+ and turns model-checking traces into deterministic implementation tests. A test manager controls message order through intercepted RPCs and compares code-level state traces with model-level oracles, targeting transcription and assumption bugs that design verification alone misses. The framework specifies CRDT operations and strong eventual consistency in TLA+, then coarsens the model by binding receive/do/send events while preserving conflict-resolution interleavings. - On the Correctness of Speculative Consensus (2022)
    - what: # Whole-paper read: On the Correctness of Speculative Consensus (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Jelle Hellings, Suyash Gupta, Sajjad Rahnama and Mohammad Sadoghi; arXiv2204.03552v1,7April2022,25pages. This is a detailed paper proof for Proof-of-Execution (PoE), a Byzantine state-machine replication protocol that speculatively executes before committing. Its main contribution is the connection between early client replies, preservation across view changes, eventual consensus and recovery of client results. The proof is mathematical prose and pseudocode, not a machine-checked development. [Q0–Q3,Q5–Q10]  ## System and required conditions  There are fixed replicas R, Byzantine replicas F, and clients C. The paper writes n=|R|,f=|F|,nf=n−f and assumes n>3f, authenticated communication and deterministic transaction execution. Byzantine replicas can coordinate and clients may all be malicious. Most exposition assumes publicly verifiable digital signatures; digest variants need cryptographic hash assumptions, and threshold variants need threshold signatures. This paper defines f from the fault set; it does not separately explain how deployments configure an upper bound used for quorum thresholds. [Q1,Q11–Q14]  Weak consensus means decisions never conflict, while termination and forcing new decisions require periods of reliable communication with some unknown bounded delay. The advertised asynchronous recovery therefore does not give unconditional progress during arbitrary loss or delay. Assumption4.6 bounds proposal size and the number W of prepared but uncommitted rounds. This makes a single finite message-delay estimate applicable to protocol messages. Timeout estimates must eventually grow sufficiently large. The displayed backoff argument also requires a positive initial estimate; multiplying zero cannot make it positive. [Q1,Q6,Q8]  ## Normal execution and recovery  The primary in view v has id=v mod n. A signed client request is proposed in a round. Each honest replica prepares only one proposal for that round/view and broadcasts Prepare. A certificate collects nf matching preparations. Replicas execute speculatively after all preceding transactions have executed and send Inform to the client. The client needs nf identical, view-specific Inform replies as a proof of execution. The familiar f+1 reply threshold for committed execution is insufficient here because speculative executions can be rolled back. Theorem4.1 establishes same-view uniqueness and normal-case service with a good primary, reliable communication and identical execution history. [Q2,Q3]  The printed Theorem4.1 contradiction proof defines T_i=S_i minus Byzantine replicas, but then treats S_i as if all its members were honest and as if those full sender sets were disjoint. Byzantine senders can vote for both proposals. The usual intersection argument applies to T_i, the honest subsets, instead. This is a notation defect in that displayed proof, not a demonstrated counterexample to same-view uniqueness. [Q3]  The four-replica failure examples distinguish omission by a faulty primary, a false accusation by a faulty backup, and network loss. Other replicas can observe the same messages in all three cases. A malicious primary can leave some honest replicas without a proposal while the client still receives a proof of execution using Byzantine replies. Recovery therefore must preserve what a client could already have observed, rather than treating an isolated replica's missing proposal as evidence that no execution occurred. [Q4]  Check-commit is decentralized. An honest replica broadcasts its prepared certificate only after execution, while still in the view, and after all previous rounds have committed. Receiving a valid certificate lets a missing replica prepare and execute. A commit certificate collects nf CheckCommit messages. Theorem4.4 relates a client proof to eventual preparation at every honest replica, relates one honest commit to eventual commits/client proof given the shared prefix, and derives that a commit certificate entails nf−f honest executions plus commitments for earlier rounds. The first two statements assume reliable communication and all honest replicas in the view. Out-of-order proposals are supported; the proved base still commits in order. [Q5]  View changes use three stages. A replica that detects failure rebroadcasts Failure. Receiving f+1 alerts induces an honest replica to join; nf alerts make it stop the old protocols and send ViewState to the next primary. State includes the latest commit certificate and every subsequently executed prepared certificate not rolled back. The next primary collects nf states and broadcasts NewView. Under reliable communication with delay δ, Lemma4.5 synchronizes entry into the proposal stage within2δ; Lemma4.7 delivers a good primary's new-view proposal within4δ of the first such entry. [Q6]  The new ledger retains the committed prefix through LC, then the latest-view prepared request in each round through LP. Missing committed history is queried; speculative requests outside the selected ledger are rolled back; the new primary must repropose selected uncommitted requests before new rounds. Theorem4.10 inducts over views to preserve any request executed by nf−f honest replicas, including every request with a possible client proof or commit certificate. Assumption4.8, uniqueness of the request named by commit certificates for a round, is a temporary proof hypothesis subsequently discharged by Corollary4.11. It is not an additional final assumption. [Q6,Q7]  Lemma4.12 supplies QueryCC/RespondCC recovery of missing committed history. Lemma4.13 and Theorem4.15 use increasing timeout estimates and eventual good primaries to establish resumption once communication is reliable. The worked δ=30ms example starts estimates7,3,5,1ms; three doublings yield56,24,40,8ms, and the four replicas need3,4,3,5 doublings respectively. Remark4.17 suggests a practical cap such as10seconds, but the theorem's unbounded-growth argument only carries to a cap when that cap exceeds actual reliable-network delay. [Q8]  Theorem4.18 combines preservation, recovery and client-request forwarding to prove weak consensus. Honest clients repeatedly send an unanswered request to all replicas; replicas forward it or trigger view changes if it is not served. Suggested defenses against malicious clients include per-client forwarding limits and treating another request by the same client as evidence of a timely proposal. These are stated heuristics, not a quantified load-admission/fairness analysis. Recoverable non-Byzantine crashes require certificates in persistent storage; Remark4.19's recovery claim depends on enough replicas recovering. [Q9]  Consensus alone does not guarantee a client obtains nf identical replies from one view. Example4.20 partitions honest replicas into A,B,C of sizes f,f,1 and alternates unreachable groups across three views. The same request becomes decided, but view-specific replies and commit certificates remain split, so no ordinary proof of execution forms. The repair is InformCC: after an honest replica commits, it can send the view-independent round/result to a retrying client. Now f+1 matching InformCC replies suffice because at least one is honest and committed execution is preserved. Theorem4.21 proves service when communication is reliable. Client request order is not automatically enforced; waiting for the first result or validating per-client counters supplies an extra application policy. [Q10]  ## Complexity, variants and evaluation  Figure1 compares seven protocols/variants; Figure12 gives13 message/certificate rows and three size variants. These are analytical accounting, not measured experiments. Base PoE takes two replica communication rounds before execution and three through check-commit; Linear-PoE takes three and five. The table's C parameter is request size, so expressions containing nC account for payload, not just the number of messages. Off-by-one terms are intentionally omitted in Figure1. Base prepared certificates have size O(nf+C); commit certificates O(nf²+C), because different replicas may attach different prepared certificates. ViewState and NewView additionally depend on W. [Q1,Q11]  Digests make most messages independent of request size but require explicit retrieval of missing request bodies and certificates. Replacing a certificate-carrying CheckCommit with a constant-size message requires f+1 matching senders before querying an honest holder. It does not eliminate the bounded-request-size assumption. Threshold signatures reduce certificates to constant size; by themselves they do not reduce all-to-all message counts. [Q12,Q13]  Linear-PoE sends preparations through the primary. Its decentralized commit replacement rotates aggregator q=round mod n, commits a digest of the last n prepared certificates, and uses a separate n:(f+1) threshold scheme for recovery certificates before n:nf commit certificates. This prevents a fixed faulty aggregator from permanently hiding committed history. The pseudocode waits for commitments through round−n and covers the preceding n−1 rounds with the resulting certificate. Failure detection still broadcasts quadratically. The authors' belief that such communication cannot be eliminated in their recovery setting is not an impossibility proof. The linear variant is explained by construction; it does not receive a separate full formal refinement proof here. [Q14]  The MAC-only variant is a proposed redesign of the two new-view stages by analogy with PBFT; the paper does not print that redesign. Out-of-order processing means proposing future rounds within W while earlier decisions finish. It does not remove the sequential execution dependence or the proved base's in-order commits. [Q15,Q16]  The n=31,C=10KiB,M=256B bandwidth example reports322KiB for the base primary and315KiB with linear aggregation, approximately2percent savings. Direct substitution gives322.5KiB and315.7258KiB, about2.10percent. The primary still transmits the full proposal to every replica. The accompanying “roughly-1/3-th increase in latency” is inconsistent with the stated increase from two to three communication rounds: relative to two, that is50percent. This is a reader arithmetic observation, not an execution measurement. [Q14]  Example5.6 assumes n=31,δ=15ms and1Gbit/s and prints22 sequential versus3028 out-of-order decisions/second. The22 figure follows1/(3δ)=22.22. The3028 figure is inconsistent with the printed bit/byte units: using10kB and256B gives about386.95 decisions/second; using10KiB gives378.51. The value3028.1 is obtained with10KiB if1Gbit/s is treated as10⁹bytes/s. Either consistent byte interpretation still gives a bandwidth-only upper estimate, excluding computation and other bottlenecks. The paper's two-orders-of-magnitude statement is therefore not supported by its stated inputs. [Q16]  Section6 compares PBFT, Zyzzyva, SBFT, HotStuff and MinBFT using communication rounds and simplified costs. It qualifies Zyzzyva/SBFT fast paths, assumes PBFT-like checkpoint costs for SBFT, and identifies trusted hardware/reliable communication for MinBFT. The HotStuff discussion and33 decisions/second example are this paper's account of a particular chained scheduling model, not an independently validated universal bound on HotStuff deployments. Its prediction that PoE outperforms PBFT “in all situations” exceeds what round counts alone establish: computation, rollback/recovery workload, implementations and resource bottlenecks are not measured here. [Q17–Q22]  The introduction/conclusion claim an “analytical and experimental” evaluation. This saved25-page version contains analytical comparisons and hypothetical numeric examples, with no experimental setup, implementation measurements, repeated trials or measured plots. Its earlier EDBT2021 paper is reference18; results from that separate paper are not imported into this record. No proof assistant, model checker, Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment is reported. [Q0,Q17–Q24]  ## Relevance and reading evidence  For distributed verification, this contributes detailed proof obligations for speculative client observations, view-change preservation, the distinction between agreement and delivered service, and communication/recovery tradeoffs. My inference for proof-agent evaluation is to check eventual-reliability and bounded-window conditions, quorum intersections, temporary proof hypotheses, persistent crash state and units in analytical evaluation separately. A successful local proof script would not by itself establish any of those model-to-implementation connections.  Read the complete25pages,40references,all15numbered figures including pseudocode and both tabular figures,all printed proofs/formulas/examples,and all25page renders. Official and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. No implementation or artifact source was linked as part of this paper's proof/evaluation and none was inspected here. This record does not audit the related ResilientDB implementation or preceding EDBT paper. No author execution/import, compiler/checker/prover/solver run or serialized scientific-result loading.

    - title: Polynomial-Time Verification and Testing of Implementations of the Snapshot Data Structure
    - what: Proves that data-independent single-writer snapshot implementations are linearizable exactly when all simple histories are, derives small automata for non-linearizable simple histories, and evaluates PAT verification and a linear-time simple-history tester. Simple histories allow only two distinguished processes to change their update value once from the initial value 0 to 1; all other processes keep 0. Theorem 5 uses differentiated histories, Anderson’s shrinking lemma and value renaming to reduce arbitrary algorithm correctness to simple histories. Theorem 10 characterizes simple-history correctness by no inversion, non-decreasing scan results and appropriate update pairs. Theorem 11 recognizes violations with O(n) states/O(n^2) transitions. Theorem 17 gives O(m n^4) verification for finite simple-history state spaces; Theorem 18 tests a fixed (i,j)-simple history in O(|h|). §6 removes vacuous reads/writes of always-zero registers. Two verification implementations compare PAT refinement on simple histories and PAT reachability with violation automata. §7 carefully identifies encoding/tool threats and distinguishes bounded exploration from full verification; its headline bug counts disagree between sections.

Linear-time testing covers simple histories, not an arbitrary already-recorded snapshot history. - TLA+ verification trifecta (2022)
    - title: Specification and Verification With the TLA+ Trifecta: TLC, Apalache, and TLAPS
    - what: Uses a TLA+ specification of asynchronous termination detection and Safra's ring algorithm to demonstrate complementary verification with TLC explicit-state checking, Apalache bounded/SMT and inductive-invariant checking, and TLAPS theorem proving, including refinement from the algorithm to a high-level state machine. The high-level module specifies active nodes, pending messages, termination detection, safety, liveness under weak fairness, and quiescence. Safra's algorithm adds white/black colors, message counters and a circulating token; termination requires an inactive node 0, no pending messages, white token/node, and zero accumulated counter. TLC finds 4,097 states for N=4,K=3 in the abstract model and 1.3 million (N=3,K=C=3,Q=9) or 219 million (N=4 with same bounds) in the algorithm model, exposing state explosion and a token-color bug. Apalache checks bounded prefixes, proves an inductive invariant for N=100 in 20 seconds, and checks quiescence for N=100 in 11 seconds. Refinement is checked for small N; TLAPS proves type, safety, liveness, and refinement for arbitrary instances, with an invariant proof taking about 230 lines and liveness/refinement about 245 lines. The conclusion recommends TLC first, Apalache for inductive invariants, TLC/random exploration for liveness, then TLAPS for higher confidence.

- Verifying Hardware Security Modules with Information-Preserving Refinement (2022)
    - what: Knox checks information-preserving refinement (IPR): an HSM circuit implements a trusted functional specification through a trusted wire-protocol driver, and arbitrary digital wire observations can be reproduced by an emulator that only queries that specification. A shared relation ties initialization, functional equivalence and physical equivalence together, including recovery after arbitrary I/O. Solver-checked symbolic execution and guided state exploration cover complete C/assembly/Verilog circuits for PIN backup, password hashing and TOTP tokens. Records exact real/ideal switching semantics, reset relation, extra crash-safety obligation, quantified fixed-point/subsumption conditions, all eight hint primitives, tool and manual-efficiency trust, FRAM model versus BlockRAM prototype, each emulator construction and commit point, subtle timing/persistence and compiler/hardware bugs, every LOC/proof-time/overhead value, deterministic-spec limitation and scaling proposals.
    - limits: §2: Adversary controls/observes digital input/output logic levels every clock cycle through a compromised host, including malformed protocol traffic and interruption/reset. No physical device attack, violating electrical specifications, analog voltage measurement, electromagnetic/temperature/power side channel. The digital timing result is relative to the modeled circuit, not an all-physical-side-channel guarantee. §§3–4: Trusted functional specification includes intended API disclosures and driver wire protocol. IPR is relative to these inputs, not proof that the API itself has desirable cryptographic/security semantics. Refinement relation, emulator, hints and proof scripts are supplied but checked; toolchain/model/solver and physical implementation correspondence remain assumptions. §3: Host may alternate functional/physical views any time. Physical→functional reinitializes driver (resetting circuit here); functional→physical reinitializes emulator auxiliary state. Emulator sees only spec-level query results, not arbitrary secret memory. A single continuing spec state must account for physical effects across recovery, ruling out treating each interval as a new empty specification. §4: Relation R need hold between operations and after reset, not at every implementation cycle. Initialization must relate initial states. Functional equivalence includes return result and final relation for each driver operation, including no-op/background running. Physical equivalence matches all per-cycle output sequences and relates reset final circuit to resulting spec state. §4.5: PE maps arbitrary wire traffic to some sequence of legal spec operations. Additional crash safety restricts interrupted protocol-following operation to its old or new abstract state. These are separate obligations: a functionally correct and crash-safe program may still leak through the commit point. §5.1: Yield permits arbitrary cycle delays. Closed overapproximating symbolic-state sets, with checked subsumption, establish fixed points. Merge may overapproximate the union and reduce proof performance burden without discarding concrete behaviors. This is not finite sampling of host schedules. §5.2: STEP checks same-cycle outputs and reset recovery for circuit/emulator/spec symbolic states. SUBSUMED closes an already-covered branch; checked full exploration and closure establish coverage for unbounded-length input. Proof script failure may time out, be slow or fail coverage; success assumes sound framework/solver/model. §6: GCC compiles application C to RISC-V ROM and Yosys translates Verilog via SMT-LIB/#lang yosys to Rosette. The binary/circuit is proof subject; this does not mechanically verify GCC/Yosys/FPGA place-and-route or general CPU ISA correctness. Initial nonvolatile and volatile/reset semantics must match hardware. §7.1.1: Persistent model uses durable atomic32-bit FRAM writes in one cycle. Experimental board substitutes FPGA BlockRAM for external FRAM. Functional proof assumes modeled persistence behavior; experiment does not validate actual power-failure retention of physical FRAM. §7.1.3: Host supplies timestamps; nondecreasing checks reject rewind but do not establish real elapsed time or trustworthy clock. Audit deliberately reveals last timestamp and helps detect future-code requests. Equal timestamps are allowed by the less-than test. TOTP cryptographic security relies on chosen functional algorithms, not a new proof of SHA1/HMAC security. §8.1: Computational security requires efficient emulator so it cannot justify a key leak by factoring/brute force. Knox does not formalize/check efficiency: manual audit supplies this obligation. Case emulators reportedly use at most one spec query per circuit cycle and roughly equivalent computation. Do not describe whole cryptographic result as fully mechanically checked. §8.2: Specs deterministic; true hardware randomness unsupported. Stateful CSPRNG plus explicit host seed/add-entropy operation is proposed compatible design, not a fourth demonstrated/verified case. §8.3: Permitted leakage can be made explicit as spec leak operation; functional equivalence need not be checked for that adversary-only operation. Enlarging allowed leakage changes guarantee and needs policy review. §8.4: Monolithic proof avoids intermediate ISA specs and proves only particular HSM program/circuit behavior. Scaling to sophisticated CPUs/crypto is unresolved; no public-key signatures in three simple cases. Delayed fixed worst-case response with separate correctness/WCET reasoning is a future proposal. §9: Noninterference/declassification/secure-compilation comparisons concern formulations described by authors. Their limitations do not establish impossibility for all generalized information-flow or simulation frameworks. No direct distributed-protocol, Rust/Verus/TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. §7.2: Single-threaded verification timings on one older CPU; no distribution of proof time or independent reproduction. Implementation latency at12MHz/2Mbaud, no confidence intervals/run count given. Claimed interactive suitability is author interpretation. Originality/relative-simplicity comparisons not independently surveyed.

- Brief Announcement: On Strong Observational Refinement and Forward Simulation (2021)
    - what: Shows by example that ordinary forward simulation need not preserve hyperliveness or strong observational refinement when finite and infinite traces are allowed. Defines progressive forward simulation with a well-founded decrease on concrete steps mapped to an empty abstract sequence; states that it implies strong observational refinement. Full theorem proof is external. The counterexample composes a forward-simulated LL/SC implementation with fetch-and-add. A particular LL/SC implementation permits SC failure merely because another thread executed LL, without any intervening write. Alternating threads can therefore prevent both operations from returning. The formal scheduler requirement is nonempty enabled actions after every consistent finite trace, plus object determinism; it does not impose per-thread fairness. Definition 1 forbids infinite internal stuttering through a well-founded concrete-state order. Necessity of the progress condition is future work.

- Fault-Tolerant Replication with Pull-Based Consensus in MongoDB (2021)
    - what: Describes MongoDB replication as a pull-based Raft derivative: secondaries fetch from any sync source, report durable positions through relayed UpdatePosition acknowledgments, and receive commit points separately. Safety requires the acknowledging server’s current term, rather than counting copies of an entry alone. Gives a quorum-intersection argument and reports TLA+ model checking, controlled chaining/failover experiments and Atlas production telemetry. Records the five-server stale-primary counterexample, acknowledgment-term repair and leader-completeness argument; log overlap/rollback and initial-sync details; weak versus linearizable options; election/priority/read extensions; all numerical benchmark/production claims and their measurement boundaries; literal appendix pseudocode inequalities. Formal evidence is a proof sketch plus reported model checking without configuration/results supplied in the paper, not a machine-checked implementation theorem.
    - limits: A single replica set replicates a log; sharding is orthogonal. Only the primary accepts writes. Normal election uses one persistent vote per term and the Raft log up-to-date order (last entry term then timestamp). OpTime=(entry term, logical timestamp) is lexicographically ordered; timestamps are logical positions, not a physical clock assumption. Correct durable storage persists term/vote/log before RPC responses. Byzantine nodes, corrupted storage and arbitrary duplicate IDs are outside the presented protocol. Safety follows Raft-style log/election assumptions despite asynchronous delay. Availability requires a communicating majority, eventual message/protocol progress and an electable primary; no partition-wide availability or deterministic asynchronous election termination is proved. Persistent term/vote/log are distinguished from volatile lastCommitted/lastApplied/lastPosition. The paper describes crash/restart operation and WiredTiger rollback, but does not prove implementation/storage refinement. PullEntries includes the last local timestamp and returns an overlapping entry plus newer entries. The first returned OpTime must match the last local OpTime before appending. A newer divergent branch triggers last-common-entry search, log truncation, rollback and replay. Same-log requests wait up to5 seconds by default; streaming database cursors batch data and avoid request-per-entry overhead. The data source need not be the primary. UpdatePosition relays per-member maximum known positions toward the primary, batches between forwarding rounds and permits one in-flight request per sync source. Commit requires a majority supporting the candidate entry and its current leader term. A higher RPC term updates currentTerm and converts the receiver to follower before commitment; the global higher-term rule covers UpdatePosition even though its local receiver block only lists merge/forward. Five-server safety counterexample is specific to separating replication from acknowledgment: a term3 voter may still pull term2 data from a stale primary. Counting durable copies alone can falsely commit an entry later overwritten by the term3 leader. Acknowledgment server terms stop the stale leader before committing. The quorum argument relies on Raft log matching/leader completeness and election restrictions; it is a paper proof sketch rather than a full separately supplied inductive proof. Authors report writing TLA+ and applying model checking (§3.3, ref33), but provide no model configuration, bounds on nodes/entries/terms, explored state counts, explicit checked invariant list, model-checking output, discovered bug count or implementation-refinement result. Unit/integration/fuzz/fault-injection testing is reported without quantified coverage. External TLA+ source was not inspected for this record. Sync-source selection only chooses a newer observed log position and checks again on PullEntries responses because the source can roll back. The paper claims cycles can never form. A per-choice newer condition alone does not constitute a proof for time-varying distributed observations; no concrete cycle counterexample was constructed and no implementation failure is asserted. WiredTiger speculatively applies entries before commitment. Stable timestamp is the locally known commit point and must not exceed the common-branch timestamp during rollback. Restore stable data then replay through the common entry. Weak-consistency clients can see/acknowledge speculative data; durability/linearizability statements must be restricted to appropriate strong options. Legacy mmap rollback uses different mechanisms omitted from the paper. Initial sync uses a possibly inconsistent collection scan rather than a snapshot: record source applied start, clone, record applied end, then replay from start beyond the recorded end point; restart on source failure. Log retention defaults to5% of free disk at startup. Insert-existing/update-or-delete-missing rules and primary-side absolute assignments make replication operations idempotent. Correctness also needs sequence ordering, schema/scan assumptions and sufficient log retention; single-operation idempotence alone does not prove every arbitrary sequence/clone state correct. A new primary can fetch old-term entries during catchup until it creates a new-term entry, sees no newer source data, or times out. This preserves weakly acknowledged uncommitted data best-effort, not guaranteed durability. Arbiters vote without holding data: a primary-secondary-arbiter set after primary failure may accept weak writes but cannot commit majority writes. Up to50 total members and7 voters; nonvoters do not count toward election/commit majorities. Planned handoff pauses writes and catches up an eligible secondary before immediate election. Priority elections use a dry-run/pre-vote to avoid needless higher-term disruption by stale candidates. It does not resolve all partition-induced repeated elections. Default election timeout10s; Atlas telemetry mentions10 or5s. Linearizable reads occur only at the primary and wait for a synchronization round trip, optionally piggybacking a concurrent oplog entry; a complete read linearization/current-term proof is not supplied. Printed Raft Appendix A p701 reverses two inequalities: AppendEntries rule1 says reject term>currentTerm; rule5 says change commitIndex if leaderCommit<commitIndex. The first reverses the conventional stale-term test (interaction with the global higher-term rule depends on evaluation order), and the second permits commit regression if followed literally; these are apparent errors in the printed comparison pseudocode, not a demonstrated MongoDB implementation defect. PDF visual checks recover >= lost by text extraction in Raft send/commit tests and MongoDB majority-position comparison. Printed MongoDB client response condition p702 is strict lastCommitted>entry.OpTime, while majority replication comparison is >= in the PDF. Literal strict response could wait for a later entry after its own entry commits, stalling an isolated write absent another/background entry; body says updates return when committed. lastApplied is described as monotonic despite rollback; distinguishing logical progress from speculative physical application needs clarification. Neither issue was reproduced in code. Controlled tests use AWS m5d.2xlarge (8vCPU/32GB/local SSD), five server VMs (three US East Virginia/two US West Oregon) and two client VMs. Primary and committing majority are East, so strong writes need not wait for WAN. Closed-loop clients replace a random document among1M documents each with one1000-byte string; vary thread count. Chaining forces one West secondary through the other West secondary, other secondaries pull primary. These settings do not isolate arbitrary topology or WAN quorum placement. Unthrottled chaining on/off throughput is approximately the same (~12–13k ops/s); primary is CPU bound with >250k context switches/s and oplog reads about5% of one core. Chaining halves cross-datacenter traffic, not total traffic or commit latency generally. In additional three-node tests (placement unspecified) with200Mbps primary limit, approximate plotted saturation increases from8800 to13200ops/s and p50 from60ms down to40ms. No repeats/confidence intervals or raw data reported. Single five-node same-datacenter failover trace,64 clients: old primary crashes at10s, election timeout10s, throughput drops around12s and recovers around21–23s; old primary recovers40s without clear throughput disturbance. This is illustrative, not exhaustive fault coverage. Version4.4 versus3.6 compares full releases, including journaling/other optimizations, so performance change cannot be attributed only to consensus protocol. Claims about old protocol assumptions/split-brain are authors’ characterization, not independently reproduced. Atlas June2020 version fractions26.86/44.17/28.54% sum99.57%; the remainder is unspecified. Failover causes89.03% planned/6.15% priority/4.82% timeout. The sample sizes, cluster selection/exclusions and variance are not given. Plotted outage CDFs stop at95%, so no extreme-tail claim follows. Production Local Write Unavailability starts at election and ends when the new primary accepts writes; Majority Write Unavailability ends when the first step-up no-op commits. These omit earlier old-primary pause/unresponsiveness and are shorter than client outage. Planned p95=.37/3.08s; timeout p95=6.41/10.24s plus typically10 or5s before election. The authors’ proposed heartbeat explanation for1/2s clusters is a belief, not a measured causal test. Week-long replication telemetry reports50% of replica sets below8.08MB/day,95% below7.94GB/day,top5% generating>92.6% of traffic. Figures11/12 instead label host count, leaving the unit of aggregation unclear. Monthly$300–5000 savings uses the paper’s historical AWS$0.01–0.147/GB estimate, not current pricing or observed customer bills. Appendix B setup describes closed-loop1000-byte inserts, while Table1 describes an adapted TPC-C benchmark with100 clients/100 warehouses and five transaction types. Preserve this workload-description inconsistency. MongoDB denormalized/query/transaction semantics are used; this is not a certified standard TPC-C result. Three server VMs/one client VM are in one availability zone, no bandwidth limit. Total throughput1453.47→1506.98 (~3.68%); modest gain is attributed to CPU offload. Primary total traffic15.56→11.70MB/s; per-secondary oplog traffic4.05MB/s. Difference3.86MB/s need not exactly equal4.05 under changed throughput/rounding. Caller must exclusively own/lock every accessed object, including reads, until completing its use. SimpleNFS proves its locking; functional GoNFS is unverified and its locking is trusted even to obtain atomicity, and that trust alone says nothing about full NFS conformance. No theorem transfers SimpleNFS correctness to GoNFS. §§1,5.6 fn3,8.1: Internals implement deferred durability and lower-level specifications can express Commit(false), but the presented top-level separation-logic API requires immediate flushing with Commit(true), sufficient for SimpleNFS. Main performance evaluation uses stable GoNFS writes although Linux can exploit unstable writes. Separately reported unstable-write rerun and appendix comparison are distinguished. §§1–2: No floating commit blocks, database-style undo, asynchronous-disk/log-bypass optimization or sophisticated B-epsilon-tree data structure. Objects must fit supported operation sizes; Commit can fail if operation is too large. Abandoning an uncommitted buffered operation is a logical ownership restoration, not undoing an already journaled operation. §§3.1,5.1: SimpleNFS is a core subset with GETATTR, SETATTR, READ and WRITE examples, not a fully verified NFSv3 implementation. Each file occupies one block; writes reject count/data-length mismatch, arithmetic overflow, beyond-block size and a starting offset beyond current EOF. Inode and data block must update together; per-inode locking owns its uniquely associated block implicitly. §§4–5: Hoare triples establish safety and postconditions if calls terminate; these are not stated liveness, fairness, deadlock-freedom or throughput guarantees. Toy-client idempotent recovery specification covers arbitrary crash/recovery repetitions within the model, not guaranteed completion under endlessly recurring crashes. §5.2: Lifting changes ghost ownership, not physical disk. Operation-local ownership permits access while durable_pred snapshots the original footprint. Exclusivity applies only to owned objects; other threads may commit changes elsewhere, including disjoint objects sharing a block. Whole-disk immutability throughout an operation is not assumed. §§5.3–5.5: ReadBuf returns mutable-buffer ownership and a separating implication to recover the operation predicate with the new contents. Footnote2 omits the actual SetDirty obligation from the displayed simplified spec. Crash-aware lock clients must preserve next-generation durable recovery obligations during every critical-section step; ordinary lock release invariants alone are insufficient. §5.5: Crash framing removes access to crash-resource Ic during proof of f and restores it afterward. It does not allow arbitrary durable-state mutation to ignore its crash consequences. Operation preparation uses only local buffered resources while the original durable footprint is framed away. §§6.1–6.3: Lock-free describes selected reads/disk-I/O regions; commits serialize read-modify-write under a global lock, and logger/installer take locks to obtain monotonic bounds. No general lock-free progress theorem is claimed. Separate header ownership allows concurrent installation/logging without holding locks during I/O. §7: Authors report all Perennial/GoJournal/SimpleNFS proofs Coq-checked and Print Assumptions used to check completeness. The article supplies specification rules and proof ideas rather than full in-paper derivations. Public artifacts were not replayed here, so this record distinguishes reported machine checking from independent reproduction. §8.1: Performance uses unverified GoNFS against Linux5.12.3 NFS/ext4 data=journal; RAM backing differs (Go array versus ext4 file in tmpfs).     - what: Introduces IC3PO, symmetric incremental induction extending finite-domain IC3/PDR. Section 5 defines permission-aware C-string predicates and indexed strstr/strchr/strcasestr wrappers that discharge pointer-subtraction obligations once. Sections 6–7 precisely identify the absent high-level request/response refinement and describe a specification-derived test client finding a liveness bug.

    - title: Formal Verification of a Fail-Operational Automotive Driving System
    - what: Defines and model-checks a distributed arbitration logic for a redundant, fail-operational highly automated driving system. The NuSMV model encodes state machines, buses, power supply, failures, and LTL/CTL safety requirements; the verification scope and tool qualification are aligned with ISO 26262.     - title: Brief Announcement: Automating and Mechanising Cutoff Proofs for Parameterized Verification of Distributed Protocols
    - what: Proposes parameterized distributed safety verification via a designer-supplied small cutoff instance, node map sim, state-effect filterΩ and action-sequence translatorτ. Generates a relation requiring relevant large-instance state effects to be included at mapped cutoff nodes; uses first-order SMT checks for preservation and violation reflection. The announcement does not formalize all RML syntax, ordering/topology axioms or state domains. Cutoff means any counterexample at a larger parameter has one at size≤k. Introduction requires checking all sizes≤k; worked transfer uses a selected size-k instance. Thus all smaller admissible sizes must also be checked or covered separately, and all relevant IDs/topology/data instances represented, not merely one concrete graph/state. No automated cutoff finder or complete procedure for arbitrary protocols claimed. Designer supplies protocol, cutoff C, map from every large-instance node to a cutoff node, filterΩ of effects relevant to a violation, and translatorτ mapping actions to zero/more cutoff actions. Automation generates/checks a candidate relation from those inputs; it does not infer all proof ingredients or eliminate human protocol insight. Ω is property-specific and must retain enough state to reflect violation. Generic relation is forallN Ω(σL(N))⊆σC(sim(N)): many large nodes collapse to one cutoff representative, so it is one-way inclusion of selected facts, not exact equality of distributed state. Ring example chooses distinguished hypothetical violating leadersLA/LB and partitions directed ring arcs, includingLB onCB side andLA onCA side; cutoff has two nodes with same IDs. Map may depend on counterexample witnesses, not one universally fixed arbitrary quotient. Ring protocol: each node has unique totally ordered ID; generate sends own ID to successor. Handle forwards IDs greater than own, elects self when own ID returns, ignores smaller ID. Safety is at most one elected node. Relation carries implication from each distinguished large leader flag to corresponding cutoff flag, and only carries pendingA/B messages while their originating distinguished node has not become leader. It is not full queue/order/multiplicity equality and requires the surrounding protocol encoding. Lockstepτ may stutter when node images coincide or a large action cannot usefully be reproduced, and may execute multiple small actions. Example handlingB atLA maps to handleB atCA followed by generatingB atCB; extra generation restores relation. Symmetric cases also required. Printed short list does not fully specify every intermediate-node/other-ID/stuttering case, parameter guard, or when a proposed action sequence is enabled. Equation1 checks unsatisfiability of R∧largeAction∧translatedSmallSequence∧¬Rprime, with safe prestateΦL/ΦC conjoined to focus on the first violation. Equation2 excludes ¬ΦL∧R∧ΦC, so related large violations force small violations. These are relation preservation and bad-state reflection. A cutoff correctness proof also needs related initial states and existence of a legal matching small sequence for every relevant large step. Neither is an explicit premise of printed Theorem1 or checked by these formulas alone. In particular, putting τ(a) in the antecedent of Equation1 only constrains already-existing matching moves. If that sequence is disabled, formula is vacuously unsatisfiable and says nothing about simulating the large step. Need an enabledness/totality obligation R∧ΦL∧ΦC∧a⇒existsσCprime τ(a), plus initial-state matching; a partial-correctness SMT check cannot substitute for it. This identifies an incompleteness of theorem as printed, not an audited flaw in an unavailable implementation/full proof. Reader simple countermodel: relationR says large bad flag implies cutoff bad flag. Both initially false; cutoff flag permanently false; a large action sets bad true, while designated cutoff action is disabled. Equation1 has false τ antecedent; Equation2 contradictory byR; small instance safe; large instance unsafe. Initial relation already holds, so even adding initialization alone does not fix missing matching-step existence. Such a node-count-dependent guarded action fits a broad relational model unless further protocol restrictions rule it out; announcement states no restriction establishing totality. A second missing obligation is initial relatedness: Rfalse makes both displayed formulas unsatisfiable for any protocol, regardless of its executions. Even when generated inclusionR disallows this exact candidate, the proof must establish the chosen initial-state relation rather than infer it from preservation. Ring pending/leader initialization plausibly makesR hold, but the announcement does not print/check that case. Adding Φ of both prestates is sound for a first-bad-state transfer only if initialization and step matching hold and all translated intermediate small states are legal. If a small execution violatesΦ earlier during a multistepτ, that already witnesses unsafety; if cutoff safe, every such intermediate stays safe. Does not require preserving after first violation. All free/quantified instance, topology and order variables must be encoded with sound restrictions for SMT UNSAT to entail the mathematical statement. Theorem1 asserts all instances safe from UNSAT of Equations1/2 and safety ofC; no proof provided beyond prose. Z3 UNSAT is reported, not an independent proof-assistant/kernel certificate. Soundness relies on correct FOL encoding, quantifiers, topology/ID assumptions, action semantics and solver. Unknown/timeout would not be proof; the paper reports only successful preliminary cases, without completeness or decidability theorem. Evaluation separates two solver cases (ring leader election, sharded key-value store) from three manually checked cases (Lock Service citing Verdi, Learning Switch citing Ivy, Distributed Lock Service citing IronFleet). Only ring cutoff2 is stated here; key-value/other cutoff sizes, exact properties, modeling effort, action counts and solver formulas not detailed.     - title: Finding Invariants of Distributed Systems: It’s a Small (Enough) World After All
    - what: SWISS searches finite spaces of quantified invariants for RML distributed protocol models. Breadth accumulates small relatively inductive clauses; Finisher searches for a final clause that, with safety, is inductive. Failed SMT verification conditions yield reusable finite-model filters, with symmetry and redundancy pruning, model minimization and parallel search. It proves selected models including Paxos/Flexible Paxos and guided Multi-Paxos, and measures successes, partial progress, costs and failed optimizations against I4 and first-order separators. Distinguishes model/spec correctness from code, safety-relative partial clauses from independent proofs, and the small-world hypothesis from general completeness.

Safety/transition semantics, solver/encoder/filter implementation and execution environment are trusted; output invariants can be independently validated but this reading did not replay them. §§2.1–2.4: Proofs address all reachable states of the supplied transition model, not just finite test runs; no liveness proof. Atomic transition/failure/network assumptions come from each input protocol. SDL running example uniquely disallows packet duplication; do not generalize that restriction to every benchmark. EPR satisfiability uses ∃*∀* with no general functions; stratified functions and quantifier alternation are admitted in the extended fragment while preserving decidability. §§3.2–3.4: Finisher checks Init⇒S, Init⇒P, TR∧known∧S∧P⇒S′ and TR∧known∧S∧P⇒P′. Breadth checks initialization and inductiveness of new clauses relative to input clauses and S. Therefore intermediate clauses can be inductive only under safety, not independently proved reachable-state properties. Reader qualification: reuse partial output with its assumptions/joint invariant obligation intact; a partial clause count is not a partial correctness theorem about arbitrary code. §3.4 Claim 1: Ideal Solve succeeds only if a finite chain exists with all earlier clauses in B, final clause in F, each earlier prefix inductive relative to S, and final conjunction including S inductive; sound pruning must preserve valid candidates and VC checks must finish. This is relative completeness for the stated chain/space, not decidability of arbitrary invariant discovery. §§4.3,5.1 reader qualification: Actual implementation retries timed-out Z3 queries with CVC4 and may skip an invariant if timeout persists. Thus practical runs with skipped candidates do not retain the ideal exhaustive coverage guarantee. Skipping rejects potentially useful proofs; it does not justify accepting an unproved candidate. Unknown/timeout and finite search failure do not establish protocol unsafety. §4.1: User supplies formula term/depth limits k,d, quantified-variable limits m,q and quantifier type nesting order to retain extended-EPR VCs. Templates can be auto-enumerated within bounds or explicitly supplied. Auto mode is not no-user-configuration; search grows exponentially. Symmetry pruning imposes syntactic term order/first-variable order, not full logical-equivalence solving. §4.2: True(M) requires P on a model; False(M) requires not-P; Transition(M,M′) requires P(M)⇒P(M′). Filters are derived from failed VC obligations and are sound for candidates satisfying the same obligation context. False models need not be reachable; they are states every acceptable strengthening for that VC must reject, rather than arbitrary actual executions proving a bug. §§4.2–4.5: Precompute base-term evaluations on every variable instantiation in finite models and evaluate candidates with bitwise operations. FastImplies is a sound but incomplete syntactic implication check using subsequences/modulo variable renaming in a trie, with limited universal/existential substitution. allInv retains redundant clauses for filtering while indInv avoids redundant output. Model minimization has a 45-second budget, so a retained model need only be partially minimized. §4.5.2: Partition/randomize B/F and run independent per-thread searches, combining only phase results. Threads do not share counterexample filters or fresh invariants during a phase. This gives good filtering parallelism but replicates SMT model construction and does not establish universal linear speedup. §5.1: Defaults B(d,k,q,m)=(1,3,1,5), F=(2,6,1,6) were adjusted per benchmark after results: increase k/q on exhausted failed searches, shrink B on slow breadth. learning-switch-ternary uses q=0; async lock and sharded-kv enlarge k; no-lost-keys needs q=2. Results include manual tuning and guided Multi-Paxos, not a fixed blind default-only experiment. §§5.1–5.2 Table 1: 27 distinct benchmarks plus duplicate guided Multi-Paxos row. SWISS times are medians of five runs with six-hour budget, on eight-core i9-9900K 3.60GHz/125GB/Ubuntu19.10, eight threads unless noted. Z3 4.8.8 then CVC4 1.8-prerelease --finite-model-find after 45s. Baseline runtime entries are published comparisons without uniform per-baseline dispersion in this paper. §5.2.1: Paxos and Flexible Paxos complete automatically within the configured candidate templates; Multi-Paxos requires correct user templates and unguided run times out in Breadth. Fast/Stoppable/Vertical Paxos remain unsolved, despite introductory phrasing that can sound broader. I4/FOL/SWISS each win on some protocols; existential support alone does not dominate larger mutually inductive universal invariants. §5.2.2: Partial progress counts handwritten invariant clauses logically implied by generated clauses, not percent of execution space, correctness or remaining proof effort. Missing one essential clause can prevent the whole safety proof. Reported 79% Vertical Paxos is 14/17, about 82.4%; preserve printed discrepancy rather than treating prose percentage as exact. §§5.3.3–5.3.5: Table 2 timings enumerate entire template spaces even after finding a proof and start with supplied Breadth invariants. The claimed 20-minute/13.4× guided result concerns proof search stopping, not the listed 2036-second full-template enumeration. Table 3 is a single-thread single-template pruning experiment, not end-to-end automatic-template run. §5.3.4: mn/mn−1 are smallest known chain maximum term sizes, drawn from human or synthesized invariants; minimality is not proved. 25/27 have mn≤8 and 22 are smaller; mn≤6/mn−1≤3 is an empirical rule of thumb. Human comprehensibility implies finite intuition is motivation for a hypothesis, not a theorem guaranteeing succinct invariants. Appendices A–B: Formula-synthesis, BMC and eager invariant accumulation were unfavorable in tested cases; this is workload-specific evidence. Figure 5 uses preselected templates and a logarithmic y-axis. Parallelism experiments deliberately finish the whole F space to remove first-hit variance and analyze longest-running threads, so speedups do not directly imply normal first-proof latency. §§5–7: No production-code performance, LLM-agent experiment, verified Rust/Verus implementation or TLA+/TLC integration is evaluated. An unexpectedly easy Fast Paxos proof uncovered a disabled-action typo in the input spec, demonstrating the need to validate intended behavior despite valid invariants. External artifacts/proofs and source-code current state were not executed or audited.

- The CakeML Project’s Quest for Ever Stronger Correctness Theorems (2021)
    - what: Historical account of CakeML’s end-to-end verification strategy: proof-producing translation of logical functions to embedded ML programs, verified compilation to concrete bytes, and application-specific proofs, with extensions through a verified Silver CPU’s Verilog implementation. Describes improvements that strengthen transported correctness, especially impure code reasoning and space bounds needed for liveness. Explains why in-logic execution supplies a concrete compile(input)=machine_code theorem, enabling a final property statement without the compiler function; how applying synthesis and in-logic compilation to the compiler’s own logical definition yields a verified executable; why finite target memory limits the default behavior theorem; how a sound space-cost semantics removes early out-of-memory exits for specific programs; and how shared characteristic-formula infrastructure connects manual verification and monadic code synthesis. Separates completed compiler/hardware layers from 2021 prospective language/compiler projects.
    - limits: This 10-page invited overview summarizes previously published mechanizations; it contains no new complete formal proof, benchmark table, theorem inventory or fresh controlled experiment. Its references identify where to inspect the underlying statements. Counts or broad performance comparisons here are author reports, not independently reproduced results. The transfer argument relies on proved source properties, formal CakeML operational semantics, a correct compiler theorem and a proved concrete compilation result. In-logic compilation removes the compiler from the final statement; it does not eliminate trust in the logic, prover implementation or fidelity of source/machine/hardware models. Source lists, arrays and integers are unbounded; target memory is finite. The default behavior preservation explicitly permits early out-of-memory errors. Source liveness alone therefore does not ensure target liveness. The separate compiler-sound space-cost semantics supports tight bounds for concrete programs and the strengthened transfer. The first compiler’s front end includes parser soundness/completeness with respect to an SML syntax grammar, type-inference soundness (completeness added later), and no runtime errors for typed source programs. That typing theorem does not rule out target out-of-memory exits. The optimizing compiler uses eight intermediate languages and multiple passes per language. Functional big-step, clocked interpreter semantics permit a single simulation proof per phase to handle termination and nontermination; the paper says most, not all, simulation directions are forward. CakeML characteristic formulae are proved sound against CakeML operational semantics, including higher-order recursive functions, mutable state, exceptions and FFI I/O. A later extension handles diverging programs, and a simplified nontermination Hoare logic is proved sound and complete. Do not extend that completeness claim to every CF feature or program-verification automation. The Isabelle/HOL source generator is for the most part verified once for all; the HOL4 generator is for the most part proof-producing. Lem generates source-semantics definitions in both provers from a common specification. The overview does not present a verified cross-prover transport theorem or certify Lem itself. The Silver result composes a verified compiler target, machine-code filesystem and CPU correctness through the formal Verilog implementation. A later verified compiler maps a supported subset of generated Verilog to FPGA technology-mapped netlists. Physical fabrication, FPGA programming and the entire external synthesis toolchain are not established by this overview. Compiler projects using CakeML for a low-level imperative language, a Haskell-inspired language and a choreographic language are described as ongoing in 2021. Project-success explanations are explicitly the author’s beliefs, not empirical causal conclusions. No Rust, Verus, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment is reported.
