- Timely progress tracking (2021)
    - title: Verified Progress Tracking for Timely Dataflow
    - what: Formalizes and proves safety of modern Timely Dataflow progress tracking in Isabelle/HOL by composing distributed progress exchange and worker-local propagation. Corrects an earlier TLA+ clocks model that excludes supported non-upright behavior and lets workers inspect/update global state. Sections 3–4 reconstruct the earlier clocks protocol, whose upright updates require introducing larger pointstamps while dropping smaller ones, then replace its global record field with worker-owned capabilities plus in-flight data. New capability creation is justified by local capabilities; a weaker justified predicate governs withheld progress updates. Sections 5–6 model weighted cyclic graphs, partially ordered timestamp summaries, frontier antichains and incremental worklists. The work_vacant-conditioned local safety theorem and implied-frontier equality compose with exchange under the could-result-in order; initialized workers’ downstream frontiers conservatively witness every existing pointstamp. The proof separates general assumptions with locales and uses signed multisets for finite-support integer counts. Section 7 compares proof engineering with the ported TLA+ proof and reports executable local-propagation comparison against Rust examples.
    - number: about 7,000 Isabelle lines: 1,000 + 3,100 + 1,700 + 1,200
    - number: one person-week and about 1,000 extra lines to port earlier TLA+ safety proofs
    - limits: Finite workers and locations, reliable FIFO progress-message queues, and partially ordered pointstamps. Timestamp summaries are nonnegative, monotone and compositional; every proper graph cycle strictly increments timestamps, and self-edges are excluded. Workers may fail-stop or pause indefinitely; the system retains safety but does not recover. Combined propagation runs to an empty worklist as one action only when it terminates. The paper explicitly does not prove general propagation termination or liveness/fair delivery. Safety covers progress tracking, not the whole dataflow runtime, user operators, or an implementation-refinement theorem for Rust. Proof sketches and more formalization details are in a separate linked extended report not included/read here.

- Wang et al. Ownership NSDI2021 (2021)
    - title: Ownership: A Distributed Futures System for Fine-Grained Tasks
    - what: Distributes task-runtime metadata to the worker that invokes each task, making that caller owner of its result futures. Local synchronous metadata plus scheduling leases reduce overhead; hierarchical reference counts and lineage/fate sharing support cleanup and optional transparent recovery. Implemented in Ray/C++, evaluated with no-op tasks, image serving and video stabilization. AppendixB reports finite TLA+ checking of core scheduling/cleanup/failure transitions, explicitly excluding first-class futures and actors. Captures API and caller-owner distinction, pending-location versus asynchronous value-location metadata, scheduling and reuse, primary pinning/secondary cache, separate value/lineage reference lifetimes, borrower transfer/nesting, failure propagation/actor restrictions/driver fate, exact finite-model bounds and missing liveness assumptions, benchmark controls/omissions and worker-versus-owner recovery tradeoff.
    - limits: Distributed future DFut is an immutable-object reference whose value may be remote or not yet computed. Calling f returns immediately; get blocks and copies the value; passing DFut to an ordinary argument implicitly resolves before task execution. SharedDFut passes the reference itself; borrowers can pass or return it again. Nested returned futures flatten for use but remain represented in reference accounting. del removes a scope reference and Table1 says the program must call it; no tracing collector is claimed. Ownership is runtime metadata responsibility, not Rust ownership or an exclusive data-access capability. The caller owns the result future, distinct from the worker executing the producing task and from physical object location. Metadata includes ID/Owner/Value/References/Task/Locations; borrowers keep a subset. TaskID hashes parent ID and invocation index, root random; ObjectID appends return index. Unique worker/node IDs distinguish incarnations, but no formal hash-collision analysis is given. Shared state includes object locations, reference holders, pending task locations and lineage. Object-directory locations can be asynchronously stale and checked against the store; pending task location must be updated before dispatch so owner can identify failures. Consistency here means metadata agrees with physical runtime state, expressly distinguished from conventional replica consistency. Immutable values avoid mutable shared-memory coherence, not the metadata protocol obligations. One or more workers per node, one local scheduler and object store; each worker executes one task at a time and can spawn children. Abstract decentralized scheduling policy chooses resources/location; owner can start with local or remote scheduler. Scheduler fetches dependencies and leases worker resources; owner records redirect/worker address before every forward/dispatch. Reuse bypasses scheduler only when resource requirements and distributed-memory dependencies match. Worst-case extra redirects cost more RTTs, despite better common-case throughput. An actor is created by a constructor task, caller-owned and represented by ARef; its worker lease lasts until no references remain. Calls can come directly after resolving/caching owner location. Ordering is per caller, not a stated total order across callers or exactly-once execution across failures. Actor restart recreates constructor; durable application state recovery is outside this work. Small values returned inline to owner and copied per holder; large values enter immutable shared-memory object store and are passed by pointer. Configurable size threshold unspecified numerically. Primary copy pinned until owner release/failure; secondary copies are evictable LRU cache. Store Get blocks without any copy until a worker creates/reconstructs it; replication is an optimization, not required durable storage. Release means evictable, not immediate physical erasure. For dereference, caller waits for Value in local table, resolving it from owner if borrower; executing worker receives inline value or store pointer. Owner tracks ordinary dependent task submissions/completions and a borrower tree, releasing value only after references disappear. Actors use analogous counting. Memory safety means avoid prematurely reclaiming referenced immutable values, not a C++ language-level memory-safety proof. AppendixA full count includes local-scope flag, submitted-task count, borrower set, nested containers and lineage count. Ordinary child result can piggyback reference release. Borrower retained after task completion if pending tasks or actor-local references remain. Owner requests quiescence, receives accumulated child borrowers, removes old borrower and merges children; borrower itself does not delete its borrower set. Dead borrowers removed after failure notice. Nested containing futures pin enclosed future value. This transfer protocol is described, not mechanized in the reported first-class-future-free model. Lineage kept separately from value: passing a DFut increments downstream lineage dependency until that task description is itself collected. A value can be released while lineage count remains nonzero, permitting recomputation. Inline results do not require their creating Task retained; referenced large results require reconstructible dependency closure. Owner discards whole record once Task and Value gone. Planned checkpointing could collect lineage earlier; automatic general lineage compaction is not established. Failure model is worker/node crashes reported by scheduler/heartbeat notifications to all workers. Non-owner waits for owner to handle loss; owner compares Locations or Owner field. No Byzantine behavior, partition safety, detector accuracy/completeness theorem or durable global-metadata failure coverage is supplied. Eventual progress necessarily requires successful task termination, usable resources, message/failure-notification progress and a sufficiently stable surviving recovery chain; the paper does not print precise fairness or failure-bound assumptions for the model. Lost object: owner first tries/promotes secondary copy, otherwise resubmits stored task and recursively reconstructs inputs, requesting their owners when borrowed. Requires idempotent computations or suitable read-only/checkpointable/transient actor state. Retrying is not proof of exactly-once external effects. Nondeterministic execution recovery is cited as complementary work, not fully provided here. Lost owner: free owned object copies or reclaim pending leases and fate-share borrowers/dependent tasks. Failed owner task is reconstructed by its parent owner, recreating children and references with new owner address. Informal argument follows pass-to-child, first-class pass and return-to-parent cases. It is not a full mechanized arbitrary-borrowing proof; AppendixB excludes first-class futures. The application fate-shares with root driver, whose recovery/persistence needs additional techniques. For transparent recovery, actors must not store borrowed DFuts in local state. AppendixA permits tracking such stored references during normal operation; that is not a contradiction because transparent recovery is optional. Manual failure handling remains available. Actor-local state recovery is out of scope despite constructor restart; application checkpoints in evaluation are explicitly external mechanisms. AppendixB specifies ownership-table transitions for task scheduling, garbage collection and worker failures. Listed properties: preserve reconstructible lineage of needed futures; eventually execute tasks/resolve Gets even with failures; eventually clean task/value state once all future references leave scope. Printed LineageInScope recursion says inline or all argument futures safe. The excerpt does not spell out its full domain/scope guards, transition system, fairness or failure limits; do not treat this brief recursive expression as a complete executable specification. Reported TLA+ Model Checker exploration bounds: at most3 recursive remote-call levels and3 futures per function; more than44million distinct states, safety and liveness reported holding. No unbounded inductive proof, TLAPS proof, C++ refinement/compiler theorem, model-check wall time/configuration or reproducible run appears here. No Resource Leakage is listed as a goal, but the run-result sentence explicitly names safety and liveness rather than separately confirming every cleanup formula. First-class futures and actors explicitly excluded; full model release planned. Implementation about14k C++ LOC, basis of Rayv1.0+ at publication. Discussion calls performance/reliable failure detection/GC anecdotal user benefits and says transparent recovery not widely used. These are historical author reports, not current Ray compatibility/deployment measurements. Artifact link stephanie-wang/ownership-nsdi2021-artifact is not fetched or executed. Experiments AWS EC2, head m5.16xlarge by default; some throughput head/intermediates m5.8xlarge. Baselines pass-by-value with futures, Rayv0.7 distributed leases, and Rayv0.7 modified to synchronously update centralized master before execution. All distributed-future variants use sharded unreplicated Redis for global metadata and Ray scheduler/store; ownership/pass-by-value use gRPC worker communication. These are shared-platform comparisons, not isolated proof all differences derive solely from metadata ownership. Tasks use predetermined placement, reducing scheduling variance and excluding arbitrary-policy behavior. Throughput leaves are no-op tasks returning short strings or1MB blobs, one intermediate driver per5 m5.8xlarge workers, up to100 workers; intermediates colocated or spread. Spreading control enables horizontal scaling; colocated baselines bottleneck at per-node scheduler, ownership improves reuse but still saturates. Centralized2shards scales about60nodes; more shards raises its threshold. Ownership≈leases for spread large objects, better for small values; unstable large pass-by-value results omitted for implementation backpressure deficiency. Plot throughput is not useful application work per second. Delegation benchmark100k no-op tasks all depend on one1MB driver-owned object on single m5.16xlarge; varying nested borrowers gives ownership about2× throughput and little baseline gain. Demonstrates hierarchy/refcount distributing load in this workload, not automatic scaling of a single sequential driver or every task graph. No general speedup guarantee. Latency microbenchmark3k tasks on one colocated/remote m5.16xlarge worker; shared1MB input, short output, measured time before task starts, not complete arbitrary-task response time. Figure13 error bars are standard deviation across tasks, not repeated-experiment confidence intervals. Reported average1.6× lower versus centralized/leases. Abstract1ms is broad architectural result, not a universal deadline. Recovery chain: tasks sleep total10s on remote m5.xlarge, return short string or10MB; kill/restart worker5s in,1s heartbeat timeout. Centralized baseline omitted for implementation effort. Normalize total runtime to ownership without failures. Leases normal runtime up to1.18× faster, but recovery more than double due to repeated lease expiration/doubling; shorter interval trades overhead/stability. Ownership total within2× normal here is a measurement, not a theorem for arbitrary graphs/failures. Model serving:4 p3.16xlarge nodes, each1Router/8ResNet50Models, batch16,2300requests/s. Median54ms for ownership/centralized; reported tail1s vs108ms,about9×. No-borrowing router copies images,p50=80ms/p100=3.2s. This ablation changes reference versus value movement, not fault-tolerance proof. Full accuracy/model training irrelevant to runtime measurement. Video:60 concurrent streams, each m5.xlarge worker, separate owner m5.xlarge hosts4drivers;29frames/s source,1s smoothing radius. Decode actor permits rereading frames for idempotence. Median≈65ms, lease/centralized tails1208/1923ms. Lease Decoder failure injected5s after start, ownership scenarios10s; acknowledge different timings rather than infer controlled identical replay cost. Leases checkpointing unavailable because implementation cannot safely collect lineage. Ownership video worker failure recovery1.9s versus owner failure8.8s (replay from beginning). Application checkpoints once/s to remote Redis, intermediate state plus sink frame-index commit, reduce owner recovery to1.1s with reported negligible overhead. This checkpoint/sink scheme is described but no exactly-once end-to-end output, Redis durability or all crash-interleaving proof supplied. Distinguish application checkpoint extension from default automatic runtime guarantee. Whole paper includes related RPC, dataflow, actors, parallel-runtime and distributed-memory work. No LLM-generated specs/proofs, Verus, verified Rust or source-to-model refinement. Bounded TLA+ evidence is directly relevant; normal borrowing/actor behavior and implementation remain outside that model. Performance/failure experiments complement, rather than establish, general liveness/resource-safety claims.

- Algorand Coq (2020)
    - title: Towards a Verified Model of the Algorand Consensus Protocol in Coq
    - what: # Whole-paper read: Towards a Verified Model of the Algorand Consensus Protocol in Coq (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Musab A. Alturki, Jing Chen, Victor Luchangco, Brandon Moore, Karl Palmskog, Lucas Peña and Grigore Roşu. arXiv1907.05523v2,25August2020,6pages. The paper reports a Coq proof that two certificates in one round carry the same value, including certificates from different periods. It models Byzantine behavior, time and partitions. The linked release contains a completed safety theorem, but its unconditional quorum axioms raise a substantial scope problem described below. No Coq check was run. [Q1,Q2,Q6,S1,S2,S6]  ## Model and claimed guarantee  A round may have several periods. Users propose, soft-vote, cert-vote and send open or value-carrying next-votes to advance periods. VRF-based self-selection chooses a different committee for each step; selected users attach ordered credentials. A user ordinarily recognizes a certificate after receiving enough cert-votes. The theorem instead defines certification by a quorum having sent votes somewhere in the trace. Authors justify this abstraction by allowing a corrupt user's sent message to reach nobody. This distinction matters when comparing certificates with local observations. [Q3,Q5]  The model uses finite types of user identifiers and abstract values, real-valued time, local states, finite message maps, a history of broadcast messages and a partition flag. Global transitions deliver messages, advance time, perform local actions, enter/leave partitions, corrupt users, replay historical messages and forge messages when the adversary has the relevant keys. Delivery deadlines constrain unpartitioned operation; partitions remove that bound. Transaction/currency details and concrete cryptographic implementations are abstracted away. [Q2,Q3,Q4,S3,S4]  The printed theorem requires an initial state before the target round and a valid finite transition trace. Given any two period/value certifications in that round, their values agree. It does not assert that any certification occurs, a bound on completion time, or implementation refinement. The same-period proof uses honest quorum overlap and the fact that an honest user cert-votes at most once per period. The different-period argument preserves an invariant excluding a quorum of open next-votes and restricting any value-next-vote quorum to the certified value. The source theorem is named `safety`, rather than the paper's `asynchronous_safety`, and ends in `Qed.` [Q6,Q7,S6,S7]  ## Assumptions and a static scope concern  The prose states: “The adversary must control less than 1/3 of the total stake participating in the consensus protocol.” The mechanized committee properties are axioms; the paper explicitly leaves the probabilistic analysis to external pen-and-paper proofs. Thus the reported symbolic theorem is conditional on these axioms, rather than a mechanized derivation of a numerical failure probability from a stake distribution. The inspected source also assumes distinct credentials for distinct users, qualifying periods at least1, positive small-message delay and ordered delay/recovery bounds. Thresholds and valid-block/hash relations are parameters. [Q2,Q3,S3,S8]  Reader deduction, not an executed Coq result: the pinned release's honest-overlap axiom quantifies over every sequence of global states, without an `is_trace` premise or a constraint on corruption. The definition of `honest_during_step` tests that a present user is uncorrupted at every listed state whose local round/period/step is at most the requested step. Global and local records impose no validity invariant on their constructors. This combination appears to rule out every committee subset reaching the assumed threshold. [S1,S2,S4,S5]  The argument is concrete. Suppose q is a committee subset of size at least tau for step(r,p,s). Construct one global state containing each q member at exactly(r,p,s), with `corrupt=true`; set timers to0, optional starting values toNone, all message/vote/proposal sequences empty and message maps/history empty. Such records need no valid transition history. On the singleton sequence containing that state, `step_leb (r,p,s) (r,p,s)` is true, so `honest_during_step` is false for every member of q. Apply the unconditional overlap axiom to this sequence with both quorums equal to q. It requires an honest member of q, a contradiction. For tau_c this excludes the quorum required by `certified_in_period`, irrespective of whether the target certification trace is valid. Therefore the release's safety conclusion appears true because its certificate antecedents cannot hold. [S1,S2,S4,S5,S9]  This is an argument about the printed definitions and pinned source, not an Algorand protocol counterexample. It does not by itself show all axioms inconsistent: if every relevant committee is smaller than its threshold, the overlap axioms can hold because their size premises are always false. A separate quorum-existence premise would conflict with the overlap property above. The intended restriction to suitable executions/adversaries is not present in this axiom. The paper displays the same unrestricted trace quantification, although it omits the helper definitions needed to complete this analysis. [Q5,S1,S2]  ## Evaluation, cases and remaining work  The work is a proof report, not a performance benchmark. Authors report “around 2000 specification lines and 4000 proof lines.” No prover runtime, independent reproduction, protocol throughput/latency result or empirical corruption experiment is reported. The linked release README calls safety complete and liveness proofs incomplete. `safety.v` imports model/helpers/quorums and does not import `liveness.v`; admitted liveness results therefore should not be described as evidence that the safety proof uses those admissions. A full dependency/assumption audit and independent proof check were not performed here. [Q8,S6,S10]  Concrete cases include delayed cert-votes allowing later periods to certify the same block, a replay action restricted to messages in history, and same-period double voting excluded for honest users. These explain the intended safety proof. The corrupt singleton sequence above instead tests the scope of a universally quantified axiom, rather than producing a legal Byzantine execution. Liveness is future work in the paper; the abstract's “exactly one block” description must not be substituted for the theorem's at-most-one guarantee. [Q1,Q4,Q6,Q7,Q8]  For this collection, the contribution is a timed Byzantine consensus model and a trace-based Coq safety development. It also supplies an evaluation lesson for specification/proof agents: a checked implication requires scrutiny of its premises and evidence that those premises allow the intended behaviors. The latter lesson is my inference from the source analysis. There is no Verus, verified-Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment in this paper.  ## Read and source scope  Read all6pages, §§1–5, all11references and every displayed record, rule, definition, theorem and lemma; inspected page4–6renders. There are no numbered figures/tables or appendices. Reference entries were read, not all referenced papers. Acquired11static files from the paper-linked release-1.1 commit3bbf1a663b3b2fdf497416efa6b01d2c1c54459d, with SHA256 and Git blob identities. Whole README, build metadata, local/global-state files and quorums.v were read; selected ranges of the large model/helper/safety/liveness files were inspected. No claim of a complete Coq-source audit. No author code, compiler, checker, prover or solver was run; no serialized scientific results or models were loaded. Official and saved inventory PDFs are byte-identical. Exact excerpts and source slices are in quotes.json; acquisition and inspection scope are recorded separately.

- Determinizing Crash Behavior with a Verified Snapshot-Consistent Flash Translation Layer (2020)
    - what: SCFTL implements a sequential read/write/flush disk interface whose completed flush commits a snapshot. Ordinary crashed operations preserve the last snapshot; a crashed flush may retain the prior snapshot or commit the new one. Stable logical-to-physical mapping uses committed delta pages/full checkpoints, and two-phase GC retains snapshot data until flush. Agda establishes the abstract simulation framework; Serval/Rosette/Z3 verify implementation obligations with manual transformations and three verified runtime validators. FEMU and modified xv6 benchmarks examine flush-frequency tradeoffs. Records precise crashed-flush nondeterminism and repeated-recovery semantics, no-op write bounds and upper-layer obligations, all five checkpoint recovery cases, GC capacity inequalities, four state/abstraction relations, SMT overapproximation/ghost/partition techniques and proof gaps. Saves all LOC cells, size-specific verification times, partial-data stress-check scope, exact filesystem labels and adverse high-flush/ext4 comparisons. Separates mathematical metatheory, solver checks, validation and unverified upper layers.
    - limits: §§1,4.2: Deterministic recovery refers to a crash during a regular operation after the last successful flush. A crash inside flush can recover either the old snapshot or the new pre-flush volatile state. The abstract specification explicitly permits both; no unique snapshot independent of crash position is promised. Repeated crashes during recovery preserve the stable state until a successful recovery. §§3.2,4.1 Figure 4: Writes outside address/counter bounds are no-ops. InBounds uses a≤amax and wcnt≤wcntmax; the counter increments after an accepted write, so exact boundary interpretation follows that inclusive condition. Upper layers must budget every atomic operation before execution, flush before insufficient capacity and split an operation larger than a whole epoch. A flush midway could persist a partial operation. §§1,6.2: Top-level SCFTL operations are sequential; concurrent FTL requests are unsupported by specification/proof. Flash commands inside or across successive unsynchronized operations can overlap and reorder across pages until SYNC. Hardware parallelism is distinct from concurrent client-operation verification. §§2,4–6: Agda mechanizes the disk/simulation metatheory; C implementation obligations are symbolically evaluated with Serval and discharged in Z3. Manual reformulation/partition of obligations is connected by pen-and-paper reasoning, explicitly leaving a gap in the formal proof. Do not call the whole C-to-snapshot proof one continuous machine-checked derivation. §§6–6.1: Three properties are not proved for the main implementation: injective L2P after recovery, enough space after recovery and enough space after flush. Verified validators establish success-flag⇒property and may only change validation variables. No notification occurred in experiments; that does not prove the implementation always satisfies these properties or always continues successfully. Failure notification is not a demonstrated recovery/fallback for these three checks. §6: TCB assumes error-free flash; correct Z3, Agda and Serval; correct LLVM-to-machine-code translation; correct LightNVM Linux module. Hardware/media faults, bad blocks, wear-out and ECC failures are outside the guarantee. No hot/cold separation or wear leveling implemented; validator-checked unverified allocator is an example of a possible extension. §§3.1,5.1: Model has erase-before-write/sequential page constraints, same-page command ordering and arbitrary cross-page scheduling. READ returns the latest modeled content irrespective of sync flag; normal I/O semantics assumes this behavior. Unsynchronized crash pages are overapproximated as arbitrary values, not enumerated physical histories. This is conservative for crash reasoning within the assumed command semantics. §§3.3–3.4: L2P is the persistent primary data; P2L/queues/counts rebuild after recovery. Invalid blocks may still hold stable-snapshot sectors, so they become erasable only after flush. No internal flush is allowed merely to facilitate GC because it would change the externally selected snapshot. Capacity bounds and reserved space are part of the implementation contract. §§4.2–4.4: Behavioral correctness compares reads in normal states following successful operations; crash states need only weaker CR/CI. Initial new disks must recover before use. Lemma 1 proves the abstract disk snapshot-consistent; Theorem 1 derives observational simulation from initial relations/per-operation Type A and invariant Type B obligations; Theorem 2 transfers snapshot consistency. These safety properties do not establish termination under arbitrary permanent crashing or concurrent request semantics. §§5.2–5.4: Ghost arrays remove existential choices while non-ghost transitions remain independent. Splitting postconditions and dropping antecedent conjuncts strengthens obligations; proof partition manually maps crash states to old/new flush outcomes. Fast solver checks still require correct semantic construction and checked side conditions; absence of one timeout is not completeness for all capacities. §6: Verification instantiates one capacity at a time: reported 8GB and 256GB results and selected write bounds 2048–20480. It is not a universally quantified theorem for all device sizes/configurations. Counts are 98 RI/AR and 17 CI/CR conditions; they are not 115 independently complete correctness properties. §7: Performance runs on FEMU/QEMU emulated Open-Channel SSD, Linux 4.15, liblightnvm/libaio with added NVMe base-command latency emulation. Not a physical SSD endurance/power-cut evaluation. Host is printed as 12-core i7-8700; retain source label without independently correcting core/thread terminology. §7.1: Stress tests compare only first few bytes of every sector; four configurations/eight hours, over 1.4TB writes, about twelve million flushes and ten thousand simulated crashes. Garbage on unsynchronized pages tests a modeled failure behavior. Passing these checks is not exhaustive byte-level recovery validation or proof that real hardware obeys the model. §7.2: async baseline does not do checkpointing and omits 2PGC and write bounds. sync uses synchronous commands and an assumed battery-backed merge page, ignoring flush. pblk receives one-thread/four-thread tests while SCFTL stays sequential. These have unequal crash guarantees and concurrency; performance ratios are conditional tradeoffs. §7.3: xv6 changes are unverified demonstration code; extending proof to upper layers remains future work. xv6-group persists through fsync and allows later system calls to roll back as a prefix, whereas comparison xv6 variants provide immediate durability at every syscall. The speedup combines lower flush frequency, log removal and changed durability timing; it is not an equal-durability implementation-only gain. §7.3 Figures 7–8: Main headline says 3–30× and at worst two times slower, but rounded printed largefile labels give 39/0.6=65× versus xv6/async (32.5× versus sync), and SQLite 142/61≈2.33× slower than ext4-data. Preserve exact labels and identify approximate headline wording rather than force agreement. Largefile Figure 7 group bar exceeds chart top; use printed 39MB/s rather than bar height. §7.3: Five runs per filesystem workload, reported standard deviation under 8%; this statement does not supply raw runs or certify every FTL/boot measurement used five repetitions. mailbench on ext4-metadata adds fdatasync to its temporary file. Benchmark-specific sync protocol/configuration matters for fairness. §§2,8: Verified layered storage, concurrent FTL operations and commercial optimizations remain future work. Relevant to crash specifications and agent proof evaluation, but no Verus/Rust, TLA+, LLM-agent study or distributed-consensus theorem. Saved PDF contains no artifact appendix/repository pointer; no external implementation or proof replay.

- Giskard specification (2020)
    - title: Specification of the Giskard Consensus Protocol
    - what: The paper gives a rigorous executable-style specification of the Giskard consensus protocol used by PlatON, defining nodes, epochs/views, message formats, local/global block stages, state transitions, and fault behavior. It proves three safety properties: same-height prepare blocks in one view are identical; same-height precommit blocks across views are identical; and same-height committed blocks are identical. The proofs reduce quorum intersections and view-change height relationships to contradictions under the one-third Byzantine bound. The specification is intended as an implementation and formal-verification reference, while liveness is left open.
    - limits: The network is partially synchronous and nodes communicate by authenticated broadcast; at most one third of participating nodes are Byzantine. Epoch/view changes can be asynchronous across nodes, and Byzantine behavior includes proposing multiple same-height blocks or voting without required messages. Safety reasoning focuses on message/block stages and does not establish liveness, performance, implementation correctness, or cryptographic assumptions beyond authenticated signatures and quorum behavior. The protocol has ten-block views and VRF-selected epoch participants as modeled in the specification.

- Leaderless SMR ROLL limits (2020)
    - title: Leaderless State-Machine Replication: Specification, Properties, Limits
    - what: Defines leaderless state-machine replication using possibly cyclic dependency graphs, separates committing from stabilization/execution, and decomposes decision into dependency discovery plus per-command consensus. Claims ROLL tradeoff 2F+f−1≤n between failure tolerance f and fast-quorum size n−F under Reliability, Optimal Latency, Load Balancing. For protocols on its parameter frontier, every chain length k has some failure-free 2-asynchronous run with a live dependency chain of length k. A five-site Google Cloud experiment illustrates EPaxos tail latency increasing with contention, unlike Mencius; proofs in conference paper are sketches with formal treatment deferred. Records graph phases, stable agreement modulo aborted dependencies, batch execution order, DDS visibility/weak agreement, exact ROLL quantifiers, quorum partition proof, skyline examples and chain induction. Separates empirical tail/correlation observations from existential worst-case chains, nice runs from synchrony, decision from execution, and stated abstract properties from a machine-checked implementation. Replaces earlier record that lacked later sections.
    - limits: Fixed n≥2 message-passing processes, fail-stop rather than Byzantine faults, deterministic replicated state machine and unbounded command/log space. Model extends asynchronous wait-free computation with failure detectors; precise detector admissibility/fairness assumptions are deferred to [22]. Do not read Reliability as solving consensus in pure asynchrony without such an assumption. Clients are not modeled; replicas proxy submissions, and different replicas may submit the same command. Conflicts safely overapproximate semantic noncommutativity, considering both final state and response values; relation is symmetric and nonreflexive. Distinct nonconflicting commands may execute in different orders. Classic logs append immutable slots; Generic SMR uses acyclic partial logs with incoming-prefix closure and compatible upper bounds. Safety properties are distinct from termination and real-time/client-response contracts; no complete client refinement proof printed. Leaderless graph maps each command to pending⊥, aborted⊤, or a committed dependency set; phases pending/abort/commit/stable/execute. Aborted commands are removed from dependency sets permanently. A committed command is stable only when no command in its transitive dependency closure remains pending. Stability agrees on stable dependencies globally; conflicting committed commands must have at least one direct dependency between them, allowing cycles rather than a prechosen total order. Algorithm1 executes the largest still-stable subset of a stable command’s closure, in reachability order between components and canonical total order within a cycle. Already executed dependencies need not execute again. Invariant1 excludes an unexecuted dependency outside an earlier batch; Invariant2 says if conflicting c precedes d within a batch then c is in d’s transitive dependencies. It is not simply arbitrary SCC iteration: batch includes eligible dependency predecessors too. Abort pruning, stable-versus-execute status and canonical order must be made explicit in a formal implementation. Theorem1 states Generic SMR reduces to Leaderless SMR without messages, with proof deferred. Direction is an implementation/refinement claim, not equivalence of arbitrary cyclic dependency states with Generic acyclic logs. Ordering all commuting commands to recover Classic SMR would require extra communication. The common dependency graph itself is not yet an agreed total execution log. Algorithm2 calls DDS.announce(c), returning dependency set D or abort⊤ and fast flag b; slow path invokes per-command consensus, then records and broadcasts outcome. Coordinator or a process suspecting it may submit/recover. A nice run has no failures and a perfect failure detector, so only the coordinator calls that command’s consensus. Leaderless does not mean no coordinator: each command has one, with no single primary ordering all commands. DDS Visibility: two conflicting nonaborted announcements include each other in at least one returned set. Weak Agreement: if one announcement of c returns a nonaborted set with fast=true, every other announcement of c returns a nonaborted set; differences contain only commands whose every announcement aborts. Thus raw dependency sets may differ, but aborted differences are removed before stable agreement. Theorem2 claims Algorithm2 correctness, proof in [22]; consensus, detector, and DDS are assumed abstract services, not implemented or verified here. Examples: rotating coordinators preassign order and always use slow flag; Clock-RSM uses timestamps and majority wait, propagates clocks for stabilization; Mencius aborts unannounced prior slots and needs everybody for fast flag; EPaxos example omits sequence numbers, unions observed conflicts, uses spontaneous agreement, and falls back/recovery to a majority; Caesar timestamps and waits/rejects inconsistent higher-timestamp conflicts. These are explanatory decompositions, not verified full protocol implementations or safety audits of recovery rules. Reliability states every submitted command eventually decided at every correct process when at most f failures. This is decision, not by itself a quantitative execution-latency guarantee. Surrounding prose inconsistently says after f failures no progress or less than f; retain the explicit inclusive property. Stable termination of dependency closures and outcomes of submissions by faulty coordinators require the detailed model. Footnote3 discusses reconfiguration/persistent recovery informally, outside the fixed fail-stop proof. Optimal Latency: in every nice run, announce returns after two message delays with nonaborted D containing only previously announced commands; if no concurrent conflicting command, fast flag true. With contention it may be slow-flagged despite two-delay DDS completion, and complete execution may wait arbitrarily longer. Load Balancing: any quorum Q containing coord(c) with |Q|≥n−F can serve its announcement in a nice run. This is freedom of quorum choice, not an empirical guarantee of equal load or geographic latency. Theorem3 ROLL assumes those properties and an available pair of noncommuting commands. Bound 2F+f−1≤n is necessary, not sufficient to construct a protocol. Together with majority-style bounds f,F≤floor((n−1)/2), skyline means no simultaneous parameter improvement. For fixed f the algebra gives quorum q=n−F≥ceil((n+f−1)/2). Do not substitute arbitrary fast-consensus quorums: ROLL quorums must contain that command’s coordinator. Proof sketch assumes violating inequality, partitions P1,P2 of sizeF−1 and Q of size n−2F+2. CAP premise 2F<n gives two coordinators p1,p2 in Q; fast quorums Q1=P1∪Q−p2 and Q2=P2∪Q−p1 have size n−F. Solo nice runs decide empty dependencies. Concurrent run delays cross messages then crashes Q; integer violation implies |Q|≤f. Survivor cannot distinguish carefully spliced runs, forcing empty dependencies for both conflicting commands, contrary to Visibility/Consistency. Detector-history equivalence and eventual stability are essential deferred proof details; the conference sketch invokes Reliability (defined as decision) to obtain stability without fully showing that bridge. Printed consequence that a plain majority fast quorum tolerates at most one failure is not implied by its displayed inequality. For odd n=2m+1, q=m+1 permits f≤2; for even n=2m, q=m+1 permits f≤3, subject also to f≤floor((n−1)/2). Its own n5(F,f)=(2,2) example gives majority q3 with f2, contradicting the unqualified consequence. This is a printed inference conflict, not a demonstrated implementation or refutation of Theorem3. Frontier examples: n5 only(F,f)=(2,2), n7 (2,3),(3,2); EPaxos attains first n7 tuple, Atlas offers(3,1). Paper calls EPaxos/Alvin optimal for n=2f+1, Atlas for f1 and even n or n3. Fast quorum floor(3n/4) for EPaxos needs integer rounding; nearby f+(f+1)/2 notation is unrounded for even f. Table1 rotating-coordinator quorum0 should not be treated as a legal coordinator-containing fast quorum; protocol lacks Optimal Latency and uses no fast DDS path. Table1 marks Caesar as having Optimal Latency, but §7 explicitly says Caesar lacks it because even contention-free commitment may need two round trips. Keep this internal classification conflict rather than certifying either claim from the unread Caesar paper. Table1 has Clock-RSM and rotating coordinator without Optimal Latency, Mencius with it but nonoptimal frontier; EPaxos/Alvin/Atlas with stated frontier conditions. Historical protocol optimality/current best claims are not checked beyond this2020paper. Chain c1…ck means ci∈deps(ci+1), so dependencies run toward the first element. §5.1 defines live as first command not stable at any process; §5 introductory overview instead says last, which is inconsistent. With pending d and deps(a)={b},deps(b)={a,c,d}, chain dba blocks a; c alone stable. A live finite chain does not assert an infinite run, inevitable starvation, or every execution having a long chain. k-asynchrony bounds overlaps: if any message overlaps both first and last messages of a causal message path, path length≤k. Overlap is real-time interval overlap, not Lamport independence of endpoint events. Formal definition is universal over all messages/paths, unlike introductory prose saying existence of a path. 2-asynchronous is not a fixed bound on wall-clock message latency, delay ratio, or clock skew; nice means failure-free/perfect detector, not lock-step synchronous. Theorem4: for every finite k>0, there exists a 2-asynchronous nice run of any ROLL-optimal protocol with live chain sizek. This is a worst-case existence theorem, not a probability distribution, expected latency, or measured percentile bound. Conference statement does not give a numeric command-latency formula in milliseconds or require every command to suffer. Full proof in [22]; conflict-pattern/termination assumptions belong to that detailed model. Chain sketch splits each announcement into request-send S, intermediate M, reply-return R. Induction constructs complete nice σi with no pending messages, chain ci…c1, and interposed Γprime whose paths have size≤1 and whose participating overlap with Qi is Pi of sizef−1. Alternate quorums and indistinguishable coordinator views force next dependency. Truncating final replies makes the chain live. Figure4 gives n5,k7 and quorums{p1,p2,p3}/{p3,p4,p5} with intersection{p3}. Exact general quorum/induction case analysis deferred; sizek need not mean k different replicas. Experiment: Google Cloud, five sites South Carolina, Finland, Canada, Australia, Taiwan (leader),128 closed-loop clients each, no-op service, synthetic key conflicts atρ=0,2,5,10,30percent for EPaxos; Paxos and Mencius baselines. Latency submission-to-execution at steady state, not commit acknowledgment. Each operation picks common key42 with probabilityρ, unique otherwise; ρ is hot-key choice probability, not directly fraction of conflicting random command pairs (under independent choices that pair probability isρ²). No-op operations commute semantically, so key conflicts are an intentional safe overapproximation. Figure1 CDF shows EPaxos tails increasing with synthetic contention and Mencius lower median; paper reports latency/batch-size correlation>0.7. No named correlation estimator, sample count, duration, repeated-run uncertainty, machine types, protocol versions, or fault injection specified in this conference paper. No exact quantiles tabulated; graph readings must not be invented. Correlation plus worst-case theorem supports a mechanism, not measured causal attribution of every tail sample or general workload performance. Mitigation discussion: pure writes may return at commit or durable f+1 receipt, but footnote5 requires later reads to wait for all preceding writes to preserve linearizability. Claimed read dependency exclusion assumes cited per-read single-process execution scheme, not arbitrary reads. Waiting for prior announcements can still allow chain of sizen by rotating coordinators, stated without proof here. These are tradeoffs, not new verified algorithms. ROLL Optimal Latency/Load Balancing enforce request-reply form with no pending messages at announcement completion. Weaker latency permitting background messages can sidestep the bound in a fully synchronous model by sharing replies among quorum members. Discussion says partially synchronous version retains ROLL and chaining requires more asynchrony. Thus theorem is relative to its formal properties, not a universal impossibility for every system called leaderless or every weaker fast-path definition. - Li et al. Pegasus 2020 (2020)
    - title: Pegasus: Tolerating Skewed Workloads in Distributed Storage with In-Network Coherence Directories
    - what: Uses a top-of-rack programmable switch as a metadata-only directory that tracks the currently observable versions and replica locations of popular keys. It can place each write on a fresh replica set and route reads to current replicas, balancing skew without storing values in switch SRAM; extends to inter-rack chain replication. Supplies a core linearizability argument, reports a safety-model-checked TLA+ specification and evaluates P4/C++/DPDK prototypes. Captures reply-based externalization invariant (including reads that expose unacknowledged writes), explicit get/put-only API, optional request-ID deduplication and its migration pause, hot-key promotion/demotion/virtual writes, version/collision/GC assumptions, read-only load-bound scope, inter-rack recovery/version contracts, printed branch reversal and actual SLO/workload/resource/scale controls.
    - limits: Basic design is an in-memory read/write key-value store over32–256 servers within a rack and one trusted programmable ToR switch. No read-modify-write, atomic cross-key operations or intra-rack fault-tolerance guarantee. Hot-key copies are for load balancing, not a complete durability scheme; most cold keys have one copy. Multi-rack chain replication separately supplies redundant copies. No Byzantine client/server/switch protocol or persistent storage proof (§3,§7). All requests and replies must traverse the same directory authority for a rack; clients initially address home servers for cold keys. Network may lose/reorder/duplicate packets. Switch assigns monotonically increasing versions and servers atomically retain the higher version/value, so older arrivals cannot overwrite new state. Safety relies on correct server/switch processing and directory consistency; arbitrary network loss does not imply termination. Fixed pipeline implementation is not accompanied by a proved P4/compiler/hardware refinement (§§4.3,5–6,8). Core switch state is global ver_next, replicated-key membership rkeys, per-key rset and ver_completed. Write request receives a fresh version; replicated writes may target any server(s), reads one current rset member. A higher-version read or write reply replaces rset with its sender and updates completed version; equal version adds sender. Lower replies do not roll back directory state. Higher writes can already exist at servers before replies expose them; rset is a routing authority, not an assertion that all physical copies are equal (§6.1–6.2,Algorithms1–2). Correctness invariant is at least one directory address with the latest externalized write plus its version. A read reply can externalize a concurrent newer write before its write acknowledgment, so monitoring only write replies is insufficient. Fixed-popularity proof orders writes by assigned versions and establishes later reads see at least preceding completed-write/read versions. Arbitrarily delayed replies may return older data for overlapping operations without violating linearizability (§6.2.3). §6 reports a public TLA+ specification model checked for safety. Paper does not supply state-space bounds, checker/version/configuration, state count/time, exact checked invariant set or whether hot-key changes, at-most-once transitions and multi-rack reconfiguration are all modeled. No model text/proof is printed, and no liveness/model-to-P4 proof is claimed. AppendixA lists the specification in the artifact but gives performance rather than model-checking workflow. This record reads the paper, not the repository, and does not independently verify or rerun that safety result. Hot-key addition first installs home-server rset and a ver_completed fence of ver_next−1, then rkeys membership. This avoids admitting stale in-flight versions as new replicas; promotion does not itself copy the object. Later writes redirect replication. Demotion marks transition, forces next write home, and removes the directory entry only after the matching reply. Read-only/infrequent-write objects require controller-triggered virtual writes preserving value while raising version and forwarding it. These ordered control-plane transitions need their own proof obligations (§6.3). Optional Pegasus-AMO suppresses retransmitted writes via client request tables and globally unique REQID. A deterministic REQID-selected detector receives original/retry, processes only a fresh request, and forwards to selected additional replicas, distributing writes independently of hot-key placement. Most-recent-request-per-client tables need an appropriate client request/retention discipline; paper does not give a general arbitrary-concurrent-request dedup proof. Transitions between popular/cold state pause writes and migrate per-client table state (home→all on promotion, aggregate latest→home on demotion). This is not an unconditional end-to-end exactly-once liveness guarantee (§6.4). Random and load-weighted round-robin selection are policies separated from coherence correctness. Replication factor is proportional to reads-per-write to bound replication overhead; writes can choose a fresh set each time. A full independent proof of all performance policies is absent. REQID-based AMO detector selection is needed to preserve write load balancing rather than route every hot-key write to its home (§§4.4,6.4–6.5). Load-balance analysis extends cited caching result: after removing hottest O(n log n) keys, residual load fits capacity up to a slack factorα, under the prior randomly partitioned cluster-service setting. Given spare total capacity byα, full replication plus suitable scheduling gives a read-only load redistribution construction. §4.5 explicitly says this initial analysis may not apply once write-dependent replica sets restrict read choices. Arbitrary read/write-ratio effectiveness then has intuition and experiments, not the same stated universal theorem. n counts servers, not keys; O(n log n) directory entries also store per-server locations and are not O(n log n) bytes. Hash collisions use server-held current popular-key sets and forwarding a misrouted cold key back home; if two hot keys collide only one is replicated. Controller must keep membership information correct.64-bit versions make overflow unlikely (claimed>100years at line rate), not mathematically impossible; wrap handling is only delegated to standard techniques. Controller GC removes stale-version/nonhome-cold copies based on reported completed versions. These features are discussed, without comprehensive modeled collision/wrap/GC state-machine evidence in the paper (§6.6). Multi-rack design maps key ranges to chains of Pegasus racks through a global configuration service. Write flows head→tail, read goes to tail; popular replicas within a rack are load-balanced by its ToR. It cannot balance a hot key across arbitrary racks; simulations are mentioned without detailed presented data. Treat each rack as one chain replica, repair failed racks via standard chain replication. Efficient individual-server repair is stated but explicitly omitted from the paper (§7). Reconfiguration must retain version monotonicity when head changes. An existing chain member has observed completed versions; a newly added head must first raise ver_next to at least other chain switches. Failure detection, configuration agreement, state-transfer fencing and in-flight-request handling are delegated/described at high level, not mechanically proved here (§7). Reader finding: §7,p.395 prints the multi-rack condition backward: stamp ver_next if VER is not null, otherwise preserve incoming VER. Adjacent explanation says only the head supplies the version and all downstream racks retain it. Those cannot both hold for normal null-initialized client requests. Intended branch is stamp when VER is null; preserve non-null and advance local ver_next beyond it. This is a rendered prose inconsistency, not an identified bug in the uninspected TLA+/P4 artifacts. Switch uses exact-match hot-key lookup/control-plane updates, two version register arrays, and rset size/bitmap/server-list arrays. The flattened per-key list index is k*n+i. Packet rewrite/multicast handles one/many destinations. Replicated keys have read/write counters; cold traffic sampled to switch CPU for access-frequency estimation, controller scans and updates. No value payload is stored in switch, permitting larger values with the same directory footprint (§8). Implementation: P4 data plane on Tofino, Python controller via Thrift APIs, C++/IntelDPDK store and clients. Single-rack testbed28nodes, dual2.2GHzXeonSilver4114/20totalcores,48GBRAM in §9, Ubuntu18.04,25GbConnectX-4,Arista7170-64S;16storage/12client nodes. AppendixA says48GB per socket, so exact RAM allocation wording differs; keep §9 configuration distinct. It is not verified Rust/Verus (§9,AppendixA). Workload is generated open-loop Poisson arrivals over one million random keys under uniform/Zipf distributions, not replay of production operations. Consistent-hashing baseline has16virtualnodes/server. Typical64Bkeys/128Bvalues enable NetCache comparison, whose limit is128Bvalue and whose switch reserves10,000suchvalues. Pegasus uses<3.5% SRAM for metadata; systems spend switch memory differently. Paper does not report confidence intervals/repeated-run counts for all figures (§9). Performance metric is maximum offered/completed throughput satisfying a99th-percentile latency SLO, selected as5×unloaded median; shown50µs. Read-only uniform→Zipfα.9/1/1.2: Pegasus nearconstant (~150Mops/s graph),10×consistent hashing at1.2. NetCache can outperform Pegasus for read-only skew because cache hits avoid servers. Headline10×/90%fewer servers is conditional on this baseline/workload/SLO, not every storage workload (§9.1,Figure7). Write-ratio test fixesZipf1.2/50µs SLO and varies0–100%writes. Pegasus/AMO maintain relative benefit, but absolute throughput falls with write contention/server cache invalidation. NetCache loses>80% throughput with10%writes and up to11.8×gap versus Pegasus in write-heavy cases. No claim that strong replication makes writes free or all workloads reach identical throughput (§9.2,Figure8). Scaling is measured1,2,4,8,16storage servers underZipf1.2/SLO; nearlinearPegasus while consistenthashing stalls after≈2. Host-directory implementation processes both requests/replies and cannot match one storage server in this prototype; this is not a theorem ruling out all software directory designs. Value-size sweep64B–1KB compares skewedPegasus to uniformconsistenthashing; operation throughput falls with size, not bit-throughput regression. Claimed arbitrary-value-size support exceeds measured≤1KB range (§§9.3–9.4,Figures9–10). Only8–16hotkeys suffice for most gain on tested16-serverZipf.9/1.2 workloads. This is nonadversarial evidence, not a fixed universal key-count bound; cited adversarial bound has different constants (~8nlogn). Half-server-capacity ablation reduces capacity of half by50%; random placement throughput halves as slowest servers bottleneck, whereas weightedroundrobin better uses residual capacity (§§9.5–9.6,Figures11–12). Dynamic tests runZipf1.2 at80%utilization and change100keys every10s. Hot-in promotes100coldest to hottest, causing latency spikes returning to normal within100ms; graph bins99thpercentile over100ms. Random swaps among10,000hottest cause no visible tail change. This is finite workload adaptation, not a hard100msfailover/directory-correctness theorem (§9.7,Figure13). Multi-rack experiment uses a different slower72-nodeXeonE5-2450/1.8GHz/10Gb-no-DPDK cluster: two24-storage-node racks and thirdclientrack. Each rack heads half the chains/tails half. Read-onlyZipf1.2 gives1.7×throughput for two replicas; one-rackfailure at t0 retains service. Text says half prior speed, but Figure14 visually ≈13→8Mops/s (roughly62%retained); treat “half” as coarse wording rather than exact measured ratio. No explicit failure detection/repair latency, write-heavy crash history or repeated-run/error analysis is supplied (§9.8,Figure14). ArtifactAppendixA documents MITlicensedP4/Python/C++/TLA+repo, Ubuntu18.04/Linux4.15, GCC7.5,SDE9.1.1/P4-14,DPDK19.11,dependencies and million64BASCIIkeys.10–60sexperiments tune clientthreads/interval to maximum throughput underSLO and vary servers,mode,α,readratio,value size/keycount. Printed badges on PDFp2 say Available/Functional/Reproduced; these are artifact-evaluation labels, not proof of implementation correctness. All appendixinstructions read, none executed; no currentrepo/status investigated.

- Modeling the Raft Distributed Consensus Protocol in LNT (2020)
    - what: # Whole-paper record: Modeling the Raft Distributed Consensus Protocol in LNT (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Hugues Evrard, MARS 2020, EPTCS 316, pp.15–39, DOI 10.4204/EPTCS.316.2; arXiv 2004.13284v1. Read all 25 PDF pages, §§1–5, the 16 references, complete Annex A model and Annex B skeleton/reliable network. Inspected all 25 rendered pages and read the entire released LNT model and README statically. Exact passages, source lines and PDF/printed pages are in quotes.json and combined.quote-source.txt. No author program, compiler, model checker, prover or solver was run.  ## What the paper establishes (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  This is a Raft modeling and experience paper. Its stated goal is “to discuss the process of developing the formal model of a distributed system using LNT” (§1,Q2). The model covers leader election and log replication, separates server and network processes, and illustrates CADP state-space development. It reports a concrete size comparison between reliable and unreliable networks. The complete printed model makes its abstractions inspectable.  The paper does not enumerate checked Raft safety/liveness formulas or report their truth values. It gives no parameterized correctness proof or implementation refinement theorem. The abstract attributes Raft correctness to “a manual proof, based on a TLA+ specification” (Q1), and §1 says that proof was presented by the Raft authors (Q2). Thus the LNT model and CADP availability should not be recorded as a new complete Raft verification result.  The paper reports two discrepancies in the original TLA+ specification: an unintended prime on matchIndex in AdvanceCommitIndex and a missing candidate-to-follower transition after a same-term leader heartbeat (§3.7,Q20). It says the former “made no practical difference” and the latter “did not impact Raft manual proof.” These are the author's assessments, not independently checked proof conclusions. The pinned historical TLA+ source credits Evrard for the apostrophe correction (Q55). That pinned snapshot already contains the candidate stepdown branch (Q54); we did not reconstruct the earlier faulty revision.  ## Assumptions and represented behavior (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The configuration fixes the number of servers and bounds terms and total client interactions, “otherwise the state space would be unbounded” (§3.2,Q9). Printed and released defaults are three servers, three terms and three client interactions. The sole measured comparison instead uses two servers, one term and one interaction. Changing server count also requires changing instantiated processes and the array range (§3.3,Q10; Q41–42). The quorum is the strict majority `(MaxServerID div 2) + 1` (Q41).  The scope is “the core of the protocol, i.e. leader election and log replication”; dynamic membership and log compaction are omitted (§3,Q6). Client actions carry only the leader ID. “We do not need to model client commands, or server responses to clients” (§3.4,Q11). Entries contain only terms (§3.6,Q14; Q44). This cannot establish distinctions between different same-term commands or full service/client response behavior.  The network can reorder, drop a message on send, or deliver while retaining a message for duplication (§3.5,Q12–13; Q43). The declared buffer is a set, despite the name msgBag. Identical pending messages collapse to one element. There is no explicit capacity bound or delivery fairness condition. The reliable alternative removes loss and retain-after-delivery branches, but still permits arbitrary message selection and provides no fairness guarantee (Annex B.2,Q40). Its smaller state space supports development under fewer network behaviors.  Timeouts are nondeterministic alternatives without elapsed time or randomized duration (§3.6.1,Q15; Q45). At the term bound only the election alternative stops; receiving and other alternatives remain possible. A candidate votes for itself directly, reducing self-message actions relative to the compared TLA+ model. Lower-term messages, including requests, are discarded; the author says this is safe, but supplies no equivalence proof (§3.6.2,Q16).  The disrupt branch permits a crash between LNT actions, including midbroadcast (§3.6.4,Q19). It ends in Crash(self), after which the server process terminates; no reboot/recovery transition appears (Q47). This is a process-level crash model, not evidence about interruption at arbitrary implementation instructions. Leaders accept client interactions, append a term entry, and replicate on a later timeout (§3.6.3,Q18). AppendEntries carries zero or one entry, enforced by an assertion (§3.6.2,Q17; Q49).  ## Concrete evaluation and cases (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  For two servers, one term and one client interaction, the unreliable network yields 11,862,015 states and 74,821,042 transitions. The reliable network yields 22,311 states and 108,176 transitions (§4.3,Q23–24). Dividing the supplied counts gives about 531.67 times fewer states and 691.66 times fewer transitions. The paper describes the reductions as “three and two orders of magnitude smaller, respectively.” Preserve its wording alongside the exact counts; the computed ratios are reader arithmetic.  No timing, hardware, tool release, repeated trials, per-property results or experiment logs are reported for this comparison. The archive contains only README.txt and raft.lnt, with no property files or reproduction script. The downloaded source uses different syntax from the print, including alt/select and card/length; exact textual identity or the exact experimental checkout is not established.  A reliable network is a development proxy. The paper says these state spaces “are not relevant for a proper verification” and that an issue found there also appears with the unreliable network (§4.3,Q24). This supports preserving finite bad witnesses under the stated behavioral inclusion, not an unrestricted transfer of liveness or arbitrary formula truth.  Figure 1 is a syntax example: two calculator operations, 1+2=3 and 3×4=12, can occur in either order in a four-state/four-transition graph (PDF p.4/printed p.18,Q8). It is not a Raft performance experiment. There are no tables.  The DLC/Consul comparison is explicitly attributed to §6 of prior thesis [2]. For 1000 commands and three servers the paper cites 2.3 seconds for DLC versus 0.5 second for Consul, and reports prior interprocess TCP communication under half a millisecond (§4.6,Q28–29). Consul batches commands while DLC sends a round for each command, so this is not an isolated measurement of formal-method overhead. The thesis and implementation were not independently evaluated here.  ## Static discrepancies requiring care (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Three local source cases qualify use of the model as a reference specification. All appear both in the visually inspected appendix and released LNT source. These are reader-created symbolic valuations; no reachable execution or protocol safety violation has been established.  - Same-term candidate: reception sets Follower only when `mTerm > currentTerm`; the AppendEntries handler receives no state argument. A Candidate at term 1 processing a valid term 1 empty heartbeat remains Candidate (Annex A.5/A.6.3,Q35–36; released source Q46/Q49). This disagrees with the paper's Raft overview that “other candidates step down to the follower state” (§2.2,Q4), and resembles the upstream omission discussed in §3.7. It does not establish that the earlier TLA+ defect causes a safety failure. - Failed replication response: `nextIndex[mFrom] := max(1 of nat, nextIndex[mFrom])` has no decrement. A local value 3 stays 3 (Annex A.6.4,Q37; Q50). This disagrees with the §2.3 description that the leader retries “with a lower index” (Q5). We have not established a reachable failed replication trace or measured its effect. - Follower commit assignment: `commitIndex := mLeaderCommit` lacks a cap by local log length or a monotonic guard. With a locally empty log, previous index 0, empty entries and leader commit 1, the handler leaves an empty log with commitIndex 1 (Q36/Q49). Reachability is unknown. The pinned TLA+ source also directly assigns the leader index and says an old duplicate request can decrease it (Q54). This may be an inherited abstraction; do not label it a newly discovered LNT safety bug.  The symbolic cases are retained in static-witnesses.json. Their purpose is to distinguish the source's actual expressions from the prose and from unproven invariants, not to substitute for model checking.  ## What this adds to the research topic (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The paper contributes an explicit distributed consensus model, reusable network/node structure, evidence that network assumptions strongly affect state-space size, and a concrete account of translation exposing specification discrepancies. It also explains the gap between a model and implementation: the Distributed LNT Compiler generates C but its synchronization protocol assumes reliable interprocess communication (§4.6,Q28). Discussion of Verdi is attribution to related work, not an implementation correctness result from this paper.  The state-space advice is qualified. Fixed broadcast order is justified informally by arbitrary receive order. The author warns that removed paths may be “irrelevant to a given verification property, but crucial to an other” (§4.4,Q26). Bypassing duplication or outdated messages is proposed as future work requiring “formal verification or proof” (§4.5,Q27), rather than a proved reduction method.  For evaluating LLM-written specifications and proofs, the reader-derived lesson is to inspect the represented state, bounds, message semantics, source/prose agreement, property statements and implementation link separately. The three static cases show why a plausible protocol narrative and a formal-language artifact do not by themselves establish the intended transitions. The paper supplies no Verus, verified Rust or LLM experiment.
    - limits: Fixed finite servers, bounded terms and total client interactions; defaults3/3/3 versus measured2/1/1. Core election/replication only, term-only entries and leader-ID client actions. Finite-set network reorders/drops/duplicates without capacity or fairness guarantee. Nondeterministic untimed timeouts, crash termination without recovery. Informal reductions and source/prose discrepancies qualify reference-model use.

- Multi-scale verification of distributed synchronisation. (2020)
    - what: Connects explicit networks of discrete pulse-coupled oscillators with counting population models; gives probabilistic correspondence proofs and a reduction eliminating non-firing states. The concrete DTMC tracks each oscillator's phase and start/update mode plus an environment firing counter; a descending-phase evaluation handles same-step firing cascades. The population model counts indistinguishable oscillators per phase and enumerates binomially weighted broadcast-failure vectors. Theorems preserve unbounded synchronisation reachability and adapted expected rewards when deterministic non-firing paths are collapsed. A counting map at round boundaries establishes two-way weak simulation and equal aggregate transition probabilities.
    - number: 41-page arXiv v1
    - number: 48,621 to 11,441 states for N=8,T=10
    - number: 128,936 to 50,883 transitions
    - number: R=5: 10.38 versus 0.047 seconds checking (N=4,T=10)
    - limits: Fixed population, fully connected network, identical oscillator dynamics, discrete bounded phases, non-negative increasing phase response and a global broadcast-failure probability. Population states erase node identity and topology. The model reduction preserves the specified unbounded reachability/reward properties, not arbitrary step-bounded properties. - T-Lease: A Trusted Lease Primitive for Distributed Systems (2020)
    - what: # Reading: T-LEASE (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Trach, Faqeh, Oleksenko, Ozga, Bhatotia and Fetzer implement a lease primitive for SGX enclaves under an OS attacker who can alter time readings, clock rates, scheduling and message delays. Read all 13 pages, nine main sections, 15 figures, two tables and 58 references. The arXiv source is a 2021 preprint of the Middleware 2020 paper. Its evidence combines a reported finite TLA+/TLC model check with C-library measurements and three separately implemented lease-based case studies. There is no proof connecting the model to the C/assembly implementation or to the CPU's hardware semantics.  The core safety condition is that the granter's real lease interval contains the holder's interval. T-LEASE measures uninterrupted enclave epochs using TSC and detects interrupts through SGX's State Save Area: a zero instruction-pointer sentinel becomes nonzero when enclave state is saved. The granter can omit interrupted intervals, conservatively extending its lease. A holder must invalidate/renew after every interrupt and finish request/reply in the same epoch, because an arbitrary pause may outlast its old lease. Sequence/epoch metadata rejects obsolete replies. Interrupt handling omits elapsed intervals; the timer cannot bound a scheduling pause from above, and its active-time estimate retains rate-estimation error.  Clock-rate verification runs six RDRAND instructions and checks TSC elapsed cycles, exploiting an empirically CPU-frequency-independent hardware RNG. The reported latency varies about 7,000–10,500 cycles (the evaluation uses 7,500–10,500). Consequently a timer can still slow roughly 40% or accelerate 45% with high acceptance probability. This is an empirical estimator with residual error, not an architectural proof of a universal deterministic rate bound. The design assumes manipulation requires an enclave interrupt, correct SGX/TSX behavior, and the stated RNG behavior. Buffer overflows and side channels are excluded.  TSX makes a lease check and shared-memory submission of a result one transaction, aborting on interrupts/conflicts. This protects the interval through result submission, not eventual message delivery or disk completion. The paper explicitly leaves tolerating delays after submission to the application; synchronous systems must budget that delay. Transactions also have cache-capacity/instruction restrictions. Implementation uses SCONE, UDP, AES-GCM-256 and pre-shared keys, in 1,037 lines of ANSI C including 26 assembly lines. A queue backoff adjustment reduced one syscall benchmark's abort rate from 79% to 0.008%; that result is not a universal transaction guarantee.  Section 5 models one granter and a set of holders, messages, current time, countdown timers, interrupts/resumes and bounded frequency changes. Holder countdown starts when requesting; the granter records holder/epoch/timestamp metadata and extends only suitable requests. ValidLease requires a currently valid, unexpired holder to have a matching granter record. Liveness is limited to no attacker, bounded MaxNow, bounded message delay, no starvation and sufficiently long uninterrupted epochs, with explicit fairness. Section 5.3 reports no safety/liveness violation on a finite no-attacker instance with equal durations, and safety with ±50% rate manipulation when the granter duration is 3× the holder's. Model size, holder count, exact constants, explored states, checker runtime and configuration are not reported here. Figure 3 is an outline with ellipses and omitted action bodies, not a complete reproducible checked artifact. No external model source was identified in the paper.  The experimental 2× lease extension does not inherit that 3× model guarantee. Section 6.1 computes (1+0.45)/(1−0.45)≈2.64, then deliberately uses 2 as a detection-probability/precision tradeoff. A source-only arithmetic witness illustrates the gap: with zero/negligible acquisition delay, holder duration L at 0.60 normal rate lasts 1.667L real time; granter duration 2L at 1.45 rate expires at 1.379L. If both empirical checks accept those reported plausible rates and no interrupt forces renewal, holder validity can outlast the granter. This is a conditional arithmetic example, not an executed attack or a demonstrated CPU trace. A factor 2 therefore needs stronger rate restrictions or a probabilistic safety statement; it is not the unconditional containment guarantee claimed in the introduction. Under an actual deterministic ±50% bound the worst ratio is 1.5/0.5=3.  The printed model also has narrower or malformed liveness statements. The first Figure 3 leads-to consequent is merely gLeaseGranted≠{}, not a grant to the particular requester. The second ends in lhState[h]={"validLease"}, a singleton set rather than the string used by TypeOK and ValidLease, and existentially chooses some holder. As printed this cannot establish the described requester-specific progress and needs source clarification. These observations do not establish that an unidentified full historical model contained the same defects. No TLC execution was performed.  Evaluation uses an SGXv2 Pentium Silver NUC at 1.5 GHz/32 GB RAM and SGXv1 Xeon E3-1270v5 Dell server/64 GiB RAM, linked at 1 Gb/s. Linux timer frequency was reduced to 100 Hz, dynamic ticks enabled, device interrupts moved to core 0, and enclave threads run at real-time priority after average epochs increased from 15 ms to 650 ms. Those settings qualify the performance results. No uniform repeated-trial count or confidence-interval method is reported.  Without interrupts, timer reads take about 30 ns. The paper reports interrupt-related minimum cost as approximately 10k cycles (20.3 µs); preserve those reported units without deriving a universal conversion. Discrete TPM/PTT reads take 220/145 ms. Rate detection is tested at 800 MHz and 1.5 GHz, which does not by itself prove behavior at every intermediate frequency or all future CPUs. Granter under-accounting can reach 14% with 100,000 instructions between updates at high interrupt rates; the authors expect ≤5% at ordinary 100–250 Hz. Long leases reach roughly 20–22 million checks/s in the plotted configurations. Interrupts drive renewal traffic even for long leases, up to about 2,000 messages/s at 1,000 Hz; retries are below 10^-6 per check for leases >100 ms, versus 0.28 per renewal with a TPM. Those retry denominators differ.  The lost-lease prose and plot disagree: §6.2 says about one loss every 2 seconds for network leases <5 ms, while Figure 12's displayed y-axis peaks around 0.025 losses/s, and its largest plotted point is about 0.024/s. Neither value is silently substituted for the other. Local experiments report no losses; this is a tested configuration, not a universal availability result.  The three cases recreate lease components rather than verify complete FaRM/Paxos/cache systems. FaRM-style failure detection counts expirations over 10 minutes; UDP/Ethernet cannot be directly compared numerically with original RDMA FaRM. No losses appear only around 100 ms leases in this test. PQL measures active-lease duration, with about 247 ms native versus 185 ms T-LEASE for long intervals: about 25% less active time, not a measured 25% throughput loss. Consistent caching uses a native granter outside the enclave and two SGXv2 cache nodes; its 5-minute experiment raises traffic from 55 to about 175 messages/s when writes appear, then reduces traffic near 100% writes. That placement does not experimentally test a malicious granter OS. The paper's broad 'up to 5% in most cases' claim must be read alongside these distinct metrics and deployment assumptions.  This paper contributes a directly relevant TLA+ lease case: compare the verified instance's rate assumptions with the measured configuration, inspect liveness predicates and fairness, and distinguish empirical hardware timing from proven time bounds. It also gives concrete PQL/failure-detector/cache integrations and shows why proof agents must preserve timing units, attacker assumptions and model-to-code boundaries. There is no Verus, verified Rust or LLM-agent evaluation. No author code, prover/model checker or serialized scientific output was executed/loaded.

    - what: VeriBetrKV verifies a single-threaded crash-safe B-epsilon-tree key-value store by combining ordinary Hoare code proofs with TLA-style state-machine refinement of program plus asynchronous disk environment. IronFleet has distributed/liveness results, but those are prior work, not VeriBetrKV results. §2.1: User trusts a 283-line top-level dictionary/crash contract, environment/OS/runtime API specifications, build system, modified Dafny/verifier/Z3, C++ backend/compiler/toolchain and hardware behaving as modeled.
