The linear typechecker changes and BoxedLinear primitives are trusted rather than a separately proved compiler/type-system soundness theorem. §§2.1,3.1: The I/O bus can reorder requests/responses but cannot duplicate or drop them except during crash. The composed StorageIOSystem nondeterministically takes a program step, disk/environment step or whole-system crash. Crash resets volatile program state; acknowledged writes survive, while unacknowledged addresses may contain old, new or corrupt bytes. Arbitrarily many crashes at arbitrary modeled points are covered, including reboot/recovery states. §3.1.1: Disk corruption can occur at any time but cannot produce a valid-checksum block. CRC32C is trusted and referenced by the disk model. Invalid checksum aborts the current query, preserving no-wrong-answer safety at the cost of availability. A malicious disk that fabricates valid checksums, checksum collisions or stale valid blocks violates the assumed model. This is not an unconditional CRC integrity guarantee or fault-tolerant recovery from arbitrary corruption. §§3.1.2,6.2.3: Without crash/corruption the visible state is a dictionary with latest writes. Crash reverts the entire dictionary to a consistent prior snapshot no earlier than the last completed sync. Spec has ephemeral and persistent states; background steps can advance persistence. sync_start/sync_end ensure that at end, persistence includes the state at start or a newer version. Unsynced operations may survive or disappear as part of a consistent snapshot; this is not independent per-key arbitrary rollback or durability of every returned insertion. §3/§6.2: Hoare reasoning verifies synchronous local implementation handlers against the program machine. Environment behavior and crashes are handled by IOSystem refinement. General real-system theorem is conditional on the actual executable, trusted API interactions and environment matching those models. TLA-style refinement is encoded/proved with Dafny, not reported TLC model checking or proof of arbitrary storage behavior. §§3.2,6.2.2: Map→abstract B-epsilon tree with infinite-map nodes→finite pivot-bucket tree separates key semantics from representation. A hypothetical purely in-memory implementation is shown gray and is not an actual second implementation. Generic CrashSafe<T>/BlockCache<T> lifting says a refinement of node/tree contents lifts through a crash-safe cache/disk composition. §6.2.3 Figure 3: Tree IOSystem and JournalIOSystem independently refine CrashSafe<Map> and JournalViewMap. CompositeViewMap applies journal operations to map snapshots. ConcreteCache adds byte marshaling; Disk<byte> refines a partitioned typed disk. Transposition rearranges program/environment components only with an invariant that tree and journal access mutually disjoint disk regions. Their models cannot simply be separated if their effects overlap. §6.2.4: Executable handler invocations refine Next transitions of ConcreteCache; I/O labels are no-op, request or response and must match trusted API actions. Proving code-to-model is insufficient without the enclosing disk composition, while proving abstract crash safety is insufficient without this implementation connection. Recovery does not write disk (§8.1), avoiding a separate write-during-recovery proof burden without excluding repeated crashes. §4: Developer policy stops feature work when verification exceeds 20 seconds, then controls definition visibility, opacity/reveal and solver instantiation profiling. The discipline reduces search burden but cannot decide arbitrary verification, distinguish all timeouts from defects, or guarantee a fixed bound. Measured final passing definitions are not a distribution of failed proof attempts or controlled developer productivity. §5.1: linear means non-aliased mutable values and shared means temporarily borrowed aliased immutable values. Static checking forbids duplication and silent discard and restricts shared values to borrow scope; explicit free is allowed. Functional sequence semantics permit in-place C++ mutation without SMT heap-aliasing reasoning. Ordinary heap references still use dynamic frames, and can be held inside linear structures. §5.1 Figure 2: Trusted BoxedLinear<A> embeds a linear value in a freely aliased heap object. Take requires Has() and sets it false; Give requires no stored value. Borrow is restricted to pure functional callers so an imperative method cannot remove ownership during the borrow. SMT proofs establish Has() where ownership is not syntactically obvious. Thus the method combines type safety with proof obligations rather than enforcing all aliasing rules in a simple Rust-like typechecker. §5.2: Backend maps immutable datatypes to structs, heap arrays/classes to reference-counted objects and immutable sequences to shared storage plus offset/length. Linear sequences use in-place operations and explicit deallocation without reference counts. Mathematical integer executable code is rejected; refined machine integers must fit C++ types. Compiler and runtime correctness are trusted. §§6.1.1–6.1.2: Uses 2 MiB nodes on HDD, 128 KiB on SSD, fanout 8. Serialized lower nodes avoid conversion, while the root uses a mutable search tree for single insertions. A ghost per-index lseq_has sequence permits taking disjoint subsets of linear children during splits. Claims about Rust needing unsafe/Option are the paper authors’ comparison, not a general impossibility theorem about all safe Rust implementations. §6.1.3: LRU BlockCache tracks inter-block references and garbage collection. Logical-to-physical indirection uses linear-probing hash table; example 1 TiB disk requires 24 MiB table. Two alternating counter-tagged superblocks select the latest checkpoint. Correctness depends on modeled write completion and checksum semantics. §§6.1.3–6.1.4: Checkpoint writes dirty nodes, then indirection table, then a superblock. At checkpoint start dirty shared nodes become write-back-before-editing, preserving the frozen snapshot. A node write must be issued before modification but need not complete before modification; crash can recover the old checkpoint. Logical journal records each insertion; sync persists journal instead of repeatedly writing large nodes. Checkpoint reclaims journal space. §7.1: Table 1 implementation proof/executable ratio is about 4:1; including refinement proofs gives 7:1. These annotation counts are a proxy for final proof burden, not person-time, maintenance cost or specification adequacy. Authors observed no runtime correctness/data-loss bugs but did observe liveness/performance bugs; no duration or exposure denominator establishes a general failure rate. §7.1: Hash-table proof LOC 1678→1063 (about 37% lower), search-tree 2220→1531 (about 31% lower), with search-tree executable LOC increasing 289→373. This compares two author implementations and supports reduced annotation burden for those components, not a universal productivity effect. Whole verification takes 1.8 CPU-hours, 11 minutes on 32 cloud machines, not 32 CPU cores in one machine. §7.1 reader qualification: Printed sentence says maximum verification time dropped 10s to 32s and 99th percentile dropped 1.3s to 4.8s. The endpoints increase in that order and conflict with dropped; the PDF visibly contains this wording. Do not silently reverse endpoints or claim a quantified speedup from this sentence without correction from source authors. §7.2: HDD/subcomponent runs use AWS d2.xlarge with four hardware hyperthreads, 2.4 GHz Xeon E5-2676 v3; SSD i2.xlarge has four hyperthreads, 2.5 GHz E5-2670 v2 and SATA SSD. All YCSB systems limited to one core and 2 GiB RAM; load 10 million operations/about 5 GiB, run phases 10000 operations. Reported medians and min/max over six runs, not confidence intervals. §7.2.1 Figure 6 reader calculation: Printed HDD Load medians are BerkeleyDB 233, VeriBetrKV-DF 5649, VeriBetrKV 5579 and RocksDB 44670 ops/s. Ratios from linear VeriBetrKV are about 23.9× faster than BerkeleyDB and 8.0× slower than RocksDB, matching abstract 24×/8× but not body/caption over 25× or caption about 9×. Preserve numerical evidence rather than reconcile by guessing different runs. §7.2.1: VeriBetrKV is slower than both other stores on most queries and roughly 4× below RocksDB, but HDD uniform U has RocksDB 35 versus VeriBetrKV 57 ops/s. SSD Load has VeriBetrKV 8986 versus BerkeleyDB 6664 and RocksDB 72645, about 1.35× faster/8.1× slower; body says 4× slower on SSD, inconsistent with printed load values. Workload-specific outcomes matter more than a universal performance claim. §7.2.1: Authors attribute slowdown to effective-cache reduction from fragmentation/conservative cgroup allocation, lack of overlap between CPU and flush I/O, and 1.5× more I/O than RocksDB, about half extra from checkpoint policy. Simulated 1.8 GiB cache exceeds 13K HDD insertions/s and matches 300K I/Os for 1M queries. These simulations/profiling attributions are not a measured optimized implementation. Query I/O usually 1.5 MiB versus RocksDB 4–8 KiB; future partial-node marshaling is unimplemented. §7.2.2: Microbenchmarks compare dynamic frames/linear on 64M random 64-bit-key hash operations and 8M search-tree pairs. Authors suspect reference-count and reconstruction overheads; no isolated causal experiment is supplied. Dafny type extension is 1900 LOC (3%) and C++ backend 3100 (7.5%). Any x86/x64 CPU with HDD/SSD, 20 GiB disk and several hours expected; source YCSB/config included.     - title: Formal Analysis and Redesign of a Neural Network-Based Aircraft Taxiing System with VerifAI.
    - what: Presents an integrated VerifAI design workflow for an industrial Boeing TaxiNet aircraft-taxiing controller: Scenic models semantic runway environments, active search drives X-Plane closed-loop simulation, counterexamples are analyzed and targeted tests confirm causes, and retraining uses discovered failures. Generic, Halton, and specialized retraining raised satisfaction to 82%, 83%, and 86%, respectively, and reduced runway departures to 3.9%, 0.6%, and 0.5%; cross-entropy sampling learned a failure-focused distribution, but augmentation experiments sometimes regressed performance.

- A Process Calculus for Formally Verifying Blockchain Consensus Protocols (2019)
    - what: # Whole-paper read: A Process Calculus for Formally Verifying Blockchain Consensus Protocols (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Wolfgang Jeltsch; arXiv1911.08033v1,19November2019,16pages. The result is the ♮-calculus, pronounced “natural calculus,” and an Isabelle/HOL theory for reasoning about process behavior. It is infrastructure for a proposed verified Ouroboros implementation. The paper says, “We plan to very soon start using our process calculus for developing a formally verified implementation of the Ouroboros family of consensus protocols.” It does not report that implementation or a consensus safety/liveness proof. [Q0,Q1,Q12]  ## Language and execution model  A process calculus describes communicating programs and the steps they may take. This one embeds its terms in a functional host language. Higher-order abstract syntax means a binder is represented by a host-language function: Receive takes a function from received data to the remainder process, and NewChannel takes a function from the fresh channel to the remainder process. The host handles variable binding, renaming and ordinary computation. The paper focuses on Isabelle/HOL; it describes Haskell execution and automatic conversion to Isabelle terms as the intended workflow, deferring discussion of that embedding. No verified Haskell translation or runtime correspondence result is supplied here. [Q2,Q3]  The five constructors are Stop, Send, Receive, Parallel and NewChannel. Processes are coinductively defined, allowing infinite terms. Examples include forwarding a received value to two channels, forwarding only when the value differs from a given value, and replication represented by p∞=p∥p∞. Send has no continuation. Although the communication rule synchronizes sender and receiver, this restriction makes synchrony unobservable in the stated calculus. There is no explicit nondeterministic-choice constructor; this does not make concurrent scheduling deterministic. Computation, branching and recursion are placed in the host language. [Q3]  The calculus permits arbitrary transmitted data, including pairs or lists containing several local channels. Publishing such data can open several channel scopes at once. A single conventional transition rule would then combine sending, scope opening and closing. The paper separates these concerns into two layers. Basic transitions expose opening as its own step. Proper transitions combine opening steps with sending, while receiving and internal communication refer back to basic transitions. The printed one-channel and two-channel publication rules show how this composition works. Some symmetric/general rules and the complete proper-residual datatype are omitted from the exposition, with formalization sources linked separately. [Q4,Q5]  A residual bundles a transition's label with its target process, because a label's bound channel can also bind occurrences in that target. Thus transitions relate a source process to a residual rather than treating source, label and target as independent entities. Basic residuals have acting and opening constructors; nesting residuals supports later composition. To compare residuals, a lifting operation extends a relation on processes to matching labels and related targets. In the opening case the targets must be related for every channel argument. Bisimilarity then means each process can match the other's transitions while preserving that relation. [Q5,Q6]  ## Generic results and assumptions  The main reuse mechanism is to prove transition theory once for an abstract residual lifting operation, then establish its axioms for each concrete residual type. Section3.1 prints preservation of equality, relational composition and converse. These are presented as the laws of a relator, a mapping on types and relations that preserves that structure. This differs from an ordinary Haskell functor on types and functions. Isabelle-generated datatype relators supply the intended concrete instances. The source locale additionally makes monotonicity explicit; the printed three-law presentation and actual locale assumptions should therefore be kept distinct. I do not establish whether that additional law is derivable from the printed ones. [Q7,Q8,S3]  Strong bisimilarity matches individual steps. Weak bisimilarity permits internal communication to be ignored. Since the generic residual interface hides labels, the paper introduces silent, which adds a silent label, and fuse, which removes silence from nested residuals. Weak transitions are inductively generated by strong steps, empty silent steps and composition through lifted weak transitions followed by fuse. Five printed laws—two naturality laws, two neutrality laws and associativity—give a monad structure on types and relations. They are assumptions of the reusable construction, not proved facts about every possible transition system. The paper reports formal proofs that weak bisimilarity equals mixed bisimilarity, where strong steps are matched by weak ones, and that strong bisimilarity is contained in weak bisimilarity. [Q9]  For the usual single silent label, Section3.3 requires a natural silent relation that is left-total and unique on both sides. It derives fuse as the union of the converse of silent and its lifted converse, and states that these satisfy the general weak-residual laws. This reduces the per-instance proof burden. These are generic behavioral-equivalence results; no fairness, adversarial stake model, probabilistic security, real-time bound or consensus termination theorem is established in this paper. [Q10]  ## Known limits and concrete counterexample  The proper transition system can open a scope even when the channel is not transmitted. The author explicitly gives νb.a◁x → a◁νb.x with target0, where x does not depend on b, and says a fix is under investigation. This is a disclosed semantic issue in the presented concrete calculus. It does not by itself invalidate the generic theorems conditional on residual laws, which are largely independent of this calculus. [Q5]  Higher-order abstract syntax also permits process structure to depend on channels, including local channels. Such channel-dependent branching is unwanted here, while branching on ordinary data is intended. Related work excludes or separately characterizes these terms; the author explains that making channels abstract does not eliminate them in classical Isabelle/HOL. Preventing channel-dependent behavior while retaining host-language binding remains future work. These unresolved expressiveness/semantics restrictions matter before treating the calculus as an adequate model of a particular network implementation. [Q11,Q12]  ## Evaluation and pinned source inspection  The evidence is mathematical construction, worked syntax/transition examples and reported Isabelle formalization. The paper says “large parts” of the calculus and the “complete theory of transition systems” were formalized, and that the document was produced from Isabelle source checked against that formalization. It gives no runtime experiment, benchmark table, proof-development time, proof-size accounting, end-to-end protocol case or comparison of verification effort. Its acknowledgements mention network-equivalence proofs, without presenting a measured evaluation of them. There are18references and no numbered figures or tables. - On the parallels between Paxos and Raft, and how to port optimizations (2019)
    - what: # Reading: porting Paxos optimizations to Raft* (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Wang, Zhao, Mu, Chen and Li study a modified Raft called Raft*, not a proof that original Raft and Paxos are interchangeable. The whole 61-page extended paper, Appendices A–C, six printed TLA+ modules, 15 figures and 67 references were read. Exact supporting passages are staged in quotes.json with section and PDF-page anchors.  The central construction starts with already-correct specifications A, its optimization AΔ, and B refining A. A non-mutating optimization introduces state/actions or conjuncts without changing A's existing state updates. Given state and action-parameter mappings, translating the added clauses produces BΔ. Section 4.3 sketches BΔ refining both AΔ and B, preserving their invariants. This is a conditional specification transformation, not a general liveness or performance theorem. Added guards can prevent progress; added actions must explicitly preserve old state, and initialization and new-variable frames must be compatible. The paper leaves implementation to developers and states in §1 that correctness is guaranteed only at specification level.  Raft* prevents deletion of accepted entries by returning extra log entries during elections, selecting safe suffix values, and rejecting shorter appends. A separate accepted-ballot field distinguishes an entry's original Raft term from its latest Paxos acceptance ballot. Figure 3 maps leader self-acceptance as well as explicit messages. One Raft* action can cover multiple Paxos operations, so porting must account for every relevant action, including implicit self-acceptance.  The two implemented cases are quorum leases (PQL) and Mencius. PQL allows a leaseholder to read locally only after relevant pending writes are applied; writes notify the leaseholders of an intersecting quorum. Translating f+1 Paxos acknowledgments to f remote Raft acknowledgments must include the leader's implicit acknowledgment and its own leaseholders. The authors describe a handwritten version that omitted those leaseholders. Mencius assigns default log-slot proposers round-robin. Nondefault recovery proposes no-ops; skipTags allow default no-ops to become executable early. The optimization must be applied to every action corresponding to Paxos acceptance, including BecomeLeader and AppendEntries, not only ReceiveAppend. Appendix B abstracts leases with one global timer; distributed-clock and real lease-expiry correctness require additional implementation assumptions.  Evaluation uses five AWS regions (Oregon, Ohio, Ireland, Canada, Seoul), two m4.xlarge instances per region for client/server, 4 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM, SSD and stated 750 Mbps network. WAN latency spans 25–292 ms. Closed-loop YCSB-like workloads use 100,000 keys, a configurable shared hot-key probability and otherwise region-partitioned uniform keys. Each trial lasts 50 seconds with a stated 10 seconds for warm-up and cool-down; whether 10 seconds applies jointly or separately is unclear. Results are medians of five trials. Implementation builds on etcd c4fc8c09, retaining custom networking/batched forwarding that the authors say improves throughput 2.4×. Oregon is the favorable Raft leader placement.  PQL uses 2-second leases, renewal every 0.5 seconds, default 90% reads and 5% conflict, and 50 clients per region for latency. About 90% of reads take 1 ms; leader-lease leader reads take 1.6 ms, while a 1% follower tail reaches approximately 137 ms from conflicting writes. PQL reports 1.6× throughput at 90% reads and 1.9× at 99%; write latency rises because leaseholders must acknowledge. Figure 9(d)'s x-axis runs from 50% conflict on the left to 0% on the right. Its rising speedup therefore agrees with the prose that lower conflict helps. An earlier apparent contradiction came from overlooking that reversed axis and is withdrawn. Figure 9 captions/legends use Raft where parts of the prose discuss Raft*; keep that baseline wording distinction.  Mencius uses 100% puts, 0% or 100% conflict, and 8-byte or 4-KB payloads. The CPU case reaches about 55,000 versus 41,000 operations/s (about 1.34×); the network case reports 70% higher throughput than Raft-Oregon. Oregon itself beats Seoul by 30% in the stated comparison. Execution can still wait for remote earlier slots: the paper reports roughly 360 ms versus 110 ms for Mencius conflict/no-conflict cases, and about 79 ms at the Raft-Oregon leader. These are workload/deployment measurements, not a verification result, fault campaign, or universal optimization guarantee.  The paper claims a machine-checkable TLAPS refinement proof in §6. Appendix C is a manual prose proof outline, and Appendix B supplies specifications and invariant statements, not executable TLAPS proof bodies. The referenced GitHub master-tree request and, after waiting over five minutes, repository metadata endpoint returned HTTP 404 on 19 October 2026 UTC. No external proof source was recovered; artifact-acquisition.json records the later response. A missing retrieval does not disprove that a historical proof existed. Appendix C calls a batch-to-sequence correspondence 'stuttering', although true stuttering leaves the mapped abstract state unchanged. Its one-step simulation statement needs an abstract batch action or a justified intermediate-state argument. Its BecomeLeader safe-prefix/suffix claims are asserted without derivation in this outline. Its mapping table also uses lastLogEntry.Term where the main text distinguishes the accepted ballot.  Several printed specifications require repair before treating them as checker inputs. These omissions can affect semantics, so they are not classified as merely cosmetic syntax errors. Figure 4 leaves unrelated state unconstrained, uses logs'[i]=v in B versus singleton {v} in A/BΔ, and BΔ initialization quantifies k while referring to i. Appendix B's quorum assumption prints Q⊆Quorum rather than Q⊆Acceptor (Raft variants print both). UpdateLog prints logBallot'[i] without the acceptor index. ProposeEntries prints IF i1=0 THEN raftlogs[a][i1−1][1] ELSE −1, reversing the expected initial-index test. Some modules omit introduced variables from vars/init and omit frames for new variables; PQL Apply, GrantLease and UpdateTimer preserve MP!vars but leave other PQL variables unconstrained. These are findings about the printed artifact, not executed counterexamples against the authors' implementation or an independently obtained historical proof.  For distributed-system verification, this contributes a concrete specification-transformation method and useful cases of implicit acknowledgments, state mappings and safe optimization transfer. It also separates invariant preservation from progress and measured speed, and highlights the need to check exact proof artifacts, initialization, frame conditions and batch simulation. It contains no Verus, verified-Rust or LLM proof-agent experiment. No author code, prover or model checker was run.

Unique IDs are checked by comparing the multiset of IDs with their ordered successors using polynomial evaluation at n+1 points; this initialization is more expensive than normal certification. All 44 pages were read: eight sections, Appendices A–E, all 17 figures, four theorems, five lemmata, four definitions, examples 1–6, all printed proof outlines and 32 references. All 11 contact sheets and individual15,18,21,22,28,32,33,44 were inspected. The original, local and official PDFs match. No author code, scientific-result artifact or formal checking tool was executed or loaded. [Evidence: Q0, frontmatter/v1 identity, PDF pp.1–1; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The paper separates two verification problems: proving single-decree Paxos through composable shared-memory object specifications, and deriving Multi-Paxos by transformations of message handling. It adapts Boichat et al.'s Paxos→Round-BasedConsensus→Round-BasedRegister decomposition. The lower specifications deliberately admit unsuccessful operations that nevertheless expose values to other operations. The aim is to preserve each unchanged module's proof when changing another module or the network implementation. Claims of being the first such modular verification belong to these authors; this reading does not establish historical priority. [Evidence: Q1, §1, two contributions, PDF pp.2–3; Q28, §7, complete comparisons/claimed novelty, PDF pp.24–25; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The setting is crash-stop, majority-quorum consensus, not Byzantine consensus or crash-recovery with durable storage. The basic network neither invents, changes, drops nor duplicates messages, delivers with unbounded delay, and has nonblocking send/blocking receive. Later transformations explicitly introduce selected read-request duplication. Leader election is omitted under an assumption that one correct process trusted by all other correct processes always exists. - Nickel: A Framework for Design and Verification of Information Flow Control Systems (2018)
    - what: Nickel verifies that deterministic sequential system interfaces and their C implementations satisfy information-flow policies. A state-dependent action-domain function and possibly intransitive flow relation define permitted influence. Noninterference compares observations after original and optionally purged action histories. Coq-proved unwinding and restricted-refinement theorems reduce system proofs to Z3 checks over individual operations. Demonstrations cover the NiStar DIFC kernel, NiKOS process isolation and a repaired ARINC 653 interface specification. Records exact purge and seven unwinding obligations, lockstep data/policy refinement, trusted policy/checker/initialization boundaries, deterministic/uniprocessor/static-policy restrictions, manual observational equivalence, all object/label/quota/scheduler mechanisms, concrete covert channels and interface redesigns, complete LOC cells, verification/effort times and the logical-time experiment. Separates mechanized metatheory from trusted SMT implementation and ARINC specification analysis from kernel implementation verification.
    - limits: §§1,3.1,3.5,6.3: Only sequential deterministic state machines, with system-call/trap handlers atomic on a uniprocessor. NiStar disables timer interrupts in kernel space and all other interrupts, using polling drivers. This does not establish security under multicore/shared-memory concurrency, weak memory or interleaved kernel handlers. §3.1 Definition1: Policy P=(D,flow,dom); domains represent exercised authority, flow is a fixed relation on domain pairs, and dom(action,state) may depend on the current thread/labels. Intransitive flow can allow p1→scheduler→p2 while forbidding direct p1→p2. A state-dependent dom does not make the can-flow-to relation dynamic; changing that relation is unsupported. §3.2 Definition2/Figures4–5: sources recursively tracks permitted direct or intermediate influence along a trace. purge is a SET of subtraces: it always permits retaining an action and permits dropping it only when its domain is outside sources, recomputing later state on the removed branch. Noninterference quantifies over every action, original trace and permitted purged trace and requires equal next-action output from the two resulting states. This is a relational security property over histories, not only memory isolation or functional refinement. §3.2: Authors establish reduction to classical noninterference for state-independent dom and monotonicity when flow is relaxed while domains/dom stay fixed. The PDF states these sanity checks but does not print their detailed proofs. Do not generalize monotonicity to changes of all policy components. §3.3 Theorem1/Figure6: Developers supply an inductive state invariant and per-domain observational equivalence. Seven universally quantified obligations cover invariant initialization/preservation, equivalence, consistency with dom, consistency with flow, output consistency, local respect and weak step consistency. Accepted invariants/equivalences are checked proof inputs, not trusted axioms; inventing an unsuitable relation can fail the checks. They remain substantial human work. §3.4 Theorem2: General refinement may introduce leaks. Supported data refinement requires same actions/outputs, related initial states, one-step preservation and equal output for related states satisfying the implementation invariant. Policy refinement additionally preserves dom for the same action/history and uses the same domain set/flow relation. No arbitrary stuttering, action splitting or nondeterministic refinement is claimed. §§3.5,6.2: Guarantees cover modeled interface observations, including logical scheduling time. Physical timing, sound, energy and microarchitectural channels outside the model are excluded. No distributed network fault, crash-recovery, availability, termination or fairness guarantee is supplied. The scheduler description assumes an infinite stream of timer interrupts rather than proving hardware progress. §4: Coq mechanizes the two general theorems. Python specifications/proof inputs and symbolic execution of C-derived LLVM IR produce Z3 obligations. Paper explicitly trusts information-flow policy, unwinding checker and Z3; implementation verification adds refinement checker and unverified initialization/glue. This is not an independently checked proof certificate for each SMT result or fully verified checker/compiler/hardware chain. §4: The intended policy is the trusted top-level requirement and needs auditing. Automated verification cannot show that an overly permissive policy matches the user’s security intention. A failed condition may reflect a genuine interface/implementation channel or insufficient invariant/observational equivalence; every solver counterexample is not automatically an exploit. §5: Determinism is obtained by exposing allocation choices as arguments, specifying allocation behavior precisely (NiStar), or hiding choices below the interface (NiKOS virtual addresses). Encrypted sequential names technically violate exact noninterference despite a claimed negligible practical leak; Nickel avoids them rather than proving probabilistic security. §§6.1–6.2: DIFC safe-flow relation combines sender and receiver ownership for controlled declassification/endorsement. Alice’s tty daemon is trusted to release secrets only to her terminal; a label proof does not verify that daemon’s declassification logic. Only threads/gates may have nonempty ownership. Fixed-size pages and finite interfaces aid SMT automation. §6.3: NiStar uses a kernel identity mapping and separate user/kernel page tables. The incomplete POSIX emulation, musl, lwIP, file-system wrapper and applications demonstrate usability; their existence does not extend the kernel proof to full application correctness, network security or durable filesystem semantics. §7: NiKOS mirrors a particular mCertiKOS interface after changing executable loading to make quotas agree. It is not a proof of every mCertiKOS variant. ARINC 653 result verifies a Python-modeled 14-operation communication interface after fixing three previously known channels; no ARINC kernel implementation/refinement proof or new bug discovery is reported. §8: Counterexamples for injected §2 examples and the round-robin workload demonstrate detection within these models. The logical-time plot supports its stated scenario, not absence of unmodeled physical channels. No Linux performance comparison, end-to-end application throughput benchmark, repeated-run confidence interval, or quantitative covert-channel capacity study is provided. §8 Figure11: LOC for interface implementation excludes shared C/x86 infrastructure; user-space LOC excludes third-party musl/lwIP. Effort figures are authors’ experience, not a controlled productivity comparison: one author six/two/one weeks for specification+verification, several researchers about six months implementing NiStar, and two months exploring framework definitions. §§9–10: Related work includes seL4/CertiKOS/Ironclad/Komodo and Covern, plus DIFC policy-synthesis tools; those citations do not mean Nickel supports concurrency or automatically synthesizes the complete policy/observational equivalence. No direct Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. Public source pointer saved; artifact/proofs not run.

- Peregrine population-protocol analyzer (2018)
    - title: Peregrine: A Tool for the Analysis of Population Protocols.
    - what: Introduces Peregrine, a web tool for designing, simulating, statistically sampling and parameterized-verifying population protocols. It verifies silent protocols over all infinitely many initial populations using layered termination and Presburger overapproximations, with LoLA confirmation and counterexample replay. The paper defines protocol/configuration/fairness semantics and illustrates majority voting. The UI supports graphical or script descriptions, manual/random simulation with rewind, convergence-speed statistics and JSON export. Verification first proves layered termination (a sufficient condition for silence), then searches an iteratively strengthened Presburger overapproximation for bad initial-to-terminal executions; candidate counterexamples are checked for concrete reachability by LoLA and replayed/exported. It distinguishes ordinary and increased-accuracy consensus classification, where LoLA checks whether a nonterminal consensus can later be broken.

Deutsch–Jozsa is a motivation for induction, not a proved case reported here [Q6–Q18].

- TCS (2018)
    - title: Multi-Shot Distributed Transaction Commit
    - what: Defines Transaction Certification Service (TCS), a repeated transaction commit interface whose committed transactions must have a legal real-time-respecting sequential order for a configurable conflict-check function. States correctness of multi-shot 2PC under algebraic conditions on shard-local conflict checks, then a simulation from a crash-tolerant protocol that weaves certification into Paxos-style replication. Provides key invariants and an agreement proof; main theorem proofs are external. Gives analytic failure-free latency reductions from seven to four message delays, or three with all-to-all acknowledgements. The correctness definition linearizes the committed projection, so it imposes safety on commits without forcing every abort to be justified by the global conflict function. It separates checks against decided-commit transactions (f_s) from stronger checks against prepared-commit transactions (g_s); conditions (6)–(8) require global/local consistency, strengthening, and a cross-order commutativity property. Abstract 2PC deliberately allows forgetting and recalling final decisions: votes/order survive recovery while a leader can temporarily lose knowledge of an abort, affecting later certifications. The concrete protocol persists transaction-vote pairs at quorums, computes votes only at leaders, synchronizes recovered follower state, and allows multiple unreplicated coordinators. Invariant 7 proves one accepted vote and slot per transaction, using preservation across ballots and transaction uniqueness.

Executables use Coq extraction to Haskell (OCaml is mentioned as an alternative). The result is not a proof of arbitrary compiled C, Rust or a native binary. §§5.2,7: Correctness is trace inclusion, with every finite prefix representing possibly infinite behavior. Only safety properties are targeted. No scheduler fairness, termination, starvation freedom, eventual successful delivery or lock acquisition follows. The proof may insert a never-executed stably enabled left-mover into an equivalent execution; it does not make the actual scheduler run it. §§1–2,8.6: Node failures are outside scope. File-system crash behavior and durability are not proved despite the Maildir motivation. Top-level intended behavior and bottom-level file-system model must be correct. Coq soundness and standard assumptions including functional extensionality, extraction/runtime, driver and concrete syscall mapping are trusted. §§1,5.3,8: SMTP/POP3 parsing and protocol implementation are unverified. The Haskell network/file-system driver lies outside the proof. Compatibility with Go SMTP, postal and rabid is testing, not protocol conformance proof. TLS, spam filtering and logging are absent. §6.1 Figures 10–12: Commutation must preserve both operations’ individual return values and final state across distinct PIDs. Atomic blocks have right-movers, at most one non-mover, then left-movers. State-dependent properties need only hold after the already-executed prefix but require proofs for all reachable modeled states, not sampled interleavings. §6.1: Disabled intermediate operations require stable enablement when moving an operation earlier: enablement survives undoing another process’s step. An existing locked-file read can be a left-mover although reading arbitrary newly created/temporary files is not. Lock ownership rules must ensure other processes cannot release this process’s lock. §6.2: Protocol semantics disables forbidden operations, such as unlocked accesses. Sound use requires proving every API user follows the protocol under unrestricted semantics. Merely restricting the environment would assume away the race; Cspec requires the refinement proof. §6.3 Figure 13: The abstraction pattern keeps operation types fixed, preserves the return value and relates successor states for every low-level step. Invariant introduction uses an identity relation. An absorbing abstract error state can relate to any low-level state, but a later protocol proof must show it unreachable before obtaining the final guarantee. §6.4: Retry-loop bodies must either perform the correct successful effect and exit, or have zero effect and retry. This supports a safety/atomicity proof without guaranteeing eventual success. Partition lifting requires proven single-shard refinement plus correct naming and disjoint decomposition at top and bottom. §§3–5 Figures 1,3,6: The displayed mail/file-system specifications permit a false delivery/link return with no effect, not solely a proved name-collision cause. They are permissive safety specifications and do not guarantee success. The paper uses atomic rename terminology later; earlier implementation/spec uses link followed by unlink, with no destination overwrite, so do not substitute unrestricted POSIX rename semantics. §8.1: With concurrent deletion, PID-filtered readdir deliberately permits a superset of existing names. It is a right-mover, not a both-mover, in that case. A name absent from the superset is free; a reported name need not still exist. Plan 2 describes random names but concretely uses the current timestamp and relies on retry rather than guaranteed collision freedom. §8.2 Figure 16: The x86-TSO case verifies a modeled counter built over shared memory and per-core store buffers. Any core may flush any portion of its buffer at each low-level operation. This is not validation of a physical processor, compiler memory model or executable counter benchmark. §8.3 Figure 17: Performance uses local simulated SMTP/POP3 requests on Linux tmpfs, avoiding network and persistent-storage bottlenecks. Authors implemented the unverified GoMail comparator. Request mix is 1:1 delivery versus read/delete over 100 random users. Message sizes, measurement durations, repetitions, error bars and raw runs are not supplied. §8.4 Figure 18: Effort is two people about six months part time, following another twelve months of failed alternative designs. Incremental deletion/naming/multi-user timings are author anecdotes, not controlled studies or independent replications. The text’s approximate 100–200 spec LOC per layer omits displayed extremes 63 and 323. §8.5 Figure 19: Proof-pattern counts are module uses and need not equal numbers of layers. The Cmail diagram describes naming plan 1; the count table also includes the retry pattern used in plan 2, which has one additional intermediate layer. §§2,8.6: The state-machine approach draws on TLA and I/O automata, but the work is not a TLA+ implementation/proof or a distributed node-failure theorem. No Verus, verified Rust or LLM-generated-specification/proof evaluation. Public artifact URL is recorded but not fetched or replayed.

- XRP Ledger Consensus Protocol analysis (2018)
    - title: Analysis of the XRP Ledger Consensus Protocol
    - what: Gives a formal network model and safety/liveness analysis of XRP Ledger Consensus Protocol (XRP LCP), a Byzantine agreement protocol operating with individually chosen trusted node lists (UNLs). Defines nodes, asymmetric UNLs, quorum qi=ceil(.8ni), tolerated faults ti, ledgers and atomic-broadcast properties. It decomposes XRP LCP into deliberation, validation and preferred-branch components and provides pseudocode. Lemmas and propositions derive overlap conditions for ledger agreement: validation propagation through honest-majority support yields Theorem 8’s pairwise overlap bound. A constructed 102-node example shows that even 99% overlap can get stuck; Lemma 10 and Theorem 11 establish progress for a single agreed UNL with leaf validators under bounded-delay/no-fault rounds.

    - number: with 80% quorums and 20% faults, roughly >90% UNL overlap is required
    - number: Example 9 demonstrates no progress despite 99% overlap and zero Byzantine faults
    - number: Theorem 11 guarantees no stuck state for a single agreed UNL of size at least k with q=n−floor((n−1)/k) plus leaves

Liveness only assumes eventual civil network delivery and no faulty nodes; FLP rules out full-asynchrony progress. Early analysis uses Byzantine accountability, explicitly rejected as tenuous; the broad theorem treats arbitrary deliberation outcomes, making the overlap condition sufficient rather than necessary. Results concern protocol rules and parameterized trust topology, not a measured deployment.

- Developing Bug-Free Machine Learning Systems With Formal Mathematics (2017)
    - what: Presents Certigrad, an implementation of stochastic computation graphs in Lean, with a reported machine-checkable proof that stochastic backpropagation produces unbiased estimates of the mathematical gradient of expected cost. It demonstrates a workflow in which formal specifications and attempted proofs guide implementation and expose both code errors and missing assumptions. It also reports verified Gaussian integration/reparameterization optimizations and an MNIST variational-autoencoder experiment with performance comparable to TensorFlow. Separates an executable stochastic program from its mathematical expectation semantics using Dist n, built by primitive sampling, deterministic returns and composition. The paper gives expectation and RNG-threading equations for each constructor. The initial all-graphs unbiasedness specification is strengthened with WellFormed, GradsExist, IntegralsExist and CanDiffUnderInts preconditions. A simple single-parameter, nonmemoizing implementation is proved first; a multi-parameter memoizing implementation is then proved equivalent. A heuristic tactic proves model-specific preconditions for the transformed AEVB graph. The verified optimization sequence integrates Gaussian KL terms and replaces parameter-dependent Gaussian sampling with standard-normal sampling followed by scale/shift, preserving the objective while changing the gradient estimator.
    - limits: Correctness is relative to the stated mathematical specification and adopted axioms. The authors assume real numbers, integration and primitive mathematical laws rather than constructing their foundations. They report repairing initially unsound axioms by restoring integrability conditions, but this reading does not independently audit that axiom set. The final displayed scalar theorem requires unique node identifiers and scalar leaves (WellFormed), appropriate differentiability for all relevant stochastic choices (GradsExist), existence of integrals (IntegralsExist), and conditions allowing gradients through integrals (CanDiffUnderInts). The implementation is reported to handle arbitrary tensor shapes and multiple parameters; the displayed specification deliberately simplifies these. Proving the generic algorithm is insufficient for an arbitrary client graph: each graph must meet the preconditions. Some are undecidable in general, so the theorem-proving tactic is heuristic rather than a complete decision procedure. The proof concerns ideal infinite-precision real arithmetic. The authors explicitly say replacing reals with floating-point numbers technically invalidates the specification and may cause numerical instability; no floating-point error bound is established here. The running system trusts optimized Eigen tensor operations and a small C++ wrapper to match the formally reasoned operations, and relies on Lean VM/runtime and primitive pseudo-random sampling. The paper describes corresponding mathematical/procedural distribution interpretations but does not establish a checked correctness theorem for the concrete RNG, Eigen, C++ wrapper or execution platform. Unbiased stochastic gradients do not establish convergence of ADAM, bounded gradient variance, statistical validity, good generalization or model fit. The empirical AEVB training comparison addresses one example, not those general guarantees. The source repeatedly says proving exposes all implementation errors. The supported guarantee is absence of violations of the modeled specification under its assumptions; specification errors, inconsistent axioms and implementation layers outside the model remain material, as the paper itself discusses. Claims of reduced cognitive burden and finding all bugs early are the authors’ development experience, not a controlled developer study or complete empirical bug census. The paper reports increased overall workload but supplies no person-hour or proof-size measurements.

- Epistemic Model Checking of Atomic Commitment Protocols with Byzantine Failures (2017)
    - what: # Epistemic Model Checking of Atomic Commitment Protocols with Byzantine faults (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Omar Ibrahim Al-Bataineh, arXiv1705.02515v3,10May2017. The official arXiv metadata calls the paper “Epistemic Model Checking of Atomic Commitment Protocols with Byzantine Failures”; the visible PDF title ends “with Byzantine faults” (M1,Q0). Official and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. The paper uses MCK to replace knowledge tests in a two-phase-commit program with concrete predicates, then studies cheating detection and termination in a synchronous reliable environment. The main qualification is its own Table2: global consistency, commit validity, abort validity and universal cheating detection fail. Eventual participant decisions and the stated coordinator/participant termination tests hold for the tested finite models. This is an analysis of a vulnerable protocol family, not a proof of Byzantine-correct atomic commitment (Q0,Q8,Q11).  ## Scope and semantics  Read all14PDFpages, sections1–8,17reference entries, all three protocol figures and three tables. Viewed individual renders7,8,9,12,13 to inspect complete pseudocode, formulas and tables. The PDF's visible version/date is2017; its creation metadata says2019, which is not substituted for the publication date. The bibliography is not a recursive reading of its cited sources. No MCK program, checker, author code or solver was executed/imported; no serialized model/experiment data was loaded.  Knowledge is defined through indistinguishability: Ki(phi) holds if phi holds at every point compatible with agent i's local information. Perfect recall retains past observations. A knowledge-based program chooses actions using such formulas, whereas its concrete implementation uses predicates of observable variables and explicit history variables. Correct implementation requires equivalence at the program points/times where each knowledge test is used. Merely obtaining the same outcome on one run, or making a safe conservative replacement, is a weaker condition (Q1,Q2,Q3).  The proposed workflow is partly automated. A human guesses a Boolean predicate/history update for each knowledge formula; MCK checks X^n(pc_i=l implies (predicate iff knowledge)). The human inspects counterexamples and revises the guess. The paper expressly says this requires “inspection and human reasoning” and possibly “some ingenuity.” It does not supply a fully automatic synthesis algorithm, a proof of search termination, or an agent evaluation. Its discussion of unique implementations depends on perfect recall and present-time knowledge tests, rather than arbitrary epistemic programs (Q3).  ## Model, cases and reported properties  One process coordinates a transaction and the others vote yes/no. An honest coordinator commits only when its own and all participant votes are yes; otherwise it aborts. It broadcasts its decision, receives acknowledgments and uses nested knowledge tests to decide when to stop. A Byzantine coordinator can choose an incorrect decision or send inconsistent decisions to different participants. The considered faults target outcomes rather than deliberately delaying or blocking termination (Q4,Q5,Q6,Q9).  The environment delivers messages, handles synchronization and exposes the trap/cheatingDetected variables to participants. Communication is synchronous and reliable in the evaluated context, with bounded delays and chosen wait parameters. The general pseudocode also mentions undefined votes and communication failures; those are not evidence that the reported Byzantine-context checks include message loss. There is no arbitrary asynchronous scheduler, unbounded delay, crash recovery or cryptographic refinement result (Q5,Q9).  A participant can detect cheating immediately when it voted no but receives commit. Participants may also open a run: they exchange their votes and received decisions, exposing contradictory decisions or a no vote paired with some commit instruction. A participant that detects cheating publishes that fact through the modeled variable. Such a publication mechanism assumes appropriate truth/correspondence in the environment; no executable authentication or dissemination implementation is supplied in the paper (Q5,Q7,Q10).  The coordinator's vote remains private to it. If every participant voted yes and the coordinator sends one consistent but incorrect decision, opening the participants' observations does not expose its private vote. The paper reports a counterexample to universal cheating detection in this case. Its speculative policy follows the received decision when the participant does not know cheating occurred. That differs from requiring knowledge that no cheating occurred; the latter conservative policy is discussed as preventing commits in this information setting (Q10,Q11).  Table1 gives three phase-specific predicate replacements. At point1, known cheating is a no vote paired with a received commit. At point2, detection also includes published cheating or an opened run with a no vote/commit pair or inconsistent decisions. Its point3 replacement for not knowing cheating is a yes vote with no publication/no trap, or a trap showing all participant votes yes and decisions equal. These are printed claimed equivalences, with the limitations below preserved (Q11).  Table2 reports:1a global consistency fails;1b eventual participant decision holds;2a commit validity fails;2b abort validity fails;3 complete cheating detection fails;4a coordinator termination holds;4b participant termination holds. Specifications2a/2b explicitly constrain the coordinator's decision variable, while1a/1b concern participant outcomes. These different variables should not be collapsed into a claim about every honest participant's valid outcome. Failure of one displayed formula does not by itself identify all possible implementation failures; no full counterexample traces for every table cell are supplied (Q8,Q11).  The models were checked for d=2,3,4,5 agents. The paper says “We conjecture that our present implementation can be shown to work for all number of agents” (§7,p13). Thus the all-size generalization is a conjecture, not a parameterized proof. It refers to “two contexts” there although this retained version presents only one Byzantine-context results row; a second unseen experiment is not inferred (Q12).  ## Formula and predicate qualifications  The explicit abbreviation Khat_i(decision) is Ki(decision=commit OR decision=abort). This says that agent i knows a decision has been made. It is weaker than knowing which decision: Ki(decision=commit) OR Ki(decision=abort). A two-point information set with commit at one point and abort at the other satisfies the first formula but neither disjunct of the second. Consequently the paper's prose “knows the final decision” should be interpreted with this written formula in view. The printed formula does not alone establish value knowledge, even if other model observations might establish it in particular phases (Q7,Q8; reader semantic example).  Table1 point3 also appears too narrow for its claimed equivalence to NOT Ki(cheating). Consider an honest coordinator sending abort after a participant voted no, with trap=false and cheatingDetected=false. Cheating is actually false. By the factivity of knowledge under the stated indistinguishability semantics, Ki(cheating) is false, so its negation is true. Yet both disjuncts of the printed replacement require the participant's vote yes, making the predicate false. The program can still retain its already assigned abort outcome; this example challenges exact epistemic equivalence rather than proving an additional disagreement execution. The paper's unreleased environment/control-point details would be needed to see whether it excludes this apparently ordinary reachable case (Q2,Q7,Q11; reader derivation).  The no-vote stopping explanation appeals to abort validity while Table2 reports abort validity fails for the coordinator's decision. Knowing the correct prescribed decision and knowing the actual Byzantine coordinator variable are different claims. The record preserves this ambiguity instead of deriving an unqualified early-stop theorem. Similarly, Specifications3/4a/4b and §7 use a free participant index i in the printed formulas; their prose talks about everyone. The coordinator pseudocode does contain an explicit conjunction over participants before breaking. Treat the displayed specifications as schematic per-participant tests unless the missing MCK model establishes their quantification (Q6,Q8,Q9).  ## Run-length method and evaluation  For a coordinator stopping condition T, the paper checks X^n(NOT T) universally over runs. Its first failed bound identifies an execution where T holds; the proposed doubling then binary search seeks the smallest such bound. To find a uniform upper bound it instead checks X^n(T), seeking the first bound where every run satisfies T; a counterexample at one step earlier illustrates a slow run. These are model time/communication bounds, not observed wall-clock latency or throughput (Q12).  Binary search requires a monotone bounded predicate. Perfect recall preserves knowledge of past facts but does not, by itself, preserve knowledge of an arbitrary proposition about a changing current state. The one-shot decision/stopping model may provide the required persistence; its complete environment/transition model is needed to establish that. An asserted universal eventual stop also need not yield a finite uniform bound for arbitrary infinite-state systems. The paper's finite tested cases and its explicit “if any” upper-bound search should remain visible (Q12; reader methodological qualification).  Table3 reports a shortest run of one round and d−1 messages, and a longest run of three rounds and3(d−1)messages. Figure3's optional participant all-to-all exchange can add2(d−1)(d−2) sends if each of d−1 participants sends both its vote and decision to each other participant. That is reader arithmetic from its loop. The paper does not explain how this optional traffic is charged in Table3, so its linear message totals should not become an unqualified bound including every opened-run exchange (Q8,Q12).  No MCK version, hardware, state-space counts, checker runtimes, iteration counts, full environment listing, complete counterexample archive or source URL appears in the retained paper. Therefore its model-checking outcomes and timing/message claims remain author-reported. This read does not reproduce them or certify its printed formulas against a saved executable model. Future work includes coordinator replication, cryptography and improved fault detection (Q12,Q13).  ## Contribution to the requested topic  This provides a concrete specification-to-predicate refinement workflow for distributed protocols: preserving local observations/history, checking epistemic equivalence at exact control points and learning from counterexamples. Its negative results demonstrate that termination and detection improvements do not establish atomic-commit safety. There is no Verus/Rust implementation, TLA+ experiment or LLM agent. A reader proposal for proof/specification agents is to check formula/prose agreement, exact versus merely outcome-preserving predicate replacements, finite versus all-size coverage, hidden environment assumptions and complete message accounting separately.
    - limits: synchronousreliablecommunication;restrictedByzantinecoordinator;perfectrecall;finitetestedagentcounts;hiddenenvironment;negativecorrectnessresults;formula/predicatequalifications;noauthorreplay

- Girault et al. MPC (2017)
    - title: Monotonic Prefix Consistency in Distributed Systems
    - what: Defines Monotonic Prefix Consistency (MPC) for replicated lists, gives a centralized toy implementation whose traces satisfy MPC, and proves that no convergent distributed implementation under asynchronous message delivery, availability, and the paper’s observability can be strictly stronger than MPC. Formalizes implementations as total update/query/message handlers, asynchronous broadcast/receive executions with causal delivery and fairness, and traces that record per-site query order/results plus an unordered set of writes. MPC requires per-site monotone reads, pairwise prefix-compatible reads across sites, and read values drawn from writes. Lemmas establish update/query availability, invisible-read deletion, fair execution limits, and convergence extension; induction then realizes every finite MPC trace and a limit argument realizes infinite traces. The paper compares MPC with causal and strong consistency and notes its observability makes MPC and strong-consistency traces indistinguishable.

Convergence means every write is absent from only finitely many queries. The impossibility does not directly cover operations that are both reads and writes, origin-sensitive traces, or probabilistic settings; the MPC implementation is centralized for simplicity.

- Gomes et al. SEC Isabelle (2017)
    - title: Verifying Strong Eventual Consistency in Distributed Systems
    - what: Builds a reusable Isabelle/HOL framework that formalizes strong eventual consistency (SEC), an asynchronous unreliable causal-broadcast network, and three operation-based CRDTs: Replicated Growable Array, Observed-Remove Set, and increment-decrement Counter. The abstract convergence theorem proves that distinct happens-before-consistent operation lists with the same set of operations yield the same state when concurrent operations commute, while a separate no-failure condition gives progress. The network locale has six axioms covering unique node histories, delivery cause, local delivery, globally unique message IDs, causal delivery, and valid broadcast operations; messages may be delayed, reordered, dropped, or nodes may crash permanently. RGA proof models immutable element IDs, tombstones, insertion ordering, causal validity, and proves concurrent operations commute and application never fails. ORSet uses add IDs and remove sets of observed IDs; Add/Remove commute only under a proved independence condition. Counter operations commute unconditionally. The framework is executable via Isabelle code generation; one counter implementation ran over TCP, but detailed performance/fault-tolerance evaluation was left for future work.
    - number: 3 CRDTs verified
    - number: 6 network axioms
    - number: ~620 lines network, ~380 convergence, ~775 RGA, ~270 ORSet, ~55 Counter
    - number: ORSet proof about four hours; Counter minutes
    - limits: Network assumptions are axiomatic: finite totally ordered per-node histories, unique events/IDs, causal delivery for dependencies, and valid-msg predicates supplied by the algorithm. The model uses crash-stop permanent node failure, not recovery, and does not model overlay implementation, timing, or resource limits. RGA retains tombstones; garbage collection is explicitly out of scope. The correctness claims are for operation-based CRDTs satisfying the five SEC locale obligations, not arbitrary distributed data types. Executable extraction demonstrates computability rather than performance.

- Parameterized leader-election abstraction for FTSP (2017)
    - title: An Abstraction Technique for Parameterized Model Checking of Leader Election Protocols: Application to FTSP
    - what: Develops a simulation-preserving abstraction for parameterized timed leader-election protocols with unique identifiers and arbitrary topologies. It abstracts non-leader nodes and network edges around a shortest path to the future leader, approximates clock drift with finite schedulers, and incrementally checks FTSP root election for all graphs bounded by leader distance K. The method first maps identifiers/messages to future-root versus non-root values and relaxes irrelevant sequence/entry variables, then completes the graph outside a chosen shortest path and merges those nodes into an environment process. Simulation lemmas establish that checking the finite abstract model implies LTL properties on every topology in G_K. Approximate-synchrony scheduler S_a(Δ) over-approximates real clocks for a finite horizon derived from σ_l,σ_u,Δ. An incremental proof initializes already-converged path nodes and uses a non-interference guard to remove spurious environment messages. A NuSMV semi-algorithm finds optimal FG bounds without storing all reachable states.

The abstraction over-approximates behavior, so spurious traces require guard strengthening and proof of the non-interference lemma. Results concern FTSP root convergence, not full time synchronization or failures during the checked interval; asynchronous K=5 timed out beyond that range.

    - title: Formal Verification of Multi-Paxos for Distributed Consensus
    - what: # Formal Verification of Multi-Paxos for Distributed Consensus (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Saksham Chand, Yanhong A. Liu and Scott D. Stoller. The original paper appeared at FM 2016, pp 119–136, DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-48989-6_8. This record reads the 37-page corrected and extended arXiv:1606.01387v4, dated 11 November 2019, classified cs.DC on its first page. The inventory's 2016 year identifies the original work; it does not date the corrected version read here (Q1,Q45; arxiv.html).  The contribution is a small TLA+ specification of Multi-Paxos and its preemption extension, an author-reported TLAPS proof of per-slot agreement, and concrete strategies for managing the much larger proof. Two qualifications matter. The authors explicitly retract the earlier completeness claim: “The claim of a complete proof in [7] was incorrect” (§1 p2, Q3), explaining a PTL backend bug and their replacement type-invariant proof. Separately, this read finds inconsistent maximum axioms in the printed appendix and pinned proof files as written (Appendix C p29, Q49,Q59,Q63). Thus the record preserves the corrected checking report but does not treat checker acceptance under those retained assumptions as independent certification of the assumption-free theorem. This is a mathematical assumption problem, not an observed execution failure or a counterexample to Multi-Paxos agreement.  ## Reading and evidence scope  Read all 37 PDF pages in extracted text and rendered images: sections 1–7, all six figures, both numeric tables, all 26 numbered equations, acknowledgments, all 63 reference entries, and Appendices A–C containing the specification, invariants and hierarchical proof. The figures are algorithm/proof listings and comparisons, not statistical plots. The two PDFs, one from the local inventory and one freshly fetched from arXiv, are byte-identical. The local PDF is the corrected v4, not the 2016 proceedings text.  Fetched the author-linked DistAlgo/proofs repository's metadata, commit and recursive tree.
