Read its full README and selected plaintext specification, assumption, type-invariant and final-theorem regions of the improved Multi-Paxos/preemption modules, plus the historical FM16 TypeOK regions. The README distinguishes these versions and says improved proofs were checked with TLAPS 1.5.6 (Q56). Downloaded Basic Paxos baseline and historical modules provide retained source context; this is not a whole-repository or whole-module audit. The explicit excerpt/range inventory is in source-scope.json. Also read the complete official issue 40 body describing the coalescing bug (Q66); metadata says opened 1 April 2017 and closed 17 May 2018. Closing an issue does not identify the fix commit or certify every installed tool version.  No author code, model, TLAPS, TLC, SMT solver or proof assistant was executed or imported. No serialized data/model/checkpoint was loaded. Reader checks use file hashes, literal source slices, arithmetic and symbolic reasoning. Raw Git files retain their bytes; .lf.txt files are identified newline-normalized derivatives for character and LF-line quote pointers. The PDF extraction renders □ as 2, primes as 0 and some negated existential/membership symbols unusually; rendered pages were used to interpret the formulas. quotes.json retains extraction bytes, including such artifacts.  ## The model and the exact theorem  The system has proposer, acceptor and learner roles, which may be colocated. Constants describe proposers P, acceptors A, quorum family Q and possible values V. Ballots B and slots S are natural numbers. Membership and the quorum family are fixed: dynamic reconfiguration is excluded. The sole stated quorum condition is Q ⊆ SUBSET A and pairwise nonempty intersection. Majority, tree or matrix quorums can instantiate it once that condition is established; the paper does not construct or evaluate those alternatives (Q6,Q13,Q19).  The state contains the set msgs of every message ever sent, proposer ballots pBal, each acceptor's highest seen ballot aBal, and aVoted, a set of ballot-slot-value records retaining the highest voted ballot for each slot. Init uses no messages/votes, proposer ballot 0 and acceptor ballot −1. Next chooses one proposer or acceptor phase. Spec = Init ∧ □[Next]_vars permits an action or stuttering at each step (Q13–Q19).  The messages-as-history abstraction lets processes select any previously sent message, repeatedly and in any order. An unhandled message models arbitrary delay or loss; repeated handling models duplication. Crashes are modeled by not scheduling the crashed process, and recovery resumes its retained state. The authors require “all state (vars) is stored in stable storage” (§3.3 p11, Q20). The model has no Byzantine message fabrication, volatile-state reset, implementation of durable storage, or explicit network delivery queue. This is a safety abstraction of benign failures.  There are no fairness or eventual-delivery clauses in the displayed Spec. Repeating Init forever is a valid behavior through UNCHANGED vars and never chooses a value. This reader witness demonstrates the absence of decision progress, without challenging agreement. A quorum of functioning processes and delivery assumptions would matter for liveness; no such liveness theorem is established here (Q9,Q15,Q19; math-witness.json).  The target is Spec ⇒ □Safe, where Safe means any two chosen values for one slot are equal. The paper identifies C1 proposed-value validity, C2 agreement and C3 learner correctness, then says C1/C3 are excluded from the formal proof; §3.3 and §4.8 discuss them informally (Q5,Q22,Q33). There are no explicit learner variables/actions. Validity means a chosen slot/value occurred in a protocol 2a proposal, not that a value came from an external client or satisfied an application invariant. Equations 24/26 use sent although the state variable is msgs; the record treats this as the printed informal derivation, not a checked new theorem.  The precise Chosen definition used in the proof is ∃b ∈ B: ∃Q ∈ Q: ∀a ∈ Q: VotedForIn(a,b,s,v). VotedForIn witnesses a sent 2b message with that ballot and slot/value. The introductory equations 3/4 place ∃b inside ∀a, allowing different ballots for different acceptors. Those predicates differ; use equations 10–12 and Appendix B for the actual theorem (Q6,Q23,Q48). A separating predicate valuation in math-witness.json makes the difference explicit, without claiming a reachable protocol counterexample.  ## Minimal algorithm changes  Basic Paxos carries one latest accepted ballot/value pair. Multi-Paxos carries a set of ballot-slot-value records in each promise. Phase1a sends a ballot. Phase1b responds only to a strictly higher ballot, returning its voted-record set and recording the promise. Phase2a waits for same-ballot promise replies covering a quorum and sends at most one 2a message per ballot. It selects the maximum accepted ballot separately per slot, retaining that slot's value, and adds new slot/value pairs. Phase2b accepts a ballot at least its promise, sends a 2b reply, and replaces voted records only for the slots in that proposal (Figures 2–5, Q14–Q18).  MaxBSV filters the voted records to maximal ballots per slot; MaxSV drops ballots; UnusedS finds absent slots; NewSV chooses a set of unused-slot/value pairs with no duplicate slot carrying different values; PropSV combines old and new pairs. Ballots are shared across slots, and old unfinished slots can be reused. The authors explain that this is more involved than separately running independent Basic Paxos instances (Q15,Q17).  NewSV has no explicit nonemptiness, finiteness or client-input requirement. The empty set satisfies its uniqueness predicate. CHOOSE denotes a fixed mathematical choice for the same argument, not a newly sampled nondeterministic result each time. The formulas are useful abstractions for agreement, but do not by themselves ensure an executable finite batch or useful new work. Finite msgs does not imply finite message payloads (Q17,Q47; math-witness.json).  Preemption adds an addressed reply containing an acceptor's highest ballot when it rejects a proposer ballot. A proposer receiving a strictly higher preempt ballot updates pBal above it. Phase1a then sends pBal, and the two acceptor actions have extra rejection branches (Figure 6/Appendix A, Q34,Q35,Q47). In Phase1b equality also enters the else branch, although the prose often says lower ballot. The proposer's strict-higher guard prevents equality from raising pBal.  Two source differences constrain exact correspondence. The printed NewBal requires only b>b2; the pinned NewBallot also excludes ballots already used by a 1a message, matching §5.1's fresh-ballot explanation. Conversely, the pinned non-preemption Phase1a omits the no-prior-1a guard displayed in Figure 2. Both retain the global no-prior-2a-per-ballot guard. These differences are documented, not silently normalized or labeled agreement violations (Q14,Q35,Q36,Q47,Q57,Q62).  Actual software must allocate ballots, for example ordered counter/process-identifier pairs, rather than inspect a global history oracle. Reconfiguration, message/state reduction and failure detection are omitted. A 1b reply can contain votes for every previously used slot. There is no verified Rust implementation, code refinement or operational throughput experiment in this paper (Q21).  ## Invariants, decomposition and final argument  Inv conjoins TypeOK, AccInv and MsgInv. TypeOK constrains every message/function/record field; the corrected preemption version additionally requires finite msgs. AccInv relates each acceptor's promise and current voted records to the historical 2b votes: stored records were actually voted, every historical vote is covered by a same-slot record at least as high, and no vote lies above the current same-slot maximum (Q25,Q26,Q48).  MsgInv1b records the sender's promise, actual historical votes in its returned set, and absence of votes between that slot's stored maximum and the promised ballot. MsgInv2a says every proposal is SafeAt its ballot, a message has at most one value per slot, and there is only one 2a message per ballot. MsgInv2b ties each vote to a matching 2a message and bounds its ballot by the acceptor's highest seen ballot (Q27,Q28).  SafeAt(b,s,v) says that for every lower ballot, some quorum consists of acceptors that voted v or have promised above that ballot and never voted there. WontVoteIn expresses the latter alternative. VotedInv carries SafeAt from proposals into votes; VotedOnce states same-ballot/same-slot votes have the same value, even from different acceptors. Their role is concrete: at equal chosen ballots use VotedOnce; at unequal ballots intersect the chosen quorum with the SafeAt quorum. The common acceptor's old vote excludes WontVoteIn, leaving equal values (Q24,Q50,Q55).  The proof first establishes Init ⇒ Inv and Inv ∧ [Next]_vars ⇒ Inv′, with separate action cases and an explicit unchanged-state case. PTL then derives Spec ⇒ □Inv and transfers Inv ⇒ Safe to the temporal Safety theorem (Q29,Q52–Q55). The final temporal QED is present; its presence still does not prove the assumed mathematics consistent.  The reusable method separates unaffected old elements from each action's new message or voted-record increment. Invariance lemmas preserve old VotedForIn/SafeAt facts; the new element is proved from the sending action and local invariants. Conjuncts and actions form a mechanical decomposition, while difficult bounds and witnesses require manual facts. The paper illustrates this fully for Phase1b and MsgInv and shows the longer Phase2a proof in Appendix C (Q30,Q31,Q51,Q54).  Proof syntax matters to performance. A common acceptor voting both values in the equal-ballot case is supplied explicitly; the authors report about 90 seconds reduced to a few milliseconds, calling it a 10,000× local speedup. Replacing direct record membership by an existential record with field equalities made another proof proceed after the original stalled for one or two minutes. These are local development observations, with no repeated-run distribution or uniform ablation (Q32). Tuple access is a concrete proof-engineering choice, not evidence of an algorithm runtime speedup.  ## The disclosed checker bug and the remaining assumption problem  The authors report that historical PTL coalescing could “prove” a primed state formula from its unprimed assumption outside a valid temporal context. It incorrectly accepted TypeOK′ under TypeOK ∧ [Next]_vars. The official issue's example falsely preserves xyz=0 while Next permits increasing xyz. Choosing increment 1 from xyz=0 gives xyz′=1, refuting that preservation claim symbolically (Q36,Q66). Historical FM16 modules retain PTL at primed message-type leaves; improved excerpts instead give explicit action proofs (Q60,Q64,Q65).  The repair proves type preservation for all phases. Preemption needs a fresh larger natural ballot to exist. With finite msgs, the used 1a ballots form a finite set T; max(T∪{received ballot})+1 supplies a larger unused witness. The authors added IsFiniteSet(msgs), proved preservation under message addition and supplied this witness. They report initial TypeOK proof growth 54→93 lines and 75→138 lines for the two variants; subsequent improvements reduce those to 54 and 77 (Q36,Q37,Q52).  A separate issue remains in the retained text. Appendix C calls two axioms “straightforward consequences” but writes MaxInSet as ∀S∈SUBSET N: Max(S)∈S (Q49). Substitute S=∅: it asserts Max(∅)∈∅, false for every CHOOSE result. The pinned source writes the domain as (SUBSET Nat) \\ {}, which subtracts no elements and still includes ∅ (Q59,Q63). Removing the empty set as an element would require {{}}. That change alone would still leave unbounded infinite subsets: applying MaxInSet and MaxOnNat to Nat gives a natural maximum k, but k+1 is a larger natural. A sound maximum lemma needs nonempty finite or bounded domains and proof that each use meets the restriction.  These are static mathematical witnesses to inconsistent assumptions as written, not TLAPS runs, discovered new protocol executions, or an assertion that every leaf exploited inconsistency. The retained files cannot alone support an assumption-free machine-certification claim. Agreement may be true and the intended invariant argument may be repairable, but repairing and replaying it is outside this literature read. The disclosed PTL repair does not address these maximum axioms. This distinction is particularly useful when evaluating automated proof agents: green obligations and completed syntax must be accompanied by an audit of explicit axioms and the actual target.  ## Evaluation and quantitative evidence  The evaluation compares Basic Paxos, Multi-Paxos and Multi-Paxos with Preemption, plus older incomplete and corrected/improved proof variants. It measures text size, proof-tree structure, lemma reuse, obligations and proof-checking cost, not network performance or application throughput. Table 2 specifies a four-core Intel i7-4720HQ at 2.6 GHz, 16 GB RAM, 64-bit Ubuntu 17.10 and TLAPS 1.5.6. Earlier elapsed times from 1.5.3 are marked separately. No raw timing logs, repeat counts, variance or matched cross-tool benchmark are provided (Q40–Q42).  The corrected new rows report specification lines excluding comments of 52, 55 and 74; proof lines 310, 787 and 831; obligations 239, 779 and 825; total CPU seconds 40, 175 and 180; total elapsed seconds 14, 51 and 90. CPU time and elapsed time are distinct; the total CPU values are close to the headline “about 3 minutes,” whereas the elapsed values are 51/90 seconds. Adding Multi-Paxos slots costs only three specification lines but 477 proof lines and 540 obligations; adding preemption costs 19 specification lines, 44 proof lines and 46 obligations. The per-slot data structure creates most of the proof expansion (Q40,Q41).  The new proof trees have maximum level 10 and degree 17, against 7 and 3 for Basic Paxos. Multi-Paxos/preemption use five/six invariance lemmas 32/35 times and three proofs using set increments each. §4.6's five lemmas used 27 times describes an earlier count; Table 2 provides the updated reuse counts (Q31,Q41). Reflowed appendix counts, including 528 proof lines excluding comments, are layout alternatives, not another method or independently smaller proof.  The three improvements factor message predicates, merge similar unchanged-state cases and remove leaf scaffolding TLAPS can establish automatically. Reported reductions for preemption include 75 lines from predicate factoring, 27 from merged cases, 110 from about 25 unnecessary-obligation instances and 61 from 22 TypeOK instances. The full repaired proofs shrink 1049→787 and 1117→831 lines; those are 25%/26% reductions from the repaired versions. Old incomplete rows marked ^^ are not valid proof-performance baselines (Q3,Q37–Q41).  Table 1 gives improved TypeOK elapsed times 8/25 seconds; Table 2 gives 7/24. Their old preemption TypeOK elapsed entries also differ, 21 versus 22. Preserve these printed differences rather than inventing a run-variance explanation. numeric_tables.json retains every metric, alternate count and footnote marker. The report that adding preemption took less than an hour explicitly excludes TypeOK; it cannot be used as total authoring time for the corrected proof (Q34,Q37,Q41).  ## Relationship to the requested research topics  This is directly useful for TLA+ and formal verification of distributed protocols: concrete fault abstraction, per-slot agreement, quorum reasoning, stronger invariants, hierarchical proof feedback, old/new-set decomposition and sensitivity to formula representation. Its strongest evaluation lesson is the explicit correction history, reinforced by the separate maximum-assumption findings in this read.  The work contains no Verus, verified Rust or LLM-agent experiment. Transfer to those topics is a reader proposal: preserve the exact property and fault model; measure changes in executable specification separately from proof scaffolding; give agents small action/conjunct obligations with explicit contexts; distinguish finite-instance testing from parameterized proof; and check axioms, omitted obligations, tool versions and source correspondence before reporting success. No agent success rate or Rust implementation result follows from this paper.  Related-work proof-size comparisons with IronFleet, Verdi, EventML/Nuprl, EPR and other systems are author descriptions of differently scoped work, not controlled evidence that TLAPS is uniformly faster or requires fewer lines. The separate executable-program work in reference 45 reportedly found a safety violation missed by testing/model checking, but that example is cited rather than reproduced and verified here (Q43,Q44). Those leads can be followed as separate full reads.

    - what: Presents a Coq-mechanized framework that models preemptive-kernel API correctness as contextual refinement from a practical C subset, with abstract specifications, concrete interrupt-aware semantics, a relational concurrent separation logic, and proof tactics. - Automatic Completion of Distributed Protocols with Symmetry. (2015)
    - what: # Automatic Completion of Distributed Protocols with Symmetry (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Rajeev Alur, Mukund Raghothaman, Christos Stergiou, Stavros Tripakis and Abhishek Udupa, arXiv:1505.04409v1. The arXiv comments identify this as the “Full version of paper presented at CAV 2015.” The paper gives a solver-and-model-checker loop that fills missing guards and state updates in finite distributed protocol sketches, requiring determinism, symmetry, deadlock freedom, safety and liveness under supplied fairness assumptions. Its empirical results cover Peterson mutual exclusion, a four-process self-stabilizing line, and five missing cache-coherence corner cases. Guaranteed correctness is explicitly limited to the finite synthesized instance (Q1,Q2,Q6,Q13,W1,W2).  ## Reading and evidence scope  Read all 21 pages, sections 1–6, all displayed definitions/formulas, nine figures, the complete five-row Table 1, and all 31 bibliography entries. There is no appendix, checklist, numbered theorem/proof or numbered pseudocode algorithm. Figure 2 is the synthesis workflow; §4 gives textual algorithms. Individually inspected page renders 3,8,11,13,14,15,16,17,18,19, covering every figure, the table, protocol diagrams and the weakest-precondition formula. This does not claim visual inspection of all pages. References were read as bibliography entries, not recursively followed.  Retained the inventory PDF, raw/layout extractions and official arXiv metadata. The paper says the custom model checker is planned for future public release; it supplies no implementation URL. No implementation/model files or historical logs were acquired or read. A web-search tool request for code returned an error without results; this is not evidence that no code exists. No author contacted, author code executed/imported, checker/solver rerun, or model/checkpoint/serialized experiment data loaded. Source versions and reported runs were not independently reproduced (Q8,W1).  ## Problem and modeling assumptions  The designer provides extended state-machine sketches, not just an English request or temporal goal. Each process has finite control locations, finite typed variables/channels, an initial valuation, known and unknown typed functions, guarded transitions and fairness sets. All type cardinalities are required finite, including process-identity symmetric types and array domains. A completed function is initially a finite interpretation table. The environment is another specified machine with no unknown functions (Q3,Q4,Q6).  Composition synchronizes matching output/input channels and sequences their updates so the receiver sees the transmitted value; independent internal actions interleave. Buffered unordered communication in the cache example is modeled within these finite-state machines, not assumed to be an unbounded reliable network. The formal product assumes disjoint process state variables and output ownership. Safety means no reachable error location. Liveness means no infinite fair accepting run of the supplied monitors; deadlock freedom is separate. Thus a finite deadlock cannot pass just because no infinite violating run exists (Q3,Q4).  Weak fairness applies to a set of transitions: either the whole set is disabled infinitely often or some member occurs infinitely often. Strong fairness requires that a set enabled infinitely often has a member taken infinitely often. Fairness sets are attached to output/internal transitions; input behavior depends on the environment/composition. These assumptions matter to the guarantees. The paper argues that using only safety in synthesis permits trivial solutions that disable progress (Q2,Q3).  Symmetry means behavior is invariant under renaming values of the designated types. Permutations act on array entries and indices, channel/process parameters and states. Unknown functions are constrained to commute with renaming, f(π(d))=π(f(d)). This is stronger than merely using the same source text while permitting special treatment of one numeric identity. Quantifiers are expanded over finite domains for the solver. The discussion mentions other symmetry notions as possible extensions; the implementation/evaluation described uses the stated finite symmetry treatment (Q5,Q7).  The designer can restrict signatures to exclude irrelevant variables, fix known read-only updates, and add constraints across functions. The formal completion requires deterministic individual machines, a symmetric product, satisfaction of initial constraints, and a deadlock-free/safe/live composition. Determinism allows simultaneous input transitions only on distinct input channels. Guarantees concern that chosen environment, monitor and fairness model, not every implementation of the informal protocol name (Q6,Q7).  ## Algorithm and what its checks establish  The synthesis loop asks Z3 for interpretations satisfying current constraints, instantiates the protocol, then model-checks it. An erroneous candidate yields further necessary conditions excluding its counterexample or repairing the reason it violates the property. A successful interpretation may subsequently be converted to a symbolic expression using an enumerative syntax-guided synthesis solver. A symbolic grammar/output is therefore a later step; the initial solver does not directly synthesize arbitrary program syntax (Q6,Q10,Q13).  The custom checker combines a symmetry-reduced annotated quotient graph with permutation tracking in a threaded graph, then searches accepting strongly connected components under fairness. Tracking the renaming matters because a compressed path can stand for multiple original paths and fairness obligations must be adjusted accordingly. The described procedure removes states enabling unmet strong-fairness sets and recomputes components until it finds a fair accepting cycle or rules one out. The authors build on cited algorithms and describe the search as sound and complete; this paper supplies no separate numbered soundness/completeness proof or implementation certification. Their historical limitations of Spin, Murphi, SMC and NuSMV are reports about their tool attempts, not a current feature comparison (Q8).  For a deadlock, the next candidate must block the witnessed path or enable some outgoing action at its end. For a safety trace it must block the error path. The paper compiles product transitions to guarded commands, coalesces assignments and computes weakest preconditions; a guarded-command obligation uses guard implication, so a disabled step can break the trace. For liveness, a stem/cycle witness must become infeasible, fail to close, or become unfair. The Peterson example shows why simply banning the waiting loop is too strong: enabling a continuously neglected critical transition can make that loop unfair under the given fairness assumption (Q9,Q10).  There is a printed indexing problem worth preserving without treating it as an implementation defect. §4.3 indexes a trace cmd1,…,cmdn but defines pre_i using cmd_(n−i−1). With n=1 and i=1 this refers to cmd_−1 rather than the sole command. The intended reverse traversal would require a corrected index/convention; no source code was available to determine what the implementation uses. The rendered page 11 confirms the printed formula. The liveness recurrence also reuses notation inconsistently around the named union of fairness sets. These are presentation limits on mechanically following the text, not reproduced failures of the tool (Q10,D1).  Search heuristics prefer each error path to exercise few unknown functions while choosing diverse paths that collectively cover many. Shorter unknown-function dependencies can give stronger pruning constraints. Candidate costs favor minimally permissive guards, unchanged updates, then fewer input dependencies; bounds relax when the solver cannot satisfy them. Such constraints are search guidance, not protocol requirements. They strongly affect runtime, and Dijkstra required a different guard heuristic. No controlled ablation quantifies each optimization's benefit (Q11,Q12).  ## Concrete cases  Peterson has two processes with my/other identity parameters, shared flag/turn variables, a critical-section safety condition and a starvation monitor. Figure 1 removes the waiting/critical guards; the experiment additionally leaves flag-update expressions unspecified and requires that at least one guard hold. Weak fairness of selected non-input transitions suffices for the stated monitor. The authors report an interpretation in under one second and expressions matching the known protocol. Table 1 reports three unknown functions; this count is retained as printed rather than inferred by counting the distinct update sites mentioned in prose (Q3,Q12,T1).  The self-stabilizing case is four processes in a line, each with Boolean x/up state. The two middle processes have two unknown guarded commands, each with two unknown updates; corresponding middle-process completions must be identical. A legitimate state has exactly one globally enabled guarded command. The specification requires reaching legitimate states from arbitrary starts, staying legitimate thereafter, and reachability among legitimate states. The successful expressions match Dijkstra's displayed rules. This is synthesis/verification for N=4; the general-N illustration is not itself a parameterized correctness proof (Q12).  German/MSI has a directory, symmetric caches and one environment per cache; permissions are invalid/shared/exclusive. Its variant adds direct cache-to-cache data/acknowledgment, silent shared eviction and coordinated exclusive eviction. These optimizations create interactions absent from the simpler base protocol. One explicit race has a directory still listing a silently evicted cache as a sharer: that cache has already requested exclusive ownership when it receives an invalidation for another requester, and must acknowledge the invalidation despite its transient state. Two related races vary the pending read/write request (Q12,Q14).  Two remaining missing behaviors arise when exclusive eviction/writeback races with another cache's request: the cache receives an unexpected invalidation, while the directory receives unexpected writeback. The synthesized behavior treats the invalidation like a writeback acknowledgment for the evicting cache; the directory accepts the latest data and forwards it to the requester without requiring an extra acknowledgment. Figures 8/9 mark the missing behaviors and recovery messages. The designer still specifies which message kinds each unknown state must handle; §5.4 says this assistance was crucial to scaling. This is completion of supplied protocol structure, not autonomous discovery of all states, messages or correctness requirements (Q14,Q15).  ## Measured results and limits  Table 1 reports five configurations. Peterson: 3 unknown functions, search space 2^36, 60 states, 14 iterations, 97 ms SMT and 130 ms total. Dijkstra: 6 functions, 2^192 possibilities, about 2,000 states, 30 iterations, 27 s SMT and 64 s total. German/MSI-2: 16 functions, about 2^4700 possibilities, about 20,000 symmetry-reduced states, 217 iterations, 31 s SMT and 298 s total. German/MSI-4: 28 functions, about 2^7614, about 20,000 reduced states, 419 iterations, 898 s SMT and 1,545 s total. German/MSI-5: 34 functions, about 2^9000, about 20,000 reduced states, 525 iterations, 2,261 s SMT and 3,410 s total. The exponents were checked in the page render because the extraction flattens superscripts (T1).  The suffix -n counts the missing transitions among five corner cases, not the number of caches. The paper does not state the exact cache-count/channel-capacity/value-domain configuration used for these rows, preventing a precise independent reconstruction from the paper alone. All runs use a Linux desktop with a 3.4 GHz Intel Core i7 and 8 GB memory. Multiple SMT seeds were run and the worst runtimes reported, but the number of seeds, dispersion and exact tool versions are absent. There is no broad benchmark population or matched competing-system comparison. Long cases spend much time solving heuristic constraints; German/MSI-5's SMT fraction is 2261/3410≈66.3%, a reader calculation, not a new measurement (Q15,T1,D2).  The authors say synthesized symbolic expressions were parametric and worked on larger instances, but explicitly qualify that interpretations are “only guaranteed to be correct for the finite instance of the protocol”. No sizes/results for the larger checks or cutoff/induction proof is supplied. Symmetry reduces a fixed instance's state graph; it does not by itself prove correctness for every process count. Nor do these finite-state experiments establish crash/Byzantine tolerance or machine-code correctness (Q13).  ## Contribution to the requested topics  This is directly relevant distributed-protocol synthesis with safety and liveness checking, predating LLM-based agents. Its distinctive combination is finite extended state sketches, symmetry constraints, fine transition-set fairness, and automatically generated counterexample constraints. Its related-work claims distinguish earlier scenario completion, safety-only concurrent sketching, and template-based self-stabilization; these comparisons are attributed to the authors, without independently reading those cited works (Q2).  For Verus/TLA+/LLM-agent work, the transfer is a reader proposal: preserve explicit environment/fairness assumptions, use deadlocks and fair cycles as separate feedback, constrain identity symmetry and keep programmer-supplied structure visible in evaluation. An SMT table, a readable symbolic expression, a finite checked instance and a general verified protocol are different outputs. The paper measures the first stages and fixed-instance checks; it contains no Verus/Rust development, TLA+ model, LLM agent or general parameterized proof.

Document histories/identity/count policy must match intended disclosure. The ten independently proved source properties are not a stated theorem of joint secrecy for all combinations of secret sources. - Graph- versus Vector-Based Analysis of a Consensus Protocol (2014)
    - what: # Whole-paper read: Graph- versus Vector-Based Analysis of a Consensus Protocol (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Giorgio Delzanno, Arend Rensink and Riccardo Traverso; GRAPHITE2014, EPTCS159, pp44–57, doi10.4204/EPTCS.159.5, arXiv1407.7931. This is a finite-state Paxos safety comparison between graph transformation in GROOVE and a PROMELA model in SPIN. It demonstrates how modeling and symmetry reduction affect reachable state counts and exploration cost. It does not establish a parameterized Paxos theorem or correspondence with a deployed implementation. [Q0,Q1,Q2,Q14]  ## Property and model assumptions  Definition1 requires every chosen value to have been proposed and all choices, including successive rounds, to agree. The general introduction permits arbitrarily delayed messages and crash/recovery retaining local information. The displayed models contain no explicit crash/recovery transitions. Each proposer sends at most one Prepare, and there is one learner. Authors argue that more proposers can mimic repeated rounds and that multiple learners have the same available information. These are modeling justifications; the paper supplies no formal cutoff theorem reducing arbitrary configurations to the finite instances measured. The one-Prepare restriction also prevents indefinite injection of new proposals; this is not a liveness proof for unrestricted Paxos. [Q1,Q2,Q3]  Prepare chooses a fresh round; Promise carries the acceptor's last accepted round/value; a quorum causes a proposer to reuse the highest previously accepted value, or its own initial value if none exists. Acceptors promise increasing rounds and accept rounds at least as high as their current promise. Learners choose a round/value after a quorum. Figure1 supplies the pseudocode, including fresh-round and maximum-prior-round selection requirements. [Q2,Q3]  ## What the two encodings do  GROOVE stores a configuration as a typed graph. Process/value nodes have no explicit identities; round numbers and counters remain integer attributes. Broadcasts are persistent message nodes connected to senders, rather than individually ordered channel contents. Isomorphic configurations can therefore merge. Nested quantification counts matching Promise/Learn nodes, negative conditions prevent duplicate Learn emission and select a maximal prior round, and control functions schedule large rule applications. onPromise removes isPrepared so a proposer accepts a quorum only once; changeMyval precedes sendAccept. A learner may choose again. Unsafe patterns test two distinct chosen values, including two choices by one learner, or a chosen value absent from all proposer values. Depth-first search stops at the first unsafe graph, or explores the complete reachable state space for that initial configuration. [Q4,Q5,Q6,Q7]  PROMELA represents each role as a process and communications as four bounded channels. Ordered send (!!) and matching receive (??) reduce irrelevant message-order variation. atomic/d_step blocks combine operations; the proposer scans Promise entries with a sentinel round9, restores them, and sends Accept after a quorum. Temporary variables are reset and learner counters saturate at the majority. Figures9–10 give proposer, acceptor, four-recipient broadcast and learner code. Printed MAX=10 bounds channels and the learner's round-indexed counter array; values use byte/short/int types. The paper does not provide separate complete experiment inputs or a formal GROOVE–PROMELA equivalence proof. The hardcoded four-recipient example is not itself every row's configuration. Atomicity, graph identity, message persistence, finite channels and representation differ together, so this is not a controlled isolation of one implementation feature. Potential blocking inside atomic blocks and fixed channel capacities are modeling limits, not independently demonstrated bugs. [Q8,Q9,Q10]  ## Evaluation and exact result scope  Table1 has22GROOVE configurations. Low majority searches all find a safety violation before exhausting the state space; their counts measure search to a counterexample. High majority searches report no violation and enumerate all reachable states of those finite models. Examples: two proposers/twelve acceptors/majority7 produce5,491,406states in14,794,452ms; three/six/majority4 produce12,247,549 in8,771,175ms; four/four/majority3 produce9,337,923 in4,523,411ms; seven/two/majority2 produce4,607,455 in1,154,561ms. Authors state that the next larger configurations exhaust memory. This is reported bounded exploration, not a proof for all process counts. [Q10,Q11]  Eight high-majority instances are also explored without graph isomorphism reduction. For two proposers/two acceptors,224states become78 (65.18% reduction); two/five:1,178,114→9,729 (99.17%); five/two:12,743,315→55,420 (99.57%). This within-GROOVE comparison more directly supports the symmetry-reduction claim. Reduction has a cost: the authors report over75% of time spent checking isomorphism for two proposers/eleven acceptors, and generation rates from under400 to over6,000states/s. Figures11–12 visualize growth/comparisons; changing quorum thresholds produces sawtooth growth. [Q11,Q12]  Table2 has11SPIN configurations, with ordinary and starred bit-hashing columns. Starred exploration is an underapproximation: finding an unsafe state supplies a witness, while finding none does not exhaustively establish safety. The caption says a hash factor above100 indicates high coverage; it is a heuristic, not a completeness guarantee. Nonempty reported factors are1.9,2.2,2.3,5.1,6.5,26, all below100. Retain distinct counts: for two proposers/five acceptors/low majority, ordinary226,306states versus starred387,982; for three/three/high,4,998,934 versus4,997,226. Larger starred counts must not be read as larger complete reachable state spaces. [Q12,Q13]  GROOVE used an i7-2600 3.4GHz, Windows7, Java6 and8GB memory; SPIN used an i7, Windows7,6GB, jSpin/SPIN6.2.5May2013 with default memory management. The paper states no repeated-run count or uncertainty estimate. Different resources and modeling choices limit causal claims about engine superiority. It reports search-state counts and verification time, not executable Paxos throughput/latency. [Q10,Q12,Q13]  ## Printed inconsistencies and presentation limits  The SPIN prose says ordinary search finds violations only through five acceptors with two proposers, and with three proposers finds violations only through three acceptors and proves safety only through two. Table2 nevertheless prints ordinary low-majority results for two/six (4,374,568states,118,000ms) and three/four (2,712,145,68,400ms), plus an ordinary high-majority result for three/three (4,998,934,71,700ms). I retain the table and flag its disagreement with the prose; I did not reproduce either. [Q12,Q13]  Two cells require literal preservation. Table2 two/two/high starred state count appears as “62 0” in layout extraction and as spaced “62 0” in the render; raw extraction yields620, matching the adjacent ordinary620. The normalized table records620 with this ambiguity. More materially, two/four/high ordinary Time is printed “3,5” while starred Time is “3,510”; caption units are milliseconds. The former is retained literally, with numeric normalization left unset, rather than silently interpreting it as3.5ms or3,500ms. [Q13]  Figure12's visible acceptor axis is labeled1–5, while its embedded spreadsheet text contains rows2–6. That text also differs from Tables1–2:234 versus224 for GROOVE/no-isomorphism/two-two;29,532 versus29,352 for SPIN/high/two-three;4,374,578 versus4,374,568 for SPIN/low/two-six. These are presentation/data discrepancies, not evidence of a model-checker defect. The record uses table values and preserves the figure's text separately. The graph compares early-stopped unsafe searches, complete safe GROOVE explorations and approximate SPIN explorations; its curves are not uniformly complete state-space sizes. [Q11,Q13,Q15]  ## Contribution and read scope  The paper contributes a concrete distributed-protocol modeling lesson: remove irrelevant process/value identity, message ordering and intermediate steps when that preserves the desired property, and measure the cost and benefit of reductions. For evaluating agents that generate specifications/proofs, my inference is to require an explicit property, finite bounds, preservation argument and completeness status for each reported result before comparing state counts or claiming verification. There is no Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment. [Q1,Q7,Q9,Q14]  Read all14PDFpages, all14references, all12figures, both result tables, all displayed pseudocode/PROMELA and graph rules; viewed all14page renders. Official arXiv and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. Publisher PDF bytes differ, but its full layout extraction is identical. No separate author artifact URL was identified in the paper's links; the printed models were inspected without execution. No compiler, model checker, solver or author-code run.

The AFP 2012 release and the current AFP source snapshot are distinct supporting artifacts, inspected statically in the ranges recorded in source-scope.json. No Isabelle, author code, model checker or solver was run.  ## What is established  The contribution is a parameterized mathematical verification of two finite-state discrete-time, time-homogeneous Markov-chain models in Isabelle/HOL. It proves formulas for ZeroConf address-collision probability, almost-sure termination and expected allocation cost, and for Crowds endpoint independence, exposure to collaborators, conditional predecessor identification and an information-leakage upper bound. “It can deal with infinite-state systems, although this paper considers only parameterized finite-state systems” (§1, p.17, Q1) is the scope to retain. Infinite path spaces still require measure theory. This is a proof about abstract global models, with formalization effort reported by the authors; it is not an implementation benchmark.  Several discrepancies constrain use of the printed results. The ZeroConf example’s named parameters do not satisfy its printed 10^-13 bound; its displayed cost formula has parentheses inconsistent with the model and retained source. The Crowds §4.2 independence display uses last-ncoll where its heading and definitions concern last-jondo. Finally, the retained information-flow theorem has an additional uniform-initiation hypothesis absent from the paper’s displayed theorem. These are separate issues, documented below rather than silently repaired.  ## Probability foundation and proof method (§2, pp.18–20)  The chain has a nonempty finite state set S and nonnegative transition weights whose row sums are 1 (Q4). Its path probability is constructed on all infinite state sequences from arbitrary product spaces, avoiding an encoding into infinite boolean choices (Q5). A specified start state precedes the measured sequence: the first measured index represents a transition from that start. Individual sequence elements need not satisfy the transition relation by the definition of path alone; the probability measure provides the operational meaning (Q4). Conditional probability is a quotient; AE means probability 1 (Q3).  The reusable tools are one-step equations for event probability, integrals and almost-everywhere predicates (Q6), qualitative reachability over nonzero transition edges and an until operator (Q7), and a theorem that almost every path is state fair (Q8). In the finite chain, if all states reachable before the target remain inside the allowed region or target, and every such non-target state can still reach the target, until holds almost surely (Q8). This is a theorem about the chain’s measure, not an extra fairness assumption on an adversarial scheduler. The model has no nondeterministic scheduler.  The hitting-time and accumulated nonnegative-reward definitions support expected termination cost (Q9). LEAST is total but underspecified if no witness exists: “If there is no such n, then the term has some arbitrary (defined!) value” (§2.1, p.18, Q2). Almost-sure termination and reachability lemmas make the meaningful cases explicit. Finiteness of expected hitting time uses the finite-state setting; it should not be generalized to arbitrary infinite chains. Likewise, the §3.4 prose that finiteness almost everywhere suffices for a finite integral is too broad in isolation. Here the finite chain, finite transition rewards and finite expected hitting time supply the needed integrability argument; the historical source explicitly invokes positive_integral_reward_until_finite before solving the cost equations (historical Zeroconf_Analysis.thy:187–196).  ## ZeroConf: model, result and concrete case (§3, pp.21–25)  The protocol allocates an unused IPv4 link-local address from 169.254.1.0 through 169.254.254.255, a pool of 65024 addresses. A new host chooses uniformly and probes using ARP. The probability q denotes choosing an occupied address; p denotes loss of the request/response exchange (Q10–Q11). This abstracts one allocation against a fixed occupancy/loss environment. Independent repeated choices and constant transition probabilities are encoded in the Markov model; changing occupancy, concurrent allocation races and correlated/history-dependent losses are not additional modeled transitions. Other cited PRISM/timed models contain more protocol features than this selected model (Q10).  The explicit assumptions are N∈Nat, 0<p<1, 0<q<1 and nonnegative real r,E (Q13). Thus zero loss, zero occupied addresses and endpoints 1 are outside the stated theorem context, even if limits can be considered separately. There are N+4 valid states: Start, Ok, Error and Probe 0…ProbeN. Ok and Error absorb. From Start, an unused choice reaches Ok with cost r(N+1); an occupied choice reaches Probe 0 with cost r. A successful probe response returns to Start with cost 0. A failed probe advances with probability p and cost r, or at ProbeN reaches Error with cost E (Fig.1, Q12,Q14). E is the repair penalty, not merely packet latency. The graph and formula use N+1 total probes; the prose step 5 says “N requests” (Q11), so N=2 means 3 probes as the numerical example and graph explicitly state.  The event is reaching Error, not proving collision impossible: P_err(s)=Pr_s(until S {Error}) (Q15). With p,q strictly positive, its derived Start probability is positive. The proof first establishes P_err(Error)=1 and P_err(Ok)=0, then the one-step recurrence. An unrestricted recurrence is unsuitable as an automatic rewrite because it loops: “using it would result in non-termination of the rewrite engine” (§3.3, p.24, Q16). State-specific rules and induction over the remaining probes yield  P_err(Start) = q p^(N+1) / [1−q(1−p^(N+1))].  The printed induction skeleton and theorem are retained in Q17; the historical source gives the same general formula (Q38). Most ZeroConf steps use rewriting, with induction and two rewrite steps for the probe recurrence (Q16–Q17). This is concrete evidence about proof organization rather than an assertion that theorem proving was automatic end to end.  The paper names 16 hosts, q=16/65024, p=.01 and N=2, then prints “Perr Start ≤ 1/1013” in extracted text, visually 10^-13 (Q18; PDF8/printed 24). Reader arithmetic with exact rational numbers gives 1/4063000001≈2.46123554×10^-10. It therefore satisfies neither 10^-13 nor 10^-12. This is an arithmetic inconsistency in the stated example, not a protocol execution or a failed prover replay.  Both inspected AFP versions instantiate locale arguments in order N,p,q,r,E/e as `2 "16 / 65024 :: real" "0.01" "0.002" "3600"` and state a 10^-12 bound (historical Q36,Q40; current Q46,Q48). That assigns p=16/65024 and q=.01, reversing the paper’s named meanings. Under that assignment the same formula gives 1/6645020000257≈1.50488637×10^-13, which does satisfy the retained 10^-12 claim, but exceeds 10^-13. Thus the retained proof text concerns a different concrete parameterization; it does not validate the numerical sentence as printed. The static source inspection establishes these statements and supplied proof scripts, without certifying that a historical checker run used precisely these downloaded bytes.  For expected cost, C_fin integrates transition rewards until Error or Ok. The chain reaches one of them almost surely (Q19,Q21). The model-consistent formula, also present in the historical and current source (Q39,Q47), is  C_fin(Start) = [q(r+p^(N+1)E+rp(1−p^N)/(1−p)) + (1−q)r(N+1)] / [1−q+qp^(N+1)].  The paper instead prints the successful-allocation term `(1−q)*(r*N+1)` (Q21, PDF9/printed 25); the model defines `r*(N+1)` (Q14). With the paper’s named parameters, r=.002 s and E=3600 s, the correct formula gives≈.006001383 s, consistent with the reported≤.007 s; the printed parentheses give≈1.004001383 s. With the retained swapped p,q values, the correct cost is≈.006020208 s and also≤.007 s. The 7 ms result is a symbolic expected rewarded-model bound under selected input parameters, not a measured latency, worst-case deadline or successful-allocation-only expectation. Both Error and Ok terminate the cost accumulation, and the error penalty is included.  ## Crowds: model and anonymity claims (§4, pp.25–29)  Crowds establishes routes by choosing a uniformly random next participant and deciding whether to forward again with probability p_f. Routes can revisit participants; Fig.2 uses J1−J4−J2−J7−J4−C1−S, while Fig.4 illustrates a different route J1−J4−J3−J5−J4−C1−S (Q20,Q25). Neither is a test trace generated by this reader. Fig.3 is a 3-participant transition-graph illustration, not the size limit for the theorem (Q23).  Let J be the number of jondos and H the number of honest/non-collaborating jondos. The set is finite and nonempty, collaborators form a nonempty strict subset, 0<p_f<1, and init is a nonnegative distribution with total 1 and zero mass on collaborators (Q24). The model states are Start, Init i for honest i, Mix j for all j and End: H+J+2 states. From Start the init distribution chooses the initiator. An Init state moves uniformly to a Mix participant; from Mix the next Mix identity has probability p_f/J, or the route ends with probability 1−p_f. End absorbs (Q26). Participants can select themselves, and collaborators follow these transitions: active route manipulation, arbitrary topology, timing observations and multiple correlated runs are outside this model.  The paper is explicit about the abstraction boundary: “We could model the individual behaviour of jondos in Isabelle/HOL and show that this induces our Markov chain model, but this is not in the scope of this paper” (§4, p.25, Q22). Hence these results do not constitute refinement from distributed node implementations, or whole-protocol anonymity against all observations. The starting state is excluded from the measured path; Init is at index 0. The displayed len value is the last zero-based Mix index, so a terminating path has len+1 Mix states. The paper’s wording calls len the number of Mix states, but its formula and i≤len lemmas count len+1 (Q27; historical Q42).  The intended §4.2 claim is that the final server-contacting participant is independent of the initiator, under the specified uniform routing. The displayed lemma instead contains last-ncoll, defined in the next subsection as the predecessor of the first collaborator, rather than last-jondo (Q28 versus Q27,Q29). Preserve this symbol discrepancy. The current AFP `server_view_indep` proves factorization of initiating and final-participant sets (Q49); the historical source has a `server_view` theorem equating the chance that final participant equals initiator to the reciprocal of the participant count; the historical source names that reciprocal J=1/card jondos (Q43; historical Crowds_Protocol.thy:97–98; Q45). The historical notation differs from the paper’s J=count notation. Independence gives no additional identity information from this modeled endpoint observation; it does not remove a nonuniform prior or give the server “no chance” of guessing in an absolute sense.  For collaborator exposure, hit-colls means at least one Mix participant is a collaborator, and last-ncoll denotes the participant immediately before the first such collaborator. Conditional identification is meaningful because the nonempty collaborator set makes the hit probability positive. The paper proves (Q29–Q31):  - Pr(hit-colls) = (1−H/J)/(1−(H/J)p_f) - Pr(first=i and last-ncoll=l | hit-colls) = init(i)[p_f/J + indicator(i=l)(1−(H/J)p_f)], for honest i,l - Pr(first=last-ncoll | hit-colls) = 1−((H−1)/J)p_f  The first expression approaches 0 when the number of collaborators and p_f remain fixed and J tends to infinity. This is not a limit with a fixed attacker fraction. The second and third account for revisiting the initiator; they concern predecessor equality, not a general optimal attacker-classification success rate. The probably-innocent bound≤1/2 requires H>1 and p_f≥J/[2(H−1)]. Since p_f<1, feasibility requires H>J/2+1, stronger than merely an honest majority. The paper gives the precise inequality 1/2<(H−1)/J and then loosely says “more than half” (Q31).  Reader-created arithmetic example, separate from the paper’s case: J=10,H=9,p_f=3/4 gives hit probability 4/13 and conditional predecessor-equals-initiator probability 2/5; its threshold is 5/8. For J=10,H=6 the threshold is 1, excluded by p_f<1. These examples clarify the parameter constraints; no simulation, model checking or author code produced them.  For information flow, the paper conditions its measure on hitting a collaborator and bounds mutual information between initiating identity and the predecessor of the first collaborator by [1−((H−1)/J)p_f]log2(H) bits (Q32). The formalization uses Radon–Nikodým-based information theory and reduces finite-range variables to the discrete probability/logarithm sum. Both retained historical and current `information_flow` theorems add `init_uniform`, requiring equal initiating probability 1/H for each honest participant (Q44,Q50). That hypothesis is absent from the displayed paper theorem and the general §4.1 context. The evidence-backed formal theorem should retain it. This inspection does not show that the numerical inequality is false for arbitrary init; it establishes that the inspected scripts prove the stated bound under an extra hypothesis. The bound covers this pair of identities under the conditional measure, not all data a real collaborator might observe.  ## Evaluation, related work and limits (§§5–6, pp.30–31)  The evaluation is two worked formal developments, exact parametric formulas and concrete rewrites for a selected ZeroConf instance. The authors report “a couple of days” and approximately 260 Isabelle/HOL lines for ZeroConf; Crowds needs approximately 1060 lines and “one person a couple of weeks,” including finding the information-gain estimate (Q34). These are author-reported effort/size figures with no controlled comparison, replication, distribution or detailed time log. The paper supplies no proof-checking runtimes, hardware measurements, packet experiments, implementation throughput, benchmark suite or user study. The two protocols are case studies, not statistical samples.  The related-work discussion matters to the opening comparison with model checking: it explicitly recognizes probabilistic CEGAR for infinite-state systems, parametric transition probabilities for a fixed state count, and quantitative invariants for linear probabilistic programs (Q33). Thus the broad opening PRISM/model-checker contrast should not become a claim that all model checking handles only one fixed numerical instance. This work builds on the authors’ previous pCTL model-checking formalization and measure theory, and compares other HOL/Coq probability frameworks and information-flow analyses. These are discussion-level comparisons, not reproduced comparative experiments. The probabilities here can be written in PCTL, while HOL permits more properties; Markov decision processes, continuous-time models and certification of model-checker runs are future work in this 2012 paper (Q34). Their presence on the modern AFP page is subsequent artifact evolution, not a result reported here.  ## What this adds to the requested topic  Directly, this is evidence that distributed-protocol questions can require quantitative guarantees over infinite executions: almost-sure termination, finite expected cost, conditional anonymity and information leakage differ from deterministic safety invariants. Isabelle’s reusable probability library supports proofs for arbitrary finite network/probe sizes and symbolic probabilities, with the global model and theorem hypotheses made explicit. The ZeroConf rewrite/induction presentation is useful concrete proof-engineering evidence. It also shows why a local literature database should compare printed statements, parameter meanings and source hypotheses, rather than treat a claimed proof as validation of every nearby prose sentence.  There is no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment in this paper. Reader inference for those areas: an agent producing a specification/proof should retain the global-model refinement boundary, distinguish probability 1 from every execution, check integrability assumptions, align locale argument order with physical parameter names, and preserve extra theorem hypotheses. Evaluating such an agent should inspect those semantic correspondences as well as checker acceptance. These are lessons drawn by this reader, not results measured by Hölzl and Nipkow.
    - limits: Finite nonempty time-homogeneous DTMCs, normalized nonnegative transitions. ZeroConf:N natural,0<p,q<1,r,E>=0; fixed global occupancy/loss abstraction,N+1 probes. Crowds:finite nonempty participants,nonempty strict collaborator subset,0<p_f<1,honest-only initiation,uniform routing; retained information-flow proof also requires uniform initiation. Global models without node-level refinement. Printed numerical,formula,symbol and source-hypothesis discrepancies retained. No proof replay.

- ownership authentication transfer protocol (2012)
    - title: Formal Verification of Safety Properties for Ownership Authentication Transfer Protocol
    - what: Models a six-message ownership-transfer protocol for a ubiquitous-computing device in CSP, expresses secrecy and authentication as CTL properties, and checks the finite-state model with NuSMV in the presence of an intruder. The protocol uses a central key server, old/new-owner nonces, a ticket, ownership-transfer confirmation and a final temporary ID. CSP processes define OldOwner, NewOwner and the server, while secrecy is marked with Claim Secret and authentication with Running/Commit events. The NuSMV model checks five concrete constraints: three intended owner properties hold, while an intruder sending UserB or UserA credentials is rejected and yields counterexamples. The paper explains each message and trace, including the fairness motivation for requiring the seller's second confirmation.

NuSMV checks a finite abstraction with finite data types, so the results establish only the modeled protocol and claims, not implementation security, cryptographic soundness, privacy of residual data, or liveness. The paper reports no state-space size, runtime, parameter sweep, or independent attack analysis beyond the five formulas.

    - title: A Case Study on Formal Verification of Self-Adaptive Behaviors in a Decentralized System
    - what: Models and verifies a decentralized traffic-monitoring system in Uppaal. Intelligent cameras form and split organizations as traffic changes, while a self-healing subsystem detects silent camera failures, elects replacement masters and restores degraded monitoring. Timed automata model environment, camera agents, organization middleware and repair controllers; TCTL-like Uppaal queries express invariants, flexibility and robustness. The case study gives concrete environment models for car arrivals, camera viewing ranges, congestion-triggered organization merges/splits and injected failures. It verifies invariant/deadlock properties plus flexibility and robustness properties F1/F2 and R1–R4, including failure detection, reorganization, continued traffic monitoring and neighbor restoration. The authors deliberately restrict failure injection with a virtual environment to control state explosion, then reuse verified models as proposed inputs for model-based testing and runtime diagnosis. Verification time is measured as camera count grows and diagnostic traces are used to inspect violations.

    - number: all specified properties were satisfied in the final model

Silent failures are detected by timeout-based ping/echo, and recovery guarantees apply to the modeled roles, communication channels and scenarios. The study verifies a model, not the prototype Java implementation; model-based testing is proposed future work.

- Verifying Safety Properties With the TLA+ Proof System (2010)
    - what: FirstpublicTLAPSrelease:hierarchical safety-proof management,backendtranslation/trust and Peterson/Bakery/incompletePaxoscases. # Verifying Safety Properties With the TLA+ Proof System (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Kaustuv Chaudhuri, Damien Doligez, Leslie Lamport, and Stephan Merz, IJCAR 2010, LNCS 6173, pp142–148; arXiv:1011.2560v1, 11 November 2010. The venue/pages are confirmed by Stephan Merz's author bibliography: “booktitle = {5th Intl. Joint Conf. Automated Reasoning (IJCAR 2010)}” and “{142-148}” (Q17; complete bibliography block in quotes.json). Read all seven PDF pages, §§1–5.1, acknowledgements and all 15 references; all seven page renders were inspected individually. The paper has no figures, tables, numbered theorems, benchmark suite, or appendix. This is the saved outside-index arxiv_all PDF, whose hash matches the reconstructed 352-path inventory. No author implementation or proof files were executed/imported, and no checkpoint or serialized data was loaded. Consultation and independent review are complete; the IJCAR bibliographic correction was applied. REVIEW.md records scope and root-only checks. The fetched author-hosted PDF has the same extracted body after removing the arXiv margin and declared glyph/spacing differences; author-copy-comparison.json records the comparison. No additional scientific content was inferred from that normalization.  The paper describes the first public TLAPS release, its proof-obligation processing, and three example developments. It directly concerns TLA+ verification of concurrent and distributed systems. Its reported support covers invariance and step simulation but excludes liveness proofs. TLA+ the language can specify liveness; this release's prover cannot establish those properties. These are historical 2010 capabilities, not a statement about today's TLAPS. The authors state: “It handles almost all the non-temporal part of TLA+ as well as the temporal reasoning needed to prove standard safety properties, in particular invariance and step simulation, but not liveness properties” (§1 p1, Q1).  ## Proof representation and what must be trusted  Specifications and proofs share the TLA+ language. A hierarchical proof decomposes a theorem into steps and ultimately leaf obligations, each citing facts and definitions. TLAPM flattens imported/instantiated modules and sends processed leaves to backends. A user can work with incomplete proofs and choose which steps to check; the release uses pragmas to exclude proofs from checking. Thus a successful check of selected leaves does not itself establish completion of every claimed theorem. This completion check is a practical evaluation requirement inferred from the workflow. Q2–Q4 preserve the architecture and selection semantics.  The backend called Isabelle/TLA+ implements the constant fragment as a dedicated Isabelle object logic. The paper explains that embedding into existing HOL/ZF logics was inconvenient because TLA+ is untyped, with no proposition/term distinction. Its single value type, classical first-order logic, equality, conditionals, Hilbert choice, Zermelo–Fränkel set axioms, and primitive function objects supply the mathematical basis. Natural numbers are introduced using a Peano structure whose existence follows from ZF; arithmetic is developed recursively. Tuples/sequences and records are functions, strings are character sequences. Ordinary “typing” facts become proof hypotheses: the paper's n+0=n example needs a numeric n. Boolean conjunction is described as Boolean-valued even on arbitrary arguments. These are semantics/proof-library facts reported by the authors, not a reader audit of the object logic. Q9/Q10 give the details.  Zenon searches for first-order proofs and emits Isabelle/Isar scripts checked against Isabelle/TLA+. The paper explicitly says “Zenon is therefore not part of the trusted code base of TLAPS” (§4.2 p5, Q11). That exclusion applies to this certificate-checking route; it does not make the entire TLAPS pipeline untrusted. TLAPM's priming rewrite engine is expressly trusted. The generic SMT-LIB backend and Cooper Presburger arithmetic backend are expressly non-certifying in this release. “Certifying veriT” is a planned integration even though veriT is already among solvers tried through the generic non-certifying interface. Distinguishing solver brand from integration mode prevents a false claim that all SMT results were certified. Q3/Q5/Q11/Q12 preserve these boundaries.  Backends reason over constant expressions. TLAPM moves primes through ordinary mathematical operators and leaves constants unchanged: (u=v+2c)' becomes u'=v'+2c when u,v are state variables and c is constant. Double priming is rejected by the syntactic analyzer. Defined operators are hidden by default and expand when made usable. Modal operators may fail substitution of equals: knowing u=42 now does not imply u'=42. Reader illustration: a transition from u=42 to u'=43 satisfies the former but violates the latter. Usable non-substitutive definitions are expanded; hidden applications become opaque hashes, conservatively losing some valid equivalences such as O(e∧f)=O(f∧e). This is a stated completeness tradeoff, not a collision/security guarantee or a proof of implementation soundness. Q5/Q6 give the transformation and example.  Positional and labelled references resolve subexpressions before later processing. In O(x,y)=x=20y+2, O(3,4)!2!1 selects 20·4. A label l on y·20 can keep referring to that term after unrelated surrounding syntax changes. The feature supports concise proof reuse, but the paper supplies no maintenance experiment. Default discharge tries Zenon, then Isabelle automation; pragmas can request tactics or other backends, often indirectly via a named standard theorem such as SimpleArithmetic. Q7/Q8 give these cases.  The generic arithmetic route rewrites obligations into SMT-LIB AUFLIRA, often dropping assumptions outside that theory, with conservative sort detection for bound variables. Reader inference: proving a conclusion from fewer assumptions is logically stronger, so omission alone is not a soundness defect; translation and sort handling must still preserve meanings. The paper reports successful use of Yices, CVC3, Z3, veriT, and Alt-Ergo, without solver-specific counts, timings or comparative accuracy. It does not prove the soundness/completeness of these translations in this note. Q12 records the exact scope.  ## Development practice and concrete evidence  The authors first check finite instances with TLC and then attempt proofs. On leaf failure, TLAPM prints usable hypotheses and the goal, expanding usable definitions. Their reported common failure is omission of a needed fact/definition. They split difficult obligations into lower-level assertions, verify the local qed, then prove those assertions in any order. The example case split proves (P1∨…∨Pn)⇒Q by each Pi⇒Q. This is a concrete incremental authoring/debugging workflow, not evidence that partial obligations are sufficient. The Toolbox then only hid proof portions; broader integration was future work, while an Emacs mode provided hierarchical viewing and proof selection. Q13/Q14 preserve this historical distinction.  The authors warn that unchecked “obviously true” assumptions can be wrong and recommend checking such data-structure facts with TLC. Finite model checking can expose counterexamples; it does not universally prove an unbounded assumption. That latter qualification is a reader inference, not a claim that the authors measured assumption-error rates. The claim that specification errors are likelier than TLAPS soundness bugs is also the authors' engineering judgment, with no quantified comparison in this paper. Q3/Q14 carry both source statements.  Section 5.1 gives these author-reported developments, without the actual full proof scripts:  - two-process Peterson mutual exclusion: about 12 PlusCal lines and a proof of about 130 lines - N-process Bakery with atomic reads/writes: an 800-line proof - high-level Paxos: 100 TLA+ specification lines covering a consensus abstraction and two refinements; first refinement completed with a 550-line proof, second mostly proved and estimated to exceed 1,000 lines  The Paxos case is explicitly incomplete, including the acknowledgement to Jean-Baptiste Tristan. The estimated second-proof length is not a measured completed artifact. Neither case length establishes checking time, human time, bug counts, proof coverage across implementations, liveness, or executable-code correctness. The N-process claim concerns the mathematical example as reported, not a finite-N experiment independently rerun here. Q15/Q16 preserve the complete cases.  The library is reported to contain more than 1,400 lemmas/theorems, about 200 pages of pretty-printed Isar. These size measures and the three case descriptions support feasibility of the release; no theorem about the verifier itself, controlled user study, performance comparison, memory result, automated success rate or systematic experiment is supplied. The full development files and checker outputs were not inspected/reproduced in this reading. “It has not turned out to be difficult once the proof idea has been understood” is an author experience report, rather than a measured proof-automation guarantee (§5.1 p7, Q16).  For the database, this is direct foundational evidence for high-level safety proofs and TLA+ proof tooling. It contributes explicit trust distinctions, partial-proof management, priming/substitution pitfalls, finite-model-checking practice, and a deliberately incomplete Paxos case. It has no Verus, verified Rust, or LLM experiment. A proposed use as an evaluation reference for proof agents is reader inference: record the precise theorem and unchecked assumptions, require every obligation, distinguish certificate-checked from trusted solver routes, and report whether the intended specification captures the requirement.

Selected/incompleteproofspossible;uncheckedassumptionsandspecificationvalidityremainhumanresponsibilities. Fullproofscripts/checkerresultsnotread/rerun;noquantitativetime/memory/successbenchmark.

    - what: A program-logic framework in Coq and Iris. Fairis proves liveness of concurrent programs under fair scheduling, by refinement of a model. The Aneris instantiation proves that distributed implementations refine TLA+ models (two-phase commit, single-decree Paxos and a CRDT).
    - number: about 1100 lines of proof scripts for Paxos
    - limits: The step from TLA+ to the Coq model was done manually. The distributed refinements give trace safety only. Distributed liveness is in a later manuscript. The notes' author read about 40%.
    - how much was read: parts read
    - [source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.07863)
    - record id: `trillium-fairis-2024`
- Yao thesis (DistAI, DuoAI, LVR) (2024)
    - title: Automated Verification of Safety and Liveness Properties for Distributed Protocols (PhD thesis)
    - what: It shows that liveness can be reduced to a list of simpler safety properties, which invariant-inference tools often prove automatically. One task is left: synthesize a ranking function (a number that decreases toward the goal) to prove termination. It was applied to 8 protocols, including Paxos. It also covers DistAI and DuoAI.
    - number: 37 of 40 generated safety properties are always true, inductive, or get an invariant automatically; 3 found manually in a few hours each
    - number: every Z3 query to synthesize a ranking function finished in under a second
    - number: manual effort 128 and 165 lines versus IronFleet's 2,093 and 7,869 lines of Dafny (16x and 47x less)
    - number: DuoAI covers 27 protocols and solves Paxos more than two orders of magnitude faster than any alternative
    - limits: It handles only "eventually" properties, not bounded time. Ranking functions are polynomials only. It works on protocol-level models, not code. It assumes fair scheduling, minimum packet delivery and a contention-free Paxos round. Part of the line-count gap is Dafny versus mypyvy. The notes' author read about 20% of the 137 pages.
    - how much was read: parts read
    - [source](https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/fexf-nt82/download)
    - record id: `yao-thesis-distai-duoai-lvr-2024`
- A Case Study on Parametric Verification of Failure Detectors (2023)
    - what: The authors model the Chandra-Toueg failure detector (a protocol that guesses which machines have crashed) in TLA+, Ivy and counter automata, assuming partial synchrony (the network is unpredictable at first, then becomes well-behaved). They prove liveness (something good eventually happens) by hand, turning it into a safety proof (nothing bad happens).
    - limits: The conversion from liveness to safety is done by hand. Ivy's automatic conversion was not used.
    - how much was read: parts read
    - [source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.08826)

- ByMC survey (2023)
    - title: Survey on Parameterized Verification with Threshold Automata and the Byzantine Model Checker
    - what: Protocols are modeled by counting messages and participants against thresholds. This lets the tool check safety, and some liveness, for any number of participants, under conditions like n>3t (n participants, at most t faulty).
    - number: Table 4: 13 asynchronous/randomized algorithms (FRB, STRB, ABA, NBACG, NBACR, CBC, CF1S, C1CS, BOSCO, Ben-Or, RABC, kSet, RS-BOSCO)
    - number: Table 6: 16 synchronous cases, 14 verified; HybridQueen and kSetOmit have no successful check
    - limits: People still supply the models and assumptions. Termination of randomized protocols holds only against adversaries that act in rounds. The Tendermint claim covers one round only. The synchronous checker is a separate prototype.

- ADO (2021)
    - title: Much ADO about Failures: A Fault-Aware Model for Compositional Verification of Strongly Consistent Distributed Systems
    - what: The ADO interface shows chosen failure cases to the user. It does not pretend that each operation either fully succeeds or does nothing. The authors use Coq and CCAL to prove that distributed C implementations (for example Multi-Paxos), and the clients built on them, match their abstract specs. The proofs sit on top of the verified CertiKOS.
    - number: multi-Paxos: 2.6K lines of C and 43.9K lines of functional correctness proofs (§6, PDF p.23)
    - limits: The results say nothing about progress (that the system eventually finishes its work). One example assumes termination. That assumption is not a proof of progress.
    - how much was read: reading depth not recorded
    - [source](https://flint.cs.yale.edu/publications/ado.pdf); [notes: Much ADO about Failures: A Fault-Aware Model for Compositional Verific](../distributed_verification_review_b/deep_1_verified_implementations.md)
    - record id: `ado-2021`
- ReSync (2020)
    - title: Programming at the Edge of Synchrony
    - what: ReSync lets a process receive messages bit by bit within a round. It also lets each protocol set its own policy for moving to the next round. The paper establishes a round-switch abstraction and evaluates runnable consensus implementations.
    - limits: The evaluated applications are not thereby fully proved.
    - how much was read: reading depth not recorded
    - [source](https://dzufferey.github.io/files/2020_Programming_at_the_Edge_of_Synchrony.pdf); [notes: Programming at the Edge of Synchrony](../distributed_verification_review_b/deep_1_verified_implementations.md)
    - record id: `resync-2020`
- Perennial (2019)
    - title: Verifying concurrent, crash-safe systems with Perennial
    - what: Perennial adds reasoning about crashes and recovery to concurrent separation logic. It separates specs for ordinary calls from specs for recovery, and durable ownership from volatile ownership. Examples are a crash-safe mail system and local replicated disks.
    - limits: It covers replication across local disks only, not a replication protocol over a network.
    - how much was read: reading depth not recorded
    - [source](https://www.chajed.io/papers/perennial:sosp2019.pdf); [notes: Verifying concurrent, crash-safe systems with Perennial](../distributed_verification_review_b/deep_1_verified_implementations.md)
    - record id: `perennial-2019`
- WormSpace (2019)
    - title: WormSpace: A Modular Foundation for Simple, Verifiable Distributed Systems
    - what: Wormspace has a write-once-register API. Clients can reason about immutable agreed values instead of the coordination protocol. Certified concurrent abstraction layers prove that C code refines the API, and links it to the verified CertiKOS.
    - number: 6 person-months core verification (4.5 functional correctness, 1.5 ghost layer) and 5 person-weeks application/linking proofs (§6, PDF p.10)
    - number: 108K verification lines
    - limits: Chain-replication registers and reconfiguration are outside the verified part. There is no availability proof.
    - how much was read: reading depth not recorded
    - [source](https://flint.cs.yale.edu/publications/socc19.pdf); [notes: WormSpace: A Modular Foundation for Simple, Verifiable Distributed Sys](../distributed_verification_review_b/deep_1_verified_implementations.md)
    - record id: `wormspace-2019`
- PSync (2016)
    - title: PSync: A Partially Synchronous Language for Fault-Tolerant Distributed Algorithms
    - what: PSync algorithms are written in communication rounds, with stated assumptions about which rounds are good. A Scala runtime runs them. SMT checks the user's invariants and progress conditions under lockstep round semantics (all nodes advance round by round together). A reduction connects these to partially synchronous executions.
    - number: LastVoting algorithm is 89 lines (Table 2, PDF p.13)
    - limits: The runtime cannot be written in PSync's round language. So the reduction theorem does not verify every statement of the runtime.
    - how much was read: reading depth not recorded
    - [source](https://dzufferey.github.io/files/2016_PSync_A_Partially_Synchronous_Language_for_Fault-Tolerant_Distributed_Algorithms.pdf); [notes: PSync: A Partially Synchronous Language for Fault-Tolerant Distributed](../distributed_verification_review_b/deep_1_verified_implementations.md)
